items.title: [RFC]: Octave KV, a native 3-bit KV cache for AMD GPUs
items.author: JartX
items.body_excerpt:
PR: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59774

### Proposal to improve performance

## Where this comes from

We serve Qwen3.8-27B (GPTQ W4A16) on boxes with four RX 7900 XTX, 96 GB in
total, with tensor parallel 4 and MTP. Our users send long prompts: whole
repositories, long documents, agent sessions that run for hours. With an fp16
KV cache and 8 GB per GPU for it, a box holds about 446k tokens, so one long
request fills it.

On ROCm today the options below 8 bits are TurboQuant, UltraQuant (#57057,
gfx950 only) and KVarN (#46613, CUDA-first). We tried TurboQuant first, since
it is merged and its idea (random rotation plus a Lloyd-Max codebook) is the
right one. On our hardware three things got in the way:

- With MTP on (`qwen3_next_mtp`, k=3) every preset produced garbage, and
  GSM8K fell to around 1%. Without MTP it was correct.
- Its multi-token path copies between host and device per layer, so it
  cannot be captured in CUDA graphs.
- Its Triton kernels are slow on RDNA3. At 380k tokens the first token took
  621 s, against 371 s with fp16.

So we wrote our own backend: same family of ideas, a few changes to the
format, and every kernel in HIP. Against TurboQuant on the same hardware it
comes out ahead on all three things we care about. It holds as many tokens or
more at each size: at about 200 bytes per slot the two hold 2.07M and 2.05M
tokens, and our 216-byte format holds 6% more than TurboQuant's 230-byte one.
It loses less: 2.5× less excess NLL at 380k at the same size, and GSM8K
stays at fp16 level (91.8-92.4 against 89.8). And it is faster: per layer at
380k, decode is 4.6× faster, MTP verification 11×, a prefill chunk takes
30% less time, and the first token of a 380k prompt arrives 2.1× sooner.

We have run it in production since October 2, 2026, and we would like to
propose it upstream. We would also like it to be more than an RDNA3 side
project: one compressed KV format for the whole AMD line, with a short
written contract that says what each architecture needs to implement. That
is the part where we most need your opinion, and AMD's help.

## Why it matters for AMD

The KV cache is usually what limits how many long requests a GPU can serve,
and on AMD it has been the hardest part to shrink: the options below 8 bits
were built for CUDA or fall back to Triton. A native compressed cache changes
that, and at any scale, because the saving is a ratio of bytes. In the same
memory it holds 4.7× more tokens than fp16 and 2.4× more than fp8 or int8,
whether that memory is a 24 GB 7900 XTX or a 192 GB MI300X. The cost is small:
no measurable change on GSM8K, and a next-token NLL increase of about 0.001
nats at 380k that stays flat as the context grows.

The smaller cache is also faster. At long context attention is limited by
memory bandwidth, so reading 4.7× fewer bytes is where most of the 4× decode
speedup comes from, as long as the kernels read the packed cache directly
instead of expanding it first. On our four 7900 XTX that turned a box that
held one long request into one that serves about four at 512k, with decode at
127 tok/s at that length.

With the kernels this tight, attention stops being the part of the step that
grows with the context. With fp16 at 380k, attention took over the decode
step and generation fell to 2.7 tok/s. With Octave KV, going from 128k to
512k (four times the context) only takes decode from 153 to 127 tok/s; most
of the step is the rest of the model again, the same weights and all-reduce
you pay at short context. Prefill shows the same thing: at 100k all the
backends we tried are within 8% of each other, because the GEMMs and the
all-reduce dominate. Long context stops being a special, expensive case and
becomes close to the normal one.

Getting this much out of the hardware makes AMD GPUs, consumer cards and
Instinct alike, more competitive for long-context serving. We think a native
compressed cache is one of the pieces that can make AMD a first choice for
long-context serving rather than an alternative: the capacity gain holds on
every card, and on the one we could measure, long context costs close to what
short context does. We would like every ROCm user to have it without writing
their own kernels, which is why we want the format to cover the whole line. To be clear about what we know: the
capacity numbers carry over to any GPU, but we have only measured speed on
RDNA3. The CDNA numbers will come with the CDNA kernels.

## What it is

`ROCM_OCTAVE` is an attention backend for the full-attention layers. You turn
it on with the cache dtype, `--kv-cache-dtype octave_k3v3` (or
`octave_k3v4`, `octave_k3v3_compact`). The name comes from the 3-bit codes:
each one indexes an eight-level codebook.

Each (token, KV head) is stored as one packed slot. Before quantizing we flip
signs at random and apply a Walsh-Hadamard rotation, which makes the
coordinates close to Gaussian, so a fixed Lloyd-Max codebook for N(0, 1) fits
any model without calibration. The kernels apply the codebook with one
`v_perm_b32` per four codes. Each vector gets one scale (four on the blocked
K layout), chosen so that `x · x̂ = |x|²`. We started with a least-squares
scale and it was clearly worse: it shrinks every vector a little, the softmax
gets flatter, and NLL at 380k came out 2-3× higher.

The three formats differ in how they treat K. V is always rotated over the
whole head:

| Cache dtype | K | V | Bytes per slot (head 256) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `octave_k3v3_compact` | whole head rotated, 3-bit | 3-bit | 196 |
| `octave_k3v3` | 4 blocks of 64: RoPE block 4-bit, the rest 3-bit | 3-bit | 216 |
| `octave_k3v4` | as above | 4-bit | 248 |

For reference, `turboquant_3bit_nc` is 198 bytes, `turboquant_k3v4_nc` 230,
int8 per-token-head 520 and fp16 1024.

Decode, MTP verification and prefill all read the packed cache directly;
there is no dequantized copy of the prefix. MTP verification was the case we
cared most about: the query tokens of one request share every K/V read,
score_reasons: 匹配 KV 与存储、Serving 与评测、Kernel 与正确性

items.title: [Bug]: Priority scheduling can un-schedule a request it already scheduled in the same step (encoder cache miss, prefix hits on unwritten KV, priority inversion)
items.author: sohom-cs
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

<details>
<summary>Environment</summary>

```text
Not hardware-specific: scheduler-level pytest reproducers, CPU only, no model forward.
vLLM main c4973d94fe (2026-10-02; re-run on 84bcbc6264, 2026-10-03, same 5 failures), Linux x86_64, Python 3.12.3, PyTorch 2.13.0,
no CUDA, VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cpu.
```

</details>

### Describe the bug

With `--scheduling-policy priority` and KV-cache pressure, I see three failures with one cause. The trigger is a lower-priority request that was admitted before a higher-priority one, for example batch and interactive traffic on one server.

1. **Crash (multimodal).** The model runner raises `RuntimeError: Encoder cache miss for <mm_hash>` ([gpu_model_runner.py L3214](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/c4973d94fed25a3bf32d601873755a9bcd951886/vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py#L3214); MRV2: [encoder_runner.py L274](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/c4973d94fed25a3bf32d601873755a9bcd951886/vllm/v1/worker/gpu/mm/encoder_runner.py#L274)). It hits the next request with the same image (R1), or a running request that hit the entry earlier in the same step (R1b).
2. **Silent wrong KV (prefix caching).** A later request with the same prefix gets a cache hit on blocks whose KV was never written: 112 tokens hit, 96 computed (R2). Mamba align checkpoints do the same: a 48-token checkpoint, 32 tokens computed (R3, already reported as #57580).
3. **Priority inversion.** Running requests get the token budget in admission order. With `max_num_batched_tokens=64` and `long_prefill_token_threshold=48`, a priority-0 prefill gets 16 tokens per step and a priority-10 prefill gets 48 (R4).

**Root cause** (links pinned to c4973d94fe)

- `self.running` is in admission order ([L1309](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/c4973d94fed25a3bf32d601873755a9bcd951886/vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py#L1309)). The RUNNING loop walks it from the front under both policies ([L641-L643](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/c4973d94fed25a3bf32d601873755a9bcd951886/vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py#L641-L643)). This is R4.
- When `allocate_slots` fails, the PRIORITY victim is `max(self.running, key=(priority, arrival_time))` ([L777-L783](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/c4973d94fed25a3bf32d601873755a9bcd951886/vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py#L777-L783)). It can be a request that this loop already scheduled. FCFS cannot hit this: its victim is `running[-1]`, at or after the cursor.
- The restore block ([L789-L813](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/c4973d94fed25a3bf32d601873755a9bcd951886/vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py#L789-L813)) returns the victim's tokens and budget. It does not undo what scheduling already did for it:
  - `encoder_cache_manager.allocate()` ([L859-L872](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/c4973d94fed25a3bf32d601873755a9bcd951886/vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py#L859-L872)): the hash stays in `cached`, but the encoder never runs (R1);
  - the eager hash registration in `allocate_slots` ([kv_cache_manager.py L608-L612](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/c4973d94fed25a3bf32d601873755a9bcd951886/vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_manager.py#L608-L612)), including Mamba align checkpoints (R2, R3);
  - `ec_connector.update_state_after_alloc` (by reading only, not tested).

This block grew in #23713, #26661, #28558, #49206 and #51725, one undo at a time. A rollback also cannot help once another request has read the entry in the same step (R1b). @heheda12345 raised the KV form of this case on #43569.

**Proposed invariant: a step never un-schedules a request it already scheduled.** Then nothing needs a rollback, and the restore block can go.

**Two fix options** (both written and run on c4973d94fe; CPU only)

- **(a) Keep RUNNING sorted under PRIORITY.** Admit with `bisect.insort(self.running, request)`; `Request.__lt__` is a total order on (priority, arrival time, id) ([request.py L357-L367](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/c4973d94fed25a3bf32d601873755a9bcd951886/vllm/v1/request.py#L357-L367)). The victim is `running[-1]` under both policies. Delete the PRIORITY branch and the restore block. `scheduler.py` +13/-37.
  - R1, R1b, R2, R3 and R4 all pass.
  - Under budget pressure, higher priority is served first. FCFS, and PRIORITY without pressure, are unchanged.
  - Existing tests: in 9 scheduler test files under `tests/v1/core`, 364 tests pass offline on main (63 need model configs I do not have offline, including `test_priority_scheduler_random.py`). With (a), one of the 364 fails: `test_deferred_block_free.py::test_allocation_retry_waits_for_fence_then_succeeds[priority-2]`. It sets priorities after admission and expects today's same-step un-schedule. If it sets them before `add_request`, it passes on main and on (a).
- **(b) Keep admission order; choose the PRIORITY victim from `self.running[req_index:]` only** (the current request and those after the cursor). `scheduler.py` +7/-25.
  - The stale state is gone (encoder and hash invariants hold), but R4 stays.
  - The request that needs blocks now often preempts itself, while a lower-priority request that is already scheduled keeps running. Five existing tests fail for this reason: `test_scheduler.py::test_priority_scheduling_preemption` and the 4 cases of `test_priority_scheduling_preemption_and_resumption_when_out_of_kv`. They assert that the lower-priority request admitted first is the victim. The deferred-free test above fails too.

**I recommend (a).** It is the only option that keeps the victim contract those tests describe, and it also fixes the inversion. The cost is a visible change in which running request gets the budget first under PRIORITY. Also, pluggable victim policies (#53723, #56897) would need to choose from `running[req_index:]`.

**Related work**

- **#43569** (@ZJY0516) rolls back eager hash registration when a request is preempted, or its KV load fails, before the worker writes the blocks. That is the generic fix for the hash si

items.title: [Feature] Implement Image Number Limitation for Image Processors
items.author: JustinTong0323
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [ ] 1. If the issue you raised is not a feature but a question, please raise a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions/new/choose Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [ ] 2. Please use English, otherwise it will be closed.

### Motivation

At present, there is no limitation on the number of images during the processing of mm data. It is necessary to impose such a limitation to prevent potential OOM and other problems.

(When using fast image processor, the GPU memory usage is roughly **1GiB** for each **4K** image)

### Related resources

Implementation Steps:
1. Define a constant, such as `IMAGE_NUM_LIMITATION = 5`, for each processor.
2. Modify the `baseprocessor` to utilize this constant for request validation.
3. Incorporate a server argument to enable modification of this numerical value.

In case you lack familiarity with the mm data processing pipeline, it is advisable to first refer to [here](https://github.com/zhaochenyang20/Awesome-ML-SYS-Tutorial/blob/main/sglang/code-walk-through/multimodal_request_lifecycle.md)

items.author: LucasWilkinson
items.body_excerpt:
In an effort to make the CMake more readable, stable and easy to use we have a few tasks we'd like to work on, creating a GitHub issue here to track that progress, some planned changes/investigations:

- [ ] Rename `define_gpu_extension_target`, currently this is used for CPU extensions too so the name is now misleading
- [ ] Add a CI test of local builds, i.e. `pip install -e .`
- [ ]  Warn that PTX builds are not currently supported (post https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/8845), currently if there is a `+PTX` in `TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST` this will be ignored. We should warn when this is the case. Alternatively we can add support for PTX builds although this is generally not desirable since PTX increases the wheel size by quite a bit (PTX is larger than SASS), and we already build for all currently supported arches.
- [ ]  Have vllm-flash-attn use [ExternalProject](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/module/ExternalProject.html) currently vllm-flash-attn uses the parent CMake scope which creates many footguns since it is in a separate repo, using `ExternalProject` will mean that the vllm-flash-attn will be run in a separate CMake scope/process
  - [ ] It might be even better to revert to the FlashMLA approach, where CMake code lives in vllm.
- [ ] Look into removing early returns in CMakeLists.txt (potentially move backends into its own files)
- [ ] Potential build both C++ and CUDA extensions when building for CUDA and using torch dispatcher to dispatch between the two, https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/8424

items.title: [Bug] --enable-linear-replayssm forces no_buffer, which degrades mamba prefix caching and inflates TTFT up to 4.7x
items.author: davidli1515
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist - [x] I searched related issues but found no solution. - [x] The bug persists in the latest version. - [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback. - [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed. - [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed. ### Describe the bug ## Describe the bug `--enable-linear-replayssm` requires `--mamba-radix-cache-strategy no_buffer`. That strategy stores the mamba checkpoint at a radix-tree depth later requests cannot reach, so prefix reuse collapses and TTFT rises sharply on any workload with a shared prefix. ### Measured Qwen3.8-27B, 1×H200, TP=1, `sglang.benchmark.serving`, `--request-rate 8 --max-concurrency 48`. Both arms use `--disable-overlap-schedule`, because `no_buffer` asserts against the overlap scheduler; holding it fixed keeps the cache strategy the only variable. - **default** = `extra_buffer`, no ReplaySSM (what most users run today) - **replayssm** = `--enable-linear-replayssm`, which forces `no_buffer` | workload | arm | prefix cache hit | out tok/s | TTFT mean | TTFT p99 | E2E mean | |---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | **rag**
2048-tok shared prefix
(8 groups × 32) | default | **88.2%** | 509.6 | 226.4 ms | 1788.2 ms | 2164.7 ms | | | replayssm | **65.9%** | 508.7 | **1062.6 ms** | **4116.2 ms** | 3876.4 ms | | | | | −0.2% | **+369%** | **+130%** | **+79%** | | **fewshot**
512-tok shared prefix
(32 groups × 8) | default | **62.2%** | 510.1 | 83.0 ms | 261.5 ms | 1959.6 ms | | | replayssm | **0.0%** | 508.9 | **159.0 ms** | **622.3 ms** | 3048.2 ms | | | | | −0.2% | **+92%** | **+138%** | **+56%** | | **sharegpt**
real conversations,
little cross-request sharing | default | 0.7% | 1136.7 | 95.9 ms | 476.6 ms | 7145.5 ms | | | replayssm | 0.0% | 1162.6 | 97.0 ms | 477.8 ms | 6929.3 ms | | | | | +2.3% | +1.1% | +0.3% | −3.0% | Hit rate is `cached / (cached + new)` summed over the server's own `Prefill batch ... #cached-token:` lines. ShareGPT is the control: consecutive requests share almost nothing, both arms sit near a 0% hit rate, and the two configurations become indistinguishable. The gap only appears where prefixes are actually shared, which is what confirms the regression comes from prefix reuse and not from some other effect of the flag. ### Why output throughput is flat Throughput is unchanged in every row, but that is a property of the load point, not evidence that the regression is free. At `--request-rate 8` with 64-token outputs the offered rate is ~512 tok/s for the two `generated-shared-prefix` runs, and measured throughput is 508–510: the server delivered exactly what arrived, so throughput was pinned by the arrival rate rather than by the server. The ShareGPT rows in the same table reach 1137–1163 tok/s on the same server, which alone shows capacity is more than twice what the shared-prefix runs asked for. Below saturation the extra prefill work has nowhere to go except queueing delay, so it lands entirely on **TTFT and E2E**. At saturation it would convert into a throughput loss instead. ### Mechanism `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/unified_cache/components/mamba_component.py:529-533` chooses the tree depth the mamba checkpoint is attached to: ```python if self.cache.enable_mamba_extra_buffer: cache_len = req.mamba_last_track_seqlen # a boundary reached DURING the prompt else: # no_buffer cache_len = token_ids_len # prompt + this request's OWN generated tokens ``` Requests share a *prompt*; their generated continuations differ. Under `no_buffer` the checkpoint sits past the end of the prompt, so a follow-up request walks the tree only to the end of its own prompt, lands on a node that carries no mamba value, and the mamba match validator rejects it. Because a forward pass resumes from a single position for all layers, a missing mamba anchor also discards the KV hit. Instrumenting the match path on a 601-token prompt whose predecessor stored 608: ``` insert: finished=True token_ids_len=608 -> cache_len=608 match: full_kv_hit_length=600 mamba_boundary=0 branching_seqlen=576 result: #new-token: 601, #cached-token: 0 ``` KV alone could have reused 600 tokens. It reused none. Severity scales with shared-prefix length: with a 512-token prefix the hit rate goes to exactly 0%, while with a 2048-token prefix it only falls to 65.9% — long prefixes contain enough grid-aligned positions that some reuse survives. ### Is this intended? `no_buffer` avoids the extra ping-pong buffer, so trading memory for reduced cross-request reuse could be deliberate. If it is, could the trade-off be documented and could the `--enable-linear-replayssm` guard mention it? Users enabling ReplaySSM for decode bandwidth are unlikely to expect a TTFT regression of this size. If it is not intended, the guard's own comment points at the cause — `donate_mamba_ping_pong_slot` (`python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/memory_pool.py:1454`) never resets `replayssm_write_pos`, unlike `MambaPool.copy_from` (`python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/memory_pool.py:997`), which is why `python/sglang/srt/server_args.py:6357` refuses `extra_buffer`: > the extra_buffer ping-pong donation path is not yet supported (follow-up) I have a candidate fix along those lines (two edits, ~7 lines) that restores the hit rate and TTFT to the default arm's numbers with GSM8K accuracy parity over 1319 questions and a clean 6.5-hour soak. I will open it as a PR referencing this issue. ### Scope of verification - Reproduced on **UnifiedRadixCache** (`Init Unified Radix Cache. Components: (FULL, MAMBA). Tree Core: UnifiedTreeCore`). The legacy `MambaRadixCache` has the same code shape (`mamba_component.py` notes it "Mirrors `MambaRadixCache.cache_finished_req`") but I have not tested

items.title: [Bug]: Wrong timestamps if audio > 30s
items.author: dr75
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment


NA

### 🐛 Describe the bug

**Segment level timestamps are incrementally offset by ~0.5s per segment.**

When transcribing long audio with vLLM Whisper, segment-level timestamps are increasingly inaccurate. Chunking uses by default a 1s window to find low-energy (quiet) regions for splitting, so the next chunk may start up to 1s earlier than the nominal chunk length. This offset is not compensated for when generating segment timestamps, resulting in an average delay of ~0.5s per segment, which accumulates (e.g., 5s after 10 segments).

Clients can workaround by subtracting 0.5s per segment, but that's obviously not accurate.

Also, the [related documentation](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/e83b7e379c11bf136c1b96bc6a67b6d2207cfde4/docs/contributing/model/transcription.md#audio-preprocessing-and-chunking) is not correct: there are no overlapping chunks, but just a window for searching the best split point. Maybe this confusion is the cause of the issue.

items.title: [Performance]: FlashAttention backend rebuilds KV-cache views on every call (+~21 µs CPU/layer since #44455)
items.author: rrranlyu
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

Cache the (canonicalized) views on the impl and reuse them while the same `kv_cache` tensor is passed in. On v0.30, a local patch doing this cuts TTFT p50 by 12–16%, and the outputs match an fp32 reference with no numerical change:


```python
# FlashAttentionImpl
def _get_kv_views(self, kv_cache, canonicalize: bool):
    c = self._kv_view_cache
    if c is None or c[0] is not kv_cache:
        k, v = kv_cache.transpose(1, 2).split(self.head_size, dim=-1)
        ck, cv = canonicalize_singleton_dim_strides(k), canonicalize_singleton_dim_strides(v)
        c = self._kv_view_cache = (kv_cache, k, v, ck, cv)
    return (c[3], c[4]) if canonicalize else (c[1], c[2])
```

Notes:
- The identity check matters. `profile_cudagraph_memory` first binds a minimal KV cache (`_init_minimal_kv_cache_for_profiling`), runs attention on it, frees it, and then allocates the real one. A cache keyed only on the first call would keep pointing at freed memory.
- There is precedent for this: `TritonAttentionImpl` already caches KV-scale views in `_k_scale_cache` / `_v_scale_cache` ([triton_attn.py#L383-L440](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/v0.30.0/vllm/v1/attention/backends/triton_attn.py#L383-L440)), and `_cleanup_profiling_kv_cache` clears them. The FA view cache could be cleared in the same place. It should also be kept per impl, not in a module-level dict, so that the replaced tensor is not kept alive.
- Hybrid models (e.g. Qwen3.5) only get this cost on their `full_attention` layers.

I'm happy to open a PR.


### Report of performance regression

Since #44455 (KV-cache layout refactor, v0.26), `FlashAttentionImpl` derives the K/V cache views on every call:

- `forward`: `kv_cache.transpose(1, 2).split(self.head_size, dim=-1)`, then `canonicalize_singleton_dim_strides` on both views ([flash_attn.py#L1232-L1250 @ v0.30.0](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/v0.30.0/vllm/v1/attention/backends/flash_attn.py#L1232-L1250))
- `do_kv_cache_update`: the same `transpose(1, 2).split(...)` ([flash_attn.py#L1454 @ v0.30.0](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/v0.30.0/vllm/v1/attention/backends/flash_attn.py#L1454))

Before #44455 this was a single `kv_cache.unbind(1)` ([v0.25.0#L816](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/v0.25.0/vllm/v1/attention/backends/flash_attn.py#L816)). The code is unchanged on current `main`.

These views depend only on the per-layer `kv_cache` tensor's storage, shape and strides. That tensor is fixed once the KV cache is allocated. The views are recomputed per layer per step anyway, and the slots each step touches come in separately via `slot_mapping` / `block_table`.

Under the default `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`, attention for prefill / mixed batches runs eagerly, so this is host time on the critical path for short prefills.

| per attention call (profiler, H100) | v0.25 | v0.26 |
|---|---|---|
| K/V view ops | `unbind` + 2× `select`: 11.6 µs | `transpose` + `split` + 2× `narrow`: 17.0 µs |
| `unified_attention_with_output` total | 134.1 µs | 155.2 µs (+21) |

For a 64-layer model that is about +1.35 ms per prefill step. On 8×H100 (TP=8), with short prompts and `max_tokens=1`, TTFT p50 went up 1–3.5 ms from 0.25 to 0.26. Only the FA backend is affected; FlashInfer is not.


### Misc discussion on performance

_No response_

### Your current environment (if you think it is necessary)

```text
vLLM 0.30.0 (vllm/vllm-openai:v0.30.0), torch 2.13.0+cu130
8x H100 80GB (TP=8), attention backend FLASH_ATTN (FA3)
--compilation-config.cudagraph_mode=FULL_AND_PIECEWISE (default)
```

items.title: [Feature][MP] Add io_uring fixed-buffer support for Lazy and Mixed L1 allocators
items.author: 2xdevv
items.body_excerpt:
**Label**

new feature

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

io_uring fixed-buffer registration is not implemented for the MP `raw_block` path. There was an initial attempt in [#3246](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/pull/3246), but MP requires a different integration from the legacy `RustRawBlockBackend`.

The legacy backend owns its CPU backend and can register allocator buffers directly during initialization. In MP mode:

- `RawBlockL2Adapter` does not own the L1 allocator.
- L1 memory is managed separately by `L1MemoryManager`.
- MP uses either `MixedMemoryAllocator` or `LazyMemoryAllocator`.
- Lazy memory is pinned and published incrementally.

Both allocators also have a boundary problem. io_uring limits each registered buffer to 1 GiB, while both allocators manage a larger contiguous address space. `AddressManager` may therefore return an allocation spanning two registered-buffer indices. One `ReadFixed` or `WriteFixed` SQE cannot handle such a request because it contains only one buffer index.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Add an MP-specific interface for exposing fixed-buffer regions and notifying `RawBlockL2Adapter` when new regions become available.

For both allocators:

1. Divide eligible L1 memory into regions no larger than 1 GiB.
2. Assign one fixed-buffer index to each region.
3. Change Rust lookup from exact base-pointer matching to range containment.
4. Split an I/O that crosses region boundaries into multiple fixed SQEs, one per registered region.
5. Advance the buffer pointer, length, and device offset for each segment.
6. Aggregate the segment completions into one logical I/O completion.
7. Fall back to ordinary io_uring I/O only when registration is unavailable or part of the request is not covered by registered regions.

### MixedMemoryAllocator

Mixed owns its complete arena at initialization, so all eligible regions can be registered once before I/O starts.

Its `BINARY_BUFFER` allocations and unsupported backing types should continue using ordinary I/O. In particular, POSIX shared-memory backing may not be eligible for io_uring fixed-buffer registration and must fall back cleanly.

### LazyMemoryAllocator

Lazy should use the sparse-buffer APIs available since Linux 5.13:

1. Reserve a sparse table based on the final L1 size.
2. Register the initially committed regions before serving requests.
3. For each expansion:
   1. Pin the new host-memory range for CUDA.
   2. Add it to the io_uring fixed-buffer table.
   3. Publish it through `AddressManager.sbrk()`.
4. Unregister fixed buffers before unpinning or releasing the memory.

The registration interface must avoid races with the background expansion thread, for example through an atomic snapshot-and-subscribe operation.

The default lazy initial size is 20 GiB, so the initial prefix requires multiple 1 GiB fixed-buffer indices rather than a single index.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

One option is to make `AddressManager` region-aware so allocations cannot cross 1 GiB boundaries. However, introducing separate address managers or changing the existing free-list behavior would be difficult and invasive. It would affect allocation, batched allocation, coalescing, fragmentation, and allocations larger than one region.

Instead, splitting crossing I/O in the Rust raw-block layer appears to be a better fit. It keeps the existing allocators unchanged and works for both `MixedMemoryAllocator` and `LazyMemoryAllocator`.

Each crossing request can be divided at registered-region boundaries, with the buffer pointer and device offset advanced for each segment. Every segment uses its corresponding fixed-buffer index, and their completions are aggregated into one logical result.

This adds completion and partial-failure handling in Rust, but keeps fixed-buffer boundary handling localized to the I/O layer where the restriction originates.

**Summary**

- Add an MP-specific interface for exposing fixed-buffer regions.
- Register Mixed regions once and Lazy regions incrementally.
- Divide L1 memory into regions no larger than 1 GiB.
- Split crossing requests into multiple fixed SQEs in Rust.
- Aggregate all segments into one logical completion.
- Fall back to ordinary io_uring when fixed-buffer registration cannot be used.

items.title: [RFC] Centralized KV Cache Orchestration
items.author: KuntaiDu
items.body_excerpt: This RFC adds a programmable orchestration layer to the centralized MP coordinator proposed in [the Master Mode RFC](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/issues/4226). ## Overall architecture: In Master Mode, the master can receive a series of events from each local deployment of LMCache. This PR describes a series of API that allows people to: * Customize how to construct a global view based on the series of events * Define new KV cache orchestration actions and triggers based on the view. ## Programming model ### View `View` is a global view of the current cluster, customizable by the user. Programming API: ```get_view(events: Stream[Event], prev_view_checkpoint: View) -> View``` ### Action Action allows you to inspect the current view and execute some actions. Two types of actions: #### IPCAction An action that will be exposed as an IPC callable by the local LMCache L1. #### ConditionalInvocationAction This type of action will be invoked when a trigger is satisfied. Definition of trigger: ``` Trigger = Callable[[View], bool] ``` And then action will be ``` Action = Callable[[View, L1Identity], Dict[L1Identity, List[KVCacheOperation]]] ``` which is a series of KV cache operations for each node. ## Examples ### LRU L1 eviction This can be implemented by: ```python # Constructing global view, for LRU it is just timestamp def get_view(events, view_checkpoint): view = view_checkpoint for event in events: if event.type == EventType.Access: view[event.l1identity][event.objectkey] = event.time # LRU eviction def get_eviction_candidate(view, L1Identity): obj_info = view[event.l1identity] time2view = [(obj_info[k], k) for k in obj_info] time2view = sorted(time2view, lambda x: x[0])[:10] return [i[0] for i in time2view] register_ipc_action("get_eviction_candidate", get_eviction_candidate) ``` ### Quota management ```python # Constructing global view, for LRU it is quota of each user def get_view(events, view_checkpoint): view = view_checkpoint for event in events: if event.type == EventType.EnterL1: view["quota"][event.objectkey.cache_salt] += event.objectkey.size view["location"][event.objectkey.cache_salt].update(event.objectkey) elif event.type == EventType.LeaveL1: view["quota"][event.objectkey.cache_salt] -= event.objectkey.size view["location"][event.objectkey.cache_salt].difference_update(event.objectkey) # Trigger def quota_exceeded_trigger(view): return any(view["quota"][cache_salt] > config.get_user_quota(cache_salt) for cache_salt in view["quota"]) # Action # for simplicity, assume that policy is fully remove all key if quota exceeded def remove_key(view): operations = defaultdict(list) for cache_salt in view["quota"]: if view["quota"][salt] > config.get_user_quota(cache_salt): for loc, key in view["location"][cache_salt]: operation[loc].append(("delete", key)) ```

items.title: [Bug] Native connector worker death leaves L2 adapter pending maps and L1 read locks stuck
items.author: Writtic
items.body_excerpt:
**Label**

Please label as `bug`.

**Summary**

`ConnectorBase`'s worker loop can exit with requests still queued, and nothing tells the Python side. Every `future_id` submitted to that worker then sits in `NativeConnectorL2Adapter`'s pending maps for the life of the process, and for stores it also pins the L1 read locks the in-flight task holds.

Raised in review on #4211 by @maobaolong. Filing it separately as agreed there, since the fix belongs to the C++ completion contract rather than the adapter.

**Details**

The adapter pairs every insert into `_pending_ops`, `_pending_store_sizes`, and `_pending_store_tasks` with a removal: the submit failure path cleans up its own entries, and the demux thread pops all three when a completion arrives. The maps grow without bound only when a submitted `future_id` never produces a completion.

`worker_loop_for_queue` in `csrc/storage_backends/connector_base.h` has two such paths:

1. `create_connection()` throws before the request loop starts. The outer `catch` prints to stderr and the worker returns, leaving its queue undrained.
2. A non-`std::exception` escapes the per-tile `catch (const std::exception&)`, unwinds to `catch (...)`, and kills the worker. That tile never reaches `handle_tile_completion`.

Both report through `fprintf(stderr, ...)` instead of the logger, so a dead worker is easy to miss.

For stores the cost is larger than dict growth. `StoreController` records `read_locked_keys` per in-flight task and releases them on completion, so a task that never completes holds L1 read locks until the process exits and those chunks cannot be evicted.

**Expected Outcome / Goal**

Every submitted `future_id` gets exactly one completion, including when its worker dies. Options worth discussing:

- On worker exit, drain the queue and push a failed `Completion` for each pending request.
- Widen the per-tile catch to `catch (...)`, so an unknown exception fails one tile instead of the worker.
- Report worker death through the logger and a metric, not only stderr.

**Actual Outcome**

The maps grow without bound and the store task never completes. #4211 adds `lmcache_mp.l2_adapter_pending_entries`, a gauge over the three maps per adapter, which makes this visible: a series that keeps climbing without returning to zero is this leak.

items.title: [Bug] fs L2 adapter: every store fails at os.open() in _write_with_odirect when use_odirect=true
items.author: h1manshu23
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**
With the `fs` L2 adapter and `use_odirect: true`, **every** chunk store fails. `FSL2Adapter._write_with_odirect` raises at the `os.open()` call, and each store is logged as failed:

```
[2026-07-31 12:39:27,361] LMCache ERROR: FSL2Adapter failed to store
/mnt/nvme0/-SEP-data-medium-SEP-text-generation-models-SEP-gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-FP8-dynamic-SEP-@0x01000100@1@246ba704d24a7690450504e0a607656c195b4e247501896d103d7d293f9b63dc.data
(fs_l2_adapter.py:629:lmcache.v1.distributed.l2_adapters.fs_l2_adapter)
```

Nothing is ever persisted to L2, so the disk tier is effectively dead while the server continues running and reporting no fatal error.

**This is not an unsupported-storage case.** `base_path=/mnt/nvme0` is a real block-backed filesystem on a 4-device NVMe RAID0 array:

```
md0 : active raid0 nvme3n2[3] nvme2n2[2] nvme1n2[1] nvme4n2[0]
```

Two distinct problems here:

1. **The failure itself.** O_DIRECT should be usable on this mount. Whatever LMCache passes to `os.open()` — flag combination, mode, or path — is being rejected on a filesystem/device stack that otherwise accepts direct I/O.
2. **The failure is undiagnosable and unrecoverable.** The log line prints the target path but not the underlying `OSError`/errno, so there's no way to tell EINVAL from EACCES from ENOENT without reading LMCache's source. And there is no fallback: rather than degrading to buffered I/O or refusing at startup, the adapter fails silently-but-endlessly, once per chunk, for the lifetime of the server.

Note the failure is at **`os.open()`**, not at the write — so this is not an O_DIRECT buffer/offset/length alignment issue, which would surface later in `_write_with_odirect`.

**To Reproduce**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. `base_path` sits on a 4× NVMe md RAID0 (512k chunk) mounted at `/mnt/nvme0`.

2. Start the LMCache server with the `fs` L2 adapter and O_DIRECT enabled:

```bash
lmcache server --host localhost --port 9000 \
  --l1-size-gb 128 --eviction-policy LRU --chunk-size 256 \
  --l2-adapter '{"type": "fs", "base_path": "/mnt/nvme0", "use_odirect": true, "num_workers": 32}' \
  --http-port 8081
```

3. Start vLLM against it on a single GPU:

```bash
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 vllm serve /path/to/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-FP8-dynamic/ \
  --port 9001 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.95 \
  --enable-prefix-caching --enable-chunked-prefill \
  --max-model-len 16384 \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"LMCacheMPConnector","kv_role":"kv_both","kv_connector_extra_config":{"lmcache.mp.host":"tcp://localhost","lmcache.mp.port":9000}}' \
  --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 --max-num-seqs 12
```

4. Send any request. Every L2 store fails with the traceback below; `/mnt/nvme0` stays empty.

**Expected behavior**

On a direct-I/O-capable filesystem like this one, stores should succeed with `use_odirect: true` — that's the whole point of running the cache on NVMe RAID0.

Failing that, LMCache should:
- include the underlying errno / `OSError` message in the `failed to store` log line, and
- probe `O_DIRECT` support on `base_path` **once at startup**, then either fail fast with an actionable message or fall back to buffered I/O — instead of raising per-chunk for the lifetime of the process.

**Screenshots**
If applicable, add screenshots to help explain your problem.
```
[2026-08-02 14:09:16,887] LMCache ERROR: FSL2Adapter failed to store /mnt/nvme0/-SEP-data-medium-SEP-text-generation-models-SEP-gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-FP8-dynamic-SEP-@0x01000100@1@2fd0d18a24695cedc65b54957836c1ddcde16bfbe2208c8c8425e4fec9c93441.data (fs_l2_adapter.py:629:lmcache.v1.distributed.l2_adapters.fs_l2_adapter)

  File "/usr/lib/python3.10/concurrent/futures/thread.py", line 58, in run

items.title: [Bug][CLI] trace replay percentiles are one sample too high at whole ranks, so p90/p99 report the max
items.author: bharadwaj-pendyala
items.body_excerpt:
**Label**

`bug`, `cli`

**Describe the bug**

`_percentile()` in `lmcache/cli/commands/trace/_stats.py` treats the nearest-rank rank as a 0-based index, so it returns one sample too high whenever `pct/100 * N` lands on a whole number.

The docstring on the function says the p-th percentile is the sample at index `ceil(p/100 * N) - 1`. The code drops the `- 1`:

https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/3b8093cf8860a39d05937af915adfb5db493a047/lmcache/cli/commands/trace/_stats.py#L88-L95

`ceil(p/100 * N)` is a 1-based rank. Using it directly as a list index skips to the next sample.

The practical effect is that `lmcache trace replay` reports the slowest single sample as p90 or p99 at the sample counts you are most likely to hit. With 10 replayed calls for a qualname, p90 equals max. With 100, p99 equals max. Fractional ranks are unaffected, so the numbers look plausible and only the tail is wrong.

There is a second, smaller error in the same expression. `pct / 100.0` is inexact for most integer percentiles, so `(7 / 100.0) * 100` is `7.000000000000001` and `ceil()` picks rank 8. Multiplying before dividing keeps the product exact.

**To Reproduce**

Tested against `origin/dev` at commit `3b8093cf8860a39d05937af915adfb5db493a047`.

```python
from lmcache.cli.commands.trace._stats import ReplayStatsCollector, _percentile

vals = [float(i) for i in range(1, 101)]
print(_percentile(vals, 50))   # 51.0, want 50.0
print(_percentile(vals, 99))   # 100.0, want 99.0  (this is max)
print(_percentile(vals, 7))    # 8.0,   want 7.0   (the float rounding case)

s = ReplayStatsCollector()
for latency_ms in range(1, 11):
    s.record("op.foo", latency_ms / 1000.0)
stats = s.summary()["op.foo"]
print(stats.p90_ms, stats.max_ms)   # 10.0 10.0, want 9.0 10.0
```

Output on `dev`:

```
51.0
100.0
8.0
10.0 10.0
```

**Expected behavior**

Nearest-rank as documented: rank `ceil(p/100 * N)`, 1-based, so index `rank - 1`. p50 of 1..100 is 50, p99 is 99, p90 of ten samples is the ninth.

**Additional context**

The existing unit test encodes the off-by-one rather than catching it. `tests/cli/commands/trace/test_stats.py::TestPercentile::test_p50_on_100_values` asserts `51.0` with the comment `nearest-rank with floor((50/100)*100)=50 → index 50 → value 51`, which is where the 1-based rank got read as a 0-based index. That test needs updating alongside the fix.

Scope check on the two other percentile helpers in the CLI, neither of which should change here:

- `lmcache/cli/commands/bench/engine_bench/stats.py::_percentile` uses linear interpolation on purpose and is documented as such. Not the same method, not affected.
- `lmcache/cli/commands/bench/l2_adapter_bench/result.py` uses a `+0.999999` ceiling approximation. Different code, worth a separate look, out of scope for this.

The changed values are user visible: terminal output from `lmcache trace replay`, plus the `p50_ms`/`p90_ms`/`p99_ms` columns in the CSV and JSON exports.

I have a fix with regression tests ready and will open a PR against `dev` shortly. Happy to change direction if you would rather keep the current numbers and correct the docstring instead, though the tail numbers are wrong either way.

items.title: [RFC][MP] Configurable L2 Load Timeout with Recompute Fallback
items.author: cage-goat
items.body_excerpt:
## Background

LMCache MP mode currently lacks a general timeout policy for L2 prefetch/load operations. When loading data from L2 is slow or never completes, inference requests may keep waiting for cached KV data indefinitely.

We would like to support a configurable waiting limit. Once that limit is reached, LMCache should allow the caller to stop waiting for the cache and fall back to recomputation.

## Motivation

Loading cached KV data is intended to reduce computation and request latency. However, when L2 queuing or loading takes too long, continuing to wait may be slower than recomputing the missing KV data.

A configurable timeout would let users set a waiting budget based on their latency requirements. Fallback should be possible when loading exceeds that budget, even if the storage system has not reported an error and the operation might eventually succeed.

## Expected Behavior

1. **A configurable L2 loading deadline**

   Users can configure the maximum waiting time for an L2 prefetch/load request, including time spent queuing and loading. This deadline is independent of the timeout for an individual message-queue request.

2. **Cache-miss fallback on timeout**

   When the deadline expires, LMCache stops making the caller wait and reports the portions that have not finished loading as cache misses, allowing the caller to recompute them. Data that is already available continues to follow the existing cache-hit semantics.

3. **Fallback for slow operations**

   The timeout policy applies to operations that exceed the waiting budget, including those that might eventually complete successfully. It should not require an explicit storage error.

4. **Correct handling of tasks and resources after timeout**

   LMCache handles late completion and resources associated with timed-out tasks correctly, preventing incorrect cache hits, duplicate completion, or persistent disruption to other requests.

5. **Compatibility and observability**

   The policy is optional, preserving the existing behavior when disabled. Logs or metrics indicate load timeouts and recompute fallbacks so users can understand their impact and tune the waiting budget.

## Discussion

We would like to discuss whether this should be a general capability of LMCache MP mode and whether related work is already planned. Configuration names, default timeout values, and implementation details can be determined in follow-up discussions.

items.title: [Documentation Request] vLLM kv_load_failure_policy doesn't apply to load failures in L2 adapters
items.author: RedL0tus
items.body_excerpt:
**Label**
Please label your issue so that it can easily be easily categorized under [LMCache Onboarding](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/issues/1882)

**Summary**
[kv_load_failure_policy](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/api/vllm/config/kv_transfer/#vllm.config.kv_transfer.KVTransferConfig.kv_load_failure_policy) doesn't seem to apply to remote KV data load failures in L2 adapters.

**Details**
vLLM supports setting kv_load_failure_policy, which defines the behavior during KV load failures. However, this configuration option doesn't seem to apply to L2 adapters. We've tested the `nixl_store` L2 adapter and the `s3` L2 adapter with injected errors, and LMCache seems to treat L2 load failures as cache misses instead of failures.

is this an intentional design choice? It would be great to document the expected behavior of failures at different cache levels in LMCache.

**Steps / Reproduction (if applicable)**
1. Start LMCache with L2 adapter set to `nixl_store` with OBJ backend, or `s3`.
2. Start vLLM, use LMCache for KV cache offloading and internal prefix caching disabled with `--no-enable-prefix-caching`.
3. Send data to vLLM and Intercept all GetObject calls to the S3 endpoint.

**Expected Outcome / Goal**
With `"kv_load_failure_policy": "fail"`, requests with external cache hits should return error code.

**Actual Outcome (if applicable)**
LMCache log errors to the console, vLLM proceed to serve all requests with recomputed KV data as if it's only a cache miss.

**Additional Context**
This issue was first discovered by [Anish Sana](mailto:anish.sana@hpe.com) under HPE's internal testing.

items.title: L1 eviction races async L2 store: chunks discarded before offload are never stored (persistent re-prefill under L1 pressure)
items.author: ShreyasBaasri07
items.body_excerpt:
**Label**
Bug

**Describe the bug**
In LMCache v0.5.5 (MP mode), under L1 (CPU) memory pressure, freshly-computed KV chunks can be evicted from L1 before the asynchronous store controller offloads them to L2, so they are silently dropped and never written to L2 — even when L2 is large enough to hold the entire working set and has no eviction configured.

The result: with a shared-prefix (prefix-caching-style) workload, ~19% of requests permanently retrieve only the shared prefix (first half of the prompt) and re-prefill the unique tail on every recurrence, indefinitely. The half-hits persist through the whole run, not just warmup.

Root cause (confirmed in v0.5.5 source):

L1 eviction destination defaults to EvictionDestination.DISCARD — L1 eviction does not offload to L2 (lru.py, eviction_controller.py:193).
The StoreController offloads L1→L2 by reserve_read-ing keys received from an L1_WRITE_FINISHED notification. If a key was already discard-evicted in the meantime, reserve_read returns KEY_NOT_EXIST, the key is silently skipped from the store (only surfaced as an L1_READ_FAILED / lmcache_mp.l1_read_failure "not_found" anomaly), and it never reaches L2 (lmcache/v1/distributed/storage_controllers/store_controller.py:600-627).
So there is a race between L1 DISCARD eviction and the async L2 offload; the loser is silently never stored.

**To Reproduce**
Environment: LMCache v0.5.5, MP mode, L1 + L2 where L2 is sized to hold the full working set and has no L2 eviction, and L1 is smaller than the shared-prefix working set.

Start the LMCache MP server with a small L1 and one large L2 adapter (e.g. S3/filesystem), no L2 eviction:
lmcache server --host 0.0.0.0 --port 6555 --chunk-size 256 \
  --l1-size-gb 60 --eviction-policy LRU \
  --l2-adapter '{"type":"s3", ... ,"max_capacity_gb":500}'

Start vLLM with LMCacheMPConnector (kv_role: kv_both), --no-enable-prefix-caching --enforce-eager.
Run a shared-prefix benchmark whose prefix pool exceeds L1. With aiperf/genai-perf
--prefix-prompt-length 4096 --num-prefix-prompts 150 \
--isl 4096 --osl 100 --num-dataset-entries 200 \
--concurrency 10 --random-seed 42 --benchmark-duration 1200

Here 150 prefixes × 4096 tokens ≈ 75 GB of prefix KV > 60 GB L1. Each request = 8192 tokens (4096 shared prefix + 4096 unique tail).

Grep the server log for Retrieved N tokens.

Observed — persistent prefix-only half-hits throughout the run (not just warmup)
Half-hits occur at ~20–32/min even in steady state, long after every one of the 200 fixed prompts has been served many times. Since retrieval is a contiguous match from token 0, Retrieved 4096 means "prefix found, tail missing → prefill." (Optionally, lmcache_mp.l1_read_failure / L1_READ_FAILED "not_found" events fire in the same window.)

Control: setting --num-prefix-prompts 10 (prefix pool now fits in L1) eliminates the half-hits — all requests become full 8192-token hits. So the trigger is specifically L1 < shared-prefix pool.

**Expected behavior**
Once a chunk is computed and admitted to L1, it should reliably be offloaded to L2 and remain retrievable regardless of L1 pressure. A chunk should not be silently dropped from the L2 store just because it was evicted from L1 before the async offload read it. Subsequent requests for the same prompt should be full L2 hits, not re-prefills, when L2 has capacity and no eviction.

**Screenshots**
N/A (server-side KV-cache behavior; log evidence included above).

**Desktop (please complete the following information):**
OS: Linux
LMCache: v0.5.5
vLLM: 0.26.0
PyTorch: 2.11.0+cu130
Python: 3.12.3
GPU: NVIDIA L40S
Mode: MP (LMCacheMPConnector, kv_role: kv_both), --chunk-size 256, --l1-size-gb 60, L2 sized to hold full working set with no L2 eviction

**Smartphone (please complete the following information):**
N/A (not a mobile/browser issue)

**Additional context**

items.title: Restart-proof KV cache for llama-server: 40K-token TTFT 155s to 6s after reboot
items.author: qqkzlm
items.body_excerpt:
Every restart wipes your prefill. Server crash, box reboot, model reload — a 40K-token agentic prompt pays the full ~155s prefill again before the first token.

I patched llama-server to persist KV-cache prefix checkpoints to disk and auto-restore the longest matching prefix on boot. Same prompt after a restart: **first token in ~6s instead of ~155s** (2.1s disk read once + decode). No client changes, no re-architecture — the server just remembers.

Measured on GTX 1080 8GB, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, `-c 92160`:

- Cold: 151s prefill → first token at ~155s
- Warm (post-restart): 2.1s disk read (first request only) → first token at ~6s
- Checkpoints keyed by model + ctx + KV quant (wrong config = ignored, never corrupted); disk-budget eviction included

Single-commit patch (86KB): https://github.com/qqkzlm/llama-cpp-prompt-disk-cache — `git am` onto the PrismML `prism` branch, four flags (`--slot-save-path`, `--checkpoint-min-step`, `--ctx-checkpoints`, `--prompt-cache-disk-budget`).

One MoE lesson from the same box: keep experts on GPU, let KV follow the layers — pushing 20 MoE layers to CPU collapsed prefill 265→30 tok/s, which no cache can fix.

Happy to upstream behind a flag if maintainers are interested.

comments.author: qqkzlm
comments.body:
Update to the README since this went up — three things worth calling out for anyone trying it:

**1. Prebuilt CUDA binaries exist for both platforms.** The `v0.2.3` release ships `llama-server-win-cuda-v0.2.3.zip` and `llama-server-linux-cuda-v0.2.3.tar.gz`. The Linux package is built for `sm_61`/Pascal, so it also runs on GTX 10-series. No build needed:

```bash
./llama-server -m model.gguf -c 32768 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \
  --slot-save-path /var/tmp/kvstore/model \
  --prompt-cache-disk-budget 20 --checkpoint-min-step 2048 --ctx-checkpoints 64
```

**2. Only one flag is actually required.** `--slot-save-path` is the only one you must pass — `--prompt-cache-disk-budget` and `--prompt-cache-disk-path` are silently ignored without it, and entries land in `<slot-save-path>/pdcache`. `--prompt-cache-disk` is **enabled by default**, so passing it is optional; use `--no-prompt-cache-disk` to turn the cache off.

**3. Cache hits require a byte-identical prompt prefix.** Only the common prefix from token 0 onward is reused. If you prepend a timestamp or a random ID, everything after it misses and the cache is effectively unused. Put stable content first (system prompt, tool definitions, long docs) and per-turn content last — opencode / Claude Code already do this, so it works out of the box.

The README now has a "when does the cache hit / when does it miss" section covering this, a flag-duty table, and a Chinese-first three-step guide (the repo README is now Chinese-primary). A Windows `start-llama-server.bat` is included in the zip if you want a prompt-driven launcher instead of a command line.

Still happy to upstream this behind a flag if maintainers are interested — the whole feature is one commit touching `tools/server/server-prompt-disk.cpp` (~900 lines) plus slot/task integration.

items.title: [Bug] --strip-thinking-cache + retraction: release_kv_cache frees KV slots the radix tree still owns (double free)
items.author: sohom-cs
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

With `--strip-thinking-cache`, `Req.owned_kv_len()` caps the owned length at the prompt once the request has reasoning tokens (#22373):

```python
if get_serving().strip_thinking_cache and self.reasoning_tokens > 0:
    return min(self.kv.kv_committed_len, len(self.origin_input_ids))
```

`release_kv_cache` then treats `[owned_kv_len, kv_allocated_len)` as over-allocated and frees it (`_release_overallocated_kv_indices`). That relies on nothing past the prompt being in the tree, i.e. on `cache_protected_len <= len(origin_input_ids)`.

A retracted request breaks that. It keeps `output_ids` and `reasoning_tokens` (`reset_for_retract` resets neither) and is re-prefilled over `prompt + output_ids`. After that prefill, `maybe_cache_unfinished_req` → `cache_unfinished_req` inserts the whole re-prefill, so `cache_protected_len = len(prompt) + len(earlier output)`. When the request finishes, or is retracted again:

- `cache_finished_req(owned_kv_len=P)` / `free_kv_row([(cache_protected_len, P)])` frees nothing, since `cache_protected_len > P`;
- `_release_overallocated_kv_indices(P, kv_allocated_len)` frees `[P, kv_allocated_len)`, and that includes `[P, cache_protected_len)`, which belongs to a tree node.

With `page_size > 1` and a prompt that doesn't end on a page boundary, the same thing happens through a different free: `cache_finished_req` frees its unaligned tail `[page_aligned(owned_kv_len), owned_kv_len)`, and that page is also tree-owned once `cache_protected_len > P` (e.g. page 4, P=10, `cache_protected_len`=12: the page holding positions 8–11 is freed while the tree keeps it).

Those slots are now both in the free list and referenced by the tree. When the node is evicted they are freed again. `available_size()` can exceed the pool size, and one `alloc()` can hand the same slot to two requests: silent KV corruption. The assert that would catch it (`start_p == end_p`) is skipped under `strip_thinking_cache`.

The PD decode resume path looks exposed in the same way (`process_prebuilt` caches the resumed request with `maybe_cache_unfinished_req`), but I have reproduced only the aggregated path.

**Reproduction** (CPU, main `0967a013c2a`, `UnifiedRadixCache`, 256-slot pool, prompt 8, 6 output tokens before the retraction, 3 decode steps after the re-prefill; real `cache_unfinished_req`, `release_kv_cache`, `evict`)

```
after re-prefill: cache_protected_len=14 (prompt=8)
owned_kv_len()=8 committed=17 allocated=17
[finish] available after release: +9 (expected +3)
[finish] slots freed while still referenced by the tree: [9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14]
[finish] after evicting the tree: free list 262 entries, 256 unique; available_size 262 > pool 256
[finish] one alloc() of the whole pool hands out [9..14] twice
```

The same numbers with `is_insert=False` (a second retraction).

**Expected:** each KV slot is freed once.

**Proposed fix:** under `strip_thinking_cache`, never report less than `cache_protected_len`:

```python
return min(self.kv.kv_committed_len, max(len(self.origin_input_ids), self.kv.cache_protected_len))
```

The output the tree already holds (from the re-prefill) stays the tree's, and only the request-private tail is freed. Without a retraction, `cache_protected_len <= prompt`, so behaviour is unchanged.

I have this with a CPU test (finish, second retraction, the no-retraction case, and page_size=4 with aligned and unaligned prompts). I'm filing the issue first because two open PRs touch this code: #41281 (@hnyls2002) and #35694 (@alphabetc1), which changes `owned_kv_len`. The test still fails on the current heads of both (`1c912a5d6bb` and `5724c337c00`), and passes on both with the one-line change. In #41281's `insert_req` flow, `cache_protected_len` is lowered to the page-aligned `P` before the tail free, so the tree-owned slots are still freed. Happy to send it as a PR on top of whichever lands first, or for it to be folded into one of them.

items.title: [RFC][NPU] INT8 (C8) KV cache for DSA models (GLM-5.2) on Ascend A2/A3 (910B/910C)
items.author: qidaye
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

This RFC proposes generalizing the existing arch35-only packed FP8 DSA KV cache
to a "packed one-byte quant" path, so that GLM-5.2 (`GlmMoeDsaForCausalLM`) and
other DeepSeek-V3.2-style DSA models can run an **INT8 (C8) KV cache on Ascend
A2/A3 (910B/910C)**. Every hardware question the proposal depends on has been
probed on a 910B (CANN 9.0.0, torch_npu 2.10.0); section 4 states measured
verdicts, not predictions.

Sections 1-4 of the full RFC follow. The remaining sections (change-surface
audit, test plan, confidence ledger) exist and can be posted here if useful;
a few forward references to them ("section 5" / "section 6" / "section 7")
remain in the text below -- the "section 7" material is summarized under
**Proposed contribution plan** at the end.

> All `file:line` references are against `sgl-project/sglang` at
> **`06008c170dae333e22caceb51f36224071f9b5b3`** (`[dsv4.1]Optimize FP4 indexer by
> skipping invisible tiles`, #40431), which is an ancestor of `upstream/main` --
> so every citation below is checkable against upstream as-is.
>
> vllm-ascend references are against **`abe8ff18a96bcd5f90d08077d1ccd068b959cab4`**
> and carry a `[va]` prefix, relative to that repo's root.
> ops-transformer references are against `gitcode.com/cann/ops-transformer` at
> **`bcc6304656c9e712b50b1faa22872a158b1e34c5`** (the commit sgl-kernel-npu's CI
> pins; `bcc6304` below) and carry an `[ops-t]` prefix.

## 1. Motivation

SGLang today supports an 8-bit ("C8") KV cache for DSA models on Ascend **only on
arch35 / Ascend 950**, in the FP8-E4M3 packed form added by
`[NPU]Support GLM5.2 and FP8 DSA&Indexer kvcache for 950` (commit `3ff226ba8f`).
On A2/A3 the DSA KV cache is unconditionally BF16.

This matters because the KV cache is the binding constraint on A2-class hardware.
A representative single-node deployment (8x 910B, 64 GB/card, GLM-5.2-W4A8, TP8,
`--mem-fraction-static 0.85`):

| item | per card |
|---|---|
| weights | 49.67 GB |
| KV cache | 1.73 GB -> `max_total_num_tokens = 16768` |
| NPU graphs | 0.75 GB |
| unused | 8.25 GB |

`context_len` is 1 M, but the whole instance holds ~16 K tokens. Raising
`mem-fraction-static` helps, but the ceiling is still set by BF16 KV bytes/token.

Per token, per layer, for GLM-5.2 (`kv_lora_rank=512`, `qk_rope_head_dim=64`,
`index_head_dim=128`):

| component | BF16 | INT8 packed | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| main MLA latent + rope | 1152 B | 656 B (512 int8 + 4x fp32 tile scales + 64x bf16 rope) | **1.76x** |
| indexer K | 256 B | 130 B (128 int8 + 1x fp16 scale) | **1.97x** |
| **total** | **1408 B** | **786 B** | **1.79x** |

The main-KV term dominates, so the expected end-to-end gain is ~1.6-1.8x more
resident tokens at the same memory budget. vllm-ascend reports a **measured
1.62x** for the equivalent change on GLM-5 W8A8 / A3 (75,600 -> 122,309 tokens,
PR #11228 / #11846) -- a second-hand figure from PR prose, but consistent with
the arithmetic above.

---

## 2. What exists today

### 2.1 The arch35 FP8 packed path (the template)

Storage is an **opaque fixed-width record**, one per token per layer, whose width is

```python
# python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/kv_cache_configurator.py, calculate_mla_kv_cache_dim
kv_lora_rank + kv_lora_rank // quant_block_size * 4 + qk_rope_head_dim * rope_storage_dtype.itemsize
# GLM-5.2: 512 + 4*4 + 64*2 = 656 bytes
```

It is produced by `_pack_dsa_fp8_kv_cache`
(`python/sglang/srt/hardware_backend/npu/memory_pool_npu.py:839`):

```python
quantized, scale = torch_npu.npu_dynamic_quant(latent.reshape(-1, 128), dst_type=self.dtype)
packed = torch.cat((quantized.view(uint8),            # 512 B
                    cache_v.to(bf16).view(uint8),     # 128 B  rope, NOT quantized
                    scale.to(fp32).view(uint8)),      #  16 B  4 per-128-tile scales
                   dim=-1)
```

and consumed by `forward_sparse`
(`python/sglang/srt/hardware_backend/npu/attention/ascend_backend.py:1228`):

```python
torch_npu.npu_kv_quant_sparse_flash_attention(
    query=torch.cat((q_nope, q_pe), -1),   # bf16 [T, H, 576]
    key=packed, value=packed,
    key_quant_mode=2, value_quant_mode=2,
    key_dequant_scale=None, value_dequant_scale=None,   # scales read inline
    quant_scale_repo_mode=1, tile_size=128, rope_head_dim=64,
    layout_query="TND", layout_kv="PA_BSND", sparse_mode=3, attention_mode=2, ...)
```

**Key observation: the record layout is not FP8-specific.** It is "512 one-byte
values + per-128-tile FP32 scales + BF16 rope tail", and INT8 and FP8-E4M3 are
both one byte, so the 656-byte width, the `quant_scale_repo_mode=1` /
`tile_size=128` descriptor, and the `npu_dynamic_quant` call site
(`dst_type=self.dtype` already) carry over structurally. The quantization is
**dynamic** (per-token, per-128-tile, computed online), so no checkpoint
calibration is required.

The scale contract is settled, from two independent implementations: the
**main-KV** per-128-tile scale is **FP32 for INT8 and FP8 alike**, symmetric,
no zero-point (`[va] vllm_ascend/attention/utils.py:87-99` hardcodes an fp32
scale term in the record width regardless of KV dtype;
`[va] vllm_ascend/attention/sfa_v1.py:1991` has the INT8 branch cast the scale
`.to(torch.float32)`). The **indexer** per-token scale is a different buffer
entirely -- FP16 under INT8 on A2/A3, FP32 under FP8 on A5 -- and belongs to
section 2.2, not to this record.

Functional acceptance of this record with an INT8 payload on a 910B is now
**measured** (section 4, V1). Numerical parity against a BF16 reference remains
test item 1 in section 6.

### 2.2 An INT8 indexer already works on pre-A5, in this repo

The DSV4 NPU backend already runs an INT8 lightning indexer on non-arch35 hardware:

```python

items.title: [Bug] deepseekv31 detector (streaming): greedy name regex drops a call and attaches the next call's arguments to it
items.author: the-Shallow
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

`DeepSeekV31Detector.parse_streaming_increment` matches the tool name with a greedy
`<｜tool▁call▁begin｜>(.*)<｜tool▁sep｜>`. When one delta carries the end of a call and the start of the next, the name group
spans the first call: the first call's arguments are never streamed and the second call's arguments are streamed
under the first call's index. `detect_and_parse` parses the same text correctly

### Reproduction

```
from sglang.srt.entrypoints.openai.protocol import Function, Tool
from sglang.srt.function_call.deepseekv31_detector import DeepSeekV31Detector

B, E, CB, CE, SEP = "<｜tool▁calls▁begin｜>", "<｜tool▁calls▁end｜>", "<｜tool▁call▁begin｜>", "<｜tool▁call▁end｜>", "<｜tool▁sep｜>"
tools = [Tool(type="function", function=Function(name="get_weather", parameters={"type": "object", "properties": {}}))]
deltas = [B + CB + "get_weather" + SEP, '{"city": "Tokyo"}' + CE + CB + "get_weather" + SEP, '{"city": "Paris"}' + CE + E]
d, acc = DeepSeekV31Detector(), {}
for x in deltas:
    for c in d.parse_streaming_increment(x, tools).calls:
        e = acc.setdefault(c.tool_index, ["", ""]); e[0] = c.name or e[0]; e[1] += c.parameters or ""
print(acc)                                                                     # {0: ['get_weather', '{"city": "Paris"}']}
print(DeepSeekV31Detector().detect_and_parse("".join(deltas), tools).calls)   # Tokyo and Paris
```



### Expected

Both calls, each with its own arguments, as `detect_and_parse` returns.



### Environment


### Environment

SGLang 0.5.20 (the latest release) and 0.5.18, CPU, Python 3.12, Ubuntu 24.04, x86_64

items.title: [RFC]: Support Layer-Specific KV-Cache Dtype & Layout in V1 Engine for Hybrid Models
items.author: zhiyuan1i
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation.

### Problem Statement
Currently, V1’s ConstantCacheManager enforces:

Uniform KV-cache dtype across all layers (e.g., cannot mix BF16 for Linear attention’s shortconv + FP32 for recurrent-cache).
FlashInfer-only layout ([num_blocks, 2, ...]), which breaks MLA (block_size=64) unless FLASHINFER backend is used.
This prevents hybrid models with layer-specific requirements from running efficiently.

### Motivation
We are developing an internal HybridModel that combines a custom Linear-attention variant (with a short convolution path) with Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA). And we successfully integrate our model to v0 engine.
After merging Minimax’s V1-engine updates from last week, we discovered that the current cache manager is too rigid for this topology.

Specifically:

We need BF16 KV-cache for the Linear-attention layers (driven by a short-convolution kernel), but FP32 KV-cache for the recurrent / MLA layers. The V1 engine presently allocates a single, uniform dtype for the entire model, forcing us to over-allocate memory when we default everything to FP32.
The engine also hard-codes the FlashInfer layout [num_blocks, 2, …] and the same block size for every layer. As a result, MLA (which we run with block_size=64) is incompatible unless we pin the backend to FLASHINFER. Skipping the safety checks produces corrupted outputs.
These constraints make it impossible to run the model without either (a) redundant memory usage or (b) a backend lock-in that we would prefer to avoid.

### Proposed Change.

We’d like to open a design discussion on how V1 could allow layer-aware KV-cache policies. At a high level:

Decouple the Linear-attention and standard-attention cache pools so that each can specify its own dtype and layout.
Lift the single-block-size requirement so that different attention mechanisms can select page sizes that match their kernels (e.g., 64 for MLA vs. 1008 for Linear).
Avoid mandating FLASHINFER for all layers when only a subset actually needs it. For example, we use cutlass kernel and triton kernel.
We are intentionally not proposing a concrete patch at this stage; instead, we’d like the community’s input on:

Whether a per-layer metadata mechanism (or another approach) is the right direction.
How to maintain backward compatibility while introducing this flexibility.
Any hidden assumptions in the current block manager that would complicate heterogeneous allocations.
Feedback and alternative ideas are very welcome.

### Feedback Period.

items.title: [Bug][Frontend]: Anthropic system-turn handling (merge or in-place) breaks prefix caching for clients that append a system turn every turn; in-place re-role to user satisfies all constraints
items.author: odeda1
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

vLLM serving DeepSeek V4 Flash behind the Anthropic `/v1/messages` frontend; client is Claude Code 2.1.x. Reproduces on any model whose template sends the frontend down the merge path, and (per #52978) will reproduce everywhere once trailing-hoist lands.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

Claude Code appends a `role:"system"` turn to the conversation on **every request** (a per-turn budget reminder, e.g. `<total_tokens>N tokens left</total_tokens>`). All three existing/proposed strategies in `entrypoints/anthropic/serving.py` for conversation-level system turns break prefix caching or the model for this traffic pattern:

| strategy | template-reject models (Qwen `loop.first`) | DeepSeek V4 Flash | prefix caching for per-turn system appenders |
|---|---|---|---|
| merge to leading block (#46025 fallback) | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ every turn's new reminder mutates the rendered **head**, shifting everything after it — the entire conversation re-prefills every turn |
| preserve in place as `system` (#46025 preferred) | ❌ 400 | ❌ garbled output (#46710) | ✅ |
| hoist only the **trailing** suffix (#52978, open) | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ the same message is *trailing* at turn N (hoisted) and *mid-conversation* at turn N+1 (in place) — it flips position between consecutive requests, mutating head **and** middle every turn |

#52978 states "Mid-conversation system turns stay in place so prefix caching … is not undone" — that holds for a one-off mid-conversation system turn, but not for the dominant real client of this API: with a per-turn trailing system message, every consecutive request pair diverges at the previous turn's reminder position, and the cache degenerates to the static system+tools prefix.

**Measured** (real captured Claude Code session, 11 consecutive requests, replayed against a single pinned replica, reading `usage.cache_read_input_tokens`):

- merge-path rendering: per-turn cache reads frozen at the static prefix; **~85% of every prompt re-prefilled every turn**; aggregate hit rate ~48% against a ~95% structural ceiling for the session shape.
- bisection: appending user/assistant turns preserves the prefix; appending one trailing `system` turn collapses the match to the static prefix.
- identical bodies with the transform below applied: **99–100% of the previous prompt re-read on every turn**, aggregate ~97%.

### Proposed fix

When a conversation-level system turn cannot be preserved verbatim, **re-role it to `user` in place** (content unchanged, block form), merging runs of consecutive user turns to keep alternation — instead of merging it into the leading block:

```python
# instead of: system_parts.append(text)  (head merge)
messages.append({"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": text}]})
# then merge adjacent user turns
```

This satisfies every constraint simultaneously:
- template-reject models: no system role remains mid-conversation → no `TemplateError`;
- DeepSeek V4 Flash: user turns are in-distribution → avoids the #46710 garbling attributed to in-place system rendering;
- #48874's trailing-system tool derail: the prompt no longer ends on a system block — the reminder folds into the adjacent user turn;
- prefix caching: renders become strictly append-only across turns (measured above).

The reminder text itself is preserved verbatim (Claude Code already self-labels it `<system-reminder>`), so the model-visible change is role framing only.

Related: #46025 (introduced the three paths), #46710 (in-place garbling on DeepSeek V4 Flash), #48874 / #52978 (trailing hoist). Happy to contribute the patch with the test matrix above if maintainers agree with the direction.

### Addendum: also allow *dropping* mid-conversation system turns, by config

Re-roling to `user` is the right **default** because it is lossless — but operators should also be able to opt into dropping these turns entirely, e.g. a per-endpoint flag on the Anthropic frontend:

```
--anthropic-inline-system-policy {reroll-to-user (default) | drop}
```

Rationale: mid-session system turns from agent harnesses are client bookkeeping (budget countdowns, environment notices), and open models were generally never trained on system content injected mid-conversation. For some of them this is out-of-distribution information however it is framed — we have seen models fixate on the countdown or echo it back. An operator who knows their model handles it badly today has no remedy short of a proxy that rewrites bodies; a `drop` policy gives the same append-only, cache-stable rendering with none of the injected content.

`drop` must stay opt-in and never become a default: it silently changes what the model sees, and a harness that sends *load-bearing* mid-session system content (tool-permission changes, file-change notices) would misbehave with no visible error.
