items.title: [Bug]: GLM required tool-call grammar accepts split marker tokens that the streaming parser treats as content
items.author: QwertyJack
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

- **vLLM:** tag [`v0.28.0`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/tree/v0.28.0), commit `2cf0a6915ce544dc493a0990f2ea38d81601128a`. Verified from the image build reference and byte-for-byte comparison of the relevant installed parser/grammar files.
- **xgrammar:** `0.2.6`.
- **vllm-ascend:** commit `c267db731d03e18042047ea1594e033673e46a6f`.
- Tokenizer: GLM-5; transformers `5.14.1`, tokenizers `0.22.2`.

The reproduction runs grammar/parser logic on CPU and needs only tokenizer files, not model weights or accelerator inference.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

With GLM `tool_choice="required"`, xgrammar accepts `<tool_call>` / `</tool_call>` assembled from ordinary sub-tokens. vLLM's streaming parser only recognizes the atomic marker IDs and emits the split markers as content. A sequence can therefore satisfy the required-tool grammar while producing **zero tool calls**.

Both encodings below decode to exactly the same text, including the stop token:

```text
<tool_call>get_current_time</tool_call><|observation|>
```

#### Minimal reproduction

Save the script below as `repro.py`, then run:

```bash
python repro.py /path/to/GLM-5-tokenizer
```

This constructs token sequences with thinking enabled and a valid `</think>` boundary; it does not run model generation. `reasoning=False` on the grammar represents the tool constraint applied **after** reasoning ends.

```python
"""CPU component reproduction; only tokenizer files are needed.
Usage: python repro_glm_split_markers.py /path/to/GLM-5-tokenizer
This constructs token sequences; it does not run model generation.
"""
import sys
from collections import Counter

import xgrammar as xgr
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
from vllm.parser.glm47_moe import glm47_moe_config
from vllm.parser.engine.streaming_parser_engine import StreamingParserEngine

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(sys.argv[1], trust_remote_code=True)
tools = [{"type": "function", "function": {
    "name": "get_current_time",
    "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {}},
}}]
# vLLM applies this tool grammar after reasoning ends.
tag = xgr.get_model_structural_tag(
    "glm_4_7", tools=tools, tool_choice="required", reasoning=False,
)
ctx = xgr.GrammarCompiler(
    xgr.TokenizerInfo.from_huggingface(tok)
).compile_structural_tag(tag)

# Captured GLM-5 encodings, with the SAME observation stop in both cases.
cases = {
    "atomic": [154843, 455, 11075, 3009, 154844, 154829],
    "split": [27, 14163, 13420, 29, 455, 11075, 3009,
              522, 14163, 13420, 29, 154829],
}
expected = "<tool_call>get_current_time</tool_call><|observation|>"
prefix = tok.encode("I need the current time.", add_special_tokens=False)
prefix += [tok.convert_tokens_to_ids("</think>")]
for label, ids in cases.items():
    assert tok.decode(ids) == expected, "Tokenizer differs from the tested GLM-5 tokenizer"
    matcher = xgr.GrammarMatcher(
        ctx, override_stop_tokens=[154820, 154827, 154829],
    )
    accepted = all(matcher.accept_token(t) for t in ids)
    engine = StreamingParserEngine(glm47_moe_config(thinking=True), tok)
    events = engine.feed(tok.decode(prefix), prefix)
    # ASCII tool text, so decoding each suffix token does not split UTF-8.
    for t in ids:
        events += engine.feed(tok.decode([t]), [t])
    events += engine.finish()
    counts = Counter(e.type.name for e in events)
    content = "".join(e.value for e in events if e.type.name == "TEXT_CHUNK")
    print(label, "grammar_accepts=", accepted,
          "reasoning_ends=", counts["REASONING_END"],
          "tool_starts=", counts["TOOL_CALL_START"],
          "tool_ends=", counts["TOOL_CALL_END"],
          "content=", repr(content))
```

Observed output:

```text
atomic grammar_accepts= True reasoning_ends= 1 tool_starts= 1 tool_ends= 1 content= ''
split grammar_accepts= True reasoning_ends= 1 tool_starts= 0 tool_ends= 0 content= '<tool_call>get_current_time</tool_call>'
```

#### Cause and expected behavior

[`StreamingParserEngine._process_lex_tokens`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/2cf0a6915ce544dc493a0990f2ea38d81601128a/vllm/parser/engine/streaming_parser_engine.py#L341) treats text-lexer matches for token-ID terminals as content once token IDs have been supplied. GLM registers its tool markers as token-ID terminals, but xgrammar accepts both encodings.

The grammar and parser should agree on valid tool-call encodings, either by constraining generation to canonical marker IDs or by recognizing the accepted encoding in the constrained tool path. Globally disabling strict parsing could misinterpret literal markup.

The same relevant parser logic is present in main at `c843f0cab78b413f2b0a5c2282cb71e3a3937b11` (source inspection only; the executed reproduction uses `v0.28.0` + xgrammar `0.2.6`).

#### Real-generation evidence boundary

A real response generated split markers, stopped normally, and returned content instead of `tool_calls`. That service had thinking enabled but no reasoning parser. Adding `--reasoning-parser glm45` while retaining thinking made 10/10 subsequent requests succeed. **We have not reproduced natural split-marker generation after correcting that configuration.** The CPU test above demonstrates the remaining encoding mismatch, not its frequency under correct configuration.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [ ] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

I searched existing issues and inspected the relevant upstream source. I have not consulted the documentation chatbot, so I am leaving the combined checkbox unchecked.

items.title: [Bug]: Engine-based parsers drop text after/between tool calls in non-streaming (streaming keeps it)
items.author: Chocolatine75
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

`collect_env.py` fails on macOS, so manually: macOS arm64 (CPU), Python 3.12, vLLM main @ 998490cd9f.
Parser-only bug, hardware doesn't matter.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

With the parsers built on `ParserEngine` (qwen3_coder, qwen3_xml, glm45, minimax_m2, ...), text that comes after a tool call is returned when streaming but dropped in non-streaming responses. Text between two tool calls is dropped too.

Repro against a real server, with the model output forced through `structured_outputs` so it's deterministic:

```
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder
```

```python
import json
import requests

URL = "http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions"
forced = ("<tool_call>\n<function=get_weather>\n<parameter=city>\nParis\n</parameter>\n"
          "</function>\n</tool_call>\nDone.")
body = {
    "model": "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Weather in Paris?"}],
    "tools": [{"type": "function", "function": {"name": "get_weather",
               "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"city": {"type": "string"}}}}}],
    "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False},
    "structured_outputs": {"choice": [forced]},
    "max_tokens": 64,
}

msg = requests.post(URL, json=body).json()["choices"][0]["message"]
print("non-streaming:", repr(msg["content"]), [tc["function"]["name"] for tc in msg["tool_calls"]])

content = ""
with requests.post(URL, json={**body, "stream": True}, stream=True) as r:
    for line in r.iter_lines():
        if line.startswith(b"data: {"):
            content += json.loads(line[6:])["choices"][0]["delta"].get("content") or ""
print("streaming:    ", repr(content))
```

```
non-streaming: None ['get_weather']
streaming:     'Done.'
```

(`/v1/completions` with the same `structured_outputs` returns exactly `forced`, so the model output is the same in both cases.)

`_events_to_delta` defers text that follows a tool event so a delta never mixes content and tool calls (`TestPostToolContentDeferral`). In streaming the next delta flushes it, but `_single_pass_parse` never does. The `tool_choice="none"` path goes through `extract_tool_calls` + `finish_streaming` and does keep it (`'\nDone.'`), and `InklingParser._single_pass_parse` already works around this for Inkling only.

I think the fix is to flush the deferred content at the end of `ParserEngine._single_pass_parse` (basically moving the Inkling override into the base class). Not sure if some models are meant to drop that text instead (Rust minimax_m2 does, in both modes), in which case it should apply to streaming too. Happy to send a PR once the direction is clear.

Related but different: #49412 is about whitespace at tool-call boundaries; here the text itself is gone.

(Investigated with help from Claude Code; reproduced locally.)

items.title: [Feature]: Logprobs on parsed path streaming `/derender`
items.author: hickeyma
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Streaming `/derender` with a reasoning or tool parser (#50550) doesn't return logprobs. #55029 added streaming logprobs but only on the unparsed path. The parsed path builds its stream choices without them. A client that streams with `logprobs: true` through a parser gets nothing back.

Agreed on #47161 (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/47161#issuecomment-5893681568): the engine is the reference for logprob token strings. Standalone `/derender`, including the parsed path should use one shared resolver built on `convert_ids_list_to_tokens` and `_correct_decoded_token` with parity tests against the engine.

Scope:

- Resolve each chunk's logprobs and attach them to whatever delta the parser emits. `/v1/chat/completions` does the same, with one `logprobs.content` list no matter which field the tokens land in.
- Update `logprob_context_token_ids` on the parsed path, like the plain path does. Keep it starting empty, like the engine.
- Drop logprobs on every chunk when `include_reasoning=false` with a parser, like the engine does.
- Fix batch derender too. `_derender_chat` clears `reasoning` but still returns the logprobs.
- Add parity tests against `/v1/chat/completions` with `include_reasoning` on and off, a chunk the parser swallows (tool-call markup) and a multi-byte char split across chunks.

`DerenderStreamState` stays as is. Chunk logprobs already cover only that chunk's tokens and replay never touches them, so no cursor is needed. #59510 handles streaming stop with a 400, so no pending text field either.

Blocked on #58181 (still open). The shared helper (`decode_token_ids`) and the parity tests depend on it.

@shimib has offered to take this. @hyeongyun0916 will review and help with repros.

### Alternatives

Re-resolving token strings separately in the parsed path. We ruled this out on #47161 because the paths already disagree (see #59241).

### Additional context

- #47161: RFC thread where this was agreed
- #55029: streaming logprobs for the unparsed path
- #50550: parser aware streaming derender
- #58181 / #57574: `GenerateLogProbs` with integer token IDs
- #59241 / #59252: SentencePiece leading space dropped in derender logprob strings
- #57052 / #59510: stop handling on derender. #59510 makes streaming `/derender` return 400 on `stop` and notes that logprobs aren't trimmed to the cut text.

items.title: [Bug]: Multimodal chat requests silently drop all images when request-level chat_template_kwargs is present (v0.30.0, Gemma-4-26B-A4B)
items.author: thorium115
items.body_excerpt: ### Your current environment vLLM version: 0.30.0 Model: Gemma-4-26B-A4B (NVFP4, ModelOpt quantization) GPU: NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell (32 GiB), driver 610.57.04 Deployment: official image docker.io/vllm/vllm-openai:v0.30.0, podman ### 🐛 Describe the bug Describe the bug On /v1/chat/completions, the presence of any request-level chat_template_kwargs causes all images in the request to be silently dropped. The rendered prompt contains only the text portion (usage.prompt_tokens ≈ 20 instead of ≈ 276 for one image), the server returns 200 OK, and the model correctly reports that no image was provided. No error or warning is logged. The identical payload without chat_template_kwargs processes images normally. To reproduce Server: vllm serve /models/gemma-4-26b \ --served-model-name gemma-4-26b \ --max-model-len 262144 \ --trust-remote-code \ --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser gemma4 --reasoning-parser gemma4 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \ --limit-mm-per-prompt '{"image":3,"audio":0,"video":0}' \ --default-chat-template-kwargs '{"enable_thinking":true}' Request A (control, works — images processed): { "model": "gemma-4-26b", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "data:image/jpeg;base64,"}}, {"type": "text", "text": "Describe this scene in detail."} ]}], "temperature": 0.7, "max_tokens": 4096 } Result: usage.prompt_tokens: 276, image-grounded description. Request B (fails — identical, adds per-request kwargs): { "model": "gemma-4-26b", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "data:image/jpeg;base64,"}}, {"type": "text", "text": "Describe this scene in detail."} ]}], "temperature": 0.7, "max_tokens": 4096, "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": true} } Result: usage.prompt_tokens: 22, response states no image was provided. Behavior is identical with {"enable_thinking": false} and with 1 or 3 images attached. Note the per-request value duplicates the server default, so it should be a no-op. Expected behavior Per the Reasoning Outputs documentation, request-level chat_template_kwargs merges with/overrides server defaults during template rendering — image inputs must still be bound into the prompt (prompt_tokens ≈ 276, grounded response). Additional context The failure is invisible in normal operation (200 OK, coherent reply); we detected it only by comparing usage.prompt_tokens across requests. At temperature 0.7 the model confabulates a fully detailed fictional scene for the image-less prompt rather than declining — silently degraded grounding for any pipeline combining per-request thinking control with images. Happy to attach minimal payload files / full server logs if useful. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Onboarding 2026] Good first issues — start contributing to LMCache in one PR
items.author: maobaolong
items.body_excerpt:
👋 Welcome to LMCache! This umbrella issue is the **single entry point** for first-time
contributors. If you've never sent a PR to LMCache before, start here.

> If you're looking for the older onboarding thread, see #627. This 2026 version
> focuses on smaller, well-scoped tasks with a friendly step-by-step PR workflow.

---

## 0. Before you start

- Read [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](../blob/dev/CONTRIBUTING.md). The most important parts:
  - Base branch is `dev`. Open PRs against `dev`, not `main`.
  - Every Python file starts with `# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0`.
  - Imports are grouped as `# Standard / # Third Party / # First Party / # Local`.
  - Line length is **88**, formatter is `ruff format`, lint is `ruff check`.
  - Never access `_private` members of other classes (SLF rule).
  - Public functions/methods need **type hints** + **docstring**.
- Set up the environment:
  ```bash
  uv venv --python 3.12 && source .venv/bin/activate
  uv pip install -e . --no-build-isolation
  uv pip install -r requirements/test.txt
  pre-commit install
  ```

## 1. How to claim a task

These tasks are mainly for new contributors to learn the LMCache issue-to-PR workflow. Please claim **only one good-first issue at a time**. If you already have an assigned good-first issue or an open good-first PR, finish that work before taking another one, and leave the remaining tasks for other newcomers.

1. Pick **one** sub-issue below that has no assignee and no `🔒 claimed` comment.
2. Comment exactly: `/claim` (or `I'd like to work on this 🙋`).
   A maintainer will assign it to you within ~2 business days.
3. If you go silent for 7 days we'll un-assign so others can pick it up — totally fine,
   just leave a comment if you need more time.

## 2. Branch & commit

```bash
git checkout dev && git pull
git checkout -b gfi/<issue-number>-short-slug
# ... do the work ...
git commit -s -m "short imperative summary"   # -s is required (DCO)
```

- **Sign-off is required** (`-s`). PRs without DCO sign-off cannot be merged.
- Keep the PR small: one issue = one PR.

## 3. Local checks (must pass before pushing)

```bash
pre-commit run --all-files
pytest -xvs tests/<the_file_you_touched>.py    # if applicable
```

## 4. Open the PR

**PR title format** (please follow):

```
[good-first-issue] <area>: <imperative summary>  (#<sub-issue-number>)
```

Examples:
- `[good-first-issue] docs: fix broken link in quickstart (#1801)`
- `[good-first-issue] tests: add unit test for FooBar.flush (#1802)`
- `[good-first-issue] lint: add SPDX header to scripts/foo.py (#1803)`

**PR description** — please use this template (the repo's PR template already
gives you the skeleton; just fill it in):

```markdown
**What this PR does / why we need it**:
Closes #<sub-issue-number>
Refs #<this umbrella issue number>

<one or two sentences describing the change>

**Special notes for your reviewers**:
- This is my first PR to LMCache 🙇 please be gentle.
- I ran `pre-commit run --all-files` locally — all green.
- I ran `pytest -xvs tests/...` — all green.

**If applicable**:
- [ ] this PR contains user facing changes - docs added
- [ ] this PR contains unit tests
```

> Tip: writing `Closes #1234` in the description auto-closes the sub-issue when the
> PR is merged. Keep `Refs #<umbrella>` so the umbrella stays linked.

## 5. Finding a reviewer

You don't need to find one yourself — `.github/CODEOWNERS` will auto-request
the right people based on the files you changed. If the PR sits idle for **3 working
days**, leave a polite comment like:

> Friendly ping — PTAL when you have a moment 🙏 cc @<one CODEOWNER from the file you changed>

If you really can't tell who to ping, default to:
- Tests / CI / packaging → @hickeyma @sammshen @ApostaC @deng451e
- Docs / examples → @sammshen @deng451e
- Storage backends → @maobaolong @sammshen @chunxiaozheng
- Core engine / memory → @ApostaC @YaoJiayi @sammshen
- Multiprocess → @ApostaC @OasisGit @hlin99

(See [`.github/CODEOWNERS`](../blob/dev/.github/CODEOWNERS) for the full map.)

## 6. Responding to review comments

This is the part most newcomers miss — please follow it, it makes everyone happier:

1. **Address every comment.** For each thread:
   - If you agree → push a fix and reply `Done in <commit-sha>`.
   - If you disagree → explain politely, propose an alternative.
   - If you don't understand → ask! Reviewers expect questions.
2. **Don't force-push** during review (it loses inline-comment context). Just add
   commits; we'll squash on merge.
3. **Re-request review explicitly** once all threads are resolved:
   > Addressed all comments, PTAL again 🙏 @reviewer1 @reviewer2

   `PTAL` = "Please Take Another Look". Tag every reviewer who left comments.
4. If CI is red, fix it before pinging — reviewers will skip red PRs.


---

## 7. How to create and claim a sub-issues

- You can extend the new cli commend line tools, ref to https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/pull/3719 and https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/pull/3678

---

Stuck? Drop a message in the `#contributors` channel of our
[Slack](https://join.slack.com/t/lmcacheworkspace/shared_invite/zt-3g8e6xzz8-KzS_HI8bPERGFK5PTB~MYg)
or comment here. We're happy to help. 🙌


**Maintainers**: please update this checklist as sub-issues are filed.

**New contributor-friendly logging cleanup queue:** #5118 is now linked as a child of this onboarding issue.

The first enforcement step has landed in #5125: Ruff `G004` is enabled repo-wide, and the remaining not-yet-migrated files/directories are temporarily ignored. I split that remaining work into small child issues under #5118 so newcomers can pick one focused slice, comment `/claim`, and send one small PR.

For anyone looking for current work: please open #5118, choose an unassigned child issue, and claim it there. The work is intentionally mechanical: convert logging f-strings to lazy `%`-style logging, preserve the rendered message text, and remove the matching `G004` ignore entry from `pyproject.toml` when the slice is clean.

items.title: [Bug][MP] Failed prefetch cleanup can publish invalid L1 data
items.author: ae86zhizhi
items.body_excerpt:
**Label**

`bug`

**Describe the bug**

In MP mode, `PrefetchController` cleans up the L1 destination of an L2 load that failed (the adapter reported the key as not loaded) with two calls in this order:

```python
l1_mgr.finish_write(failed_keys)
l1_mgr.delete(failed_keys)
```

(`lmcache/v1/distributed/storage_controllers/prefetch_controller.py`, "Clean up failed keys" in the load-completion handler; the same pair runs in `_cleanup_in_flight_requests` on `stop()` for every request still in its load phase.)

`finish_write` makes the destination readable and notifies the write-finished listeners even though the load has not been confirmed successful; its contents may be incomplete or uninitialized. `StoreController`'s listener enqueues the key and its loop calls `reserve_read` on it, which now succeeds. If the store controller acquires and still holds that read lock when the `delete` runs, the `delete` returns `KEY_IS_LOCKED` and the entry stays; the destination is then stored to the policy-selected L2 adapters under a valid key, and a later lookup returns it as a hit.

The shutdown path has the same shape without needing a failed load: every in-flight request's `write_reserved_keys` goes through the same two calls while the store controller's loop is still running.

Even when the `delete` wins the race, the key is announced to every `L1ManagerListener` as write-finished, and `finish_write` publishes `L1_WRITE_FINISHED`, so metrics and coordinator cache events report an unconfirmed destination as a completed write.

**To Reproduce**

With the regression test of the linked pull request (`tests/v1/distributed/test_prefetch_failed_load_cleanup.py`), against `dev`:

1. Store one key in a `MockL2Adapter` and wrap it in `FaultInjectL2Adapter(gap_indices=(0,))`, so the key is present at lookup and its load is reported as failed.
2. Register an `L1ManagerListener` that records `on_l1_keys_write_finished`, and start a `StoreController` with a second, empty `MockL2Adapter` as its target.
3. Submit a prefetch for the key and wait for its result (0 retained keys).
4. The recording listener has received the failed key as write-finished (`assert key not in listener.write_finished_keys()` fails). Depending on scheduling, the empty adapter may also receive a store of the destination.

The second test checks L1 absence and listener silence when `stop()` interrupts an unfinished load (an adapter that accepts a load which then stays pending); it fails on `dev` for the same reason.

**Expected behavior**

A reservation whose load failed or was cancelled is removed while it is still write-locked. The key never becomes readable, is never announced to the write-finished listeners, and no store task is created for it. `reserve_read` on the key returns `KEY_NOT_EXIST`.

`L1Manager.delete(keys, force=True)` already does this; the fix is to call it instead of the `finish_write` + `delete` pair at both sites. A pull request with the change and the two tests follows.

**Environment**

- LMCache `dev` at 45e019df (2026-09-08); the same two call sites are in v0.5.4.
- Linux x86_64, Python 3.12, torch 2.13.0. The tests use the pinned-memory L1 and no model.

items.title: [Performance] NVFP4 KV cache regresses Qwen4Exp decode ~29% on DGX Spark (SM121) vs fp8_e4m3 — consider arch-gating the default
items.author: leego
items.body_excerpt:
# [Performance] NVFP4 KV cache regresses Qwen4Exp decode ~29% on DGX Spark (SM121) vs fp8_e4m3

## Summary
`--kv-cache-dtype nvfp4` (the new default, `NVFP4_KV_CACHE=1`) costs **~29% single-stream
decode throughput** for Qwen4Exp-style models (QSA sparse attention) on GB10/SM121,
versus fp8_e4m3 KV. The FP4 packed-KV path's gather-side dequant is expensive on this
silicon; on datacenter parts the tradeoff may differ, but on Spark the pool-size win
is pointless (262K native context already fits with fp8) and the decode cost is real.

## Data (2× DGX Spark TP=2, NEXTN 3/1/4, decode CUDA graphs on, n=7-10 median)
| KV dtype | single-stream decode | notes |
|---|---|---|
| nvfp4 (default since the NVFP4-KV change) | 44.0 tok/s | also occasional deep dips |
| **fp8_e4m3** (`NVFP4_KV_CACHE=0`) | **56.8-58.6 tok/s** | stable |
| bf16 | 54-59 (more variance) | |

Same cluster, same weights (RadixArk/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4), same bench
(`completion_tokens`-based streaming, 400-token runs).

## Suggestion
- Gate `NVFP4_KV_CACHE` default by arch: keep 1 on SM100+, default 0 on SM120/121 for
  QSA models (or autotune at first capture).
- Alternatively add a fused gather+dequant path for FP4 KV in the QSA Triton varlen
  fallback kernel (`qsa_fa_fallback.py` pattern used on SM121).

## Environment
Image lmsysorg/sglang:qwen38flashnext (+SM121 QSA fallback), 2×GB10, RoCEv2 TP2.
Full methodology: MiaAI-Lab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Dual-DGX-Sparks → OPTIMIZATION-2026-08-28.md.

items.title: [Bug] HiCache backup thread dies on any storage backend exception; queued backups and their host memory are never released
items.author: qidaye
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

`HiCacheController.backup_thread_func` (and the `HybridCacheController` override) only catches `queue.Empty`:

```python
while not self.storage_stop_event.is_set():
    try:
        operation = self.backup_queue.get(block=True, timeout=1)
        if operation is None:
            continue
        if not self.backup_skip:
            self._page_backup(operation)
        self.ack_backup_queue.put(operation)
    except Empty:
        continue
```

Any exception raised by the storage backend while writing a page (I/O error, timeout, malformed response from a remote store such as Mooncake / NIXL / 3FS / HF3FS / file backends) escapes the loop and kills the daemon thread. From that point on:

- every backup operation stays in `backup_queue` forever and is never written to L3;
- `ack_backup_queue` never drains, so `HiRadixCache` / `UnifiedRadixCache` never release the host memory held by those operations (`entry.release_host()` in the backup drain path);
- the only visible symptom is host pool exhaustion much later. There is no log line pointing at the dead backup thread, and `hicache_*` metrics keep reporting as if backups were in flight.

A backend that returns `False` from `batch_set` already stops the current operation, but the acked `StorageOperation` carries no information about the failure, so the ack consumer cannot distinguish a partial or failed write from a complete one.

Expected: a failing backup should be logged, the operation should still be acked (so host memory is released and the queue keeps draining), and the ack should say what went wrong.

### Reproduction

Drives the production `backup_thread_func` with a controller stub whose backend raises once. No GPU or model needed.

```python
import threading
from queue import Empty, Queue
from unittest import mock

import torch

from sglang.srt.managers.cache_controller import HiCacheController, StorageOperation

controller = mock.MagicMock()
controller.storage_stop_event = threading.Event()
controller.backup_skip = False
controller.page_size = 16
controller.backup_queue = Queue()
controller.ack_backup_queue = Queue()

calls = [0]
def page_backup(operation):
    calls[0] += 1
    if calls[0] == 1:
        raise RuntimeError("storage backend I/O error")  # e.g. remote store timeout
    operation.completed_tokens = 16 * len(operation.hash_value)
controller._page_backup = page_backup

def make_op(n):
    return StorageOperation(torch.zeros(n * 16), list(range(n * 16)), hash_value=[f"h{i}" for i in range(n)])

controller.backup_queue.put(make_op(4))
controller.backup_queue.put(make_op(2))

t = threading.Thread(target=HiCacheController.backup_thread_func, args=(controller,), daemon=True)
t.start()
t.join(timeout=3)
print("backup thread alive:", t.is_alive())
acked = []
try:
    while True:
        acked.append(controller.ack_backup_queue.get(timeout=1).id)
except Empty:
    pass
print("acked operations:", acked, "(2 expected)")
print("still queued:", controller.backup_queue.qsize())
```

Output on `main` (2358916d5a):

```
Exception in thread Thread-1 (backup_thread_func):
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  File ".../sglang/srt/managers/cache_controller.py", line 1289, in backup_thread_func
    self._page_backup(operation)
RuntimeError: storage backend I/O error
backup thread alive: False
acked operations: [] (2 expected)
still queued: 1
```

The same happens in a real deployment whenever the L3 backend raises during `batch_set` (observed with a remote storage backend timing out under load): the backup thread disappears and host memory is never reclaimed.

In a server the trigger is any exception from the configured `--hicache-storage-backend` during a write; e.g. `--enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-storage-backend <backend>` with a backend that becomes unreachable.

### Environment

Reproduction above is CPU-only and does not depend on the accelerator.

```
sglang: main @ 2358916d5a (editable install from source)
python: 3.12.13
torch: 2.13.0+cpu
OS: Ubuntu 24.04, Linux 7.0.0-30-generic
```

`python3 -m sglang.check_env` currently fails on a CPU-only host with `NameError: name 'env' is not defined` (no branch in `check_env.py` for the CPU case), so the versions above were collected manually.

A fix is in #38427.

items.title: [Bug] HiCache write_through does not fully persist first-seen prefixes before eviction
items.author: donghyq
items.body_excerpt:
# [SGLang] HiCache `write_through` does not fully persist first-seen prefixes before eviction

## Summary

When `--hicache-write-policy write_through` is used with Mooncake Store, a first-seen prefix can be evicted from L1/L2 before all of its KV is backed up to storage. Replaying that prefix after eviction restores only part of it from L3; the rest is recomputed.

Using `--hicache-write-policy write_back --hicache-storage-prefetch-policy wait_complete` on the same workload restores the full prefix from Mooncake Store, so the storage backend and restore path are functional.

## Environment

- SGLang commit: `bdf8886ad3`
- Branch: `main`
- Model: Qwen3-4B
- GPU: 1 × NVIDIA H20-3e
- Attention backend: Triton
- HiCache:
  - `--enable-hierarchical-cache`
  - `--hicache-size 4`
  - `--hicache-write-policy write_through`
  - `--hicache-storage-backend mooncake`
  - `--hicache-storage-backend-extra-config '{"standalone_storage": true, "client_server_address": "127.0.0.1:50300", "enable_group_semantics": false}'`
- Mooncake Store:
  - master/client started independently
  - `root_fs_dir` and `cluster_id` configured
  - global segment size: 16 GiB
- Prompt: 5 distinct 16,011-token prefixes, `max_new_tokens=1`
- L1 capacity: 42,763 tokens
- L2 capacity: 27,127 tokens

## Reproduction

1. Start SGLang with the `write_through` configuration above.
2. Flush the cache.
3. Send five distinct 16,011-token prefixes sequentially.
4. Replay prefix A after prefixes B–E have displaced it from L1/L2.

## Expected

Prefix A should be restored from Mooncake Store with roughly:

```json
{
  "cached_tokens": 16010,
  "cached_tokens_details": {
    "device": 0,
    "host": 0,
    "storage": 16010,
    "storage_backend": "MooncakeStore"
  }
}
```

## Actual

Prefix A restores only part of the KV from storage:

```json
{
  "cached_tokens": 2551,
  "cached_tokens_details": {
    "device": 0,
    "host": 0,
    "storage": 2551,
    "storage_backend": "MooncakeStore"
  }
}
```

A second replay then reports a full device hit:

```json
{
  "cached_tokens": 16009,
  "cached_tokens_details": {
    "device": 16009,
    "host": 0,
    "storage": 0,
    "storage_backend": "MooncakeStore"
  }
}
```

## Control experiment

The same workload with:

```text
--hicache-write-policy write_back
--hicache-storage-prefetch-policy wait_complete
```

returns:

```json
{
  "cached_tokens": 16010,
  "cached_tokens_details": {
    "device": 0,
    "host": 0,
    "storage": 16010,
    "storage_backend": "MooncakeStore"
  }
}
```

This indicates that Mooncake Store can persist and restore the full prefix when the write path is forced.

## Possible cause

In `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/hiradix_cache.py`:

- `_inc_hit_count()` at line 926 skips chunked requests.
- `write_backup()` at line 856 is only called after `hit_count` reaches `write_through_threshold`.
- For a first-seen prefix, the leaf node may therefore not be backed up before eviction.
- `write_backup()` also requires the parent node to already be backed up, so a long first-seen prefix may only be partially persisted.
- `_evict_write_back()` at line 1105 shows the working control path: it stages the node to host, waits for the backup, and then writes storage.

## Suggested fix

One of the following would make the behavior clearer:

1. Add a true “write-through on insert” mode that persists the full prefix chain when a request finishes.
2. Document that `write_through` means “second-hit persistence” rather than “insert-time persistence”.
3. Keep the current optimization, but add a warning when a first-seen prefix is evicted before its backup completes.

## Impact

This affects long first-seen prompts that are evicted before a second request arrives. It can silently reduce L3 hit rate and make shared-cache routing less effective.

items.title: [Bug] Large HiCache UCX startup timeout on downstream build; not reproduced on v0.5.20
items.author: ByronHsu
items.body_excerpt:
### Result

**Not reproduced on the latest upstream image (v0.5.20).** A large HiCache pool triggered a UCX startup timeout on our earlier downstream build, but both HiCache and no-HiCache starts passed with the unmodified upstream image.

| Build | HiCache per rank | UCX initialization, all 8 ranks | Server ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Downstream `869abc0605`, NIXL 1.3.0 / UCX 1.21.0 | 234 GB | Six ranks explicitly timed out at 60s; none completed | No |
| Same downstream build, no HiCache | 0 | 3–4s | Yes |
| **Upstream v0.5.20, NIXL 1.4.1 / UCX 1.22.0** | **234 GB** | **~2s** | **234s after launch** |
| Same upstream image, no HiCache | 0 | ~2s | 62s after launch |

Each HiCache/control pair ran on the same eight-H200 node with fresh processes. The upstream pair used a different physical node from the downstream pair, and multiple software components changed: this does **not** identify a fix or prove the cause. Only startup was tested, with no inference requests. Both upstream runs registered all eight KV buffers, passed passive `/ready` checks for 30 seconds, and exited cleanly.

### Reproduction settings

8 H200s, approximately 2014 GiB host RAM; public `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V2-Lite` real weights, revision `604d5664dddd88a0433dbae533b7fe9472482de0`.

Upstream image: `lmsysorg/sglang:latest` resolved to **v0.5.20**, source `94602c9c2b7cbdb8efd5c52802dac6a1c180089e`. Tested amd64 image digest:

```text
lmsysorg/sglang@sha256:b27fce60bc5494c118c4910702812bcfa8cee67abcdd1ff8b0902f21647552f4
```

No source overlay, serving patches, or dependency replacements. Download the model revision above into `$MODEL_DIR`, then run:

```bash
export SGLANG_DISAGGREGATION_ENGINE_INIT_TIMEOUT=60
export SGLANG_NCCL_ALL_GATHER_IN_OVERLAP_SCHEDULER_SYNC_BATCH=1
export SGLANG_FORCE_STREAM_INTERVAL=1
export SGLANG_FORCE_CPU_IMAGE_PREPROCESSING=0

python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path "$MODEL_DIR" --trust-remote-code \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 30000 \
  --tp-size 8 --dp-size 8 --ep-size 8 --enable-dp-attention \
  --disaggregation-mode prefill --disaggregation-transfer-backend nixl \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.7 --dtype bfloat16 --kv-cache-dtype bf16 \
  --page-size 64 --tokenizer-worker-num 4 \
  --context-length 150000 --max-running-requests 1024 \
  --skip-server-warmup --log-level debug --decode-attention-backend fa3 \
  --enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-size 234 \
  --hicache-write-policy write_through \
  --hicache-mem-layout page_first --hicache-io-backend kernel
```

Remove the five HiCache options for the control. CUDA graphs stay enabled; NIXL is the PD transport, not L3 storage. Actual pool allocation: **234,001,612,800 bytes per rank**, about **1.872 TB total**. Size is per rank and requires sufficient host/cgroup headroom.

### Original failure

The downstream run failed **during UCX backend creation, before KV registration**:

```text
RuntimeError: NIXL create_backend('UCX', {'num_threads': '8'}) did not return within 60s
```

Five seconds before failure: **141.6 GiB host headroom**, **39.2–39.4 GiB free per GPU**, no host OOM-counter increase or CUDA OOM. Host memory pressure and compaction were high. No native stack inside UCX was captured. A later audit found rank 0 in a debugger tracing stop at 21:29:30 UTC, inside the 60-second UCX window, as well as earlier allocation-stage attachments. The retained samples do not establish total pause duration. Other ranks also timed out without a recorded tracing stop, but this run was not free of measurement interference. A telemetry gap further limits the evidence.

The upstream HiCache run kept at least **120 GiB host headroom**, logged no OOM, and completed UCX startup quickly. The underlying reason for the older failure remains unresolved.

<details>
<summary>Upstream runtime</summary>

Python 3.12.3; PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130; NIXL/nixl-cu13 1.4.1; bundled UCX 1.22.0; CUDA 13.0; driver 595.71.05; Linux 6.8.12; FlashInfer 0.6.18; Transformers 5.12.1. THP mode remains `madvise`. The 60-second UCX deadline and eight prefill backend threads were unchanged.

</details>

### Follow-up: the extra host memory is DC receive buffers

On one exclusive node, with the same upstream source/image and **232 GB/rank** HiCache, we compared fresh server processes:

| Native backend | DC interfaces | Receive-buffer chunks | Scheduler anonymous huge pages | UCX startup span |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| NIXL 1.4.1 / UCX 1.22 | 0 | 288 | 12.498 GiB | 2s |
| NIXL 1.3.0 / UCX 1.21 | 288 | 576 | 23.188 GiB | 4s |
| Same 1.3.0 package, only `UCX_TLS=^dc_mlx5` added | 0 | 288 | 12.502 GiB | 3s |

All three initialized all eight ranks, registered KV buffers, and held passive readiness for 30 seconds. No compaction stalls, THP fallbacks, or OOM occurred. No inference or PD transfers were tested. The third case is a diagnostic intervention, **not a verified timeout fix**.

UCX debug logs and per-scheduler memory maps identify the difference: **8 ranks × 9 workers × 4 ports = 288 DC interfaces**, each eagerly allocating a **38 MiB** receive buffer through `rc_recv_desc`. Those extra buffers account for **10.6875 GiB** of huge pages. Excluding only DC on the old package removes them and matches the newer package. Actual loaded UCX versions were verified in server logs.

The old binary includes DC; the new wheel omits it. [NIXL PR 1708](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/nixl/pull/1708) disables DC in the manylinux build. The v1.3.0 source tag also contains that flag despite the tested wheel including DC, so we report observed binary features rather than infer build history from tags.

During the **original failing UCX initialization window**, kernel counters rose by **10,496 compaction attempts, 10,492 failures, 3,407 THP fallbacks, and 3,668 direct-reclaim stalls**. They were flat just before UCX started. The examined SGLang NIXL startup and host-pool files are byte-identical between the downstream and upstream revisions.

This supports a host-memory compact

### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

### MOTIVATION.

[PR #26468](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/26468) moved vLLM config hashing toward an opt-out model so new compilation-relevant config fields are less likely to be accidentally omitted from torch.compile cache keys. 

This issue tracks the follow-ups and to-dos.

## TODOs
1. Refactor all locations of `compute_hash` to `compile_factors`.  `compute_hash` isn’t the right name because real computation of the hash is actually done by `utils.hash_factors`.
2. before calling `normalize value` in `get_compile_factors`, it needs to check if .compile_factors exists on the subobject. This allows us to avoid handling `PassConfig` specially as in the case for compilation.py 
4. Uniform use of `normalize_value` & `hash_factors` across configs with a compute_hash function.
5. address this comment: [comment here](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/26468#discussion_r2545031784)
6. Create a shared helper instead of inlining both `_compute_code_hash` and `compilation_config_hash_factors`
7. Refactor all locations of `compute_hash` to `compile_factors`
8. Follow up on docstrings not being up-to date in the opt-out configs
9. typing cleanups (e.g., return {} where configs don’t affect graphs; use Path for traced files; consistent DP hash validation.

always print hashed configs into cache_key_factors.json

items.title: [RFC]: Streaming Derender for Disaggregated Serving
items.author: hickeyma
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation.

The batch derender endpoints (`/v1/chat/completions/derender`, `/v1/completions/derender`) landed in #43606 (detokenization) and #45919 (non-streaming reasoning/tool parsing). They consume `GenerateResponse` and emit a complete `ChatCompletionResponse`.

Many real world disaggregated consumers cannot use a batch only post processing tier:

- **Interactive serving** (llm-d, Dynamo) returns tokens to end clients as they are generated. Streaming is a **hard gating requirement** (ref: @bbrowning in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/42729#issuecomment-4631310758).
- The producer side already streams e2e. `/inference/v1/generate` returns an SSE `StreamingResponse` when `request.stream` is set (`scale_out/token_in_token_out/api_router.py`), emitting `GenerateStreamResponse` chunks whose `GenerateResponseStreamChoice` carries the delta token IDs per step (`scale_out/token_in_token_out/serving.py`). `/render` already forwards `stream` / `stream_options`. **It therefore needs to be implemented on the  derender side.**

This RFC specifies a streaming derender that is the inverse of the streaming render path.

Partial:
- #34407
- #22817

Companion to:
- #42729

#### Why is this not a flag on the derender batch endpoint?

1. **Different input type.** The batch path (#42729) consumes a complete `GenerateResponse`. Streaming consumes `GenerateStreamResponse` *deltas*. It is therefore a distinct request shape and not a parameter on the existing endpoint.
2. **Incremental detokenization is stateful.** `IncrementalDetokenizer` carries `prefix_offset` / `read_offset` / prior tokens across `update()` calls. A naive per chunk `tokenizer.decode()` produces wrong spacing and can split multi-byte characters (see #44620). The per step delta `token_ids` are the right incremental input. `GenerateStreamResponse` however does **not** carry the detokenizer offsets and that state has to come from somewhere.
3. **Streaming parsers are stateful too.** Reasoning/tool parsers maintain incremental parse state across deltas (the reasoning to content/tool transition, partial tool call JSON). This compounds the state transport question below.

### Proposed Change.

#### New endpoints

| Method | Path | Input | Output |
|--------|------|-------|--------|
| `POST` | `/v1/chat/completions/derender` (`stream: true`) | `DerenderChatStreamRequest` | JSON `{ "chunk": ChatCompletionStreamResponse, "stream_state": DerenderStreamState }` |
| `POST` | `/v1/completions/derender` (`stream: true`) | `DerenderCompletionStreamRequest` | JSON `{ "chunk": CompletionStreamResponse, "stream_state": DerenderStreamState }` |

> [!NOTE]
> Streaming reuses the same `derender/` path with a `stream: true` flag, mirroring the producer (`/inference/v1/generate`). FastAPI validates a typed union discriminated on the `stream` literal and the handler dispatches with `isinstance`. The existing non-streaming types keep `generate_response` required.

Both endpoints run on the existing render server (GPU-free, only the `Renderer`/tokenizer) and are **stateless**.

#### Response format: plain JSON per call, not SSE

The derender is a **stateless per chunk translator**: one request in to one `{ "chunk", "stream_state" }` out. SSE out was rejected because it requires either a long lived connection or buffering all chunks before calling derender. This both conflict with the stateless design (Option A). The SSE protocol lives on the generate side and the final usage chunk are the client's responsibility.

#### Core design decision: incremental state (Option A, stateless)

The server returns updated state in each chunk. The client echoes it back on the next chunk. Server stays stateless and idempotent. There is no `request_id` keyed session and no lifecycle/eviction on the render tier.

Other design decision considered:

- **Option B (server-side session keyed by `request_id`)**: rejected because it breaks statelessness and adds session lifecycle + eviction + memory pressure.
- **Option C (shm state transport)**: deferred as a future optimization for large round tripped state on long generations. Only consider after Option A's payload cost is measured.

#### Parser state: replay (no opaque serialization)

Tool parsers hold internals we can't cheaply round trip (`prev_tool_call_arr`, `current_tool_id`, `streamed_args_for_tool`, engine lexer buffers). Rather than serialize them, the streaming chat derender **rebuilds a fresh parser each chunk by replaying the output tokens through it**, then feeds the new chunk and emits whatever the parser hands back.

Replay keeps the producer's chunk boundaries. `stream_state` carries `output_chunk_lens` (the token count of each chunk as it arrived) next to `output_token_ids`. Every chunk, replayed or live, goes through one `parse_delta` call. That matches standard serving which calls `parse_delta` once per engine step, so a multi-token step (e.g. speculative decoding) rebuilds the same parser state. Per token replay could diverge because some parser state (e.g. `history_tool_call_cnt`) advances once per `parse_delta` call. Text comes from a throwaway incremental detokenizer with `skip_special_tokens=False`, so the parser sees `</think>` / `<tool_call>` markers exactly as generate emits them.

Here are a few things to be aware of:

- **Cost:** transport is O(n) per chunk → O(n²) over a generation. Replay is one `parse_delta` call per prior chunk → O(n²) calls over a generation. `parse_delta` is itself O(n) for parsers that re-scan the accumulated text (Hermes tool call JSON, DeepSeek-R1 reasoning), so compute is O(n³) character work. `prompt_token_ids` is also sent and re-scanned on every chunk, so on long prompts it dominates the payload. Prompt + history + delta is bounded by `max_model_len` and rejected past it. Replay runs off the event loop on the renderer's executor (`renderer_num_workers`, default `1`), so size it for concurrent parser configured streams. Documented in `derenderer.md`.
- **Measured

comments.author: hickeyma
comments.body:
#50550 has merged, so streaming chat derender now does reasoning and tool call parsing. Thanks @sagearc, @chaunceyjiang, @NickLucche  and @bongwoobak for the reviews.

### What landed in #50550

- Replay through `parse_delta` on a fresh parser each chunk. It emits the same `reasoning` / `content` / `tool_calls` deltas that `/v1/chat/completions` streams for the same tokens.
- Replay keeps the producer's chunk boundaries. `DerenderStreamState` now carries `output_chunk_lens` alongside `output_token_ids`, so a multi-token step (e.g. spec decode) goes through one `parse_delta` call on replay, just like in serving. 
- `prompt_token_ids` on the request, so the parser knows whether the prompt left reasoning open.
- Tool call ID pinning, the `finish_reason` rewrite to `tool_calls` and parallel tool call filtering.
- Fail closed 400s for:
  - a parser configured without `chat_request` (the batch path now checks this too)
  - missing `prompt_token_ids`
  - more than one choice per chunk
  - prompt + history + delta over `max_model_len`
- `model_config` passed to the batch parser, so it knows the model's `tool_call_id_type`. Batch derender still discards the parser's tool call ID, though. That's tracked under #42729.
- A "Streaming cost" section in `derenderer.md`.

### The replay cost has been measured

@shimib benchmarked the derender tier with #50550 applied (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/56851#issuecomment-5685698033), on 1×A100-40G with Qwen3-8B and the hermes + qwen3 parsers. At matched load, detokenizing and parsing on the derender tier cost ~9× the in-process CPU. E2E p50 rose 15% on multi-thousand-token reasoning outputs. With the default `renderer_num_workers=1`, the tier also saturated under concurrent parsed streams until the pool was made bigger.

This RFC deferred a parser cache and parser state serialization "until the cost is shown to matter". For latency sensitive interactive traffic, it matters. Rather than add server side state to the render tier, I propose:

- **Latency sensitive P/D (llm-d):** #56851. Detokenization and parsing move onto the decode pool per request and the parser lives as long as the request does. There's no replay, no echoed state and no extra hop per chunk.
- **Stateless consumers (RL, batch, gateways that own postprocessing):** streaming derender as it is. An LRU of live parsers keyed by `(request_id, choice_index)` stays an optional optimization with no protocol change (#57571).
- Serializing parser state was tied to #32713 which was closed as not planned. I'm therefore  dropping it for now.

### Remaining to close this RFC

- [x] **PR3: streaming parity CI.** Extend `test_derender_parity.py` to the chunked path (plain, reasoning, tool, reasoning + tool) including a multi-token chunk and a finish only final chunk.
- [x] **PR3: docs.** A streaming example, the client loop contract and the `stream: true` symmetry with `/inference/v1/generate`. The client loop contract covers echoing `stream_state`, one choice per chunk, `n > 1` as N streams and the client sending the final usage chunk.
- [ ] **Streaming logprobs.** #55029 (@shimib) covers the plain path. It does conflict and needs a rebase onto #50550 and the parsed path needs the same treatment, including dropping logprobs when reasoning is hidden, as batch does. I'd like to bring this into scope instead of leaving it as a known limitation. Batch already has logprobs and the parity plan in #56851 depends on them.
- [x] **Plain path off the event loop.** #57528 (fixes #57350) moves `_detokenize_delta` onto the renderer executor, so raising `renderer_num_workers` actually helps the plain streaming path.
- [x] **Tracking issues for deferred work:** the parser cache / server side state (#57571), including tool call ID stability across retried calls. Shared per choice `ChatStreamProcessor` used by both chat serving and derender (#57572). Integer token IDs for logprobs in `/inference/v1/generate` responses (`GenerateLogProbs`) (#57574)

comments.body:
Parser path logprobs. #55029 covers the plain path, and the remaining list just says "then the parsed path". Will the parsed path be a separate PR? I couldn't find an issue for it.

Streaming stop strings. #42729 tracks this as #57052 bug A, and the two fixes listed there — #47313's `stop_reason`, or a derender-side stop string pass — both assume you already have the whole text. Streaming doesn't: `stop_reason` only arrives on the final chunk, and by then a prefix of the stop string may already have been emitted. So it seems to need the hold-back buffer the coupled path has, and since derender is stateless that buffer would have to ride in `DerenderStreamState`. That would be a protocol change. What do you think?

comments.author: hickeyma
comments.body:
@hyeongyun0916 on (a), who owns parsed-path logprobs? I think we need to settle which code produces the token strings before anyone writes that path. Right now there are three candidates and they already disagree. #59241 is one case where derender drops the SentencePiece leading space that the engine restores.

My proposal is the same rule we're using for text. The engine is the reference.
  
- `output_mode=text / derender`: use the engine's `Logprob.decoded_token as-is` and don't re-resolve.
- Standalone /derender, including the parsed path: one shared resolver built on `convert_ids_list_to_tokens `plus a shared `_correct_decoded_token`, with parity tests against the engine.

If that works for you and others, I'll open a separate issue for parsed path logprobs, blocked on this. Any per chunk cursor it needs would go into `DerenderStreamState` but I'd like to agree on how that state evolves before adding fields to it.

On (b), agreed that streaming stop strings need a hold-back. I'd rather not build it into derender yet, though. Stop strings only matter when the engine has a tokenizer (#57058 already rejects `stop` on `--tokens-only`), so the engine can apply them itself through `output_mode` (#56851) with the hold-back it already has. For now I'd have streaming `/derender` reject `stop` and point people at `output_mode=text`. If a tokens-only consumer turns up that really needs it, the pending text can be one more optional `DerenderStreamState`  field.

Let me know what you think.

I can't reproduce this on stock v0.21.0, and after tracing the whole streaming path I don't think stock code can produce this exact signature. Writing up what I found.

**What the glyphs are**

`Ċ`, `åĹ¯`, `ï¼Į` are exactly what `tokenizer.convert_ids_to_tokens()` returns for those token ids (verified with a DeepSeek-R1 family tokenizer: 198 -> `Ċ`, 106287 -> `åĹ¯`, 3837 -> `ï¼Į`). So the reasoning stream is raw token strings that never went through the byte-level decode step.

**Why stock v0.21.0 shouldn't be able to emit that**

The streaming chain with `--reasoning-parser deepseek_r1` is:

1. The engine detokenizer produces `output.text` (already byte-decoded, incremental).
2. serving_chat sets `delta_text = output.text` and feeds it to the unified parser that `ParserManager.get_parser(reasoning_parser_name="deepseek_r1")` builds, which delegates to `DeepSeekR1ReasoningParser`.
3. That parser only slices `delta_text` around the `</think>` boundary. I audited every branch of `basic_parsers.py` and `deepseek_r1_reasoning_parser.py`: each return value is a substring of `delta_text`. There is no `convert_ids_to_tokens` anywhere in `vllm/entrypoints`, `vllm/parser`, or `vllm/reasoning` (the only hit is the unrelated `/tokenize` endpoint).

Your control experiments are the tell. Without the parser, the same `output.text` arrives as clean content, and non-streaming is clean too. So your detokenizer output is clean. The parser can only cut up what it receives; slicing clean text cannot turn one field back into raw token strings while the other stays clean. Something in your deployment is replacing the reasoning path with a token-string implementation between the detokenizer and the wire.

In-process simulation of the exact serving chain (real tokenizer, CJK reasoning stream, token-at-a-time detokenization, then the same `_WrappedParser.parse_delta` the server uses):

One related landmine worth knowing about for this exact checkpoint: `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-0528-Qwen3-8B` declares `tokenizer_class: LlamaTokenizerFast` on the Hub while shipping a byte-level BPE `tokenizer.json`. items.title: [Bug] lmcache CLI crashes on every subcommand without openai: bench engine imports it at parser registration
items.author: aeon-x
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

After a plain `pip install lmcache`, **every** `lmcache` CLI subcommand crashes at startup, including `lmcache server` and `lmcache --help`:

```
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'openai'
```

Root cause:

1. `lmcache/cli/main.py` registers every subcommand's argparse parser at startup, regardless of which subcommand is run.
2. Registering `bench engine` calls `EngineBenchCommand.add_arguments()`, which imports `engine_bench/command.py` → `engine_bench/config.py`, and `config.py:14` does a top-level `from openai import OpenAI`.
3. `openai` is not a dependency of the `lmcache` wheel. It is only listed in `requirements/cli.txt`, which is consumed by the separate `lmcache-cli` distribution (`pyproject_cli.toml`). The main `pyproject.toml` still installs the same `lmcache = "lmcache.cli.main:main"` console script, without those dependencies, and no `lmcache[cli]` extra exists (the only extras are `kafka` and `nixl`).

So the `lmcache` wheel ships an entry point that cannot start. It is masked in the `vllm-openai` images and in any environment where vLLM is installed, because vLLM itself depends on `openai`.

**To Reproduce**

```bash
python -m venv v && . v/bin/activate
pip install lmcache torch   # no vllm, no lmcache-cli
lmcache --help              # ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'openai'
lmcache server --help       # same
```

Reproduced on current `dev` (found while testing #5400's wheels in a clean venv): `lmcache --help`, `lmcache server --help`, `lmcache describe --help` all fail identically.

**Expected behavior**

`lmcache server` (and every subcommand that does not need it) works without `openai`. Only `lmcache bench engine` should require it, with a clear message.

**Possible fixes** (any one)

- Lazy-import `openai` inside the engine-bench code path that uses it (e.g. move `from openai import OpenAI` into the function that builds the client), so registration doesn't import it. Smallest change; other optional CLI imports may need the same treatment.
- Add `requirements/cli.txt` as a `cli` extra of the main package, and have `bench engine` raise a clear "pip install lmcache[cli]" error.
- Drop the `lmcache` console script from the main package if the CLI is meant to ship only via `lmcache-cli`. Note `lmcache server` is the documented way to start the MP server, so this probably isn't desirable.

items.title: llama-quantize: GGML_ASSERT(size mismatch) when quantizing mmproj files containing 3D conv tensors (gemma4v audio conv1d)
items.author: mrBenBern
items.body_excerpt:
Quantizing the gemma-4-E2B combined mmproj (vision+audio, gemma4v/gemma4a projectors) from F16 to Q8_0 aborts with:

  llama-quant.cpp:1365: GGML_ASSERT(gguf_get_tensor_size(...) == new_size) failed

Repro:
  llama-quantize --allow-requantize mmproj-F16.gguf out.gguf Q8_0

Fails at tensor `a.conv1d.0.weight` — shape [3,3,1,128] (3D conv1d from the audio encoder). The f32→f16 conversion changes the tensor size, and the split-output writer asserts on the mismatch. Every subsequent 3D tensor fails the same way (a.conv1d.1.weight [3,3,128,32], ...).

Workaround (verified): keep 3D tensors in f32 via tensor-type overrides —
  llama-quantize --allow-requantize \
    --tensor-type "a.conv1d.0.weight=f32" \
    --tensor-type "a.conv1d.1.weight=f32" \
    mmproj-F16.gguf mmproj-F16-q8_0.gguf Q8_0

This works and the resulting Q8_0 mmproj is functionally correct on-device (Android, llama.cpp 4ebdf2c): vision outputs verified same-in-quality as F16 (sign-text reading), encode on a Helio G99 CPU improved 6.4x vs BF16 (37s -> 5.8s for a 91-token image).

Expected behavior: either skip/conversion-preserving handling for N-D tensors whose element count doesn't allow requantization, or a clean error message listing the offending tensors instead of an assert.

items.title: [Bug]: vllm.utils.system_utils.suppress_stdout silently suppresses stderr when sys.stdout is bound to fd 2
items.author: the-Shallow
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment
The output of python collect_env.py ```text OS: Debian GNU/Linux 13.7 (trixie), x86_64, running under WSL2 Kernel: Linux 6.6.87.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2 glibc: 2.41 Python: 3.12.14 NumPy: 2.5.3 PyTorch: 2.13.0+cpu CUDA available: No vLLM package: Not installed; validation executed relevant code extracted from the vLLM v0.30.0 tag ```
### 🐛 Describe the bug Summary The docstring states "Only suppresses stdout, not stderr, to preserve error messages", but the implementation redirects whatever fd `sys.stdout` happens to point at. Under the common `sys.stdout = sys.stderr` idiom, that fd is 2, so `suppress_stdout()` sends **stderr** to `/dev/null` — silently discarding error messages and tracebacks emitted by C libraries during `torch.distributed` group creation. Reproducing the Bug Run as `python repro.py 2> err.txt`; `err.txt` is empty. ```python import os import sys from vllm.utils.system_utils import suppress_stdout sys.stdout = sys.stderr with suppress_stdout(): os.write(2, b"CRITICAL ERROR MESSAGE\n") sys.stdout = sys.__stdout__ ``` ## Fix Target `STDOUT_FILENO` explicitly, so stderr is never a candidate. ```diff --- a/vllm/utils/system_utils.py +++ b/vllm/utils/system_utils.py @@ -76,7 +76,9 @@ def suppress_stdout(): if envs.VLLM_LOGGING_LEVEL == "DEBUG": yield return - stdout_fd = sys.stdout.fileno() + # C libraries write to STDOUT_FILENO regardless of what `sys.stdout` is + # bound to; deriving the fd from `sys.stdout` can wrongly target stderr. + stdout_fd = 1 stdout_dup = os.dup(stdout_fd) devnull_fd = os.open(os.devnull, os.O_WRONLY) ``` ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [RFC]: CPU backend support for the vLLM connector + Mooncake Store L2 for multi-instance CPU serving
items.author: amd-lalithnc
items.body_excerpt:
## 1. Summary

This RFC proposes upstreaming two related contributions that enable **LMCache on the vLLM CPU backend** and make **cross-instance KV reuse** work for CPU serving:

1. **A CPU GPU-connector** (`VLLMCPUConnector`): a pure-torch gather/scatter path between vLLM's paged CPU KV cache and an LMCache `MemoryObj`, handling vLLM's 4D fused K/V CPU layout. This is the missing piece that lets LMCache run at all on `device=cpu`.
2. **Fixes to the Mooncake Store L2 connector** so it works on the CPU backend and shares KV **across instances** (fork-safe per-process client init, a correct `exists()`/lookup path, and a config-key alias).

Together these let multiple vLLM CPU instances behind a load balancer share one KV cache (SHM on a single box, or Mooncake Store over TCP across a cluster), instead of each instance recomputing the same prefixes.

Note that the CPU connector (contribution 1) is **backend-agnostic**: it is the shared foundation that unlocks the *entire* LMCache backend ecosystem on CPU (local DRAM L1, the shared SHM server, pickle, and remote L2s). Contribution 2 is one representative distributed L2 (Mooncake). We enable and validate **both** the default (SHM) and Mooncake paths because they target different deployment scopes (see §3.4).

We propose **two stacked PRs** (CPU connector, then Mooncake-on-CPU) plus this RFC to tie them together.

## 2. Motivation

- **CPU inference is growing** (cost, availability, disaggregated/CPU-tier deployments), and vLLM has a maturing CPU backend.
- **Multi-instance CPU serving needs *shared* KV.** vLLM's Automatic Prefix Caching (APC) is **per-instance**: behind a load balancer, instance B cannot reuse instance A's prefix KV, so shared system prompts / few-shot / documents are recomputed on every instance.
- **LMCache already solves cross-instance reuse**, but had **no CPU connector**, so it could not run on vLLM CPU at all; and the **Mooncake Store L2** path did not work on CPU or across instances (fork-safety + lookup bugs).
- **Measured impact** (Section 5): on a single-socket AMD EPYC, an external shared KV cache gives **+27-31% aggregate throughput at 3 instances** and **-28%/-34% p95/p99 tail latency** vs APC.

## 3. Design

### 3.1 Topology

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    LB[NGINX load balancer] --> V1[vLLM CPU inst 1]
    LB --> V2[vLLM CPU inst 2]
    LB --> V3[vLLM CPU inst 3]
    V1 <-->|store / load KV| L[(LMCache)]
    V2 <-->|store / load KV| L
    V3 <-->|store / load KV| L
    L <-->|put / get| S{{Shared KV: SHM  or  Mooncake Store L2 / TCP}}
```

### 3.2 CPU connector (`VLLMCPUConnector`)

**Why a CPU connector is needed.** Every existing GPU connector relies on CUDA custom ops (`c_ops`) and CUDA streams and assumes the GPU KV memory layout. None of that exists on CPU, so LMCache previously could not run on vLLM's CPU backend at all. `VLLMCPUConnector` fills that gap.

**What it implements.** The same connector interface, using **plain PyTorch tensor operations** (indexing + copy) with no CUDA kernels or streams:

- `from_gpu(...)` (**STORE / gather**): copy the KV for tokens `[start, end)` out of vLLM's paged CPU buffer into a contiguous `MemoryObj`.
- `to_gpu(...)` (**LOAD / scatter**): copy KV from a `MemoryObj` back into vLLM's paged buffer, placing each token's K/V into the slot given by vLLM's slot mapping.
- `batched_from_gpu(...)` / `batched_to_gpu(...)`: batched variants that handle several token ranges in one call.

**Handling vLLM's CPU KV layout.** vLLM's CPU backend stores each layer's cache as a single **4D fused K/V tensor** (K and V packed together), which is laid out differently from the GPU cache. For each layer the connector derives logical views shaped `[num_blocks, block_size, num_heads, head_size]` for K and for V (`_kv_token_views`), then uses the request's block/slot offsets to move exactly the right rows. This keeps gather/scatter correct without copying the whole buffer.

**Selection.** The connector is picked automatically when the device is CPU (`torch_device_type == "cpu"` in `CreateGPUConnector`), so no user config change is required.

**Plugging in as a `GPUConnectorInterface`.** So the CPU connector can subclass `GPUConnectorInterface` without importing the CUDA-heavy `gpu_connectors`/`utils` modules (which import `c_ops`, absent in NO_GPU_EXT builds), the interface ABC is extracted into a small `c_ops`-free `interface.py` that `gpu_connectors.py` re-exports. Existing GPU connectors are unaffected.

### 3.3 Mooncake Store L2 on CPU

The Mooncake client (Go runtime + multithreaded C++) is **not fork-safe**, and vLLM forks its scheduler/worker processes. Fixes:

- **Fork-safe, lazy per-process init**: the store/lookup client is created inside each process on first use (`_ensure_store()`), never inherited across a fork.
- **Correct lookup path**: `exists()`/`exists_sync()` now call `_ensure_store()` first (the contains/lookup path can run before any put/get on an instance) and compare `is_exist() == 1` (it returns `1/0/-1`) so an error never reads as a cache hit. Without this, cross-instance lookups were swallowed as misses and the instance recomputed.
- **Config-key alias**: accept `master_server_address` as an alias for `master_server_addr` in dict-based setup.

**Cross-instance key consistency (usage requirement, not connector code):** for a prefix computed on instance A to be found by instance B, the KV keys must hash identically across processes. Python's default randomized hashing breaks this; deployments must use a stable algorithm (e.g. `LMCACHE_PRE_CACHING_HASH_ALGORITHM=sha256` with `PYTHONHASHSEED=0`). This will be documented.

### 3.4 Why enable both paths (default SHM and Mooncake L2)

The CPU connector is transport/backend-agnostic, so a natural question is *why validate two L2 paths instead of one*. Because they are **complementary, not competing**: the right choice is dictated by deployment topology, and we want CPU users to be able to pick either without changing the connecto

items.title: [RFC] Consolidate O_DIRECT handling: nine independent implementations, none of which handles a filesystem refusing the flag
items.author: xiangping-chen
items.body_excerpt:
**Label**

`RFC`, `Refactoring`, `backend`, `mp_mode` — also touches `nixl`, `localdisk`, `gds`, `fs_connector`.

---

## Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

O_DIRECT gating is reimplemented independently in **nine** places, and no two agree on behaviour. Verified against `upstream/dev`:

| # | Site | Mode |
|---|------|------|
| 1 | `lmcache/v1/storage_backend/local_disk_backend.py` | in-process |
| 2 | `lmcache/v1/storage_backend/connector/fs_connector.py` | in-process |
| 3 | `lmcache/v1/storage_backend/nixl_storage_backend.py` (static pool + dynamic = 2 copies) | in-process |
| 4 | `lmcache/v1/storage_backend/raw_block/core.py` + `rust/raw_block/src/lib.rs` | shared |
| 5 | `lmcache/v1/gpu_connector/gds_context.py` | shared (GDS L1) |
| 6 | `lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/fs_l2_adapter.py` | **MP** |
| 7 | `lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/nixl_store_l2_adapter.py` | **MP** |
| 8 | `lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/nixl_store_dynamic_l2_adapter.py` | **MP** |
| 9 | `csrc/storage_backends/fs/connector.cpp` (drives MP `fs_native`) | **MP** |

### 1. No site handles a filesystem that refuses O_DIRECT

Every site detects support by asking the **platform** — `hasattr(os, "O_DIRECT")`, `getattr(os, "O_DIRECT", 0)`, or `#ifdef O_DIRECT` — then opens without classifying the errno. Across all nine files:

```
grep -c 'errno\.(EINVAL|EOPNOTSUPP|ENOTSUP|EPERM)'   ->   0   in every one
```

The platform check answers a different question from the one that matters. `open()` may refuse the flag with `EINVAL` (documented), a filesystem may report `EOPNOTSUPP`/`ENOTSUP`, and `EPERM` is possible under policy. Because none of that is classified, the failure modes are inconsistent and none is a fallback:

- **`nixl_store_l2_adapter`** — the `OSError` escapes pool construction and the **MP server fails to start**, immediately after logging *"Falling back to buffered I/O"*, which did not happen:

```python
# nixl_store_l2_adapter.py — upstream/dev
if use_direct_io:
    if hasattr(os, "O_DIRECT"):
        flags |= os.O_DIRECT
    else:
        logger.warning(
            "use_direct_io is True, but O_DIRECT is not available on "
            "this system. Falling back to buffered I/O."
        )
for i in range(num_files):
    ...
    fd = os.open(tmp_path, flags)     # unguarded, and no try/finally
    fds.append(fd)
```

- **`fs_l2_adapter`** — swallowed by a blanket `except Exception`; the read helper returns `0`, the write helper re-raises. Net effect: **every load misses and every store fails, permanently, while `report_status` keeps reporting `is_healthy: True`.** A 0%-hit L2 tier that reports itself healthy is a worse outcome than a crash.
- **`fs_native`** (C++) — `throw std::runtime_error`.
- **`raw_block`** — fails fast at init, which is at least honest.

### 2. Alignment is checked inconsistently, and mostly incompletely

O_DIRECT requires the **offset**, the **length**, *and* the **buffer address** to be aligned. Most sites check only length:

```python
# fs_l2_adapter.py:549 and :624 — length only; the address is never inspected
aligned = self._os_disk_bs > 0 and size % self._os_disk_bs == 0
```

`raw_block` is the one implementation that gets this right: `_is_buffer_aligned()` (`core.py:1001`) plus `posix_memalign` bounce buffers in Rust (6 call sites).

The assumption elsewhere is not safe. `torch.empty(..., pin_memory=True)` does **not** guarantee page alignment — torch's caching pinned allocator sub-allocates, so once it has served an unaligned-sized request later pointers come back offset. Measured offsets of 2048 and 2560 bytes against a 4096 requirement. In `GdsBackend` this caused O_DIRECT to silently degrade to buffered I/O depending on nothing but allocation history, and it was only caught because a test began failing when reordered.

Granularity is also inconsistent: most sites use `statvfs.f_bsize` (the filesystem's *preferred* block size), `raw_block` uses a config value defaulting to 4096, and the real requirement is the device **logical block size** — 512 on hardware where `f_bsize` reported 4096. Too large needlessly disables O_DIRECT; too small yields `EINVAL`.

### 3. Short transfers are unhandled or mishandled

Under O_DIRECT a partial transfer is necessarily a multiple of the logical block size, so a retry *can* be aligned — but only if the code computes it that way. Several sites retry at `buf[total:]` with no alignment consideration, and `fs_l2_adapter`'s write path issues `os.write(fd, buf)` and **discards the return value**, so a short write silently publishes a truncated file via `os.replace` and reports success.

## Describe the solution you'd like

A small, dependency-free `direct_io` module owning the O_DIRECT decision, adopted at the Python sites.

```python
_DIRECT_IO_UNSUPPORTED_ERRNOS = frozenset(
    {errno.EINVAL, errno.EOPNOTSUPP, errno.ENOTSUP, errno.EPERM}
)


class DirectIOPolicy:
    # Decides whether a transfer may use O_DIRECT, and degrades safely.
    # One instance per (path, alignment) domain. Thread-safe; the support flag
    # is a one-way latch.

    def __init__(self, path: str, requested: bool, align_bytes: int | None = None): ...

    @property
    def align_bytes(self) -> int:
        # From the device logical block size where determinable, else statvfs
        # f_bsize, else 4096.
        ...

    def aligned(self, *, offset: int, length: int, address: int) -> bool:
        # True when all three O_DIRECT constraints hold. Warns once when not.
        ...

    def open(self, path: str, flags: int, mode: int = 0o644) -> tuple[int, bool]:
        # Open, adding O_DIRECT when requested, supported and not latched off.
        # Returns (fd, is_direct). A refusal carrying one of the unsupported
        # errnos latches O_DIRECT off for this policy and retries buffered; any
        # other OSError propagates.
        ...

    def aligned_buffer(self, nbytes: int) -> memoryview:
        # Address-aligned buffer for

items.title: [MP][engine_driven] ~0.55s fixed cost per transfer object on retrieve swamps wire time on PCIe hosts (pickle transport)
items.author: kaka86mm
items.body_excerpt:
## Environment
- PR #4410 head `2a79594` (hybrid multi-group engine-driven), CPU-only MP server `--supported-transfer-mode engine_driven`, transport = pickle (`Using pickle non-GPU transfer strategy`)
- 4× CMP 170HX (sm80, GPUs on PCIe 2.0 x4 host links, no P2P), vLLM 0.13.0 fork, PP=4
- MiMo-V2.6-Flash: 1 full-attention group + 5 sliding-window groups

## Measurement
Retrieval of a 69,376-token prefix across a restart (server untouched, engine restarted) shows a per-transfer-object fixed cost of ~0.55 s that dominates the wire time (~1.6 s total):

| server `--chunk-size` | transfer objects | retrieve TTFT | wire time (server log) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 256 (default) | 68 | 37.8 s | 1.6 s |
| 4096 | 17 | 9.8 s | 1.17 s |
| 8192 | 9 | 8.8 s | 0.28 s |

Plain local recompute of the same prefix is 26-30 s, so large chunks make the connector a ~3× win — but ~0.55 s of *fixed* cost per object means small-object workloads (many short prefixes, or default chunking) still lose to recompute on slow interconnects.

## Profile (with caveats)
py-spy `record -d 25 -r 50` on one PP worker during the retrieval phase. Caveat: py-spy samples **active threads only**, so this is a CPU-time profile, not wall-clock attribution — it can show where CPU went, not what blocked the main thread.

- MainThread (execute loop): essentially **absent** from CPU samples — blocked the whole time (separate stack dumps show it in `recv` / `shm_broadcast.acquire_read`)
- `_report_usage_worker` telemetry thread: burns a full core throughout retrieval (co-observation; not claiming causality)
- pickle-side work (`prepare_retrieve_multigroup_pickle`, `_load_from_bytes`, `msgspec_decode`): ~6-10% of CPU samples

So the wall-clock gap is not CPU-bound work in the worker; we suspect per-object round-trip/pacing in the transport.

## Questions
1. The server exposes `--shm-name` / pool size (`ShmTransferStrategy` with pickle fallback). Is the per-object cost expected to disappear under SHM (no serialize/TCP/unpickle per object)? We plan to A/B it in the next maintenance window and will report back.
2. The C++ transfer op records phase timings (`phase_timing_enabled` ← `is_observability_enabled()`, `pop_completed_phase_timings`). On the CPU-only server the `/metrics` endpoint only exposes lookup/lifecycle series — what is the supported way to export **engine-side** transfer-phase timings so the 0.55 s can be decomposed exactly?

Happy to share the raw flame data or a repro script (ffmpeg-free synthetic prompts against any checkpoint) if useful.
