items.title: EAGLE/MTP prefix-cache last-block drop causes a 1,648-token recompute per hit on one hybrid Qwen3.8 GDN layout — ~30-40% batch throughput loss on prefix-reusing workloads with speculative decoding
items.author: Suppressor72
items.body_excerpt:
EAGLE/MTP prefix-cache last-block drop causes a 1,648-token recompute per
hit on one hybrid Qwen3.8 GDN layout — ~30-40% batch throughput loss on
prefix-reusing workloads with speculative decoding enabled

## Environment

- vLLM `0.26.1rc1.dev926+gb05ae5dc0`, V1/V2 model runner, async scheduling
- Dual RTX 5090 TP=2, FP8 weights + FP8 KV, prefix caching on
- Model: Qwen3.8-27B (hybrid: GDN/Mamba layers + full attention → 15
  MambaSpec KV groups + full-attention group; scheduler/hash block = 1648
  tokens); other hybrid layouts should be evaluated by their own scheduler
  alignment
- Speculative: dflash (DFlash2, K=7) and mtp — both reproduce; also
  reproduces with an always-K=0 tiered config `[[1,16,0]]` +
  `skip_draft_when_k0: true` (drafter provably never runs at c ≥ 3; without
  `skip_draft_when_k0`, K=0 draft-state sync may still run)

## Summary

With any EAGLE-family `speculative_config` set, multi-round / repeated-prompt
workloads lose ~6-10 points of prefix-cache hit rate versus an identical
no-spec boot (97.5% → 86.9-91.7% in our harness). The cause is the EAGLE
last-block drop (`drop_eagle_block`) in the prefix-cache hit path:

1. `kv_cache_coordinator.py` flags **all** KV groups as eagle when the model
   has no `is_eagle_group` annotation (conservative fallback).
2. The EAGLE-marked dense/full-attention group drops one alignment unit from
   its hit (protecting against (a) draft-layer KV for the last block depending
   on the writer's continuation and (b) prefill-lookahead pollution at chunk
   boundaries); hybrid reconciliation then limits the combined hit to that
   shorter boundary, so the request recomputes one 1,648-token scheduler-
   aligned unit.
3. On dense-attention models that alignment unit is a 16-token block. On this
   hybrid GDN/Mamba layout it is **1,648 tokens**. The same protection
   therefore costs ~100× more cache hit here; other hybrid layouts should be
   evaluated by their own scheduler alignment.

Measured per-request-per-round (32k identical prompt re-sent, cache trace of
`get_computed_blocks`):

| Config | warm lookup hit | tail recompute | c=8 tok/s (vs no-spec 327) |
|---|---|---|---|
| no speculative_config | 31360 (20×1568) | 640 tok | 327 |
| dflash K=7 + tiers | 29664 (18×1648) | 2336 tok | 206 (−37%) |
| dflash + drop disabled (ablation) | 31312 (19×1648) | 688 tok | 322 (−1.6%) |

Disabling the drop recovers essentially the entire warm prefix-reuse gap
(+56% at c=8) on this workload — the last-block rule, not spec-decode step
machinery, accounts for it (a separate cold-prefill drafter cost exists on
unique-prompt traffic; see below) (we profiled the
engine loop: per-step decode time is within 0.6% of no-spec at resolved K=0).

The regression is easy to miss: single-request benchmarks with unique prompts
don't reuse prefixes, and aggregate token/s hides where the time goes. Watch
`vllm:prefix_cache_hits_total` and the re-prefill chunk census instead.

## Why the drop is still needed (and why "just disable it" is not the answer)

The drop is load-bearing for consumers that draft: draft-layer KV in the last
matched block depends on tokens past the matched prefix (the writer's
continuation), and chunked prefill with drafting combines a lookahead token
into boundary KV. Serving such a block to a request that will draft from that
boundary gives it stale/foreign draft KV. Speculative decoding stays
lossless (the target verifies every token), so the damage is acceptance
degradation rather than wrong outputs — but for K>0 consumers the recompute
the drop forces is the correct behavior.

The asymmetry is that a consumer running at **resolved K=0** (dynamic
speculation tiers with `skip_draft_when_k0`, or any K=0 tier) never executes
the drafter at all, so it never reads draft-layer KV: the drop protects a
consumer that does not exist. Our proposed fix makes the drop conditional on
exactly that (reference implementation on our fork — over our open-PR limit
on main right now, will open the PR when a slot frees:
https://github.com/Suppressor72/vllm/tree/feat/eagle-k0-consumer-drop @
dfb6eeae79): skip it when the admission's projected
resolved K is 0 under `skip_draft_when_k0`. Result on the same harness:
c=8 206 → 304 tok/s (no-spec 327, hard-disable ceiling 322), prefix-cache hit
rate 91.7% → 95.4%, zero change at c=1/c=2 where K>0 still drafts.

## Repro

Measured on nightly `0.26.1rc1.dev926+gb05ae5dc0` + local patches (DFlash2
backport #52816, `skip_draft_when_k0` #53420/#53426 lineage, dflash tier
validation) — the cache-path code under discussion is upstream code; config:

```json
{"method": "dflash",
 "model": "<DFlash2 drafter for the target>",
 "num_speculative_tokens": 7,
 "num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size": [[1, 2, 7], [3, 16, 0]],
 "skip_draft_when_k0": true}
```

The causal comparison stays within one 1,648-token geometry: stock hit
29,664 (18 blocks) → drop-disabled 31,312 (19 blocks), same boot layout. The
no-spec arm (31,360 at a different 1,568-token layout) is context, not the
proof.


1. Any hybrid-GDN target with dflash/mtp/eagle `speculative_config`,
   `enable_prefix_caching=true`.
2. Client: re-send the same ~32k prompt (chat completions), 4 rounds × 8
   concurrent sessions, 256 tokens each.
3. Compare against the same boot without `speculative_config`:
   aggregate tok/s, `vllm:prefix_cache_hits_total`, and (instrumented)
   `KVCacheManager.get_computed_blocks` hit lengths — hits land exactly on
   block-size multiples and are one block shorter under spec.

## Additional observation (separate, not addressed by the PR)

With fully unique prompts (`--salt auto`: no reuse possible) the spec boot
still runs at ~0.59× no-spec on this target (150.7 vs 255.8 tok/s at c=8,
prefill-dominated legs) — a cold-prefill drafter-context cost that is
inherent to running the drafter, distinct from the cache issue above. We have
not yet decomposed it; happy to file separately if maintainers prefer.


*Measurement and instrumentation for thi

items.title: [Bug] enable_blending with LMCacheConnectorV1 crashes at startup: VLLMModelTracker.register_model is never called
items.author: matu79go
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

Enabling CacheBlend (`enable_blending: true`) with the vLLM V1 connector (`LMCacheConnectorV1`) crashes the engine at startup:

```
ValueError: vllm model for vllm-instance not found.
```

Root cause: `LMCBlenderBuilder.get_or_create()` calls `VLLMModelTracker.get_model(ENGINE_NAME)`, but **nothing in the current tree ever calls `VLLMModelTracker.register_model()`** — grepping the repo shows the only references are in `lmcache/v1/compute/models/utils.py` (definition) and `lmcache/v1/compute/blend/utils.py` (the `get_model` call). The registration call appears to be a leftover from the old `lmcache_vllm` fork era.

## Environment

- LMCache: main @ `668a1fd`, built from source
- vLLM: 0.19.1 (official `vllm/vllm-openai:latest-cu130-ubuntu2404` image, aarch64 / GB10)
- Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, `--enforce-eager --no-enable-prefix-caching`

## Reproduction

```yaml
# lmcache config
chunk_size: 256
local_cpu: true
max_local_cpu_size: 32
enable_blending: true
use_layerwise: true
blend_special_str: " # #"
blend_check_layers: [1]
blend_recompute_ratios: [0.15]
```

```
vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"LMCacheConnectorV1","kv_role":"kv_both"}' ...
```

EngineCore dies during `_initialize_kv_caches` → `LMCacheConnectorV1Impl.__init__` → `LMCBlenderBuilder.get_or_create` → `VLLMModelTracker.get_model` raises.

## Workaround that made blending work for us

A tiny vLLM general plugin that wraps `GPUModelRunner.load_model` and registers the model right after load:

```python
# entry point group "vllm.general_plugins"
def register():
    import importlib
    for mod in ("vllm.v1.worker.gpu_model_runner", "vllm.v1.worker.gpu.model_runner"):
        try:
            cls = importlib.import_module(mod).GPUModelRunner
        except Exception:
            continue
        orig = cls.load_model
        def load_model(self, *a, _orig=orig, **kw):
            out = _orig(self, *a, **kw)
            from lmcache.v1.compute.models.utils import VLLMModelTracker
            VLLMModelTracker.register_model("vllm-instance", self.model)
            return out
        cls.load_model = load_model
```

(Note vLLM 0.19 has two runner modules — the default flat `gpu_model_runner.py` and the V2 `gpu/model_runner.py` — so both need the hook.)

## Additional friction points hit on the same path (worth doc fixes at least)

1. `blend_check_layers` / `blend_recompute_ratios` default to `None`; with blending enabled, `process_qkv` crashes with `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`. Either give working defaults or validate at config load.
2. The default `blend_special_str: " # # "` (trailing space) never matches in-stream tokens for Llama-3 BPE: `encode(" # # ")[1:]` = `[' #', ' #', ' ']`, but in a real prompt the trailing space merges into the next word (`' all'` etc.), so `SegmentTokenDatabase._fast_split_by_subtensor` finds **zero separators** and every lookup misses. Using `" # #"` (no trailing space, `[674, 674]`) works. Also, the *first* document of a prompt tokenizes without a leading space, so its segment hash differs from the same document appearing mid-prompt — prepending a fixed dummy segment (`"docs:" + SEP`) restores position-invariant reuse.
3. Setting `blend_special_str` via env var strips the meaningful leading/trailing whitespace — it only works via `LMCACHE_CONFIG_FILE` yaml.

Happy to turn the workaround into a PR if you can advise where the registration should live properly (connector init? runner wrapper?).

items.title: [RFC][MP] Runtime Management Policy Configuration
items.author: haowu1234
items.body_excerpt:
## 1. Problem

The Q3 roadmap lists **"Configure the management policy (eviction, store, and prefetch policies) during runtime"** under the KV Cache Management Interface (#4025).

Today, MP server management policies are selected mostly at startup:

- L1 eviction policy: `--eviction-policy`
- L1 eviction tunables: `--eviction-trigger-watermark`, `--eviction-ratio`
- L2 adapter eviction config: embedded in each adapter config
- L2 store policy: `--l2-store-policy`
- L2 prefetch policy: `--l2-prefetch-policy`

This is too static for production operation. Operators may need to adjust cache behavior while preserving warm cache state:

- Raise eviction watermarks during a warm-up period.
- Lower watermarks during memory pressure.
- Switch between normal L1 retention and buffer-only L2 store behavior.
- Change prefetch selection behavior after adding or removing L2 adapters.
- Validate a policy update before applying it across a fleet.

This RFC proposes a runtime policy-control surface with an explicit safety boundary: hot-update stateless selectors and safe tunables first, and reject stateful policy migration until policies define migration support.

## 2. Design principle: policy planes

Rather than treating every config field independently, runtime management policy should be split into four planes.

### 2.1 Selector plane

Policies that choose future behavior but do not own durable state.

Examples:

- `store_policy`
- `prefetch_policy`

These are good Phase 1 hot-update targets. A new selector applies to future planning only.

### 2.2 Tunable plane

Numeric or boolean knobs on an existing policy instance.

Examples:

- eviction trigger watermark
- eviction ratio
- optional eviction logging knobs

These are good Phase 1 hot-update targets if the controller reads them from a shared runtime config each loop.

### 2.3 Lifecycle plane

Settings that change the shape of storage resources or data representation.

Examples:

- L1 size
- chunk size
- L2 adapter type
- serde/backend configuration
- object key schema
- memory layout

These are not policy updates. They require restart or an existing adapter reconfiguration path.

### 2.4 State plane

Policies that own internal state whose meaning differs across policy classes.

Examples:

- `LRU`
- `IsolatedLRU`
- `noop`
- future policies such as `S3FIFO`

Changing between these safely requires a state migration contract. This RFC does not propose that for Phase 1.

## 3. Goals

1. Add a node-local MP server API for reading, validating, and updating runtime management policy.
2. Support hot updates for selector-plane and tunable-plane changes.
3. Reject lifecycle-plane and state-plane changes with explicit errors.
4. Define in-flight semantics so updates are predictable.
5. Provide a capability model so future policies can declare what they support.
6. Leave room for coordinator fan-out later without requiring it in the first PR.

## 4. Non-goals

- No runtime changes to L1 capacity, chunk size, object key schema, memory layout, serde, or backend type.
- No hot migration between eviction policy classes in Phase 1.
- No persistence of runtime overrides in Phase 1.
- No new authentication model for MP HTTP management APIs.
- No serving-engine connector protocol changes.

## 5. Capability model

Each policy/controller should expose runtime capabilities instead of forcing the API layer to hard-code every field forever.

Example capability response:

```json
{
  "store_policy": {
    "current": "default",
    "registered": ["default", "skip_l1"],
    "hot_swappable": true,
    "stateful": false,
    "effective_on": "next_store_plan"
  },
  "prefetch_policy": {
    "current": "default",
    "registered": ["default", "retain"],
    "hot_swappable": true,
    "stateful": false,
    "effective_on": "next_prefetch_request"
  },
  "l1_eviction": {
    "policy": "LRU",
    "policy_hot_swappable": false,
    "stateful": true,
    "runtime_tunables": {
      "trigger_watermark": {
        "current": 0.8,
        "minimum": 0.0,
        "maximum": 1.0,
        "effective_on": "next_eviction_loop_tick"
      },
      "eviction_ratio": {
        "current": 0.2,
        "minimum": 0.0,
        "maximum": 1.0,
        "effective_on": "next_eviction_loop_tick"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

For Phase 1 this can be implemented with static controller methods. The important part is the API shape: callers learn what is safe to change from the server, not from out-of-band documentation.

## 6. Proposed API

### 6.1 Read policies and capabilities

`GET /config/policies`

Alternative if maintainers prefer a dedicated management namespace: `GET /management/policies`.

Returns current policy state, runtime version, and capability metadata.

```json
{
  "version": 7,
  "capabilities": {
    "store_policy": {
      "current": "default",
      "registered": ["default", "skip_l1"],
      "hot_swappable": true,
      "effective_on": "next_store_plan"
    },
    "prefetch_policy": {
      "current": "default",
      "registered": ["default", "retain"],
      "hot_swappable": true,
      "effective_on": "next_prefetch_request"
    },
    "l1_eviction": {
      "policy": "LRU",
      "policy_hot_swappable": false,
      "runtime_tunables": {
        "trigger_watermark": {"current": 0.8, "minimum": 0.0, "maximum": 1.0},
        "eviction_ratio": {"current": 0.2, "minimum": 0.0, "maximum": 1.0}
      }
    },
    "l2_eviction": [
      {
        "adapter_id": 0,
        "adapter_name": "fs",
        "policy": "LRU",
        "policy_hot_swappable": false,
        "runtime_tunables": {
          "trigger_watermark": {"current": 0.8, "minimum": 0.0, "maximum": 1.0},
          "eviction_ratio": {"current": 0.2, "minimum": 0.0, "maximum": 1.0}
        }
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

### 6.2 Validate an update

`POST /config/policies/validate`

Same body as `PATCH`, but does not mutate state.

This is useful for operators and future coordinator fan-out: validate all targets first, then apply only if ever

items.title: [Bug][MP] FSL2Adapter serialises every key inside a load batch (2.2x slower on 24 MiB chunks, measured)
items.author: xiangping-chen
items.body_excerpt:
**Label**

`bug`, `performance`, `mp_mode`, `backend` — also relevant to `fs_connector`.

---

## Describe the bug

`FSL2Adapter` never parallelises the keys inside a `submit_load_task` batch. Each key's I/O
is awaited before the next begins, so a batch of N keys takes N sequential round trips.

`lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/fs_l2_adapter.py`, `_execute_load`:

```python
for i, key in enumerate(keys):
    ...
    if self._use_odirect:
        num_read = await self._loop.run_in_executor(   # awaited in-loop
            None, self._read_with_odirect, file_path, dst_buf,
        )
        ...
        continue
    async with aiofiles.open(file_path, "rb") as f:
        num_read = await _async_readinto_full(f, dst_buf)   # awaited in-loop
```

Dispatching to `run_in_executor` does not help, because the result is awaited immediately.
The same shape appears in the store path (`for key, obj in zip(keys, objects, strict=True)`,
which awaits `exists` → write → `replace` per key, i.e. three sequential round trips each)
and in the lookup path (`for i, key in enumerate(keys)` awaiting `_key_exists_on_disk`).

**There is no outer concurrency to compensate.** `submit_load_task` schedules exactly one
coroutine per batch, and the caller puts a whole request into one batch —
`storage_controllers/prefetch_controller.py:931`, "Step 7: submit load tasks per adapter":

```python
for adapter_idx, bitmap in trimmed_plan.items():
    per_adapter_keys = bitmap.gather(request.keys)
    ...
    task_id = self._l2_adapters[adapter_idx].submit_load_task(
        per_adapter_keys, per_adapter_objs
    )
```

So all of a request's keys for a given adapter are serialised. Concurrency exists only
*across adapters*, which does nothing for the common single-`fs`-adapter deployment.

## Measurements

`lmcache bench l2` on XFS over a 4-drive NVMe RAID-0. The experiment holds total work
constant and moves concurrency from *within* a batch to *across* batches, so the only
variable is where the parallelism sits.

**24 MiB keys** (a real KV chunk: Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, `chunk_size: 256`, TP=1 → 98,304
B/token × 256 = 24 MiB), 32 keys total, `use_odirect: true`:

| Layout | Lookup | Store | **Load** |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 32 keys, 1 batch | 2.43 ms | 82.84 ms | **68.75 ms** (11,202 MB/s) |
| 4 keys × 8 batches | 4.79 ms | 79.11 ms | **31.60 ms** (24,308 MB/s) |

**Load is 2.2× slower** when the same 32 keys arrive as one batch instead of eight.

Store is *not* materially affected at this size (1.05×) — it appears write-bandwidth-bound
on the device, so the serialisation is masked. Lookup is too small here to measure
meaningfully. **The defect is in all three code paths, but only Load demonstrably suffers
at this size.**

The mechanism is confirmed by a batch-size sweep at `--in-flight 1` (256 KB keys), where
duration scales linearly with batch size — the signature of a serial loop:

```
--num-keys      1      4      8     16     32     64    128
duration     0.34   1.87   6.63   9.02  16.00  25.91  46.16   ms
```

128× the keys, 136× the duration.

### Reproducing

```bash
# one batch of 32
lmcache bench l2 --l2-adapter '{"type":"fs","base_path":"/mnt/nvme/l2bench","use_odirect":true}' \
  --num-keys 32 --in-flight 1 --data-size-kb 24576 --l1-align-bytes 4096 --rounds 3

# eight batches of 4 -- identical total work
lmcache bench l2 --l2-adapter '{"type":"fs","base_path":"/mnt/nvme/l2bench","use_odirect":true}' \
  --num-keys 4  --in-flight 8 --data-size-kb 24576 --l1-align-bytes 4096 --rounds 3
```

Note `lmcache bench l2` needs the `native_storage_ops` extension (it imports `Bitmap`);
`NO_GPU_EXT=1 python setup.py build_ext --inplace` is enough to get it.

## Expected behavior

A batch API should exploit the batch. Loading N keys should overlap the N I/Os, as the
other adapters already do:

- `nixl_store_l2_adapter` builds one vectorised descriptor list and issues a single
  transfer;
- `raw_block_l2_adapter` uses dedicated `ThreadPoolExecutor`s (`_load_pool`, `_store_pool`,
  `_lookup_pool`);
- `s3_l2_adapter` gathers per-key futures with `asyncio.gather`.

`fs` is the odd one out, and it is the default file-backed adapter.

The fix looks small: build the per-key coroutines and `await asyncio.gather(*tasks)`
instead of awaiting in the loop, with a bound on in-flight I/O so a large batch cannot
swamp the executor. Worth noting from the data that unbounded is not automatically better
— at 24 MiB keys, `1 key × 32 batches` measured *worse* than `4 keys × 8` (65.72 ms vs
33.37 ms), so a concurrency limit belongs in the design rather than a bare `gather`.

## Caveats

- **Buffered numbers are page-cache reads, not disk.** The same comparison with
  `use_odirect: false` shows a much larger spread (121.83 ms vs 19.09 ms, 6.4×), but the
  bench writes then reads 768 MiB on a host with ample RAM, so those figures are memory
  bandwidth. The O_DIRECT row above is the one that reflects storage, and 2.2× is the
  figure I would rely on.
- 3 measurement rounds, 1 warmup, single host. Enough to establish the effect and its
  rough size, not a precise characterisation.
- The `1 key × 32` O_DIRECT anomaly noted above suggests executor or queue-depth limits at
  high concurrency; I have not investigated it.
- I have not measured the end-to-end TTFT impact in a live MP deployment — only the
  adapter in isolation.

## Environment

- LMCache `v0.5.1.dev52`, `upstream/dev`
- Ubuntu 26.04, kernel 7.0.0-28-generic
- torch 2.11.0+cu130, CUDA 13.0
- XFS on `/dev/md0`, software RAID-0 over 4 × Dell PM1735a MU 1.6 TB NVMe

## Related

Same defect class as the in-process `LocalDiskBackend`, whose `batched_get_blocking`
defaulted to a serial `for key in keys: get_blocking(key)` and was given a thread pool
(#3961, hardened further in #4348). The MP interface removed that particular footgun — it
is batch-native, with no single-key `get` to loop over and a `Bitmap` result for partial
success — but `FSL2Adapter`'s implementation reintroduces the behavi

items.title: [Bug] fs_native L2: files left by a previous process are never counted toward max_capacity_gb or evicted (disk grows unbounded across restarts)
items.author: OscarSavNS
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

With the `fs_native` L2 adapter, chunk files persist across a server restart and are still served (lookup is a `stat` on the file), but the new process never registers them. They don't count toward `max_capacity_gb`, and the eviction policy never sees them, so **they are never evicted**. Each restart can strand up to a full cap of untracked files, and disk usage grows without bound until the filesystem fills.

## Observed

`lmcache/vllm-openai` image, LMCache `0.5.6rc1` (commit `9a7b6050`), MP server with:

```
--l2-adapter '{"type":"fs_native","base_path":"/lmcache/l2","num_workers":32,"use_odirect":true,
  "max_capacity_gb":1000,"eviction":{"eviction_policy":"LRU","trigger_watermark":0.9,"eviction_ratio":0.1}}'
```

1. Wrote ~1.2 TB of KV. LRU eviction worked as documented: usage hit the 0.9 watermark three times and dropped to 871 GB each time (`L2 usage 0.90 above watermark 0.90; triggering eviction`).
2. Restarted the server with the same `base_path`: 298,340 files, 911.7 GB on disk.
3. After the restart, `GET /status` reported `l2_eviction_controller.adapters[0].total_bytes_used = 0`.
4. Requests over the pre-restart prefixes were served from those files: 16.76M tokens, every full chunk, `lookup_hit_l2_tokens_total` +16,760,832. After that, tracked usage was 0.49 GB, i.e. only the new writes, while 911.7 GB of served files stayed untracked.

## Root cause (on `dev` at dc68527c)

- Byte accounting and eviction order are fed only by stores that the current process completes: `_notify_keys_stored` in `l2_adapters/base.py`, called from the native adapter's store completions. Neither `fs_native_l2_adapter.py` nor `native_connector_l2_adapter.py` scans `base_path` at startup.
- Reads of pre-existing files fire `on_l2_keys_accessed`, and `LRUEvictionPolicy.on_keys_touched` ignores keys it doesn't track (`if key in self._order`).
- `NativeConnectorL2Adapter` decrements usage on delete only for keys in `_key_sizes`, i.e. stored by this process.
- Re-storing an existing key is a no-op on disk (`csrc/storage_backends/fs/connector.cpp`: "Skip if already stored on disk").

RFC #4738 mentions this in passing ("Restart recovery: ... Existing files on disk are not automatically registered again"), but as part of a larger multi-disk design, and there is no standalone bug for it.

## Impact

With `max_capacity_gb` sized to the disk (the natural configuration), one restart with a full cache followed by a refill exceeds the disk. Any deployment that restarts routinely (rollouts, crashes) accumulates untracked files. Operators have to choose between wiping `base_path` on every start, which loses the persistence, and eventually running out of space.

## Proposed fix (prototyped, tested)

File names are already reversible: `fs_l2_adapter._filename_to_object_key` inverts the names the C++ connector writes. The prototype:

- adds `L2AdapterInterface.recover_persisted_objects() -> int` (default no-op), delegated by the serde and fault-inject wrappers;
- `StorageManager` calls it for each adapter **after** the L2 eviction states have registered their listeners, at init and in `add_l2_adapter`;
- `NativeConnectorL2Adapter` takes an optional `persisted_object_scanner`. `recover_persisted_objects` records each object in `_key_sizes` (so eviction deletes decrement usage) and announces it through `_notify_keys_stored`. It goes newest-first, so LRU's reverse insertion puts the oldest file at the eviction head. Keys already tracked are skipped;
- `fs_native` gains `recover_on_start` (default `true`) and a scanner that `os.scandir`s `base_path`. It decodes `.data` names, takes `st_size` and `st_mtime`, and skips `.tmp` files, undecodable names and directories.

Tests: 13 new (scanner, adapter recovery/ordering/delete/double-count, config, and `StorageManager` end-to-end: leftover files are accounted, over-cap leftovers are evicted oldest-first, `recover_on_start: false` keeps today's behaviour). The existing tests in `test_native_connector_l2_adapter`, `test_fs_native_l2_adapter_config`, `test_runtime_adapters`, `test_l2_adapter_base`, `test_fault_inject_l2_adapter`, `test_storage_manager_l2_keys` and `test_l2_adapter_factory` still pass (185 passed). Run on the 0.5.6rc1 commit; the patch also applies cleanly to current `dev`.

**Validated on a real cache:** 0.5.6rc1 plus the patch, restarted over the 911.7 GB directory above, with the cap lowered to 800 GiB:

```
fs_native: found 298492 persisted objects (849.44 GiB) in /lmcache/l2 in 3.0 s (0 entries skipped)
L2 adapter 0: registered 298492 objects recovered from persistent storage (usage 912076931072 bytes)
L2 usage 1.06 above watermark 0.90; triggering eviction.
L2 usage 0.96 above watermark 0.90; triggering eviction.
```

- **Settled usage:** 0.86. The disk went from 912.2 GB to 738.85 GB, with 738.78 GB tracked, within 0.01% of `du`.
- **Oldest first:** the evicted files were the oldest by mtime; the newest were kept.

Open questions for maintainers:

- **Default:** should `recover_on_start` default to `true`? It changes startup behaviour, since eviction can run immediately when leftovers exceed the watermark.
- **Scan cost:** the scan is synchronous at startup. ~300k files took 3.0 s to scan plus 0.5 s to register here; a very large directory might want a background scan.
- **Other adapters:** the same gap likely applies to other persistent adapters, e.g. `fs` and `nixl_store`; the hook is generic.

Happy to open a PR.

items.title: [Bug] LFUCachePolicy state desync causes KeyError crash under memory pressure
items.author: Chocolatine75
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

With `cache_policy: "LFU"`, the local-CPU backend can crash with a `KeyError`
under memory pressure. `LFUCachePolicy.get_evict_candidates()` removes the keys
it returns from its internal frequency bookkeeping (`key_to_freq` /
`freq_to_keys`), treating *selection* as *eviction*. But the caller does not
always evict every returned candidate, so the policy ends up tracking fewer
keys than are actually resident — and a later access to a still-resident but
untracked key raises `KeyError`.

LRU/FIFO/MRU are unaffected because their only state is the cache dict itself.

### Where it goes wrong

`LocalCPUBackend.batched_allocate()` requests up to 64 candidates, then:
- evicts the first fully-evictable one and `break`s, and
- `continue`s (skips) any candidate whose layer is pinned
  (`lmcache/v1/storage_backend/local_cpu_backend.py`, the `continue` at the
  per-layer check).

Every candidate `get_evict_candidates()` returned was already dropped from LFU
bookkeeping, but only the evicted one is actually removed from `hot_cache`. The
rest stay resident but untracked. The next `update_on_hit()` on one of them
does `self.key_to_freq[key]` → `KeyError`.

### Reproduction (policy level, no GPU needed)

```python
from collections import OrderedDict
from lmcache.v1.storage_backend.cache_policy import get_cache_policy

class Entry:
    def __init__(self, can_evict=True): self.can_evict = can_evict

p = get_cache_policy("LFU")
p.update_on_put("k")
cache = OrderedDict({"k": Entry(can_evict=True)})

assert p.get_evict_candidates(cache, num_candidates=1) == ["k"]
# caller selected "k" but did NOT evict it (e.g. a pinned layer) — "k" is still
# resident, so a later hit must be fine:
p.update_on_hit("k", cache)   # -> KeyError('k')
```

FIFO/MRU/LRU run the same snippet without error.

### Impact

- Only affects deployments configured with `cache_policy: "LFU"`.
- Crash (`KeyError`) in the allocation hot path once the CPU tier is under
  memory pressure and eviction kicks in; worse with layerwise models where
  `batched_allocate` requests many candidates and evicts one.

### Suggested fix

- Make `LFUCachePolicy.get_evict_candidates()` selection-only (no internal
  mutation), consistent with the other policies.
- Notify the policy on every actual removal in `LocalCPUBackend.remove()` (not
  just forced ones). `update_on_force_evict()` is a no-op for LRU/FIFO/MRU, and
  lets LFU drop a key when it is really evicted (including internal
  `force=False` evictions).

I have a PR ready with this fix plus regression tests for all four policies.

items.title: fs L2: per-rank group payloads collide on shared keys — half-size group-5 objects abort lookup promotion (hybrid groups, PP>1)
items.author: kaka86mm
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

On a PP>1 hybrid-KV-group model, the fs L2 tier never survives a server restart: lookups find the keys but abort promotion with `Incomplete read` size mismatches, so `lmcache_mp_lookup_hit_l2_*` stays 0 and everything recomputes. Evidence points to **per-rank group payloads colliding on shared keys** — one PP rank writes group-5 objects at exactly half the size the reader's spec-derived buffer expects.

## Environment

- 4× CMP 170HX (sm80), vLLM fork v0.13.0, PP=4 (`12,12,12,12`), MiMo-V2.6-Flash-RL — 6 hybrid groups, `group_tokens_per_block=[256,128,128,128,128,128]`
- `lmcache server --chunk-size 8192 --shm-name ... --max-gpu-workers 4 --supported-transfer-mode engine_driven --l1-size-gb 100 --no-l1-use-lazy --eviction-policy LRU --l2-adapter '{"type":"fs","base_path":"/lmcache-l2","relative_tmp_dir":"tmp"}'`
- lmcache 0.5.6.post4410 (PR #4410 head)

## Repro (deterministic)

1. Send a unique 200K-token prefix (same token ids both times) → prefill completes, objects written to L2.
2. Gracefully restart server and engine (`docker stop -t 60` both; no kills).
3. Resend the identical prefix.

Result: full recompute (~57 s), `lookup_hit_l2_tokens_total` / `lookup_hit_l2_keys_total` = **0**, and 27 warnings:

```
Incomplete read for -SEP-model@0x04000400@5@<hash>.data: expected 1310720, got 655360
```

## Evidence for per-rank payload collision

File-size census of the L2 dir after one 200K store:

| group | files × size |
|---|---|
| @0 | 243 × 41,943,040 + 81 × 62,914,560 |
| @1..@4 | 324 × 1,310,720 each |
| @5 | **243 × 1,310,720 + 81 × 655,360** |

- 324 = 4 ranks × 81 chunks; the 81 bad @5 files are exactly one rank's share. The PP ranks carry different layer compositions (rank 0 hosts the vision encoder, rank 3 the lm_head), so per-rank group payloads legitimately differ in size (see @0's 40 MB vs 60 MB classes).
- All 27 lookup-time mismatches are `@5` keys whose on-disk size (655,360) is exactly half of `expected = len(dst_buf)` (1,310,720) — the buffer comes from the engine-side group spec (`fs_l2_adapter.py`, standard async path: `expected = len(dst_buf)`), not from any per-object metadata.
- Atomic writes were enabled (`relative_tmp_dir=tmp`, `os.replace`), and these files were written by a fresh clean process with no interruption — truncation is ruled out; the writer wrote half.
- The reader `continue`s on mismatch, so the first bad object in a chain truncates the contiguous hit to zero → no promotion at all, not even partial.

This also retroactively explains the partial adoption we reported earlier (168/192 keys after a restart) and why `lookup_hit_l2` was 0 all day in production.

## Suggested directions

- Include the rank (or a payload-size discriminator) in the L2 object key, or assemble the full-group payload before writing under the shared key; or
- store the object's true byte length in a sidecar / the key name and size the read buffer from it, instead of deriving `expected` from the model group spec.

Happy to run instrumented builds or share the full server logs / file census on request.

(Prior context from the same rig: #5440 — the per-object cost thread; #4410 review.)

items.title: Eval bug: Speculative decoding (draft-mtp / draft-dspark): greedy output diverges from vanilla on quantized targets
items.author: Ankk98
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

Under greedy sampling (`temperature=0`, `top_k=1`), **draft-model** speculative decoding can produce different text than a non-speculative run when the **target is quantized** (e.g. Q4_K_M). The same setups match on a **bf16 target**. **Ngram** speculation on the same quantized target stays lossless even when drafts are accepted.

This contradicts the expected property that speculative decoding is lossless for greedy decode (draft proposes; target verifies).

Related: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/25173 (`draft-dspark`), but the issue is **not DSpark-only**.

## Environment (local repro)

- Hardware: AMD Strix Halo iGPU
- Backend: Vulkan (`-DGGML_VULKAN=ON`)
- Branch: PR #25173
- Others have also reported similar mismatches on **CUDA** (not re-run here)

## Expected

Greedy speculative output == greedy vanilla output for the same target weights / seed / prompt.

## Actual / evidence

Probe prompt (thinking off):

> What happens when a browser requests https://example.com? Five bullet points.

### Matrix (Vulkan)

| Setup | Spec active? | Match vanilla? |
|-------|----------------|----------------|
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, vanilla ×2 | n/a | **OK** (deterministic) |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `ngram-simple` (drafted, 0 accepted) | yes | **OK** |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `ngram-mod` (4/8 accepted) | yes | **OK** |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `draft-dspark` n_max=7 | yes (e.g. 80/336) | **BUG** |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `draft-dspark`, `-fa off` | yes | **BUG** (still) |
| Qwen3-8B **bf16**, `draft-dspark` n_max=7 (4 prompts) | yes | **OK** (4/4) |
| Gemma-4-12B Q4 + `draft-mtp` n_max=4 | yes (169/340) | **BUG** |

Example Q4 DSpark fork (both `finish=stop`):

- vanilla: `...checks if it has a cached copy of the website's SSL/TLS certificate...`
- dspark: `...checks if the system has a valid certificate for **example.com**...`

## What this is / is not

- **Is quantization-related:** yes (Q4 breaks; bf16 OK for DSpark).
- **Is not “all speculative”:** ngram paths match on the same Q4 target, including with accepts.
- **Is not DSpark/DFlash-only:** Gemma **MTP** also diverges on Q4.
- **Is not Qwen-only:** Gemma-4 + MTP also fails.
- **Is not vanilla Q4 nondeterminism:** two vanilla Q4 runs match.
- **Is not FA-only:** DSpark still mismatches with `-fa off`.
- **Target weights likely fine:** ngram uses the same greedy accept/verify sampler path (`common_sampler_sample_and_accept_n` in server) and stays lossless → points to **draft-model speculative paths** (MTP / DSpark: draft ctx, KV, embd/injection, multi-token target batching) interacting badly with **quantized** target compute—not permanent weight corruption.
- **Type-cast root cause:** not isolated; path-dependent Q4 numerics remain a plausible contributor.

items.title: [Kernel] Optimize triton decoding kernels for long context
items.author: merrymercy
items.body_excerpt:
We noticed the current triton decoding kernel is very slow on long context. This is due to a missing flash decoding like optimization.

## Reproduce
We test the decoding speed with a context length of 200 and 2,000.

triton backend: The decoding speed drops from 147.64 token/s to 126.41 token/s
```
$ python3 -m sglang.bench_offline_throughput --model meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct --dataset-name random --num-prompt 1 --random-input 128 --random-output 2048 --random-range 1 --attention-backend triton

[2024-11-30 05:10:04 TP0] Decode batch. #running-req: 1, #token: 234, token usage: 0.00, gen throughput (token/s): 147.64, #queue-req: 0
... 
[2024-11-30 05:10:18 TP0] Decode batch. #running-req: 1, #token: 2154, token usage: 0.00, gen throughput (token/s): 126.41, #queue-req: 0
```

flashinfer backend: The decoding speed only drops from 144.17 token/s to 143.35 token/s
```
$ python3 -m sglang.bench_offline_throughput --model meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct --dataset-name random --num-prompt 1 --random-input 128 --random-output 2048 --random-range 1

[2024-11-30 05:11:40 TP0] Decode batch. #running-req: 1, #token: 234, token usage: 0.00, gen throughput (token/s): 144.17, #queue-req: 0
...
[2024-11-30 05:11:54 TP0] Decode batch. #running-req: 1, #token: 2154, token usage: 0.00, gen throughput (token/s): 143.35, #queue-req: 0
```

## Possible solutions
We can learn from the flash decoding triton kernel from lightllm and improve the [current triton decoding kernel](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/python/sglang/srt/layers/attention/triton_ops/decode_attention.py). Related links:
- https://github.com/ModelTC/lightllm/blob/main/lightllm/models/llama/triton_kernel/gqa_flash_decoding.py
- https://pytorch.org/blog/flash-decoding/
- https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.01282

items.title: Refactor: TRTLLMHAAttnBackend should not inherit from FlashInferAttnBackend when reuse is small
items.author: merrymercy
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

`TRTLLMHAAttnBackend(FlashInferAttnBackend)` (in `python/sglang/srt/layers/attention/trtllm_mha_backend.py`) inherits from `FlashInferAttnBackend`, but it reuses very little from the parent. Almost all attention-specific behavior is overridden, and some inherited setup is allocated-but-never-used. We should reconsider this inheritance: **if the reuse is small, we should not inherit from `FlashInferAttnBackend`** — inheriting directly from the base `AttentionBackend` (and pulling in only the small bits of plumbing that are actually shared) would be cleaner.

### What is actually reused

The only real reuse comes from `super().__init__(...)`:
- `req_to_token_pool`, `token_to_kv_pool`
- `max_context_len`, `skip_prefill`, `use_sliding_window_kv_pool`
- the `kv_indptr` / `kv_last_page_len` buffers (used by the companion `TRTLLMHAAttnMultiStepDraftBackend` draft steps)
- `forward()` dispatch — which actually comes from the base `AttentionBackend`, not from FlashInfer.

### What is overridden (not reused)

Essentially all the attention logic:
- `init_forward_metadata`, `init_cuda_graph_state`, `init_forward_metadata_out_graph`
- `forward_decode`, `forward_extend` (call `flashinfer.decode.trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache` / `flashinfer.prefill.trtllm_batch_context_with_kv_cache` directly)
- `get_cuda_graph_seq_len_fill_value`, `_resolve_swa_kv_pool`
- it uses its own `TRTLLMMHAMetadata` and its own page-table builder.

### Inherited-but-unused / redundant work

Because the TRTLLM kernels use a completely different API, part of the parent `__init__` is wasted:
- Parent builds `prefill_wrapper_ragged`, `prefill_wrappers_paged`, `decode_wrappers`, and the `FlashInferIndicesUpdater*` objects — TRTLLM-MHA never uses them.
- Parent sets `self.workspace_buffer` to the shared `global_workspace_buffer`, but the child **replaces** it with its own zero-init `global_zero_init_workspace_buffer`.
- `max_context_len` and `_swa_kv_pool` are set by the parent and then re-set by the child.

### Proposal

- Evaluate inheriting `TRTLLMHAAttnBackend` directly from `AttentionBackend` instead of `FlashInferAttnBackend`.
- Move the small amount of genuinely shared init plumbing into a thin shared helper/mixin (e.g. pool/buffer setup) rather than dragging in the full FlashInfer wrapper/indices-updater allocation.
- Avoid allocating FlashInfer wrappers and updaters that the TRTLLM path never uses.
- Apply the same review to `TRTLLMHAAttnMultiStepDraftBackend(FlashInferMultiStepDraftBackend)`.

As a general guideline: **do not inherit from `FlashInferAttnBackend` when the reuse is little** — prefer inheriting from the base `AttentionBackend` and sharing only what is actually common.

### Good first issue

This is a good first issue: it is well-scoped, localized to `trtllm_mha_backend.py` (plus the base classes), and mostly a refactor with clear before/after behavior to validate against existing tests.

items.title: [Bug] Interrupted Mooncake trace download is reused as a complete cache
items.author: unravel1020
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

When SGLang downloads a Mooncake JSONL trace and the streamed HTTP response raises an exception after one or more chunks have been written, the partially written destination file is left in place. On the next `MooncakeDataset.load()`, the file-existence check treats that path as an available dataset and skips the download. The benchmark then reads only the records present in the partial file (or fails while parsing a truncated final line) instead of retrying the download.

This report concerns a path written by a failed download. It does not ask SGLang to remove arbitrary pre-existing user-provided dataset files.

### Reproduction

The following CPU-only reproduction uses a temporary destination that does not exist before the first load. The mocked response yields one complete JSONL record and then raises a connection error while the body is being streamed:

```python
import os
import tempfile
from unittest.mock import patch

import requests
from sglang.benchmark.datasets.mooncake import MooncakeDataset


class InterruptedResponse:
    headers = {"content-length": "200"}

    def raise_for_status(self):
        pass

    def iter_content(self, chunk_size):
        yield b'{"timestamp": 1, "hash_ids": []}\n'
        raise requests.exceptions.ConnectionError("simulated interrupted transfer")


with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as temp_dir:
    path = os.path.join(temp_dir, "trace.jsonl")
    dataset = MooncakeDataset(path, "conversation", 10)

    with patch(
        "sglang.benchmark.utils.requests.get",
        return_value=InterruptedResponse(),
    ):
        try:
            dataset.load()
        except requests.exceptions.ConnectionError:
            pass
        else:
            raise AssertionError("the first load should raise ConnectionError")

    print("final path exists:", os.path.exists(path))
    print("rows returned by the next load:", len(dataset.load()))
```

Observed on the commit below:

```text
first load: raises ConnectionError
final path exists: True
rows returned by the next load: 1
```

The second load does not issue another HTTP request because the destination path exists.

### Expected behavior

After a streamed download fails, SGLang should not leave a final path that a later load treats as a complete downloaded dataset. A subsequent load should retry the failed download or report that the downloaded dataset is unavailable; it should not silently benchmark from the partial trace.

### Environment

- SGLang source: `main` at `41812afe432a54308be1c361a4d587952356f958`
- OS: Ubuntu on WSL2, Linux 6.18.33.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2 x86_64
- Python: 3.12.14
- PyTorch: 2.13.0+cpu; `torch.cuda.is_available() == False`
- No model, server, or GPU is needed for this reproduction.
- `PYTHONPATH=python python -m sglang.check_env` currently fails on this CPU-only environment with `NameError: name 'env' is not defined`; this is unrelated to the reproduction above.

items.title: [Bug]: Qwen3.5 4b incompatibility
items.author: aminsamir45
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

## Environment
- vLLM: 0.16.1rc1 (nightly)
- TRL: 0.28.x
- Model: Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B (text-only checkpoint)
- Mode: GRPOTrainer with `vllm_mode="colocate"`

## Problem

When using a Qwen3.5 text-only checkpoint with vLLM's colocate mode in TRL's GRPOTrainer, vLLM instantiates `Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration` (the full VLM class) — the only registered class for this architecture. This causes a hard weight naming mismatch:

- vLLM expects weights under: `language_model.model.layers.*`
- Text-only checkpoint has weights at: `model.layers.*` (no `language_model.` prefix)

## Root Cause

There is no `Qwen3_5ForCausalLM` text-only class registered in vLLM. The entire Qwen3.5 family uses a hybrid architecture (Gated DeltaNet + sparse MoE), and vLLM currently only exposes the full multimodal class `Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration`. When a text-only checkpoint is loaded through this class, the weight prefix mismatch causes a hard failure.

This is distinct from the standalone vLLM server use case (e.g., serving `Qwen3.5-27B` as a full VLM), which works correctly because the checkpoint includes the vision encoder and weight names match.

## Expected Behavior

Either:
1. A `Qwen3_5ForCausalLM` text-only class is registered in vLLM, OR
2. The `--language-model-only` flag correctly handles text-only checkpoints by remapping the weight prefix (`model.layers.*` → `language_model.model.layers.*`) and skipping vision encoder initialization

## Impact

This completely blocks using vLLM with TRL GRPOTrainer for GRPO/RL training on Qwen3.5 text-only models — which is a primary use case for small models like 4B. Currently forced to fall back to `model.generate()`, which is 10-24× slower and defeats the purpose of vLLM integration in training loops.

## Workaround

None currently. Disabling vLLM (`use_vllm=False`) and accepting the throughput penalty.

## Question for maintainers

Is `--language-model-only` support with correct weight prefix remapping planned for 0.17.0? Is there a recommended path for using text-only Qwen3.5 checkpoints with vLLM today?

### Reproduction

```
"""Base Modal container image builder."""

import modal
from shared.constants.modal import CLOUD_SQL_PROXY_URL

BASE_PIP_PACKAGES: list[str] = [
    "trl>=0.28.0,<0.29.0",
    "peft>=0.18.0",
    "accelerate>=1.4.0,<2.0.0",
    "bitsandbytes>=0.44.0",
    "datasets>=2.16.0",
    "numpy>=1.24.0",
    "pandas>=2.0.0",
    "pyyaml>=6.0",
    "scikit-learn>=1.3.0",
    "tqdm>=4.66.0",
    "google-cloud-storage>=2.10.0",
    "gcsfs>=2024.2.0",
    "pydantic>=2.12.5",
    "matplotlib>=3.10.8",
    "psycopg[binary]>=3.3.2",
    "opentelemetry-api>=1.37.0",
    "opentelemetry-sdk>=1.37.0",
    "weave>=0.51.0",
]

# TRL 0.28.x unconditionally imports vllm_ascend (Huawei Ascend NPU)
# which doesn't exist on NVIDIA GPUs. Stub it so the import succeeds.
# Remove when: TRL drops the unconditional import (huggingface/trl#3545).
_STUB_VLLM_ASCEND = (
    "SP=$(python3 -c 'import site; print(site.getsitepackages()[0])') && "
    "mkdir -p $SP/vllm_ascend/distributed/device_communicators && "
    "touch $SP/vllm_ascend/__init__.py "
    "$SP/vllm_ascend/distributed/__init__.py "
    "$SP/vllm_ascend/distributed/device_communicators/__init__.py && "
    "echo 'class PyHcclCommunicator: pass' > "
    "$SP/vllm_ascend/distributed/device_communicators/pyhccl.py"
)


def build_base_image(
    *,
    extra_pip_packages: list[str] | None = None,
    extra_env: dict[str, str] | None = None,
) -> modal.Image:
    """Build a Modal container image with CUDA, shared deps, and app code."""
    pip_packages = BASE_PIP_PACKAGES + (extra_pip_packages or [])
    env_vars = {"PYTHONUNBUFFERED": "1", "PYTHONPATH": "/app"}
    if extra_env:
        env_vars.update(extra_env)

    return (
        modal.Image.from_registry(
            "nvidia/cuda:12.6.2-cudnn-runtime-ubuntu24.04", add_python="3.12"
        )
        .apt_install("git", "gcc", "python3-dev", "curl")
        .run_commands(
            f"curl -fsSL {CLOUD_SQL_PROXY_URL} -o /usr/local/bin/cloud-sql-proxy",
            "chmod +x /usr/local/bin/cloud-sql-proxy",
        )
        .pip_install(*pip_packages)
        # vLLM nightly for Qwen3_5ForCausalLM (Gated DeltaNet) support.
        # vLLM pins transformers<5 and installs 4.57.x, but Qwen3.5 was only
        # added in transformers 5.x. We re-install transformers 5.x afterward.
        # The train script monkey-patches vLLM for cross-version compat
        # (language_model_only=True to skip the VLM pipeline, plus relaxed
        # config type check for Qwen3_5Config vs Qwen3_5TextConfig).
        .run_commands(
            "pip install -U vllm --pre --extra-index-url https://wheels.vllm.ai/nightly"
        )
        .run_commands("pip install 'transformers>=5.2.0'")
        .run_commands(_STUB_VLLM_ASCEND)
        .env(env_vars)
        .add_local_dir(".", "/app", ignore=[".venv", "__pycache__", "*.pyc", ".git"])
    )
```

items.title: cumem allocator: double-free and stale error codes during sleep/wake cycles
items.author: markrogersjr
items.body_excerpt:
## Your current environment

vLLM v0.17.0 (also reproducible on main) with cumem allocator enabled, using sleep/wake cycles for colocated GRPO training.

## How would you like to use vllm

Colocated training where vLLM's GPU memory is released via `sleep()` during training steps and reclaimed via `wake_up()` for inference.

## Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] I have searched for [similar issues](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues).

## Description

Several bugs in the cumem allocator cause CUDA driver errors during sleep/wake cycles:

### 1. Double cuMemRelease on already-unmapped allocations

`sleep()` iterates all allocations and calls `unmap_and_release` unconditionally. If some allocations are already unmapped (e.g. from a previous partial sleep or external release), this causes a double `cuMemRelease`. Similarly, `wake_up()` calls `create_and_map` on already-mapped allocations. There is no per-allocation tracking of mapped state.

### 2. CUDA ops on freed memory during sleep

When the allocator is sleeping, PyTorch's garbage collector can trigger `my_free` on tensors whose backing memory was already released by `sleep()`. The C++ `my_free` then calls `unmap_and_release` on invalid handles, causing CUDA driver errors. Additionally, `gc.collect()` and `torch.cuda.empty_cache()` at the end of `sleep()` can trigger these frees while the allocator is in the sleeping state.

### 3. Stale global error_code propagation

`error_code` is a file-scope global in `cumem_allocator.cpp` that is not cleared between calls. A non-fatal error in one operation (e.g. `create_and_map`) can persist and cause a subsequent unrelated call (e.g. `unmap_and_release` or `my_free`) to take the wrong code path.

### 4. Size mismatch in my_free

`my_free` passes its `size` argument to `unmap_and_release` and `cuMemAddressFree`, but the correct size is `recv_size` returned from the Python callback. This can cause incorrect unmapping.

### 5. Flash Attention 4 rotary embedding import failure

`find_spec("flash_attn")` succeeds with FA4 installed, but `from flash_attn.ops.triton.rotary import apply_rotary` fails because FA4 restructured its module layout. This causes an unhandled `ImportError`.

## Fix

https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/36535

items.title: [Bug]: Fast Start WeightCacheKey hashes only safetensors headers, so an ipc_cache engine can silently map another checkpoint's weights
items.author: nien-hui
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment
The output of python collect_env.py ```text vLLM Version : 0.30.1rc1.dev426+g863475eb9 (git sha: 863475eb9) PyTorch : 2.13.0+cu130 Python : 3.12.14 OS : Ubuntu 22.04.3 LTS (x86_64) GPU : NVIDIA RTX A6000 (driver 580.178.04) ```
### 🐛 Describe the bug #### Summary `hash_checkpoint()` builds the `checkpoint` field of `WeightCacheKey` from each shard's file name and safetensors header only ([`protocol.py#L239-L272`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/863475eb9cd78ae6a4a22f1b90df7fe85e0af438/vllm/model_executor/model_loader/weight_cache/protocol.py#L239-L272)). The header holds tensor names, dtypes, shapes and offsets, but no weight values. Two local checkpoints with the same architecture and file layout (a base model and its fine-tune, `step_0` and `step_100`) therefore get the same key. If a daemon preloaded from checkpoint A is still running and an engine starts on checkpoint B with `--load-format ipc_cache`, the daemon's check ([`daemon.py#L399-L403`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/863475eb9cd78ae6a4a22f1b90df7fe85e0af438/vllm/model_executor/model_loader/weight_cache/daemon.py#L399-L403)) finds no mismatched field and serves A's tensors. The engine never reads B from disk and logs no warning, while the CLI and the API `model` field both say B. The [docs](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/863475eb9cd78ae6a4a22f1b90df7fe85e0af438/docs/features/preload.md?plain=1#L21-L23) promise a "Safe fallback" when the daemon's cached weights don't match the engine, and say the fingerprint covers "checkpoint content". A user would therefore expect a daemon that still holds a different checkpoint to be rejected. #### Reproduction with `vllm preload` Make two checkpoints that differ only in weight values. `q` is `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B`; `q_mod` is a copy with `model.norm.weight` zeroed and the safetensors header untouched. ```bash hf download Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --local-dir q cp -r q q_mod ``` ```python import json import struct with open("q_mod/model.safetensors", "r+b") as f: (n,) = struct.unpack("

items.title: MP mode: remaining unbounded request-state retention in vLLM client and sidecar prefetch bookkeeping
items.author: wuwanxu
items.body_excerpt:
## Deployment

We run a production **3P1D** deployment with vLLM and `LMCacheMPConnector`. Each serving node has a per-node LMCache sidecar; LMCache uses `fs_native` as the L2 adapter backed by local SSD. P2P, CacheBlend, and engine-driven transfer are not enabled.

The previous client-side MQ no-response leak is tracked separately in #5270. During a follow-up audit of upstream `dev` (checked at `05fc77a`, 2026-09-24), we found the two request-state retention paths below. This issue only reports the observed behavior and asks maintainers to determine the intended lifecycle and remediation.

## 1. vLLM client: `_returned_finished` grows for the worker lifetime

`LMCacheMPWorkerAdapter` creates:

```python
self._returned_finished: set[str] = set()
```

`_process_finished_stores()` uses this set to prevent a request ID from being reported repeatedly through `finished_sending`, then records returned IDs with:

```python
self._returned_finished.update(ret_stores)
```

We could not find a `discard`, `clear`, TTL, or capacity-based removal path. Therefore every request ID once returned as `finished_sending` remains resident until the vLLM worker exits. This path is exercised by normal successful requests as well as failure paths.

The set appears to be needed for async-scheduling deduplication after neighboring tracking sets are drained, but it also produces monotonic process-lifetime growth. With UUID-like Python request IDs, the retained footprint is roughly 150-200 bytes per request before allocator overhead; at sustained high QPS this can become material in a long-lived worker.

Relevant code:
- `lmcache/integration/vllm/vllm_multi_process_adapter.py` (`_returned_finished`, `_process_finished_stores`)

### Questions for maintainers

1. Is process-lifetime retention of every completed `finished_sending` request ID required by the vLLM connector contract?
2. What lifecycle or retention semantics should this deduplication state have in a long-running worker?

## 2. sidecar: abandoned prefetch jobs and completion Bitmaps are never reclaimed

`LookupModule` registers every lookup in:

```python
self._prefetch_jobs: dict[str, _PrefetchJob] = {}
```

The job is removed when `QUERY_PREFETCH_STATUS` or `WAIT_PREFETCH_STATUS` obtains a non-`None` completion result. If a client aborts or disconnects after LOOKUP, or stops polling after an RPC timeout/unhealthy transition, the job is not consumed by that path.

The corresponding `PrefetchController` completion state has the same consumer-driven ownership:

```python
self._completed_lookups: dict[PrefetchRequestId, int] = {}
self._completed_results: dict[PrefetchRequestId, Bitmap] = {}
```

`query_prefetch_result()` pops both the Bitmap and the lookup result. The source comment notes that failing to consume the prefetch result leaks memory. `Bitmap` is native/C++ memory, so its growth may not be visible in Python GC or tracemalloc. `END_SESSION` removes the session and touches L1 keys but does not remove the prefetch job or controller completion state.

In production we also see frequent `Session ... not found, skipping touch` warnings (roughly 378-953 over two hours), consistent with request-lifecycle skew and making normal client polling an unreliable sole ownership mechanism.

Relevant code:
- `lmcache/v1/multiprocess/modules/lookup.py` (`_prefetch_jobs`, `query_prefetch_status`, `end_session`)
- `lmcache/v1/distributed/storage_controllers/prefetch_controller.py` (`_completed_lookups`, `_completed_results`, `query_prefetch_result`)

### Questions for maintainers

1. What is the intended owner of a prefetch job and its completion result after the original client has abandoned the request?
2. Is there an existing cancellation or reclamation lifecycle that this MP path should use?
3. What cleanup ordering is required for an in-flight prefetch so that late completion cannot expose invalid L1 data or retain completion state?

## Expected behavior

For healthy-sidecar and abort/error paths alike, client and server request bookkeeping should have a defined bounded lifecycle. Abandoned request state should be reclaimable without requiring a vLLM worker or sidecar restart, while preserving correctness for normal in-flight requests.

## Reproduction direction

1. Run vLLM + `LMCacheMPConnector` + sidecar with an SSD-backed `fs_native` L2.
2. Send sustained requests and observe the vLLM worker: `_returned_finished` grows monotonically.
3. Submit LOOKUPs, then abort/disconnect before prefetch polling completes, or induce a prefetch-status timeout.
4. Observe `lmcache_mp.active_prefetch_jobs` and `PrefetchController.report_status()["completed_results_count"]`; entries can remain after the client has abandoned the request.

comments.author: neevmodh
comments.body:
Read through both paths in `upstream/dev` to check the analysis — can confirm both observations.

**Part 1 (`_returned_finished`):** Confirmed there's no eviction path on this set anywhere in `vllm_multi_process_adapter.py`. Looking at `_process_finished_stores`, the set's only real job is to stop the same `req_id` from being re-added to `ret_stores` if `finished_req_ids_from_engine` reports it again in a later call — but once vLLM's own engine stops mentioning a `req_id` (i.e. it's fully retired from the engine's tracking), `_returned_finished`'s entry for it can never be hit again by the loop that checks it, so it's dead weight from that point on. A conservative fix that doesn't touch the dedup semantics: at the end of `_process_finished_stores`, intersect `_returned_finished` with the union of `self.finished_stores` / `self.store_futures` / `finished_req_ids_from_engine`, so an ID is only retained while it's still reachable through one of the sets that could re-report it. Happy to send that as a small PR if a maintainer confirms there's no other call site relying on longer retention.

**Part 2 (prefetch jobs):** Confirmed `end_session` (`lookup.py:514`) is already the natural per-request teardown hook — it's called on `MP_REQUEST_END` and already knows the `request_id`. Adding `self._prefetch_jobs.pop(request_id, None)` there looks safe on the `LookupModule` side. The harder part is `PrefetchController`'s `_completed_lookups`/`_completed_results` (a *different* class, presumably reachable through session/controller wiring I didn't fully trace) — and your question #3 is the real blocker here: popping a `Bitmap` out from under a prefetch that completes *after* the client has already been torn down risks exactly the late-completion/invalid-L1-data race you flagged, since it's native memory. I don't think this half should be fixed without a maintainer confirming the intended ownership handoff at session end — happy to implement once that's settled, but I'd rather not guess at a fix that touches native memory lifecycle across processes.

comments.author: neevmodh
comments.body: Following up on my earlier analysis: opened #5363 for part 1 (the `_returned_finished` set). Rather than guess at exact removal timing (which depends on the vLLM engine-contract question I couldn't answer myself), it bounds the set with a small LRU cap instead — converts unbounded growth into bounded memory without needing that question resolved first. Part 2 (sidecar prefetch/completion state) is intentionally left alone, per my earlier comment on the native-memory ordering risk.

items.title: OTel tracing overhead cliffs at c=50 on TP=2 deployments — level/flush tuning has no effect
items.author: wangxf1987
items.body_excerpt:
## Title

OTel trace overhead benchmark on a production-style K8s deployment (TP=2, 2 replicas): throughput loss of 20-33% at c>=50, trace level and flush threshold have negligible effect

## Summary

We benchmarked `--enable-trace` overhead on a production-shaped K8s deployment (RBG + LeaderWorkerSet, not docker-compose), Qwen3.6-27B-CHO on sglang v0.5.18, TP=2 per replica x 2 replicas (4 GPUs total, not an exclusive full node). This complements the larger-scale results already discussed elsewhere for TP=8 exclusive-node setups, and shows the overhead shape is very different at smaller TP.

Full report (charts + tables): attached PDF (`report-en.pdf`). Raw data (`result.csv`, GPU/CPU logs) available on request.

## Environment

- sglang `v0.5.18` (community image), `SGLANG_TRACE_ASYNC=1`
- Deployment: K8s RBG + LeaderWorkerSet, TP=2 per replica, 2 replicas, 4x H20 GPUs
- Trace path: sglang engine -> local OTel Agent (DaemonSet, node-local endpoint) -> Gateway -> backend, i.e. a two-hop agent-gw architecture, not a direct hardcoded Gateway connection
- 4 configs compared:
  | Group | trace level | async | flush threshold |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | G1 baseline | disabled | - | - |
  | G2 | 2 | 1 | default |
  | G3 | 3 | 1 | default |
  | G4 | 2 | 1 | 50 |
- Load generator: fixed-prompt benchmark client, concurrency swept across 1/10/50/100/200, 3 repeats per level (median)

## Findings

1. **Overhead is mild at low concurrency (c<=10)**: ttft_p99 +6~71%, throughput loss only 3~4%.
2. **c=50 is a clear inflection point**: ttft_p99 jumps 4.6x (172ms -> 965ms) going from G1 to G2 — roughly equivalent to the G1 baseline's own c=100 latency level being pulled forward to c=50. In other words, enabling trace shifts the whole latency-saturation curve left by one concurrency tier.
3. **From c>=50 onward, throughput loss is stable at 20~33%**, and grows with concurrency (-20.3% at c=50, up to -33.1% at c=200).
4. **Trace level 2 -> 3 produced no measurable incremental overhead** at c>=10 (all deltas within noise, ±2%).
5. **`SGLANG_TRACE_ASYNC_FLUSH_THRESHOLD=50` vs. default also produced no measurable benefit** at c>=50 (within ±16%, mostly ±2%; one anomalous +132.9% ttft_p99 spike at c=10 looked like a transient one-off, not reproduced at other levels).
6. **Root cause for (4) and (5): CPU was never the bottleneck in this setup.** Host CPU utilization on the GPU node stayed at 2~3% across all 4 groups (vs. GPU sm% rising from 14.8% baseline to 16~19% with trace enabled). Both trace-level and flush-threshold tuning target CPU-side span processing cost — with only 2 TP ranks, span volume is low enough that CPU headroom is never exhausted, so those knobs have nothing to bite on at this scale.
7. This is a **much smaller overhead** than what we see at TP=8 on an exclusive full node (throughput loss there was 75~79%, itl_p99 spiking ~28x, with CPU pegged at 99% — happy to share that data too if useful). The magnitude gap tracks roughly linearly with TP rank count, since span generation scales with the number of ranks, and the TP=8 test used synchronous export while this one used async by default.

## Why we're filing this

- The community advice we've seen elsewhere ("lower `SGLANG_TRACE_LEVEL` to reduce overhead", "tune the async flush threshold") holds at high TP / high CPU pressure, but **doesn't transfer to smaller TP configs** — those knobs are simply inert until CPU saturates. Worth calling out in docs/guidance so users at TP<=2-4 don't spend time tuning a lever with no effect.
- The **c=50 inflection point** (throughput loss going from ~4% to ~20% within one concurrency step) suggests there may be a queueing/lock-contention effect on the trace export path that kicks in once concurrent in-flight spans cross some threshold, rather than a smooth linear cost per request. Might be worth profiling `trace_async.py`'s buffer/flush path under concurrent load to see if there's a lock or queue that serializes once request volume rises (in our TP=8 investigation, we found `trace_req_finish()`/`abort()` and `__getstate__` all trigger unconditional flushes regardless of the configured threshold, and `trace_req_start()`'s `tracer.start_span()` + `propagate.inject()` calls are synchronous OTel API calls on the request path — happy to dig further if maintainers think that's a productive direction).
- Production guidance: for small/mid TP deployments (TP<=2-4), default trace config (level=2, async on) is fine as-is. For TP=8-class deployments, overhead is materially higher and level-tuning is the effective lever — but this should probably be stated explicitly since it's not obvious from the trace docs which regime a given deployment falls into.

## Attachments

- `report-en.pdf` — full benchmark report with charts (ttft_p99 / itl_p99 / e2e_p50 / throughput vs. concurrency, delta% overview, GPU/CPU resource usage)
[Uploading report-en.pdf…]()

items.title: [Bug] Potential hybrid GDN Radix-cache selected-logprob drift on repeated branch scoring
items.author: furedericca-lab
items.body_excerpt:
## Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues and did not find an existing report that fully covers this request shape.
- [ ] I have not re-run this on today's latest main; the reproduction was observed on pinned main commit `2f5c9ac43d76eef11e8561c89c55a79db7db715a` (2026-09-25).
- [x] Environment details and a standalone `/generate` reproducer are included below.
- [x] This is a possible correctness issue rather than a general usage question.
- [x] Report is in English.

## Describe the bug

With a hybrid GDN Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 checkpoint, repeated selected-token logprob scoring is stable when Radix Cache is disabled, but the first Radix-enabled branch scoring pass differs substantially from subsequent identical passes.

The observation is:

| Cache configuration | Max repeated selected-logprob delta | Pattern |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Unified Radix Cache enabled | `2.551527976989746` | run 1 differs; runs 2 and 3 match exactly |
| Radix Cache disabled | `0.0` | runs 1, 2 and 3 match exactly |

The prefix is explicitly warmed before the repeated branch batches. With Radix enabled, the server log reports `#cached-token: 0` for the first branch batch and `#cached-token: 128` for later identical branch batches. With Radix disabled, the three repeated branch batches are bit-stable.

This strongly correlates the drift with the cache-hit execution path, but I do **not** want to over-attribute the root cause: the current evidence does not prove that a specific GDN recurrent-state checkpoint, restore, split, or other hybrid-cache internal operation is responsible.

This was found while gating a decision workload that consumes candidate-token logprobs directly, so cache-hit equivalence matters even when the top-1 decision itself does not change.

Related work:

- #22935 — Mamba Radix cache prefix/split behavior
- #34899 — bit-exact correctness coverage for Unified Radix Cache
- #38625 — interior/no-buffer checkpoint work

I am not assuming that #22935 or #38625 has the same root cause or fully covers this request shape. In particular, I would like to know whether a shared prefix followed by divergent option branches is expected to preserve selected-token logprobs under deterministic inference when the later identical branch requests hit the hybrid cache.

## Environment

Tested environment:

- SGLang source: `2f5c9ac43d76eef11e8561c89c55a79db7db715a`
- SGLang package: `0.5.21.dev612+g2f5c9ac43`
- Model: `ukisai/Swift-1.5-Qwen3.8-27b-NVFP4`
- Model revision: `332d277a083ca395aa2f822842b82f5f2f3913a2`
- Architecture: `Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration`, hybrid GDN / full attention
- Quantization: ModelOpt mixed FP8/NVFP4
- GPUs: 2 × NVIDIA RTX 5090 (SM120), TP=2
- NVIDIA driver: `610.57.04`
- Kernel: `7.0.0-34-generic`
- Python: `3.13.11`
- PyTorch: `2.14.0a0.post20260925` (CUDA 13.4)
- Triton: `3.7.0`
- `sglang-kernel==0.4.7`
- `flash-attn-4==4.0.0b19`
- Attention backend: Triton
- Deterministic inference: enabled
- Prefill CUDA Graph: disabled
- Decode CUDA Graph: retained
- Unified Radix Cache: enabled for the failing case
- Observed Mamba strategy: `extra_buffer`
- Comparison case: identical server settings plus only `--disable-radix-cache`

A literal `python3 -m sglang.check_env` dump was not retained for this run; the exact pinned runtime versions above are from the same project environment used for the reproduction.

## Reproduction

Launch the candidate server with Radix Cache enabled:

```bash
python -m sglang.launch_server \

items.title: [Bug] Hybrid-SWA + radix cache: admission livelock when the SWA prefix lock pins a finished request's untrimmed last chunk
items.author: bill-h-lin
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

With a hybrid-SWA model, the radix cache on and a tight SWA pool, the scheduler can stop admitting a request forever: 1 waiting, 0 running, GPU idle, no log line. We hit it on MiMo-V2.6-Flash (sliding window 128, page size 1) and traced it to `SWAComponent.acquire_component_lock` pinning a whole tree node that holds a finished request's untrimmed last chunk of SWA, instead of one window.

**Sequence** (`--chunked-prefill-size 8192`, `--swa-full-tokens-ratio 0.06448` → SWA pool 8,451, `--context-length 131072`, `--max-running-requests 1`, overlap scheduler on):

1. A 32,768-token request with `max_new_tokens=1` (it finishes at its first token).
2. A request with the same 32,768 tokens, a different next token, then 4,999 more (37,768 in all).

Request 2 matches 32,768 cached tokens, needs 5,001 SWA slots and never runs. `/v1/loads` stayed at 1 waiting, 0 running for 43 minutes. The same sequence runs fine with `--chunked-prefill-size 4096` or with a 16,643-token SWA pool.

### Root cause (line numbers on `main` @ 6624999385)

1. Under the overlap scheduler, a request that finishes at its first token still gets one decode step prepared before its prefill result is processed: `alloc_for_decode` (`allocation.py:587`) commits one more token, and `release_kv_cache` → `insert_req(req, up_to=req.owned_kv_len())` keys `(origin_input_ids + output_ids)[:kv_committed_len]`. So it is cached with 32,769 tokens, its output token included.
2. `cleanup_after_caching_req` (`swa.py:1011`, the `not is_finished` guard at `:1023`) frees out-of-window SWA only for unfinished requests. So the request's final 8,192-token chunk keeps its SWA live. In the tree that is a node `[24,576, 32,641)` holding 8,065 live SWA slots, then the 128-token window leaf that `_maybe_split_leaf_for_swa_lock` (`swa.py:555`) capped "so locking it pins only one window".
3. Request 2 diverges at position 32,768, so its match splits the window leaf into 127 + 1. `acquire_component_lock` (`swa.py:811`) pins whole nodes until it has covered 128 tokens: the 127-token node, then the whole 8,065-token parent. **8,192 slots pinned** for a 128-token window.
4. `SWAPrefillBudget.check_prefill` (`prefill_budget.py:213`) sees 5,001 needed and 259 available. Since 5,001 fits an empty pool, it is not a permanent shortfall ("Transient pressure waits"), so the request waits for running requests to free slots. None exist.

The bound: only an untrimmed final chunk holds more than about one window of live SWA, so the lock over-pins by at most one chunk, while a request needs at most one chunk + 1. A pool of 2 × chunk + window + slack therefore always leaves enough (by 258 slots here), and one of chunk + window + slack, as above, can deadlock whenever a request reuses the path of one that finished at its first token (`max_tokens=1`, an immediate EOS or stop) and diverges inside its last window.

### Reproduction

- End to end: on a GPU (RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell) with SGLang at 542a043, reproduced with the sequence above. That build carries local changes (an MoE expert-offload tier, and #41263's chunked-prefill SWA free order); none of them changes the radix tree, the SWA lock or `check_prefill` (#41263 only moves when a chunked request's out-of-window SWA is freed).
- On CPU, on the same build: the same four steps, with the scheduler's own `UnifiedRadixCache`, SWA allocator and `PrefillAdder` plus the orphan decode step, give 259 / 5,001 available / needed (not admitted) at chunk 8,192 / pool 8,451, and admit at chunk 4,096 (4,355 / 4,097) and at pool 16,643 (8,451 / 5,001).
- On `main`: the unit test in the linked PR builds a live parent + capped window leaf, matches a key that diverges on the last page and locks it; the lock pins the whole parent. Links 1, 2 and 4 are unchanged in the code on `main`; we have not run the end-to-end sequence on `main`.

### Proposed fix

In the lock walk, split a live, unlocked device-SWA node that is longer than what the window still needs, so only the in-window tail is pinned (the same idea as the leaf cap, applied to whatever node the walk reaches). PR: #41580.

Related: #27210 caps compute locks by splitting the lock's endpoint node. It does not cover this case: at page size 1 the match ends inside the capped leaf, the endpoint is shorter than a window, and the over-pin comes from its parent. #32379 fixed a different SWA admission livelock (decode headroom double-counted for cached resumes).

### Environment

SGLang 542a043 (end to end) and `main` 6624999385 (unit test), CUDA 13.0, torch cu130, one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (sm120), `--tp-size 1`, radix cache on, overlap scheduler on.
