items.title: [Bug] GLM-5.3-Flash on SM120: fa4 attention backend crashes at CUDA-graph capture (hybrid extend reshape) — triton is the only working backend
items.author: Lei-010
items.body_excerpt:
# GLM-5.3-Flash on SM120 (RTX PRO 6000): attention backend matrix — fa4 crashes on hybrid extend, triton is the only working path

## Environment

- 8× NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (SM120, 96 GB each), driver/CUDA as stock
- SGLang `lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.20` docker image (built 2026-09-18)
- Model: `zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash` (official FP8 weights, TP8)
- Draft (for spec decoding legs): `incoai/GLM-5.3-Flash-DFlash2` (DFlash2DraftModel, sha256-verified)
- `--trust-remote-code`, `--context-length 131072`, `--mem-fraction-static 0.85`

## Summary

We systematically tested every attention backend that boots for Glm5Next on SM120. **Only `triton` works.** Both `flashinfer`-default (trtllm-gen fmha — already tracked in #40558) and `fa4` crash during engine init / CUDA-graph capture. The fa4 failure is a distinct bug: a shape reshape error in `forward_extend` that also reproduces **without** speculative decoding, i.e. it is not DFlash2-specific.

## Backend matrix (all TP8)

| Config | Result |
|---|---|
| default (trtllm-gen fmha) | ❌ `TllmGenFmhaRunner ... Unsupported architecture` (see #40558) |
| `--attention-backend fa4` + DFLASH | ❌ see below |
| `--attention-backend fa4`, no spec | ❌ same error — **reproduces without spec decoding** |
| `--prefill-attention-backend fa4 --attention-backend triton` + DFLASH | ❌ same error at decode capture |
| `--attention-backend triton` + DFLASH | ✅ healthy, accept len 2.73–3.90 |
| `--attention-backend triton`, no spec | ✅ healthy |

## fa4 failure signature

```python
RuntimeError: shape '[-1, 64, 8, 0]' is invalid for input of size 753975296
```

Stack (abridged):

```
sglang/srt/model_executor/runner/decode_cuda_graph_runner.py, line 464, in __init__ → self.capture()
  ... capture_one_shape → self.backend.capture_one
sglang/srt/layers/radix_attention.py, line 290, in forward
sglang/srt/layers/attention/hybrid_linear_attn_backend.py, line 1327, in forward → 1276, forward_extend
sglang/srt/layers/attention/flashattention_backend.py, line 1704, in forward_extend
RuntimeError: shape '[-1, 64, 8, 0]' is invalid for input of size 753975296
```

Observations:

1. The failing view has a trailing **0** dimension — with Glm5Next's hybrid layout (KDA linear-attention layers interleaved with full-attention layers) the fa4 `forward_extend` path receives a zero-length draft/extend token axis and `reshape` fails instead of short-circuiting.
2. `flash_attention_v4_sm120` (selected automatically when `device_capability[0] == 12`) handles decode `flash_attn_with_kvcache`, but the extend path reshaping assumes a non-empty second batch axis.
3. Repro is deterministic across ≥3 containers; failure occurs at first CUDA-graph capture (bs=48, ~90 s after weights load).

## Reproducer

```bash
docker run --gpus all --network host --ipc host \
  -v /path/GLM-5.3-Flash:/model:ro \
  --entrypoint python3 lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.20 \
  -m sglang.launch_server --model /model --tp 8 --trust-remote-code \
  --attention-backend fa4 --port 8000 --mem-fraction-static 0.85
# → RuntimeError: shape '[-1, 64, 8, 0]' is invalid ... at decode graph capture
```

## Working config (for anyone blocked on this)

```bash
... --attention-backend triton [--speculative-algorithm DFLASH --speculative-draft-model-path /draft]
```

With `triton`, GLM-5.3-Flash FP8 TP8 serves fine on SM120, and DFLASH spec decoding reaches accept len ~3.3 (block_size 8). Note prefill throughput with triton is low (~140 tok/s on an 8K prompt, single stream), which is why a working fa4/flashinfer path on SM120 matters.

Happy to provide full logs if useful.

items.title: [Bug] `--bf16-gemm-backend gemv` is accepted but unquantized linear layers never use it
items.author: SamMausberg
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

`--bf16-gemm-backend gemv` is accepted, but unquantized linear layers never use it.

The flag loads the Hopper BF16 GEMV in `initialize_bf16_gemm_config` ([unquant.py#L225-L236](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/41cbe65de05b209f3263942389267f79bd749d6a/python/sglang/srt/layers/quantization/unquant.py#L225-L236)), and `_bf16_gemm_dispatch_impl` uses it for one-row GEMMs ([#L327-L334](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/41cbe65de05b209f3263942389267f79bd749d6a/python/sglang/srt/layers/quantization/unquant.py#L327-L334)). But `UnquantizedLinearMethod.apply` calls that dispatcher only when the backend is `cutedsl` ([#L484-L501](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/41cbe65de05b209f3263942389267f79bd749d6a/python/sglang/srt/layers/quantization/unquant.py#L484-L501)). Otherwise, on CUDA, it returns `F.linear`.

The dispatcher's only other callers are the packed GDN input projection in `qwen3_5.py`, which on CUDA only Qwen4-Exp finalizes, and `apply_with_addend` (Nemotron-H's latent projection). So on SM90 the server accepts `--bf16-gemm-backend gemv`, and every other unquantized linear layer, for example all of Qwen3.5's, still runs on cuBLAS. It has been this way since the backend was added in #34859.

Expected: the flag's help text says it chooses "the backend for unquantized BF16 GEMM operations". So `--bf16-gemm-backend gemv` should route one-row BF16 GEMMs in `UnquantizedLinearMethod.apply` through `_bf16_gemm_dispatch_impl`, as `cutedsl` does. If `gemv` is meant only for the dispatcher's existing callers, the help text should say so, and the server should not accept the flag on its own as if it applied to every unquantized linear layer. (`gemv` arrived with the Qwen3.8 support, whose packed input projection is one of those callers.)

The kernel looks worth reaching. In a per-GEMM microbenchmark on a GH200 (SM90), `hopper_bf16_gemv` was the fastest kernel for every Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B projection at M = 1. Its outputs were bitwise equal to cuBLAS's on 99.6-100% of elements. I have not measured serving, since the kernel cannot be reached there.

<details>
<summary>Microbenchmark</summary>

- In isolation, against `F.linear`, using the projection shapes of Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B with each layer's real weights. One CUDA graph per kernel compared, torch 2.13.0+cu130 and cuBLAS 13.1.
- At M = 1, `hopper_bf16_gemv` was the fastest kernel for every projection. For example, 8.57 us against 11.20 us for the 2560 x 4096 `out_proj`, and 2.75 against 5.43 us for the 64 x 2560 `in_proj_ba`.
- Run on SGLang bd66ce34, whose GEMV sources are identical to main's.
- [Method and results](https://github.com/SamMausberg/verified-progress/blob/dbebf4000a30e9283fc9428647a881e1b0f4ad2a/evidence/backbone/README.md#the-fastest-kernel-reading-the-same-weights).

</details>

If `apply` starts dispatching for `gemv`, it should also get a guard. `initialize_bf16_gemm_config` rejects `cutedsl` under `--enable-deterministic-inference` because it is batch-size dependent ([#L237-L242](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/41cbe65de05b209f3263942389267f79bd749d6a/python/sglang/srt/layers/quantization/unquant.py#L237-L242)). It does not reject `gemv`, which is batch-size dependent in the same way: it takes only M = 1, so a request's outputs would depend on whether it was decoded alone.

### Reproduction

This runs on CPU and replaces the GEMV with a recording stub, so it needs no GPU:

```python
import torch

from sglang.srt.layers.quantization import unquant

# State that initialize_bf16_gemm_config() leaves for --bf16-gemm-backend gemv,
# with the Hopper GEMV replaced by a recording stub.
calls = []
unquant._BF16_GEMM_BACKEND = unquant.Bf16GemmBackend("gemv")
unquant._use_hopper_bf16_gemv = lambda m, n, k: m == 1
unquant._hopper_bf16_gemv = lambda x, w: calls.append(tuple(x.shape)) or x @ w.t()

layer = torch.nn.Linear(64, 32, bias=False, dtype=torch.bfloat16).requires_grad_(False)
x = torch.randn(1, 64, dtype=torch.bfloat16)

unquant.UnquantizedLinearMethod().apply(layer, x)
print("GEMV calls from UnquantizedLinearMethod.apply:", len(calls))
unquant._bf16_gemm_dispatch_impl(x, layer.weight, None)
print("GEMV calls from _bf16_gemm_dispatch_impl:", len(calls))
```

On main at 41cbe65de0 it prints:

```
GEMV calls from UnquantizedLinearMethod.apply: 0
GEMV calls from _bf16_gemm_dispatch_impl: 1
```

### Environment

The reproduction above ran on main at 41cbe65de05b209f3263942389267f79bd749d6a, CPU only. Below is `python3 -m sglang.check_env` on the GH200, from the venv the reproduction used. Its `sglang` line is that editable install, built at 40e1bb0f3. The microbenchmark ran in SGLang bd66ce34's venv, with the same torch, CUDA and driver.

<details>
<summary>check_env output</summary>

```

CUDA available: True
GPU 0: NVIDIA GH200 480GB
GPU 0 Compute Capability: 9.0

items.title: [Bug] DeepSeek V4 Pro loading on Lustre takes 95 minutes despite prefetch; limiting tensor-copy workers reduces it to 3.3 minutes
items.author: janbernloehr
items.body_excerpt:
## Describe the bug

Loading a DeepSeek V4 Pro FP8/NVFP4 checkpoint from Lustre on one 8-GPU B300
node takes approximately 95 minutes inside SGLang's model-loading phase,
even with `--weight-loader-prefetch-checkpoints` enabled. Prefetch finishes
in approximately 62–73 seconds, while the longest wait for outstanding
per-tensor loader futures is approximately 94 minutes.

In one sequential A/B experiment on the same node and container image,
changing only the tensor-copy executor in
`DeepseekV4ForCausalLM.load_weights` from the Python default of 32 workers
per rank to two workers per rank reduced the reported model-loading time
from **5717.04 s to 199.72 s**. Startup through HTTP readiness fell from
**6115.90 s to 325.52 s**. Both arms completed and served benchmark requests.

This concerns the executor used for per-tensor weight-loader calls, which
is separate from the checkpoint-prefetch and shard-reader thread counts.
The two arms retained mmap, four prefetch threads per rank, the serial
shard iterator, TP=8, and the same server arguments. DP-attention was disabled.

## Related upstream reports

- [Issue #20842](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/20842) proposed
  coordinated checkpoint prefetch for network storage. This report covers
  a remaining slowdown with that prefetch path already enabled.
- [Issue #29268](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/29268) reports
  DeepSeek loading hangs on network storage with async mmap-to-CUDA copies.
  It was closed after a suggestion to enable prefetch; the issue has no
  linked closing PR. Our case adds evidence with prefetch already enabled
  and without DP-attention. Our baseline eventually completed, so we are
  reporting an extreme slowdown rather than proving a deadlock.
- [PR #37806](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/37806), currently
  open, proposes automatically enabling prefetch on NFS/Lustre. Its stated
  scope leaves `should_async_load()` and executor width unchanged. Since
  prefetch was explicitly enabled in both of our arms, auto-enabling that
  flag alone would not change our configuration.
- [PR #29821](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/29821) explored
  synchronous DeepSeek V4 tensor loading for an AMD/HIP slow-tail case.
  It closed without merging. That is related evidence about copy
  concurrency, but a different backend and experiment.

At inspected upstream commit
[`e8fab85a02c23e01260fb1adb030b00886f5999d`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/e8fab85a02c23e01260fb1adb030b00886f5999d/python/sglang/srt/models/deepseek_v4.py#L5556),
the DeepSeek V4 loader still constructs `ThreadPoolExecutor()` without an
explicit worker limit. Its
[`should_async_load()` helper](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/e8fab85a02c23e01260fb1adb030b00886f5999d/python/sglang/srt/model_loader/utils.py#L295)
still selects ordinary CPU tensors for async loading. This is a source
inspection; the measurements below use the pinned version listed under
Tested revision, not a GPU reproduction on latest main.

## Measurements

One allocation, one node, default arm first and two-worker arm second:

| Measurement | Default: 32 copy workers/rank | 2 copy workers/rank |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Startup through HTTP readiness | 6115.90 s | 325.52 s |
| Native model-loading duration, maximum of 8 ranks | 5717.04 s | 199.72 s |
| Outstanding copy-futures wait, maximum of 8 ranks | 5632.56 s | 131.71 s |
| Prefetch completion duration, range across ranks | 62.04–73.11 s | 66.59–75.82 s |
| Major page faults during copy-futures wait, sum across 8 rank processes | 143,578,881 | 318 |
| MHC JIT compile duration, maximum of 8 ranks | 289.0 s | 2.1 s |
| MHC rank synchronization, maximum of 8 ranks | 3880.9 s | 41.6 s |

The model-loading timer includes nested phases; these rows must not be
added together. The futures-wait measurement starts after iterator
consumption, so it does not cover all work performed by the executor.
Per-rank phase durations and fault deltas came from begin/end instrumentation
and process resource counters, present in both arms.

During the slow arm, sampled thread wait channels included
`cl_sync_io_wait` and `folio_wait_bit_common`. Earlier-finishing ranks then
spent a long time in MHC rank synchronization. This points to the loading
and page-fault path as a useful target, rather than treating the barrier
wait alone as the cause. We did **not** capture native CUDA stacks proving
the driver-lock mechanism described in #29268.

For a limited serving smoke test, aggregate output throughput with 1000-token
input/output requests was:

| Concurrency | Default (output tokens/s) | 2 workers (output tokens/s) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 110.30 | 109.32 |
| 16 | 1244.75 | 1294.89 |
| 64 | 2976.88 | 3051.67 |
| 128 | 4847.49 | 4847.73 |

These are single observations, not statistical performance or accuracy results.

## Reproduction

Use a single node with eight B300 GPUs and the checkpoint on a Lustre mount.
The measured checkpoint was `nvidia/DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813-NVFP4`, revision
prefix `a6ed51e`, with **66 safetensors shards totaling 941,115,855,096 bytes
(876.48 GiB)**. The checkpoint contains mixed FP8/NVFP4 weights and E8M0
scales. It was already downloaded before either arm.

Run the pinned SGLang revision below. The command below uses generic paths and ports and omits the site's
NUMA binding. Both measured arms used identical NUMA placement:

```bash
python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path /path/on/lustre/DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813-NVFP4 \
  --served-model-name deepseek-v4-pro-861b \
  --tp 8 --nnodes 1 --node-rank 0 \
  --dist-init-addr 127.0.0.1:29500 \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.79 \
  --context-length 2048 \
  --cuda-graph-max-bs-prefill 2048 \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 \
  --enable-metrics \
  --weight-loader-prefetch-checkpoints \
  --trust-remote-code \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 30000
```

For the second arm, stop all server processes and apply this one-line change
inside `DeepseekV4Fo

items.title: [Bug][KV Cache] nvfp4 KV silently reuses the checkpoint's fp8-calibrated k/v_scale as NVFP4 global scale → deterministic long-context corruption (single-variable proof, sm_120)
items.author: chengye75-star
items.body_excerpt:
## TL;DR

Serving an NVFP4 KV cache (`--kv-cache-dtype nvfp4`) on a checkpoint whose `quantization_config.kv_cache_scheme` says `num_bits: 8` (e.g. unsloth's NVFP4 quants, which ship fp8-calibrated `k_scale`/`v_scale`) silently corrupts the KV cache: 32 tiny `[1]` bf16 scalars are loaded verbatim and consumed as the NVFP4 **global scale**. Removing exactly those 64 **bytes** flips long-context needle from 1/4 to 4/4 on an otherwise bit-identical 22.5 GB checkpoint. No log line ever mentions scales. Related but distinct: [#36121](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/36121) (fp4 scales not traveling through HiCache host transfers; footnote has our hybrid-path measurement), [#39942](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/39942) (fp8 KV scales silently *dropped* — opposite failure, same blind spot: nothing validates KV scale provenance).

## Setup

SGLang 0.5.21 (official PyPI wheel), torch 2.13.0+cu130, 2× RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB (sm_120, TP2), driver 595.91.07. Model: `unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4` (hybrid 16 full-attention + 48 GDN layers, head_dim 256, compressed-tensors). Flags: `--kv-cache-dtype nvfp4 --prefill-attention-backend flashinfer --decode-attention-backend trtllm_mha --disable-prefill-cuda-graph --context-length 195000 --page-size 64`, greedy, chat format. (Same rig as my [#36010 evidence post](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/36010#issuecomment-5788493111); this bug is **independent of spec decode** — it hits the plain no-spec nvfp4 path.)

## Symptom

With scales as shipped, long-context retrieval collapses: needle **1/4 (d50) / 0/4 (d500)**; answers degenerate into question-echoing after a short thinking block. Everything else looks healthy — boot logs clean, short prompts / tool calls / vision normal. Deterministic: completion tokens reproduce byte-for-byte across boots and repeats.

## Root cause (source walk; mechanism marked as inference)

1. The checkpoint carries 32 per-layer `*.self_attn.{k,v}_scale` tensors — `[1]` bf16 scalars calibrated for **fp8** KV (`config.json → kv_cache_scheme: {num_bits: 8, static_minmax, symmetric}`).
2. *(inference, from source)* At load, `weight_utils.maybe_remap_kv_scale_name()` attaches them to the attention modules unconditionally; the fp4 path (`layers/attention/kvfp4_tensor.py`, comment: *"The KV cache path passes preloaded per-layer scales already on device"*) consumes them as the NVFP4 `global_scale` in `x_fp4 * block_scale * global_scale`.
3. *(inference)* Nothing validates the checkpoint's KV scheme against the runtime `--kv-cache-dtype`. An fp8-geometry scalar (amax/448 family) applied under NVFP4 geometry (amax/6 family) is off by ~75× → every stored K/V is systematically mis-scaled.

## Single-variable proof (same box, same day, same prompts)

| config (one variable per row) | needle d50 | needle d500 |
|---|---|---|
| unsloth + nvfp4, scales as shipped | 1/4 | 0/4 |
| **unsloth + nvfp4, 32 scale tensors stripped (64 bytes total), `kv_cache_scheme=null`** | **4/4** | **4/4** |
| unsloth + fp8_e4m3 (scale geometry matches dtype) | 4/4 | 2/4 |
| `sakamakismile/Qwen3.8-27B-MTP-NVFP4` + nvfp4 (checkpoint ships no scales) | 4/4 | 1/4 |

The stripped copy is a hardlink farm with only `model.safetensors` rewritten (header offsets recomputed; post-check: 0 leftover scale tensors) — the rest of the ~22.5 GB is byte-identical. Same-checkpoint before/after is the control: 64 bytes of metadata move the score by three needle questions.

## Why this is not an edge case

The filename pairing (`…-NVFP4` weights + `--kv-cache-dtype nvfp4`) is the natural reading, and unsloth's NVFP4 releases ship fp8-calibrated KV scales as a matter of their recipe. Everyone doing that pairing gets silently wrong KV with zero log evidence; needle-style evals are the only thing that notices, and most people don't run those. Checkpoints without shipped scales (dynamic path, row 4) are unaffected — which is presumably why this hasn't surfaced loudly.

## Asks

1. **Validate at load**: if the checkpoint carries `k_scale`/`v_scale` and `kv_cache_scheme.num_bits` disagrees with `server_args.kv_cache_dtype`, warn loudly and skip them (fall back to dynamic scales) instead of reinterpreting an fp8 scalar as an fp4 global scale.
2. Checkpoints whose scheme says `num_bits: 4` (e.g. NVIDIA/ModelOpt NVFP4-KV exports) *should* consume their scales — the bug is specifically the mismatched pair, not scale loading per se.
3. Optional `--load-kv-scales {auto,never}` for quick A/B without safetensors surgery (our workaround rewrites a 22 GB file's header — works in 3 minutes, but terrifying to recommend).

## Verified workaround & production numbers

Drop the 32 `*.self_attn.[kv]_scale` tensors from `model.safetensors`, rewrite header offsets, set `quantization_config.kv_cache_scheme = null`. The healthy config now serves our production: 185K-token cold prefill ~176 s, decode ~25 tok/s; with HiCache L2 (20 GB host, `write_through`, `page_first`, slru) a post-eviction 185K re-ask lands in **2.4–5.5 s** (vs 178 s cold) with the secret code word intact across the L2 round-trip (2/2 rounds, backup counters confirm real transfers); needle 4/4+4/4; tool-calls live. sm_120 hybrid-attention reference points are thin here — happy to post logs/transcripts.

Footnote re #36121: its fail-fast covers paths our hybrid assembly doesn't traverse (UnifiedRadixCache picks host pools in `hybrid_pool_assembler`), and in our exact combo (nvfp4 + HiCache + page_first + write_through) the fp4 block scales evidently *do* survive L2 as measured above — so the guard as drafted wouldn't cover this configuration either way. Full hybrid-path measurements posted as a review note on that PR.

items.title: [RFC]: Limit the use of envvars in vLLM
items.author: zhuohan123
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation.

vLLM's envvars are on the edge of getting out of control. There are many envvars should instead be configs. Like the attention backend, all2all kernel backend, and even there is a flag to control KV cache layout. envvars are evil because:

1. It is equivalent of using global variables everywhere in the code, which is a bad programming practice.
2. envvars have no advanced structure like, hierarchy, typechecks, etc. 

In summary, I think envvars are the kind of thing that is very easy to add so people tend to add envvars as the shortest path to implement their feature, but this can quickly becomes unmanageable and makes the project very hard to use. 

### Proposed Change.

I think we should:

1. Spend some effort on reviewing the current envvars and move many of them to configs.
2. Have very strict bar on what can be an envvar and question every new envvars in vllm.

### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

_No response_

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [RFC]: Bound frontend drain latency for bulk aborts and long non-streaming completions
items.author: aoshen02
items.body_excerpt:
# Motivation.

Bulk abort is expected to be the fast path for pausing online RL generation,
but its latency can scale with all output retained by the frontend. In a
DP8/EP8/TP1 deployment with eight API server processes, aborting 2,000
non-streaming completion requests at a reported approximately 3,500 generated
tokens per request produced 96-177 seconds of frontend tail latency. Actual
returned means were 4,850-5,445 tokens because generation continued while the
frontend lagged. The engines had already accepted the abort; API processes
were still draining queued outputs,
detokenizing sampled logprobs, constructing response models, materializing
Python dictionaries, and encoding JSON.

The largest amplifier was API-process load imbalance. The parent enabled
`SO_REUSEPORT`, but all workers inherited copies of one socket and therefore
shared one accept queue. In one run, the busiest API process owned 1,492 of
2,000 requests. Balanced DP-engine load did not imply balanced frontend load.

This matters beyond RL pause. The same work appears when long non-streaming
completion requests finish or are aborted together, especially when sampled
logprobs or token IDs are returned. A fast model can produce outputs faster
than one Python frontend process can consume and serialize them.

This RFC follows the completed pause/resume API RFC #32103, whose follow-up
list explicitly called out better abort handling. It does not change pause
mode semantics or DPEP coordination. At RFC creation, searches of issues and open PRs using
pause/abort, frontend serialization, logprobs, API server, and reuseport terms
found no overlapping proposal or implementation. Related work is
complementary:

- #56754 drains in-process requests before sleep.
- #52875 reduces per-frame cost for simple streaming completions.
- #47933 preserves `finish_reason="abort"` for scale-out token streams.

## Reproduction and evidence

The primary setup used two GB200 nodes, DP8/EP8/TP1, eight API servers, 2,000
requests, and sampled `logprobs=0`. A four-layer checkpoint made the frontend
bottleneck easy to reproduce; the final candidate was also validated with the
full 78-layer MXFP8 checkpoint.

On the reduced model, the unmodified frontend took 96.18 and 177.12 seconds
from pause to its last response serialization in two runs. The measured
seven-file candidate took 3.38 seconds at 7.28 million returned tokens, and
5.18 seconds at 10.08 million returned tokens versus 96.18 seconds at 10.89
million unmodified. The six-file patch proposed here differs only by removal
of a null-result lazy-context change and was itself measured as the valid
2.924-second `no_lazy_context` leave-one-out arm.

On the full model, one unmodified baseline was 6.97 seconds frontend and 7.44
seconds through all client results, with a balanced 187-270 requests per
frontend. Four additional unmodified runs using a two-process client that
concentrated connections on fewer workers reached 8.92-21.10-second frontend
tails, with 462-907 requests on the busiest process. Two used the 3,500-token
trigger and two used 3,800. They have no patched counterpart and are baseline
evidence, not an A/B comparison.

Two seven-file-candidate repeats completed frontend serialization in 3.63 and
3.90 seconds and all client parsing in 3.81 and 4.19 seconds; waiting for both
the pause HTTP response and all client results took 3.81 and 7.67 seconds. This
validates parity and absence of regression at full scale. It does not reproduce
the reduced model's 100+ second tail in a matched A/B or isolate the listener
change. GPU response parity was also captured on this measured seven-file
candidate; equivalence to the shipped six-file state rests on hash identity
with the measured `no_lazy_context` arm rather than a separate post-trim GPU
capture.

We then ran an eight-arm, same-allocation leave-one-out experiment. Every arm
aborted and rendered exactly 2,000 responses. The complete candidate was
bracketed at 2.953 and 3.054 seconds, giving a 0.102-second drift bound.

| Removed optimization | Frontend-tail regression |
| --- | ---: |
| Independent `SO_REUSEPORT` listener per API worker | +6.199 s |
| Bounded single-token decode cache | +1.075 s |
| Flat sampled-logprob storage | +1.039 s |
| Direct Pydantic JSON serialization | +1.176 s |
| Explicit event-loop yields | +0.125 s |
| Lazy byte-fallback context lookup | -0.080 s |

The first four effects are 10-61 times the measured run drift. The lazy
context change was removed. Event-loop yields are retained for a deterministic
fairness invariant: without them, a ready output queue can consume 100 batches
before a waiting control task runs. Leave-one-out effects interact and must
not be summed to reconstruct the original 100+ second result.

The listener result is one stochastic draw for a client opening approximately
2,000 connections. Its +6.199-second effect is not a general point estimate;
keep-alive-heavy clients can see a different distribution or no benefit.

## Implementation update — 2026-09-23

Phase 1 is proposed in **#58278: [Frontend] Give API workers independent reuseport listeners** (draft, not merged). The narrowed implementation changes only listener selection and per-worker socket ownership. General CLI startup/shutdown behavior stays identical to the base; lifecycle refactoring is deferred. The following GPU measurements belong to historical head `377818881b`, not the current revision.

A prior **listener-only** GPU/HTTP ABBA experiment completed on node18 using one node with four GB200s, four-layer HY4-preview BF16, DP4/EP4/TP1, four default API processes, 250 requests per replica (1,000 total), non-streaming completions and sampled `logprobs=0`.

| Metric | Shared listener (A, two runs) | Independent listeners (B, two runs) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Last frontend serialization | 8.298 / 10.698 s | 4.551 / 4.746 s |
| Median frontend serialization tail | 9.498 s | 4.649 s (51.1% lower) |
| Last client response body received | 9

items.title: [Feature] L1/L2/L3 cache hit rate observability — Prometheus metrics, OTel spans & per-request JSONL trace
items.author: grissomsh
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation

LMCache's current `PrometheusLogger` provides basic metrics (`time_to_retrieve`, `num_retrieve_requests`), but is missing:

1. **Per-tier cache hit rate** — no way to distinguish whether a hit came from L2 (CPU RAM), L3 (NVMe Disk), or a remote backend.
2. **TTFT decomposition** — `frontend_latency` (API server → engine core) and per-request `kv_lookup_time` / `kv_retrieve_time` are not surfaced.
3. **Per-request tracing** — no way to correlate cache-hit details to an individual request for debugging latency spikes.

These gaps make it hard to answer operational questions like: *"Why did TTFT spike — was it a slow disk read, CPU cache contention, or GPU prefix cache eviction?"*

---

### Design Goals

1. **Three-layer observability model**: throughput → latency → cache hit rate
2. **Minimally invasive**: extend existing `LMCStatsMonitor`, `PrometheusLogger`, and `cache_engine` — no breaking API changes
3. **TP-aware**: cross-process bridge via `/dev/shm` for Worker ↔ EngineCore per-request data relay when TP > 1
4. **Self-verifying**: every trace carries token identity equations for automated correctness validation

---

### Proposed Design

#### Layer 1 — Throughput: Token Source Decomposition

```
Tokens/s = local_compute + L1_hit + L2_hit + L3_hit + remote_hit
```

**Approach**: Extend `cache_engine.py`'s `retrieve()` / `retrieve_layer()` to classify hit tokens by storage backend. Add a `_BACKEND_NAME_TO_HIT_TIER` mapping:

| Backend | Tier |
|---------|------|
| `LocalCPUBackend` | L2 |
| `LocalDiskBackend` / `GdsBackend` | L3 |
| `RemoteBackend` | Remote |

**New Prometheus metrics** (6 total):

| Metric | Type |
|--------|------|
| `lmcache:l2_hit_tokens` / `lmcache:num_l2_hit_tokens` | Histogram + Counter |
| `lmcache:l3_hit_tokens` / `lmcache:num_l3_hit_tokens` | Histogram + Counter |
| `lmcache:remote_hit_tokens` / `lmcache:num_remote_hit_tokens` | Histogram + Counter |

#### Layer 2 — Latency: TTFT Decomposition

```
TTFT = frontend_latency + queue_time + prefill_time
prefill_time ⊃ kv_lookup_time + kv_retrieve_time
```

**Approach**: Add `LMCacheKVConnectorStats` (extending vLLM's `KVConnectorStats`) on the vLLM side, and expose per-request timing through `vllm_v1_adapter.py`'s `request_finished()` via `EngineCoreOutput.kv_transfer_params`.

**New Prometheus metrics** (9 bridge metrics + 1 framework metric):

| Metric | Type | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| `vllm:lmcache_kv_lookup_seconds` | Histogram | KV lookup latency |
| `vllm:lmcache_kv_retrieve_seconds` | Histogram | KV retrieve latency |
| `vllm:lmcache_retrieve_process_tokens_seconds` | Histogram | Retrieve: process_tokens phase |
| `vllm:lmcache_retrieve_to_gpu_seconds` | Histogram | Retrieve: CPU→GPU DMA phase |
| `vllm:lmcache_num_l2_hit_tokens` | Counter | vLLM-side L2 bridge |
| `vllm:lmcache_num_l3_hit_tokens` | Counter | vLLM-side L3 bridge |
| `vllm:lmcache_num_remote_hit_tokens` | Counter | vLLM-side remote bridge |
| `vllm:request_frontend_latency_seconds` | Histogram | API server → engine core latency |

#### Layer 3 — Cache Hit Rate & Per-Request Trace

One JSONL `[trace]` line emitted per request at completion:

```json
{
  "ts": 1782023561.679,
  "rid": "chatcmpl-xxx",
  "prompt_tokens": 3934,
  "output_tokens": 32,
  "TTFT_ms": 169.2,
  "queue_ms": 0.04,
  "prefill_ms": 130.1,
  "decode_ms": 144.6,
  "e2e_ms": 314.3,
  "frontend_ms": 39.0,
  "input_tokens_cache_hit": 3840,
  "L1_hit": 0,
  "external_kv_hit": 3840,
  "L2_hit": 0,
  "L3_hit": 3840,
  "remote_hit": 0,
  "input_tokens_no_cache_hit": 94,
  "kv_transfer_mode": "non_layerwise",
  "kv_lookup_ms": 1.2,
  "kv_retrieve_ms": 101.5
}
```

**Token identity equations** (verifiable by automated scripts at runtime):

```
prompt_tokens = input_tokens_cache_hit + input_tokens_no_cache_hit
input_tokens_cache_hit = L1_hit + external_kv_hit
external_kv_hit ≈ L2_hit + L3_hit + remote_hit   (≈ due to chunk_size=256 granularity)
```

#### Cross-Process Bridge (TP > 1)

When TP > 1, `retrieve()` runs on Worker_TP0 while `request_finished()` runs on the EngineCore/scheduler process. Per-request data is relayed via file-based bridge in `/dev/shm/lmcache_bridge/` (tmpfs, memory-backed):

- Per-tier counters: file + `fcntl.flock` for atomic cross-process updates
- Timing data: `write-tmp + os.replace` for atomic JSON
- Cleanup: throttled periodic sweep + retry limit (3) to prevent `/dev/shm` exhaustion

#### OTel Span Attributes

8 attributes on the `"llm_request"` span:

| Attribute | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| `gen_ai.latency.time_in_frontend` | API → engine |
| `gen_ai.latency.time_in_kv_lookup` | KV lookup |
| `gen_ai.latency.time_in_kv_transfer` | KV retrieve |
| `gen_ai.usage.l1_hit_tokens` | L1 (GPU prefix cache) |
| `gen_ai.usage.l2_hit_tokens` | L2 (CPU RAM) |
| `gen_ai.usage.l3_hit_tokens` | L3 (NVMe/SSD) |
| `gen_ai.usage.remote_hit_tokens` | Remote backend |
| `gen_ai.latency.kv_transfer_mode` | layerwise / non_layerwise |

---

### Metrics Summary (16 new Prometheus metrics)

**LMCache side (6):**

| Metric | Type |
|--------|------|
| `lmcache:l2_hit_tokens` / `lmcache:num_l2_hit_tokens` | Histogram + Counter |
| `lmcache:l3_hit_tokens` / `lmcache:num_l3_hit_tokens` | Histogram + Counter |
| `lmcache:remote_hit_tokens` / `lmcache:num_remote_hit_tokens` | Histogram + Counter |

**vLLM bridge (9):**

| Metric | Type |
|--------|------|
| `vllm:lmcache_kv_lookup_seconds` | Histogram |
| `vllm:lmcache_kv_retrieve_seconds` | Histogram |
| `vllm:lmcache_retrieve_process_tokens_seconds` | Histogram |
| `vllm:lmcache_retrieve_to_gpu_seconds` | Histogram |
| `vllm:lmcache_num_l2_hit_tokens` | Counter |
| `vllm:lmcache_num_l3_hit_tokens` | Counter |
| `vllm:lmcache_num_remote_hit_tokens` | Counter |
| `vllm:lmcache_kv_transfer_mode` | Info |

**vLLM framework (1):**

| Metric | Type |
|--------|------|
| `vllm:request_frontend_latency_seconds` | Histogram |

---

### Verification

The design has been validated end

items.title: [RFC] Native PD disaggregation in MP mode
items.author: limarkdcunha
items.body_excerpt:
## 1. Problem

Current behavior: Today, the user must manually deploy, configure, and maintain an external, unmanaged reference script (examples/disagg_prefill_mp/disagg_proxy_server.py) to handle control-plane orchestration. While LMCache natively handles the data plane handoff (prefill stores to the server; decode reads from it), routing decisions and prefill-completion signaling are bolted onto this loose example script.

This introduces severe problems such as :

- Slow "done" signal. To learn "prefill finished," it runs a separate mini server just for that message, and waits on it. That's an extra network round-trip and a thread hand-off sitting right in the path before the user gets their first token — pure delay, nothing gained.

- Rigid setup that breaks easily. It always pairs prefill #2 with decode #2, in that fixed order, using host/port lists typed in at startup. Want to add or remove a machine? Restart the whole proxy. And it has no way to notice a machine died — it'll happily send requests to a dead one.

- Reinventing what already exists. LMCache already has mp_coordinator, which tracks live instances, checks their health, and holds fleet-wide metadata (quota, blend fingerprints, and so on). The proxy ignores all of that and rebuilds a worse version of instance tracking from scratch — static host/port lists, no health, no roles.

Expected outcome:
Ship PD orchestration as a **separate, native router/proxy service**. It owns routing, request forwarding, and completion signaling. `mp_coordinator` keeps its existing job — tracking fleet state (membership, health, roles) — and just exposes that data for the router to read. Coordinator never handles a request; router never owns fleet state. This retires the standalone example proxy script and makes PD disaggregation native.

## 2. Non-goals

Worth being explicit about what this RFC does not touch:

- No changes required on the vLLM or SGLang side — both already expose the hooks LMCache needs (`kv_transfer_config` connector). This is entirely an LMCache-side orchestration change.
- The KV data-transfer path itself (CUDA IPC / SHM / socket fallback) stays exactly as-is. Only orchestration — routing and completion signaling — changes.
- The prefill/decode scheduling policy inside the serving engine isn't touched. LMCache orchestrates the handoff; the engine still does the compute.
- Coordinator high availability is out of scope here — see Open Question 4.

## 3. Proposal

Router/proxy owns all PD orchestration (routing, forwarding, completion signaling); coordinator only exposes fleet metadata, per §1.

Three changes:

1. **Role-aware membership (coordinator metadata).** Instances declare `prefill` or `decode` at registration, extending the existing register/heartbeat path. Only piece that touches the coordinator.

2. **Native completion signaling.** Replaces the HTTP telemetry hop with an internal "prefill done, decode may proceed" signal. The main open decision — options below.

3. **Fleet-aware routing (in the router service).** The router picks prefill/decode targets from live membership and health, instead of static round-robin pairing. In v1 this means round-robin over live, role-matched, healthy instances — a real improvement over today's static pairing, even though it isn't load-aware yet. True load-aware selection is deferred; see Open Question 2.

   **Fleet discovery**, part of this change: the router caches its own copy of the fleet metadata and routes from that, rather than calling the coordinator per request. Keeps the coordinator out of the request path.

   **How it gets that copy.** No push/subscribe mechanism on the coordinator today — only `GET /instances` (a pull). "Coordinator pushes to router" would be net-new work.

   Cheaper path for v1: router polls `GET /instances` every second or two, refreshes its cache. Reuses what's already there; staleness window is small enough to be covered by the retry-and-resync rule further down.

   True push can come later if polling proves too coarse.

That covers routing and membership — the harder piece is completion signaling, since it's the one place where getting it wrong means decode reading garbage or hanging. Worth walking through where the signal actually comes from today before picking an approach.

## Completion signaling — the options

Where does "request X is fully stored, across every worker" actually get decided today? Not on the LMCache MP server — it's assembled in LMCache's own vLLM adapter (`get_finished`, in `vllm_multi_process_adapter.py`), triggered by vLLM calling that method. That adapter already handles cross-worker aggregation, dedup, and the healthy/unhealthy cases correctly, and once it's satisfied it fires `on_request_store_finished(...)` — today, an HTTP POST to the proxy's telemetry server. Since that adapter is LMCache's own code (it just happens to run inside vLLM's process), we can change how it announces completion without touching vLLM at all. The MP server itself never sees this — it only sees individual store commits, with no concept of "all workers done for this request."

Three ways to build the native signal:

**Option 1 (recommended) — swap the transport.** Keep the adapter's `get_finished` detection exactly as it is, and just replace the HTTP POST with a native notify (ZMQ, straight to the proxy). Reuses cross-worker logic that's already correct and battle-tested, so it's the smallest change we can make. The signal still originates in the adapter rather than the MP server — fine, since the adapter is our code either way.

**Option 2 — move the aggregation server-side.** Rebuild "all workers done" tracking inside the MP server itself: count `COMMIT_STORE`s per request across every rank, and emit the signal from there. Fully decoupled from vLLM's loop, but it re-implements, as new work, something the adapter already does correctly. Not worth the cost for what it buys.

**Option 3 — skip the signal, block on retrieve instead.** Send th

items.title: [Bug] store_layer raises StopIteration in the vLLM worker when the store is skipped (freeze mode or unhealthy engine)
items.author: elbourne12345
items.body_excerpt:
**Labels:** `bug`

## Describe the bug

`LMCacheEngine.store_layer` is a generator whose callers advance it a fixed
number of times. Two of its exit paths — freeze mode and an unhealthy engine —
yield fewer times than that, so advancing the generator raises `StopIteration`
inside the vLLM worker and takes down the engine.

Both paths are reachable on a live server: freeze is toggled at runtime, and the
health monitor can flip a healthy engine to unhealthy mid-serving.

## The contract

`LMCacheConnectorV1Impl` commits to the advance count before it can know whether
the store will be skipped:

- `save_kv_layer` advances once per model layer — `vllm_v1_adapter.py:1093`
- `wait_for_save` advances once more — `vllm_v1_adapter.py:1124`

So every exit path must yield `num_layers + 1` times. The two normal paths do
(the per-layer loop, then the final `yield` at the end of the method). These two
do not:

| path | `cache_engine.py` | yields | expected |
|---|---|---|---|
| normal (hit or miss) | 732–776 | `num_layers + 1` | ✔ |
| **freeze mode** | 648–656 | `num_layers` | ✗ one short |
| **unhealthy** | 620–622 | `0` | ✗ none at all |

```python
        # Health check: block operation if LMCache is unhealthy
        if not self.is_healthy():
            logger.warning("LMCache is unhealthy, skipping store_layer operation")
            return                      # <- yields nothing at all
        ...
        if self.is_frozen():
            logger.debug(...)
            # Still need to yield to avoid StopIteration
            for layer_id in range(self.num_layers):
                yield                   # <- one short: no final yield
            return
```

The comment on the freeze path shows the hazard was known; the count is just off
by one.

## To Reproduce

Confirmed on `dev` @ `913016b`. Driving the real generator exactly as the
adapter does (`num_layers` advances, then one more):

```
contract: adapter performs 4 + 1 = 5 advances

NORMAL  (healthy, no chunks)     yields=5   advances_survived=5   OK
FROZEN  (freeze mode on)         yields=4   advances_survived=4   *** StopIteration in wait_for_save ***
UNHEALTHY (health check fail)    yields=0   advances_survived=0   *** StopIteration in save_kv_layer ***
```

Both parametrizations of the test added in the accompanying PR fail on
unpatched `dev` and pass with the fix, with the full
`tests/v1/test_cache_engine.py` suite green (69 passed) afterwards.

The normal path establishes the contract at 5 empirically. Freeze dies on the
final advance in `wait_for_save`; unhealthy dies on the *first* advance in
`save_kv_layer`, mid-forward-pass.

To hit it on a live server with `use_layerwise: true`:

1. Start vLLM with the LMCache v1 connector and `use_layerwise: true`.
2. Enable freeze mode — `POST` the freeze endpoint
   (`lmcache/v1/internal_api_server/vllm/freeze_api.py`), **or** let the cache
   controller run a full sync, which calls `lmcache_engine.freeze(True)` itself
   (`full_sync_sender.py:217`) and holds it for the whole sync.
3. Send any request that stores KV. `wait_for_save` raises `StopIteration`.

The controller path is the nastier one: LMCache puts *itself* into the failing
state, for the duration of a sync, with no operator action.

## Expected behavior

Skipping the store degrades gracefully — the generator still yields
`num_layers + 1` times and the request completes without caching.

## Additional context

- The retrieve-side twin of this bug is #4133 / #899, fixed by the still-open
  PR #4574. That PR's author noted the same inconsistency in `retrieve_layer`'s
  unhealthy path and deliberately left it out of scope; `store_layer` was never
  in scope there. This issue is the store-side case.
- Earlier `StopIteration`-in-the-save-path crashes (#1844, #2453) were fixed by
  #2268, which is the PR that introduced the yield-padding loop that is off by
  one here.
- Freeze mode itself came from #2169.

items.title: Starting a localization (l10n) effort for LMCache
items.author: quaid
items.body_excerpt:
I'd like to propose we start building a localization community around LMCache, beginning with blog posts and expanding to documentation and other parts of the website over time.

tl;dr – 
- localizing content and software is valuable to all of us;
- we can automate the toil of translation but we need human editors who can review the translations and make sure they are properly localized;
- localization means words and phrases are fixed so the final product makes more sense to a native reader;
- we can use RHLF to improve this process and reduce toil over time.

## What is the problem

We already receive blog posts written natively in Mandarin and English. This is a good thing.

But we also need to localize this content without putting a burden on people. Fortunately this content has completed a technical review before being translated, so the focus can be on fixing idioms and grammar for better understanding by the widest audience.

## Why this matters

Ultimately this is about attracting more users to LMCache, some of whom will become intentional contributors over time.

Twenty-five years ago, localization (l10n) projects were one of the main ways Linux distributions and communities like the Fedora Project made headway into new parts of the world. It usually wasn't a corporate initiative. It was people who were enthusiastic about bringing free and open source software to their fellow country members, and who put in the effort to translate strings and make the software make sense locally. That work produced translations AND collaborations. It grew contributors, built regional communities, and carried the free software and open source ethos into places it hadn't reached before.

LMCache has users and watchers all over the world, and there are almost certainly people already adjacent to this project who could help bring information and education about the software to their local communities.

## What I'm proposing

We form loosely as `l10n-sig` out of anyone who wants to be an editor and approver for one or more languages. Languages get added when someone steps forward to take one. Rather than announcing a target list and hoping it fills in, we start with whoever volunteers.

I'm volunteering to be an editor and reviewer for anything translated to English, and I'd love more help with that role. I'm confident we can get Mandarin covered right away. But what else and how?

Japanese and Korean are the obvious early candidates given where our users are, but the principle is that a language becomes active when a person is willing to own it.

It only takes one person to get things started and be the gravity to bring another language.

As I said above, this isn't only English needing localizing. I currently have an original blog post written in Mandarin that I want to bring into English through this same process. I'd like to stop doing one at a time reviews by asking around in Slack to see who might need a break from creating features or fixing bugs. I'd rather offer the opportunity to people who aren't or can't create features or fix bugs.

Therefore, posts written originally in any language are welcome, and translation should flow in whatever direction it needs to.

## This is not a request for volunteer translation labor

LLM translation is pretty good now, and we should lean on it for the first pass. What we need is a human review step, and there are two kinds of people who can do that well.

The first is someone capable in both the source and target language, who can read the machine translation and confirm the meaning carried over and the tone is right. Not necessarily final-polish copy editing — a human or AI copy edit can always be applied later — just confirmation that it makes sense and reads naturally.

The second, and possibly just as valuable, is someone technical who knows their own language well and doesn't necessarily read the source language at all. Because the models are good enough now, a domain expert can look at a translated technical passage and say "ah, I see what this was trying to say" and correct the terminology so it's actually right in their language. Technical accuracy matters as much as idiomatic flow, and that person is well placed to catch it.

So the ask is much closer to "read this and tell us if it sounds right" than "translate three thousand words."

## How the workflow might look

Initially all of this can be manual, while we work out which models produce the best tone for technical writing in each language and we develop any necessary skills.

Longer term this could be automated — a GitHub Action that sends a published post to a translation model, then loads the result into WordPress as a draft where a translation editor reviews and approves it. It could also live partly outside the repo, with approval happening after the fact rather than as a gate. The goal is to distribute this work rather than make it dependent on a paid staffer, and to remove the need to ask permission before contributing.

If anyone already knows of a toolchain or process for this, please say so. I'd much rather adopt something that works than stand up and maintain our own infrastructure.

## What I'm looking for

Ideas or helping hands for:

- Thoughts on the approach
- Pointers to existing tooling
- Anyone in

items.title: [Bug][MP] lmcache_mp.l1_read counts released read reservations even when no GPU retrieve occurs
items.author: 0andy
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

`lmcache_mp.l1_read` is documented as "Number of chunks read from L1"
(`docs/source/mp/observability/metrics.rst`).

However, the counter also increments when L1 read reservations are only
released and no LMCache-driven CPU→GPU retrieve is submitted.

With the vLLM connector, this can happen when the requested prefix is already
available in vLLM's local GPU prefix cache.

LMCache lookup/prefetch finds the matching chunks and retains/read-locks them.
Later, `update_state_after_alloc()` determines that no external retrieve is
needed and calls `free_lookup_locks()`.

That path eventually reaches `L1Manager.finish_read()`, which publishes
`L1_READ_FINISHED`. The `lmcache_mp.l1_read` metric therefore increases even
though no LMCache-driven retrieve was submitted.

In my repro:

- 5 retained L1 keys with no retrieve caused `l1_read` to increase by 5.
- Another 6 retained L1 keys with no retrieve caused it to increase by 6.
- After restarting vLLM, the same 6 retained keys were actually retrieved from
  L1, and `l1_read` again increased by 6.

So `lmcache_mp.l1_read` increases by the number of retained/released keys in
both cases and does not distinguish a real retrieve from a lookup reservation
that is later released unused.

---

**To Reproduce**

Environment:

- LMCache dev @ `1ca53a8a` (`0.5.6rc3.dev31`)
- vLLM `0.30.0`
- MP mode
- ZMQ transport
- `lmcache_driven` transfer
- `--chunk-size 16`
- 1x A100

Steps:

1. Start the LMCache MP server with `--chunk-size 16`.
2. Start one vLLM instance using `LMCacheMPConnector`.
3. Send prompt P (85 tokens) once to populate the cache.
4. Send P plus a short suffix (97 tokens) twice using the same vLLM process.
5. Observe the LMCache logs and `/metrics`.
6. Restart only vLLM, leaving the LMCache server running.
7. Send the same P + suffix request again from the fresh vLLM process.
8. Compare `lmcache_mp_l1_read_chunks_total` with the actual retrieve metrics.

Observed before restarting vLLM:

```text
=== 1: P, cold ===
Stored 80 tokens
Stored 16 tokens
lmcache_mp_l1_write_chunks_total 6.0
(no l1_read)
(no num_submitted_retrieves / num_finished_retrieves)

=== 2: P + suffix, same vLLM process ===
Prefetch request completed (L1+L2): 5/6 retained keys (5 L1, 0 L2) in 1.2 ms
Stored 16 tokens
Stored 16 tokens
(no "Retrieved" line)

lmcache_mp_l1_write_chunks_total 8.0
lmcache_mp_l1_read_chunks_total 5.0
(no num_submitted_retrieves / num_finished_retrieves)

=== 3: same request again, same vLLM process ===
Prefetch request completed (L1+L2): 6/6 retained keys (6 L1, 0 L2) in 0.9 ms
Stored 16 tokens
(no "Retrieved" line)

lmcache_mp_l1_write_chunks_total 9.0
lmcache_mp_l1_read_chunks_total 11.0
(no num_submitted_retrieves / num_finished_retrieves)
```

The `l1_read` counter increased:

```text
0 -> 5    (+5)
5 -> 11   (+6)
```

exactly matching the number of retained keys, while no GPU retrieve was
submitted.

The extra `Stored 16 tokens` in step 3 is unrelated to this issue. The two
requests produced different completions, so the final chunk containing
generated tokens differed.

As a control, I then restarted vLLM while keeping the same LMCache server
running. This removes vLLM's local GPU prefix cache, so the cached prefix has
to be retrieved from LMCache.

The same request then produced:

```text
Prefetch request completed (L1+L2): 6/6 retained keys (6 L1, 0 L2) in 1.7 ms
Retrieved 96 tokens in 0.001 seconds

lmcache_mp_l1_read_chunks_total 17.0
lmcache_mp_num_submitted_retrieves_total{device="cuda:0"} 1.0
lmcache_mp_num_finished_retrieves_total{device="cuda:0"} 1.0
```

The previous reading, taken after step 3, was:

```text
lmcache_mp_l1_read_chunks_total 11.0
```

No other requests were sent in between, so the real retrieve also increased
`l1_read` by exactly 6:

```text
11 -> 17   (+6)
```

This gives the following A/B comparison:

```text
Case A: 6/6 retained, no retrieve
l1_read +6
num_submitted_retrieves +0
num_finished_retrieves +0

Case B: 6/6 retained, real CPU->GPU retrieve
l1_read +6
num_submitted_retrieves +1
num_finished_retrieves +1
```

`lmcache_mp.l1_read` therefore grows by the same amount in both cases. Only the
`num_*_retrieves` metrics distinguish whether a real retrieve occurred.

Relevant code path at `1ca53a8a`:

- `lmcache/v1/mp_observability/subscribers/metrics/l1.py:49`

  `L1MetricsSubscriber` subscribes to `L1_READ_FINISHED`.

- `lmcache/v1/distributed/l1_manager.py:433`

  `finish_read()` publishes one `L1_READ_FINISHED` event containing the keys
  whose read locks were released; the metric subscriber counts those keys.

- `lmcache/integration/vllm/lmcache_mp_connector.py:1381` →
  `lmcache/v1/multiprocess/modules/lookup.py:481`

  `free_lookup_locks()` → `finish_read_prefetched()` → `finish_read()`,
  without a data-transfer request on the no-retrieve path.

---

**Expected behavior**

The metric semantics and documentation should be consistent.

If `lmcache_mp.l1_read` is intended to represent chunks actually read from L1,
it should not increase for the `free_lookup_locks()` path when no retrieve was
submitted.

If it is intentionally a read-reservation lifecycle counter, its description
should make that clear and documentation should not use it as proof that a
retrieve occurred.

This is especially relevant because the SGLang quickstart
(`docs/source/getting_started/quickstart.rst`) currently tells users they can
"confirm the retrieve" by checking:

```text
lmcache_mp_l1_read_chunks_total
```

The repro above shows that this counter can increase even when no
LMCache-driven retrieve was submitted.

I reproduced the no-retrieve behavior with the vLLM connector. I have not
tested whether the same no-retrieve path is reachable through SGLang.

---

**Screenshots**

Not required for reproduction. The relevant LMCache server logs and metric
values are included above.

---

- OS: Ubuntu 24.04
- Browser: N/A
- LMCache: `1ca53a8a` (`0.5.6rc3.dev31`)

items.title: Performance comparison for dense shared prefix + block-diagonal local mask: custom mask in BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper vs MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper
items.author: catnanami
items.body_excerpt: I am trying to evaluate the best way to implement an attention pattern with a dense shared/global prefix plus a local block-diagonal suffix. The mask pattern is shown below: I am considering two implementations: BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper with a custom mask MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper Questions: 1. For this pattern, is cascade attention expected to be faster than paged prefill with a custom mask? 2. Or is this pattern better handled by a custom kernel/backend? My use case is speculative decoding, where all verification tokens share the same prefix KV, but each local block should only attend to its own block.

comments.author: VectorPeak
comments.body:
For the mask in the image - a dense shared prefix on the left plus independent block-diagonal local regions on the right - `MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper` is usually the better fit than `BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper` with one large custom mask.

The reason is that the custom-mask prefill path does not really exploit this structure as well: it still treats the problem like one masked attention problem over the full layout, so the block-diagonal sparsity mostly becomes masking overhead. Cascade attention lets you model this as:

- shared/global prefix KV: attended by all verification tokens
- local suffix KV: split into independent blocks/requests
- final result: merge prefix-attention state with each local block’s attention state

For speculative decoding, this is exactly the kind of case where cascade can help, especially when the shared prefix is large and the local verification blocks are relatively small. Each local block can be represented as a separate batch item sharing the same prefix. If the local part also needs causal masking inside each block, use the normal causal/local mask for that per-block suffix attention.

items.title: [Windows 11] AMD Adrenalin driver (32.0.31007.5012) causes R9700  VRAM to offload to system RAM on idle - crash with 32GB RAM
items.author: realsheox-max
items.body_excerpt:
## Problem
AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700 on Windows offloads entire VRAM content 
to system RAM after ~15 seconds idle, causing system crash 
(32GB RAM fills up instantly).

Reproduces with both Vulkan and ROCm backends.
Also reproduces in LM Studio (Vulkan backend).

## Root Cause
AMD Adrenalin Software (driver 32.0.31007.5012, dated 12.05.2026) 
installs aggressive DPM power management that evicts VRAM on idle.
The basic Windows driver without Adrenalin does NOT have this behavior.

## System
- OS: Windows 11 (Build 26200.8457)
- GPU: AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700 (32GB VRAM)
- CPU: Intel i7-11700KF
- RAM: 32GB DDR4
- Affected driver: 32.0.31007.5012 (Adrenalin, 12.05.2026)
- Working driver: 32.0.22042.14002 (09.03.2026, no Adrenalin)

## Fix
1. Uninstall AMD Adrenalin, rollback to driver 32.0.22042.14002
2. Use --no-mmap without --mlock

## Working command
.\llama-server.exe --device Vulkan1 \
  --model "model.Q4_K_M.gguf" \
  --ctx-size 65536 \
  --threads 8 \
  --parallel 1 \
  --n-gpu-layers -1 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 \
  --port 8080 \
  --cache-type-k q4_0 \
  --cache-type-v q4_0 \
  --cache-ram 0 \
  --no-mmap

## What does NOT fix this
- DisableGpuMemoryTrim registry key
- KMD_EnableContextBasedPowerManagement=0
- PCI Express Link State Power Management=Off
- WSL2 with ROCm (same issue)

## Additional Notes
The R9700 is marketed as a dedicated AI workstation card.
The target use case is exactly keeping LLMs permanently loaded
in VRAM for inference workloads.

Ironically, AMD ships the same consumer Adrenalin driver with
aggressive laptop-style power management on this workstation card.
When the LLM is idle between requests, the GPU already draws only
~8W — there is absolutely no reason to evict VRAM contents to
system RAM at that point.

This DPM behavior makes sense on laptops/integrated GPUs to save
battery. On a dedicated 32GB AI accelerator it actively destroys
the primary use case.

AMD should either:
1. Ship a compute/workstation driver profile without aggressive DPM
2. Add an option in Adrenalin to disable VRAM eviction on idle
3. Document this behavior clearly for AI/LLM workloads

## Related Issues
- #22871 - Similar symptoms on Linux/Docker
- https://github.com/ROCm/ROCm/issues/4903 - --mlock forces shared memory on Windows AMD
- #12800 - AMD DPM offloads VRAM to GTT on Linux (fix: amdgpu.runpm=0)

items.title: Analysis: Volta (SM70/SM72) Flash Attention Optimization Paths
items.author: hernandez42
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

This issue documents a systematic investigation into Volta-class GPU (SM70/SM72) flash attention performance in llama.cpp, motivated by 1Cat-vLLM's FLASH_ATTN_V100 backend which achieves significant improvements on V100 via TurboMind SM70 WMMA kernels and split-D attention design.

Benchmarking was performed on Jetson AGX Xavier (SM72, aarch64, CUDA 11.4) with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B MoE D=256 GGUF models.

## Key Findings

### Current Config is Already Reasonably Tuned

Attempting custom Volta flash attention configs (doubling nbatch_K2/nbatch_V2, adjusting occupancy) showed no improvement — in fact, decode throughput regressed ~5% due to increased shared memory pressure reducing occupancy.

| Scenario | Current (Ampere fallback) | Custom Volta config |
|----------|:---:|:---:|
| Pure decode | 20.85 t/s | 19.68 t/s |
| 256 gen | 20.85 t/s | 21.08 t/s |

### MMA Architecture Gap is Fundamental

The ~2× throughput gap between Volta (m8n8k4, no ldmatrix, no cp.async) and Turing/Ampere (m16n8k8, ldmatrix, cp.async) is architectural and cannot be closed by config tuning alone.

### No Code Change Required Now

The existing dispatch logic in `fattn.cu` (Volta branching at line 491) and Ampere config fallback in `ggml_cuda_fattn_mma_get_config_volta()` at `fattn-mma-f16.cuh:123` are already producing near-optimal results for this kernel design.

## Potential Future Optimization Paths

1. **Volta-specific split-D WMMA attention kernel** (following 1Cat-vLLM's FLASH_ATTN_V100 design): Split D=256 into 4×64-dim slices processed by separate warps, reducing per-warp shared memory from 32KB to 8KB. Estimated gain: ~35% on SM72.

2. **MTP speculative decoding support for Qwen3.x**: llama.cpp already supports `--draft-model`, but Qwen3.x's native MTP heads are different — they're model-integrated, not a separate draft model. Adding MTP head support would benefit all architectures.

3. **Persistent thread block design**: Keep warps alive across KV slices instead of re-launching kernels, with pipelined loads into shared memory.

## Next Steps

If maintainers are interested, I can develop a Volta-specific flash attention CUDA kernel following approach #1. The work would include:
- New kernel file (e.g., `fattn-volta.cu`)
- WMMA integration via `nvcuda::wmma` (already used in `mma.cuh`)
- Test coverage via `test-backend-ops`
- Benchmark data on AGX Xavier (SM72) and, if provided access, V100 (SM70)

## Benchmark Environment
- GPU: Jetson AGX Xavier (SM72, Volta)
- CUDA: 11.4, aarch64
- Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B MoE (Q4_K_M, 20GB GGUF)
- llama.cpp v0.3.0-dev

items.title: RFC: Persistent expert slot pool for MoE CPU offload (--moe-expert-cache), +84% decode
items.author: memoriaru
items.body_excerpt:
This follows up on #24528 (leloch's CUDA-side adaptive cache, whose PR #24524 was closed for scope) with a different design point: zero kernel changes via id remapping, plus a prefill fallback rule

# RFC: Persistent expert slot pool for MoE CPU offload (`--moe-expert-cache`)

> Draft for a ggml-org/llama.cpp discussions post. Follows up on feature request
> [#20757](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/20757). Companion branch:
> `moe-expert-pool`. **Status: validated on consumer hardware (RTX 4090, CUDA):
> perplexity-equivalent, long-session stable, +34% decode on a real code-generation
> workload on top of +84% on the neutral benchmark.**

## Summary

Add `--moe-expert-cache N` (-mec N): for every MoE expert weight tensor that offloading
placed in host memory, keep a persistent pool of `N` expert slots in accelerator memory.
Cache hits serve a decode step with **zero** host-to-device traffic; misses copy the
expert in and evict the least recently used slot. Expert ids are remapped to slot ids
through a per-tensor map table applied with `ggml_get_rows` — **no new ggml op and no
backend-specific code** — so CUDA, Vulkan, Metal and CPU all work unchanged.

Measured on a single RTX 4090 24 GB, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (qwen4exp, 48 MoE layers, all
experts on CPU, UD-Q3_K_XL, 8 K context, greedy):

| -mec | decode tg512 (t/s) | vs baseline | prefill          |
|-----:|-------------------:|------------:|------------------|
| 0    | 11.55 ± 0.41       | —           | pp512 104.5 ± 9.9 / pp2048 113.4 ± 5.7 |
| 16   | 12.89 ± 0.33       | +12%        | —                |
| 32   | 17.54 ± 0.15       | +52%        | pp512 119.1 ± 10.9 / pp2048 112.9 ± 4.8 |
| 48   | 19.09 ± 0.62       | +65%        | —                |
| 64   | 21.21 ± 0.46       | **+84%**    | —                |

On a real code-generation workload served through `llama-server` (173-token prompt,
512 generated tokens, warm rounds): 12.82 → 14.10 (+10%) at N=32 and → 17.14 (**+34%**)
at N=64; a long multi-task session (2561 tokens with pool-churning 1 K-token
generations interleaved) held anchor outputs **byte-identical across four runs** with
no throughput decay. Greedy decoding with the pool active is **perplexity-equivalent**
to the host-copy path (PPL 3.3096 ± 0.053 vs 3.3262 ± 0.053, deterministic reruns;
difference well inside the error bars).

Prefill is unchanged within noise by construction (below). A backend-level matrix test
passes **bit-exact** on CUDA (RTX 4090) and Metal (AMD dGPU): 5 quant types × dual pools
sharing one routing × ubatch sizes 1/3 × cold / full-eviction / hit+reload /
graph-rebuild. Server-level greedy A/B initially diverged deterministically from the
host-copy path; root cause was found and fixed (details in *Validation* — including one
invalid verification round we are disclosing rather than hiding).

## Problem

With `--cpu-moe` / `--n-cpu-moe` (or the auto-fitter), decode re-streams every selected
expert over PCIe on every token: the selective expert copy added in #15346 removed the
*unused* experts but still copies the same *hot* experts token after token. Routing is
skewed, so for code-generation-style workloads the same small expert set is re-read
thousands of times. #20757 requests a cache for exactly this.

## Why not the other approaches on the table

- **`--prefetch-weights` ([#21067](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/21067))**
  overlaps next-layer transfers with compute but cannot know the next layer's routing;
  for MoE it was measured moving 2.06× the bytes with +47.8% TTFT. Complementary, not
  competing: prefetch targets dense/prefill transfer overlap, this targets decode
  residency. The two can share the copy-stream infrastructure.
- **Dynamic caches with SLRU/probation (original #20757 proposal)** let prefill bursts
  evict the decode hot set; a frequency-gated admission filter was needed to recover.
  This design sidesteps the problem structurally: **a ubatch that can touch more
  distinct experts than the pool has slots never goes through the pool at all** — it
  takes the existing selective-copy path. Prefill therefore behaves exactly like
  master (verified: pp512/pp2048 unchanged), and prefill never evicts decode state.
- Prior PRs in this space (#21614/#21620/#24524) were closed for scope/review reasons;
  this branch is deliberately small in backend impact: zero kernel changes, one
  scheduler hook, ~700 lines total of which ~350 are the scheduler core.

## Design

1. `ggml_backend_sched_register_expert_pool(sched, w, backend_id, n_slots, &table)`
   allocates `n_slots * expert_size` (+ a small NaN-safe tail) on the compute backend
   and a host-side I32 `map_table` shaped `[1, n_expert]` (flagged as a graph input).
2. `llm_graph_context::build_lora_mm_id` — the single funnel for all MoE expert
   matmuls — routes through the pool when one is registered for the tensor **and** the
   ubatch cannot select more distinct experts than slots (`n_expert_used * n_tokens ≤
   n_slots`). The remap is `get_rows(table, cont(ids))`: existing ops only.
3. The map-table buffer is registered with the scheduler's pooled-split boundary check,
   so the remap `GET_ROWS` always anchors its own split. In that split's prologue the
   scheduler reads the (original) expert ids back to the host, updates LRU state,
   issues async H2D copies for misses and rewrites the map table — *before* the same
   split's input copies upload the fresh table. (This ordering is the fix described
   below; anchoring the update anywhere later lets the remap consume a stale table.)
4. Safety rails: total pool memory is capped at half the device's free memory at load
   time (tensors beyond the budget silently keep the selective-copy path); pools are
   disabled under pipeline parallelism; slot-overflow is a hard assert instead of
   silent corruption.

Slot sizing: `N` must cover the decode working set, not just to

items.title: Misc. bug: Router mode loads wrong GGUF when multiple files share a subdirectory
items.author: Kalix-Green
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

version: 0.3.0-dev (build 0, commit unknown)
built with GNU 13.3.0 for Linux aarch64

### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server

### Command line

```shell
llama-server --models-dir ~/LLM/models --models-max 1 --fit on --flash-attn on --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

### Describe the bug

In router mode (`--models-dir`), when a subdirectory contains multiple `.gguf` files (e.g., a main model and a draft model), and the client sends a `model` name that matches the subdirectory name, the server may incorrectly select a different file inside that subdirectory (e.g., the draft model) instead of the one with the same name as the subdirectory.

This leads to loading the wrong model, which often fails due to tensor count mismatches (since the draft model has a different architecture).

### To Reproduce

1. **Directory structure** (example):
~/LLM/models/
└── Laguna-S-2.1-UD-Q4_K_XL/
├── laguna-s-2.1-DFlash-BF16.gguf # draft model (should NOT be chosen)
└── Laguna-S-2.1-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf # main model (expected)



2. **Start server**:
```bash
llama-server --models-dir ~/LLM/models --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080 --models-max 1
Send a request:
```


```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "Laguna-S-2.1-UD-Q4_K_XL",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]
  }'
```

Expected behavior
The server should load Laguna-S-2.1-UD-Q4_K_XL/Laguna-S-2.1-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf – the file that most closely matches the requested model name (i.e., the one with the same name as the subdirectory).

Actual behavior
The server attempts to load laguna-s-2.1-DFlash-BF16.gguf (the draft model) and fails:

[llama_router.log](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/31801437/llama_router.log)

[start-llama_router.sh](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/31801452/start-llama_router.sh)

text
[60737] 0.00.297.698 E llama_model_load: error loading model: done_getting_tensors: wrong number of tensors; expected 76, got 69
[60737] 0.00.392.537 E cmn  common_init_: failed to load model '/home/.../laguna-s-2.1-DFlash-BF16.gguf'
9.25.860.746 W srv    operator(): got exception: {"error":{"code":500,"message":"model name=Laguna-S-2.1-UD-Q4_K_XL failed to load","type":"server_error"}}

### First Bad Commit

**Possible cause**

The router's model matching logic appears to use case‑insensitive substring matching and may pick the first file that matches any part of the requested name. In this case:

The requested name "Laguna-S-2.1-UD-Q4_K_XL" contains "laguna-s" (case‑insensitive).

The draft file laguna-s-2.1-DFlash-BF16.gguf also contains "laguna-s" and appears earlier in alphabetical order, so it is selected before the exact‑name file.

This ambiguous matching causes the wrong model to be loaded.

**Suggested fixes**

Prioritise exact matches – if the requested model string exactly matches a file name (or exactly matches subdirname/subdirname.gguf), load that file first.

Introduce a model alias/preset system – allow users to define explicit mappings between model names and file paths (e.g., via a --models-preset file).

Change matching priority – give higher precedence to files whose name exactly matches the subdirectory name.

Improve matching algorithm – switch from substring matching to prefix‑based or exact‑match‑first logic.

**Related issues**

[#20199 Web UI: Ambiguous Parsed Model name](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/20199) – similar ambiguity in Web UI.

[#18312 Feature Request: Model group support](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/18312) – could be extended to address this.

[#24434 PR: --models-preset-only](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/24434) – restricts router to a preset list, but does not solve the matching ambiguity.

Thank you for considering this report. I hope this can be fixed or at least documented to avoid confusion.

items.title: Vulkan: mul_mat_vec bf16 pipelines are created even when the device has no bf16 support
items.author: JulianPscheid
items.body_excerpt:
`ggml_vk_load_shaders` creates `mul_mat_vec_bf16_f32_f32`, `mul_mat_vec_bf16_f16_f32` and `mul_mat_vec_id_bf16_f32` unconditionally:

https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/ggml/src/ggml-vulkan/ggml-vulkan.cpp#L5374

Every other bf16 pipeline in that function is behind a support check. `pipeline_matmul_bf16` is guarded by `device->coopmat_bf16_support` at :4870 and :4916, and the non-coopmat creates at :5009 and :5185 sit inside branches that have already excluded it.

On a device whose compiler cannot build that shader, this turns an unsupported format into a process abort. Pixel 11 Pro, PowerVR C-Series CXTP-48-1536 MC1, `VK_DRIVER_ID_IMAGINATION_PROPRIETARY`, which reports `bf16: 0`:

```
ggml_vulkan: Compute pipeline creation failed for mul_mat_vec_bf16_f32_f32
ggml_vulkan: vk::Device::createComputePipeline: ErrorUnknown
libc++abi: terminating due to uncaught exception of type vk::SystemError
```

Reproduce with `test-backend-ops test -b Vulkan0 -o MUL_MAT`, which walks the type list and dies when it reaches bf16. Everything after that point goes untested, which is how I originally missed the k-quant failures on this device.

In practice a bf16 model would not run on this hardware anyway. The problem is that it aborts instead of reporting the type as unsupported, and that it takes the rest of `test-backend-ops` down with it.

Pipeline compilation is lazy, so this only fires when something actually requests a bf16 mul_mat_vec. A real bf16 model or a full `test-backend-ops` run will.

I have not written a patch. Gating these three creates on bf16 support looks straightforward, but I do not know whether any device relies on these pipelines existing without advertising bf16, and I have no way to test that.

items.title: GSP: grammar-conditioned sparse LM-head projection - replication and SGLang integration feedback wanted
items.author: StealthEyeLLC
items.body_excerpt:
I am sharing an open research artifact that may be relevant to SGLang's structured-generation path.

GSP (Grammar-Conditioned Sparse Projection) consumes a packed grammar legality mask before/during the target-model LM-head projection instead of computing the full vocabulary projection and masking afterward.

The current artifact includes:
- packed-mask row-sparse Triton projection for latency-oriented decoding
- batched block-GEMM that skips grammar-inactive vocabulary tiles
- density-aware dense fallback for permissive/mixed states
- support/top-1 correctness checks
- raw paired end-to-end Qwen3.5-2B results

On the reference RTX 5060 Laptop GPU, 30 paired AB/BA trials gave median end-to-end ratios of 1.0756x (enum JSON), 1.0642x (tool-call JSON), and 1.0842x (nested-array JSON). The free-string control is not claimed as a reliable mean speedup.

This is not claiming first invention of batch-1 grammar-aware LM-head filtering; the contribution boundary is the packed-mask batched execution, heterogeneous routing, and controlled target-model evaluation.

I would especially value:
- SGLang integration feedback
- datacenter GPU replication
- heterogeneous-batch measurements
- negative results / dense-winning crossover cases

Release, verified preprint, source, raw evidence:
https://github.com/StealthEyeLLC/grammar-sparse-projection/releases/tag/v0.1.1
