items.title: [Feature][RFC]: Compact active beam rows during VBWS decode in the PyTorch backend
items.author: yifanQi98
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

This is a request for design feedback on executing only the active beam rows during Variable-Beam-Width Search (VBWS) in the PyTorch backend.

TensorRT-LLM currently keeps generation rows in a static admission-width layout (`py_beam_width` / `max_beam_width`). That layout is useful for persistent beam state, KV-cache slots, cache indirection, and sampler offsets, but it also means the model forward may execute the full beam capacity when only a much smaller per-iteration width is live.

For example, with:

```python
SamplingParams(
    n=500,
    best_of=500,
    use_beam_search=True,
    beam_width_array=[20, 300, 500],
    max_tokens=3,
    temperature=0.0,
)
```

the context step produces 20 beams, followed by decode steps operating on 20 and 300 live input beams. A static-capacity forward still lays out 500 generation rows per request for both decode steps.

I propose separating:

- **beam capacity**: persistent physical state/KV/cache layout; and
- **beam execution width**: rows that participate in the current model forward.

The prototype keeps physical KV page IDs and capacity-stride request state unchanged, creates a compact attention-metadata view for the active rows, runs the model on those rows, and restores the logits layout expected by the existing sampler.

This builds on the VBWS correctness fixes merged in #19407 (for #19337): correct Python width tracking and terminal-step finalization make the active width well-defined at each step.

#### Current-main context

I checked current `main` at `ae3531adf3edcd833844559ecb791ab29b398d5d` (2026-09-29). The PyTorch ModelEngine still lays generation rows out at the static admission width, and CUDA Graph token sizing uses `batch_size * max_beam_width`. This proposal targets that remaining compute over-provisioning; it does not change VBWS search semantics.

### Proposed design

1. Compute a batch execution width from `LlmRequest.get_beam_width_by_iter()` for the stage being executed.
2. Preserve the request-major capacity layout for persistent beam/KV state.
3. Select the leading active rows from each request into a compact execution view.
4. Build/update compact attention metadata while preserving physical KV page IDs.
5. Add execution width (or equivalent active-generation-row count) to the CUDA Graph key.
6. Capture/replay graphs for configured VBWS widths.
7. Either:
   - initially restore logits to capacity stride with `-inf` padding; or
   - preferably teach the sampler to consume packed logits and explicit request offsets, avoiding the large-vocabulary repadding cost.
8. Fall back transparently to the existing static-capacity path for unsupported batches.

A conservative initial eligibility scope could be:

- PyTorch backend;
- decoder-only, pure-generation batches;
- no speculative decoding or cross attention;
- all non-dummy requests in a batch have the same execution width;
- single GPU initially, unless maintainers prefer distributed support in the first implementation;
- non-decreasing `beam_width_array` values already accepted by VBWS.

### Prototype results

Environment:

- TensorRT-LLM `1.3.0rc26`
- PyTorch `2.12.0+cu130`
- BF16 Qwen3-family model, full vocabulary
- single RTX PRO 5000 72GB
- `max_batch_size=64`, `max_beam_width=500`
- `beam_width_array=[20, 300, 500]`, `max_tokens=3`
- CUDA Graph enabled; baseline and compact arms used identical settings
- only the active-beam compaction flag differed

#### End-to-end fixed-rate service results

Each level ran for 60 seconds with five load-generator processes.

| Target QPS | Metric | Static capacity | Compact | Change |
|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 10 | Average latency | 44.03 ms | 36.68 ms | -16.7% |
| 10 | P95 latency | 46.82 ms | 39.33 ms | -16.0% |
| 30 | Average latency | 46.49 ms | 38.94 ms | -16.2% |
| 30 | P95 latency | 54.44 ms | 45.46 ms | -16.5% |
| 30 | Average GPU utilization | 61.83% | 40.58% | -21.25 pp |
| 40 | Average latency | 89.46 ms | 51.06 ms | -42.9% |
| 40 | P95 latency | 123.11 ms | 72.74 ms | -40.9% |
| 40 | Average GPU utilization | 73.66% | 50.15% | -23.51 pp |
| 45 | Average latency | 142.15 ms | 68.08 ms | -52.1% |
| 45 | P95 latency | 199.33 ms | 102.51 ms | -48.6% |
| 50 | Success rate | 92.32% | 100% | +7.68 pp |
| 50 | Successful throughput | 44.49 req/s | 49.23 req/s | +10.6% |

At target QPS 50, the static-capacity path was overloaded, so its mixed success/failure latency is intentionally not used as a compute-efficiency comparison. The compact path still completed all requests with 83.11 ms average and 134.01 ms P95 latency.

#### Direct Nsight Systems profile

To attribute the improvement, I also profiled synchronous batch-4 execution after warmup, using 50 measured iterations (200 requests). The profiler used a TP1 single-process worker and bypassed MPS so CUDA activity remained visible to Nsight; these absolute numbers are not intended to represent HTTP serving throughput.

| Metric | Static capacity | Compact | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Elapsed time, 200 requests | 7.163 s | 5.809 s | -18.9% |
| Direct requests/s | 27.92 | 34.43 | +23.3% |
| Total GPU kernel time | 3671.85 ms | 2171.99 ms | -40.8% |
| Attention kernel time | 1479.91 ms | 601.39 ms | -59.4% |
| GEMM kernel time | 1321.68 ms | 708.28 ms | -46.4% |
| Norm/RoPE kernel time | 63.03 ms | 33.97 ms | -46.1% |
| Sampling/selection kernel time | 131.19 ms | 131.64 ms | +0.3% |

The compact path executed 3.2% more kernel instances and increased D2D copy time from 68.20 ms to 86.23 ms (+26.4%), but the model-compute reduction was substantially larger. Compact metadata update took 6.50 ms total across 200 updates (32.5 microseconds per update).

### Correctness and numerical stability

Both paths were internally deterministic across repeated runs (100% self-consistency).

Across five prompts with 500 returned beams per prompt, full-set overlap was approximately 98%. For one representative prompt:

- full-set overlap: `494 / 5

items.title: [Feature]: SM120 Cake sparse-MLA: DeepSeek-V4.1 formats (FP8 SWA + FP4 compressed, BF16 Q)
items.author: xqoasis
items.body_excerpt:
### Before submitting

- [x] I have searched existing issues and this request has not been filed yet.

### Problem

Follow-up to #5690 / #5914.

### Summary

While evaluating DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on SM120, we found the Cake sparse-MLA decode from #5914 much faster than the `backend="sparse"` path. On SM120 it currently serves only the DSv4 NVFP4 cache (`kv_cache_format="nvfp4"`, 384 B for both the SWA and the compressed cache), and it quantizes Q's NoPE part to NVFP4. Both differ from the format DeepSeek-V4.1 was trained for.

Would the Cake generator be able to emit an SM120 variant that keeps the schedule but reads:

- compressed cache: the V4.1 288 B FP4 record (512 E2M1 values incl. RoPE + 32 E4M3 group-16 scales), i.e. the extra cache that `fp8_dsv41_fp4_ca` already reads;
- SWA cache: FP8 (the 584 B DSv4 record or the 528 B V4.1 MXFP8 record);
- Q: BF16 (or FP8) rather than NVFP4?

The SM100/SM103 Cake programs already cover FP8 E4M3 inputs, so this is mainly about the SM120 variant.

### Measurements

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash decode attention shapes (64 heads; 128 SWA + 512 top-k candidates per query row), a few dozen to ~100+ query rows per call, CUDA graphs, cold L2. Latency is relative to `backend="sparse"` with the 584 B FP8 cache on FlashInfer main (lower is better):

| configuration | relative latency |
|---|---|
| `sparse`, `fp8` (584 B) | 1.00× |
| `sparse`, `fp8_dsv41_fp4_ca` | ~1.2–1.6× |
| Cake, `nvfp4` (384 B) | ~0.42–0.43× |

Part of Cake's gain comes from the format (fewer bytes, FP4 MMA), but most of it appears to come from the schedule; the `sparse` kernel is latency-bound at these shapes (low tensor-pipe utilization, barrier and shared-memory stalls dominate). `fp8_dsv41_fp4_ca` (FP4 upconverted to FP8 at gather time) is slower than the FP8 path, so there is currently no fast SM120 reader for the V4.1 trained format.

### Why the 384 B NVFP4 contract is a concern for V4.1

1. **SWA precision.** The DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash tech report (§2.4.4) applies QAT only to the main/compressed KV cache (quantized after RoPE, RoPE included) and states: "We retain FP8 for the SWA KV cache due to its sensitivity to quantization." Cake requires the SWA cache in NVFP4 as well.
2. **Query precision.** The report dequantizes the cache before attention; Cake quantizes Q's NoPE part to NVFP4 for the `mxf4nvf4` QK MMA, which V4.1's QAT does not cover.
3. **The V4.1 format is validated end to end.** vLLM's V4.1 `nvfp4_ds_mla` (288 B FP4 compressed record + FP8 SWA, BF16 Q) matched the FP8 cache on GSM8K and GPQA-Diamond in vllm-project/vllm#56935.

A synthetic check on the same shapes (Gaussian latents, peaked softmax, attention-output relative error vs. an fp32 reference on unquantized latents) points the same way:

| configuration | relative error |
|---|---|
| `sparse`, 584 B FP8 cache | ~5% |
| KV in NVFP4 only (Q in BF16), exact math | ~19% |
| Q in NVFP4 only (KV exact), exact math | ~17% |
| Cake (KV and Q in NVFP4) | ~25% |
| `sparse`, `fp8_dsv41_fp4_ca` | ~19% |

Synthetic data overstates absolute error, but it suggests quantizing Q costs about as much as quantizing the KV, and that path is outside V4.1's training.

### Request

An SM120 Cake variant for the V4.1 formats would give SM120 a fast, QAT-validated FP4 KV path that matches the record vLLM uses for DeepSeek-V4.1 on SM100. We're happy to test a branch on SM120 and share relative latency and accuracy.

### Requested outcome

On SM120/SM121, `trtllm_batch_decode_sparse_mla_dsv4(..., backend="cake")` should accept the DeepSeek-V4.1 cache formats, with performance in the same range as the current Cake `nvfp4` path:

- SWA (main) cache in FP8: the 584 B DSv4 record and/or the 528 B V4.1 MXFP8 record;
- compressed (extra) cache in the V4.1 288 B FP4 record (512 E2M1 values incl. RoPE + 32 E4M3 group-16 scales, page-footer layout), i.e. what `kv_cache_format="fp8_dsv41_fp4_ca"` describes today;
- the query kept at BF16 (or FP8) precision in the QK product rather than quantized to NVFP4.

In short: on SM120, a DeepSeek-V4.1 deployment using the format the model was QAT-trained for (FP8 SWA + FP4 compressed KV, high-precision Q) should get Cake-level decode latency, instead of choosing between the fast `nvfp4` path (FP4 SWA + FP4 Q, outside the model's training) and the slower `fp8_dsv41_fp4_ca` path.

### Target hardware

SM120 (RTX PRO 6000, RTX 50-series)

### Inference engine

vLLM

### Affected model or model family

DeepSeek-V4.1

items.title: [Testing] Triage of red tests that still need a fix (90-day sweep)
items.author: bolubo
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

A 90 day sweep of the Actions history (2026-06-26 to 2026-09-25) turned up 455 failed runs. Most of them are already fixed, tied to a PR branch that was still iterating, or environmental. This issue is about what is left: tests that are still going red and do not have a fix, with enough evidence attached that someone can pick one up without redoing the whole investigation.

Two of the items reproduce locally on main today (A). Four more keep showing up in CI across branches, where the mechanism is narrowed down but there is no local repro yet (B). The appendices cover the one-off flakes and the families that are already fixed, so nobody has to dig through them again.

The coverage side already has tracking issues (#2637, #2708, #2737); this list is a different axis, tests that are failing right now.

If you want to take one, please comment on the item first so two people do not end up on the same thing, and link the PR here when it is up. Small focused PRs are the easiest to review.

## Items

- [ ] A1. Gateway rate limiter windows follow the wall clock, and three tests flake on the bucket boundary.
- [ ] A2. Two tests have been skipped since April 2025, and both pass when re-enabled.
- [ ] B1. The SLO queue spec times out on the release path.
- [ ] B2. The RoleSet topology spec hits a 409 conflict.
- [ ] B3. Batch e2e: a restored job does not reach `completed` within the 60s budget.
- [ ] B4. The planner unit test hangs and trips the 10 minute package timeout.

Grading:

- A: reproduced locally on main (`544204ae`), with a measured failure rate over repeated runs.
- B: repeated red in CI on main or across branches; no local repro yet.
- Watch: seen once; kept for reference.
- Fixed: already covered by a merged PR; do not re-triage.

## A. Reproduced locally on main

### A1. Gateway rate limiter windows follow the wall clock

`pkg/plugins/gateway/ratelimiter/redis.go:77` builds the counter key as `name:key:<unix/window % 64>`, so the counter changes on wall-clock bucket boundaries. A pair of calls that should share one window can land in two buckets instead, and the second call gets a fresh counter and is admitted. The TTL side is already anchored to the first write (`incrAndExpireScript`), so the key rotation is the remaining race.

- Affected tests: `pkg/plugins/gateway/replica_rps_test.go:96` (`TestModelReplicaRPS_Half_AllowsOneRequestEveryTwoSeconds`), `pkg/plugins/gateway/replica_inflight_test.go:335` (`TestHandleRequestBody_ReplicaInflightCoexistsWithReplicaRPS`), and `pkg/plugins/gateway/gateway_ratelimit_test.go:270` (`TestEnforceModelRPS_RejectDoesNotPostponeNextWindow`, added with #2726).
- How often it fails on main (one process per run, `-count=1`): 3 red in 100 runs for the first pair, 14 red in 450 runs for the third test, so roughly one run in thirty. The failure messages are "a second request within the same 2s window should be rejected" and "immediate retry should be rejected by the still-open window".
- CI hit: [run 35654425095, job 106514390571](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/actions/runs/35654425095/job/106514390571), Go Race Tests on 09-21, same assertion at `gateway_ratelimit_test.go:270`.
- Repro: `for i in $(seq 1 50); do go test ./pkg/plugins/gateway -run 'TestModelReplicaRPS_Half_AllowsOneRequestEveryTwoSeconds|TestHandleRequestBody_ReplicaInflightCoexistsWithReplicaRPS' -count=1; done`
- Two ways to fix it, and this is a real tradeoff: (1) anchor the window at the first write so every call in the same window computes the same key, which is what the tests already assume, at the cost of changing behavior at bucket boundaries; or (2) keep the wall-clock bucket and make the tests independent of it by injecting the clock, which is a smaller change but leaves the boundary burst in the product.

### A2. Two tests skipped since April 2025

- `pkg/utils/prefixcacheindexer/tree_test.go:33` (`Test_LPRadixCacheE2E`) and `:71` (`Test_RadixMatchPrefix`) have carried `t.SkipNow()` since `d546795a` (#933, April 2025). Removing the two lines makes both pass locally, in under 0.1s including subtests.
- `apps/console/api/resource_manager/provider/kubernetes/catalog_test.go:33` skips unconditionally with `t.Skip("skip for now")`, which also makes the kubeconfig checks below it dead code. Either delete the line or gate it on the environment with a stated reason.
- Repro: `go test ./pkg/utils/prefixcacheindexer -run 'Test_LPRadixCacheE2E|Test_RadixMatchPrefix' -v`

## B. Repeated red in CI, no local repro yet

### B1. SLO queue spec times out on the release path

- `pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/slo_test.go:253` ("Queue router should be blocked and released successfully") fails with `context deadline exceeded` at `:270`, after the 10s per spec budget.
- Hits since June: 06-28 `exclusive_topology`, 08-17 `route-dev` and `feat/align-job-time-window`, 09-05 `ui-aiconfigurator`, 09-09 `feat-pd-hybrid-cache-load`, 09-12 `roshpr/feat-stormservice-pooled-scale`, 09-20 `andreafeat/disable-gateway-rate-limiting` (race job). #2335 reported this spec in June and was closed after #2328 and #2353 merged, but it still recurs.
- A 150 run local loop is green, so it needs a CI style repro first. Fixing it likely means either making the assertion event driven or making the fixed wait budget explicit and generous.

### B2. RoleSet topology spec hits a 409 conflict

- `test/integration/controller/roleset_test.go:1062` ("applies topology policy updates only to newly created pods") fails at `:1118` with `Operation cannot be fulfilled on rolesets... the object has been modified; please apply your changes to the latest version and try again`. Latest hit: [35814726502](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/actions/runs/35814726502) on main, 09-23, 89 of 90 specs passed. Two more on 08-04.
- The spec updates the RoleSet while a reconcile is in flight, so `retry.RetryOnConflict` around the update (or `Eventually`) should close the race. Test side, no product change expected.

items.title: bug(sampling): top_k_arr/min_p_arr are validated against input rows but indexed by output row, reading out of bounds when indices is longer than probs
items.author: kahyunnam
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

`top_k_sampling_from_probs` and `min_p_sampling_from_probs` validate their per-request parameter tensor against the **input** batch but index it by the **output** row. When `indices` is longer than `probs.size(0)`, every output row at or past `probs.size(0)` reads past the end of the parameter tensor and silently samples with a garbage `top_k` / `min_p`.

- `check_tensor_param(maybe_top_k_arr, probs)` — [`csrc/sampling.cu:216`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/csrc/sampling.cu#L216) — requires `top_k_arr.size(0) == probs.size(0)`, via [`csrc/sampling_utils.h:34`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/csrc/sampling_utils.h#L34). Same for `min_p` at [`csrc/sampling.cu:262`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/csrc/sampling.cu#L262).
- The kernels read [`top_k_arr[bx]`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/include/flashinfer/sampling.cuh#L872) and [`min_p_arr[bx]`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/include/flashinfer/sampling.cuh#L1129), where `bx` is `blockIdx.x`, i.e. the output row.

The sibling kernels get this right and index by the input row: [`top_p_arr[row_idx]`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/include/flashinfer/sampling.cuh#L1006) in `TopPSamplingFromProbKernel`, and [`top_k_arr[row_idx]` / `top_p_arr[row_idx]`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/include/flashinfer/sampling.cuh#L1228-L1229) in `TopKTopPSamplingFromProbKernel`. So only the two `[bx]` sites are wrong.

### Reproduction

On a B200 (SM100), 4 input rows, 16 output rows via `indices = arange(16) % 4`, vocab 512. The parameter tensor is a length-4 view carved out of a 4096-element buffer whose tail holds a conspicuous value, so an out-of-bounds read returns that tail instead of faulting:

| Call | Parameter tensor | Output rows violating the parameter |
|---|---|---|
| `top_k_sampling_from_probs` | length-4 `top_k`, all `1`, buffer tail `500` | **12 / 16** — exactly rows 4–15 |
| `min_p_sampling_from_probs` | length-4 `min_p`, all `1.0`, buffer tail `0.0` | **12 / 16** — exactly rows 4–15 |
| `top_p_sampling_from_probs` (control) | length-4 `top_p`, all `1e-6`, buffer tail `1.0` | **0 / 16** |

With `top_k = 1` every output row must return `argmax(probs[indices[i]])`; rows 4–15 do not. The `top_p` control isolates the cause to the `bx` / `row_idx` choice rather than anything about the harness.

Note that `compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck` does **not** flag this: the read stays inside the PyTorch caching-allocator segment, so a memcheck-clean run is not evidence of safety here.

<details>
<summary>Repro script</summary>

```python
import torch
from flashinfer import sampling

torch.manual_seed(0)
IN, OUT, V = 4, 16, 512
probs = torch.softmax(torch.randn(IN, V, device="cuda"), dim=-1)
indices = torch.arange(OUT, device="cuda", dtype=torch.int32) % IN

# Length-IN views carved out of a larger buffer whose tail holds a conspicuous value.
k_buf = torch.full((4096,), 500, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
k_buf[:IN] = 1
top_k = k_buf[:IN]

p_buf = torch.zeros(4096, dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda")
p_buf[:IN] = 1.0
min_p = p_buf[:IN]

tp_buf = torch.full((4096,), 1.0, dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda")
tp_buf[:IN] = 1e-6
top_p = tp_buf[:IN]

argmax = probs.argmax(dim=-1)


def violations(out):
    return [(i, int(out[i])) for i in range(OUT) if int(out[i]) != int(argmax[indices[i]])]


out_k = sampling.top_k_sampling_from_probs(probs, top_k, indices=indices, deterministic=True)
print("top_k=1  violations:", len(violations(out_k)), "/", OUT, violations(out_k)[:6])

out_p = sampling.min_p_sampling_from_probs(probs, min_p, indices=indices, deterministic=True)
print("min_p=1  violations:", len(violations(out_p)), "/", OUT, violations(out_p)[:6])

# Control: top_p indexes by input row, so it must be unaffected.
out_tp = sampling.top_p_sampling_from_probs(probs, top_p, indices=indices, deterministic=True)
print("top_p    violations:", len(violations(out_tp)), "/", OUT)
```

```
top_k=1  violations: 12 / 16 [(4, 189), (5, 226), (6, 216), (7, 345), (8, 459), (9, 92)]
min_p=1  violations: 12 / 16 [(4, 320), (5, 147), (6, 350), (7, 300), (8, 42), (9, 113)]
top_p    violations: 0 / 16
```

</details>

### Fix

Two options, and the choice is a contract decision rather than a mechanical one:

1. Index by the input row — change `top_k_arr[bx]` to `top_k_arr[row_idx]` and `min_p_arr[bx]` to `min_p_arr[row_idx]`, matching the existing validation and the two sibling kernels.
2. Keep output-row indexing and fix the validation to use the output batch instead of `probs`, which is what `top_k`/`min_p` being *per-request* arguably implies.

Option 2 matches what the docstrings suggest (`indices` maps outputs to distributions, so a per-request parameter is naturally per-output) and is the convention #5745 uses for `seed`/`offset`, which validates against `output.size(0)`. Option 1 is the smaller change and keeps all four kernels consistent with each other. Either way the four kernels should agree, and a test with `len(indices) > probs.size(0)` plus a tensor-valued parameter would have caught this.

### Environment

NVIDIA B200 (SM100, CC 10.0), CUDA 13.0, torch 2.14.0+cu130, Python 3.10, `main` @ `1cad38165`. Nothing about this is architecture-specific.

items.title: [Roadmap]Fast Engine Recovery: Weight Cache Daemon
items.author: liusy58
items.body_excerpt:
# [Roadmap] Fast Engine Recovery: Weight Cache Daemon 
@liusy58 @QiuMike @alexnails 
Phase 1 landed in #27139 — a per-rank daemon holds post-quantized weights and serves them over CUDA IPC; weight load drops from ~306–327s to <1s on Qwen3-235B FP8 ([blog](https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2026-08-21-sglang-fast-recovery)). This issue tracks the next steps. Contributions and feedback are welcome.

Related: #27052 (Fast Recovery framework), #27310 (GPU Memory Service / VMM)

Goals: <10s cold restart and <1s warm standby switch; broaden model & quant coverage; make the cache outlive the daemon; make resident weights usable beyond the one GPU they sit on.

Where Phase 1 stands: TP + PP, single-node and multi-node launch (each node spawns its share of ranks and joins one dist group), zero-copy IPC per GPU, unquantized + block-wise FP8. Not yet: cross-node daemon coordination / failover, DP & EP shard keying, spec-decoding draft models, weight update / sleep-wake, cache surviving daemon death.

## Model & quantization coverage

- [ ] parity harness — disk-load vs daemon-load `state_dict` diff (names / shape / dtype / stride / byte hash) + short GSM8K gate; required evidence for every new allowlist entry
- [ ] carry post-processing metadata in the manifest (final shape/stride, layout tag, whitelisted module attrs) instead of reproducing `process_weights_after_loading` on a meta-init model — this is what blocks most quant methods today
- [ ] quant methods: per-tensor fp8 / w8a8 int8 / mxfp8 / nvfp4 / compressed-tensors / awq / gptq-marlin #32398 
- [ ] archs: MoE (DeepSeek V3/V4, Ling, Kimi K3) / hybrid linear attention / multimodal (vision tower + projector) / LoRA base weights https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/33684
- [ ] MTP & EAGLE draft models (per-rank draft daemon), removing the `--speculative-algorithm` rejection in `server_args.py` #32744
- [ ] generic post-map rebuild hook to replace the hardcoded `_rebuild_stale_views`; make tied storages, param→buffer flips and non-persistent buffers explicit in the manifest
- [ ] publish the support matrix in docs; unsupported combinations keep hard-erroring (no silent wrong numerics)

## Transport: CUDA VMM shareable handles (#27310 §4.2)



- [ ] `vmm_fd` backend (skeleton already in `weight_cache/transport.py`): `cuMemCreate` + FD handles over `SCM_RIGHTS`, VA reservation on import, `torch_ipc` stays the fallback, `--weight-cache-transport {auto,torch_ipc,vmm_fd}` #33279
- [ ] `mooncake` backend https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/36293


## Weight update without reload

- [ ] epoch handoff on stable VAs: readers unmap → writer commits → readers remap at the same VAs, so captured CUDA graphs stay valid
- [ ] daemon as the weight delivery agent for trainer pushes (NCCL/RDMA); un-gate the `update_weights_*` rejections in `weight_updater.py`
- [ ] colocated RL: engine itself takes the writer role, same protocol, no daemon in the loop

## Multi-instance & cross-GPU sharing

- [ ] key the cache by physical GPU UUID + config fingerprint (plus optional `--weight-cache-namespace`) under a configurable runtime dir. Today the socket is `/tmp/sglang_weight_cache_rank{global_rank}.sock`, so 2× tp=4 on one 8-GPU node collide and rank 0 of the second instance attaches to the GPU 0 daemon
- [ ] discovery: replace static socket paths with a lightweight registry (file-based dir, optionally etcd) so an engine rank selects a daemon by `CacheConfig` match rather than by process rank, and locates daemons across nodes without a manual `--weight-cache-socket`
- [ ] `--weight-cache-peer-copy` — when no daemon holds the shard on the local GPU, `cudaMemcpyPeerAsync` it from a peer-GPU daemon (NVLink-domain check, chunked on a low-priority stream, bandwidth cap so a serving neighbour is not disturbed). 1× memory per instance, sub-second over NVLink vs ~300s from disk
- [ ] preference order local zero-copy > peer copy > disk, reported per rank
- [ ] fleet fill: a daemon fills itself from a peer daemon instead of disk (P2P on-node, NCCL/RDMA cross-node), so a fleet cold start pays one disk read per shard group — the real bottleneck for 1T+ models on shared FS; align with the checkpoint-engine broadcast path
- [ ] out of scope for now: resharding across TP/EP topologies (tp=4 daemon → tp=8 engine)

## Multi-node, DP & EP

- [ ] primary–secondary daemon coordination for multi-node TP (e.g. TP=16 = 2 nodes × 8 GPUs): primary orchestrates daemon startup, cross-node NCCL process-group formation and readiness signalling; secondaries load their local shards in parallel and serve IPC handles to engines on their own node. Basic multi-node launch already works via `--nnodes/--node-rank/--dist-init-method`; what is missing is the cluster state machine
- [ ] cross-node daemon lifecycle: primary tracks which secondaries are alive, triggers coordinated restarts, signals engines on a dead secondary's node to fall back to disk; promote a secondary when the primary dies
- [ ] DP support: every DP rank on a GPU maps the same daemon's handles, so a model is read from disk and quantized exactly once per GPU regardless of DP degree (today each DP rank disk-loads independently). This is about supporting SGLang's DP deployment model, not cross-GPU sharing
- [ ] EP support: expert shards differ per EP rank, so cache and key them by `ep_rank`; handle partial expert loading when a rank owns a subset of experts
- [ ] `CacheConfig`: add `ep_rank`, `dp_rank` and `node_rank` for correct shard identification under EP and multi-node (`dp_size`/`ep_size` are already there)

## Ops & reliability

- [ ] `daemon status` command + Prometheus metrics (resident bytes, attached clients, load time, hit / mismatch / fallback), and an engine endpoint reporting how each rank got its weights
- [ ] runtime dir with owner-only permissions + `SO_PEERCRED` check before handing out handles (no world-writable `/tmp` sockets)
- [ ] `protocol_version` in the handshake with a documented skew policy (the env stamp alrea

items.title: Concurrent multi-process compilation with a shared TRITON_CACHE_DIR on a network filesystem crashes: EBUSY from os.removedirs in cache put, FileNotFoundError reading back just-published files
items.author: zkyue
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

When several processes JIT-compile the same kernels concurrently into one shared
`TRITON_CACHE_DIR` on a network/distributed filesystem, individual compilations
crash with one of two signatures:

1. `OSError: [Errno 16] Device or resource busy` raised from
   `FileCacheManager.put` -> `os.removedirs(temp_dir)` — the staged file has already
   been renamed to its final name when this cleanup step runs, so the exception aborts
   a `put` whose real work had completed;
2. `FileNotFoundError` in `CompiledKernel.__init__` reading back files the process
   itself just published.

Both reproduce with the stock 3.4.0 wheel and the script below. Both code paths are
unchanged on current `main`
([cache.py L103-L127](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/5f2ca3a88c52b80b601e3e243fb3d6079de0f61f/python/triton/runtime/cache.py#L103-L127),
[compiler.py L407-L432](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/5f2ca3a88c52b80b601e3e243fb3d6079de0f61f/python/triton/compiler/compiler.py#L407-L432)).
We first hit both in real 8-rank torchrun jobs (four EBUSY occurrences across three
distinct `put` call sites — IR-stage put, metadata put, `put_group` — plus several
FileNotFoundError ones); there a single crashed rank left the remaining ranks blocked
in collectives, so the whole job hung.

## Environment

- Triton 3.4.0 (pip wheel), Python 3.12.3, Linux 5.15 (Ubuntu), x86_64, single node
- Shared `TRITON_CACHE_DIR` on a Kubernetes PVC backed by a vendor distributed NVMe
  filesystem (`findmnt` fstype `storage`, mounted `rw,noatime`); proprietary — we do
  not have visibility into its client/server internals or documented POSIX guarantees
- Control run on local overlayfs on the same machine: zero failures
- The reproducer does not touch a GPU (explicit `GPUTarget("cuda", 90, 32)`, ptxas
  from the wheel); the original crashes were in GPU jobs on the same mount

## Signature 1: EBUSY in `put` cleanup

```
  File ".../triton/compiler/compiler.py", line 383, in compile
    metadata_group[metadata_filename] = fn_cache_manager.put(json.dumps(metadata, default=vars), metadata_filename,
  File ".../triton/runtime/cache.py", line 119, in put
    os.removedirs(temp_dir)
  File "<frozen os>", line 243, in removedirs
OSError: [Errno 16] Device or resource busy: '/path/to/cache/7CDGTACI.../tmp.pid_2958216_a306aa55-5495-45ce-8a85-cf7f77b01ead'
```

In the reproducer this fires both at the metadata `put` (as above) and at `put_group`; in our real jobs also at IR-stage `put`s.

`put()` writes to a per-writer temp dir (unique: pid + uuid4), atomically
`os.replace`s the file to its final name, then removes the temp dir. `os.removedirs`
only propagates an error from the leaf `rmdir` (parent-pruning errors are swallowed),
so the filesystem is refusing to remove the writer's own just-emptied temp dir. We
have not traced the fs internals; empirically it happens only while sibling processes
are hammering the same key dir with their own staged writes and renames. Whatever the
fs-side reason, the failing operation is pure cleanup of a private directory whose
only file was already renamed out — aborting the compilation at that point turns an
ignorable condition into a crash.

Two incidental observations on this line: `os.removedirs` also tries to prune the
*shared* key directory and its ancestors after removing the temp dir (normally stopped
by `ENOTEMPTY`, but clearly unintended), and #4295 — which introduced the temp-dir
scheme — did not discuss the cleanup step's failure modes.

## Signature 2: FileNotFoundError reading back just-published files

```
  File ".../triton/compiler/compiler.py", line 403, in compile
    return CompiledKernel(src, metadata_group, hash)
  File ".../triton/compiler/compiler.py", line 448, in __init__
    metadata = json.loads(metadata_path.read_text())
  File "/usr/lib/python3.12/pathlib.py", line 1030, in read_text
    return f.read()
FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory
```

(an earlier run of the same reproducer, and our real jobs, also hit the same
failure in the `read_bytes` loop over the other group files a few lines down)

Note where it fails: `open()` succeeded — the ENOENT comes out of the `read()` of an
already-open file. `metadata_group` holds final paths this process itself just
published. Nothing in the workload deletes published files; the only concurrent
mutation of those names is other writers `os.replace`-ing their own copies of the
same content over them. On a fully POSIX filesystem an open file survives its name
being replaced; the failures are consistent with the open handle being invalidated
by a concurrent same-name replace (we did not capture a syscall trace tying an
individual failing read to an individual competing rename). #4295 fixed
an earlier FileNotFoundError in this loop (glob picking up other writers' temp
files); this is a distinct remaining window in which the reader loses to a same-name
replace rather than to temp-file listing.

## Reproducer

<details><summary>repro_cache_race.py</summary>

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Reproducer for Triton JIT cache crashes under multi-process compilation
with a shared TRITON_CACHE_DIR on a network filesystem.

Per round: N fresh processes compile the same 8 kernel variants (same cache
keys) into one fresh shared cache dir, barrier-aligned per variant. No GPU is
used: compilation targets are given explicitly and ptxas comes from the wheel.

Expected failure signatures (both fail the compilation; the harness catches
and records them — in real jobs they crash the process):
  (a) OSError [Errno 16] Device or resource busy
      from FileCacheManager.put -> os.removedirs(temp_dir)
  (b) FileNotFoundError
      from CompiledKernel.__init__ reading back just-published group files

Rounds where a failure occurred are preserved on disk for inspection; clean
rounds are deleted. Each round validates that all N workers reported back and
exited 0, so the failure counts have a trustworthy denominator.

Usage:

items.title: [Performance] XQA sm90 decode (head_dim 256, fp8 KV, page 16), batch 10 / 124K ctx: 18% of HBM peak, 66-block grid, 12.5% warp occupancy — 65% of the decode step
items.author: wenzhelee
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

Long-context, small-batch decode with **XQA** (`kernel_mha`, from `csrc/xqa/mha_sm90.cu`) runs at **18% of HBM peak** and accounts for **65% of the decode step** on an H20 (sm90). In the *same step on the same device*, a `deep_gemm` FP8 GEMM reaches 32%. The traced grid for `kernel_mha` is only **66 blocks for 78 SMs**, 1 block/SM (129.6 KiB smem) → ~12.5% warp occupancy, so we suspect a long serial KV chain rather than a bandwidth limit.

We may well be mis-configuring something (e.g. `page_size`), and we'd appreciate a pointer to the relevant knob or to the right kernel for this shape. Happy to run further experiments if useful.

### Environment

- vLLM `v0.30.0` (`vllm/vllm-openai:v0.30.0`), **flashinfer 0.6.18.post1**, torch 2.13.0+cu130 (CUDA 13.0)
- 2 × NVIDIA H20 (sm90, **78 SMs**, 97,871 MiB each), `--tensor-parallel-size 2`
- Model: Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 — hybrid: **16 full-attention layers (4 KV heads, head_dim 256)** + 48 GDN (linear-attention) layers
- KV cache: **fp8 (e4m3)**, `--block-size 16` → `page_size = 16`, `--max-model-len 1000000`, MTP `num_speculative_tokens=2`
- Attention backend `FLASHINFER`; `--max-num-seqs 128`, `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.88`
- Load: **10 concurrent requests**, 124,026-token prompts (94.6% prefix-cache hit, so prefill is negligible), 3000 decode tokens each, greedy
- The precompiled kernel that matches this run is exactly
  `xqa_input_bf16_kv_cache_e4m3_output_bf16_page_size_16_head_dim_256_head_group_ratio_2_use_sliding_window_False_use_spec_dec_False_spec_q_seq_len_1`
- For reference, swapping in `FLASH_ATTN` (FA3) made the *whole step* 1.8x slower (82.7 → 45.6 ms/step), i.e. XQA is already the better of the two available paths.

### Evidence

torch-profiler / CUPTI kernel events, one **42.2 s** steady-decode window = **955 engine steps** (steps derived from `spec_decode_num_drafts_total`), batch 10, 124K ctx. Per-step totals:

| kernel family | ms/step | share | grid | block | smem/block | bytes/step/card | effective BW |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **`kernel_mha` (XQA)** | **27.51** | **64.9%** | — | — | — | KV 19.84 GB | **721 GB/s = 18.0% of 4.0 TB/s** |
| ↳ the dominant call | 26.78 | 63.2% | **[3, 2, 11] = 66 blocks** | [128,1,2] = 256 thr | 129.6 KiB | | |
| `deep_gemm::sm90_fp8_gemm_1d2d_impl<…17408,5120…>` | 3.27 | 7.7% | [78,1,1] | [256,1,1] | 214.8 KiB | | |
| GEMM family (all deep_gemm/nvjet) | 10.51 | 24.8% | | | | weights 13.65 GB | **1,299 GB/s = 32.5%** |
| quant / copy / elementwise | 1.56 | 3.7% | | | | | |
| GDN (`gdn_decode_post_conv_mtp_kernel`) | 1.45 | 3.4% | [11,24,1] | [256,1,1] | 44.1 KiB | | |
| allreduce (`oneshotAllreduceFusionKernel`) | 1.18 | 2.8% | | | | | |
| **total** | **42.38** | 100% | | | | | |

`kernel_mha` is called **17 times per step** (16 full-attention layers + the MTP draft layer), 1552 µs per call.

Context control — same batch size, same everything, only ctx = 8K:

| | 124K | 8K |
|---|---|---|
| attention ms/step | **27.51** | **3.03** |
| GEMM family | 10.51 | 9.38 |
| GDN | 1.45 | 1.44 |
| allreduce | 1.18 | 1.09 |
| quant/copy | 1.56 | 1.44 |

**Every non-attention family is ctx-independent ( ±0.1 ms); the 25.9 ms step delta is 100% this kernel.** Fitting `t_attn ≈ 1.31 ms + 2.055e-4 ms × ctx` ⇒ marginal KV read bandwidth ≈ 758 GB/s. Impact on throughput: engine-peak 1716 tok/s at 8K ctx vs 696 tok/s at 124K with identical batch.

### Questions

1. For this variant, how is the KV/context split factor chosen (grid.z = 3 here → 3 × 2 KV heads × 11 requests)? With 124K ctx that leaves each block serially covering ~41K tokens of KV, which 66 blocks / 8 warps-per-SM apparently cannot hide. Is the split factor a build-time constant, or can it be increased?
2. Would a different `page_size` change the tiling/occupancy? The JIT cache already contains `page_size ∈ {16,32,64,128} × head_dim 256 × head_group_ratio 2`, so we plan to A/B `--block-size 32/64` next — if you already know the answer we'd rather not burn restart cycles.
3. Is there a recommended alternative decode kernel/flag for this shape on sm90 (**long context, small batch, GQA group ratio 2, fp8 KV, head_dim 256, page 16, MTP/spec-decode enabled**) that we should compare against — e.g. a non-XQA / non-tensor-core path?
4. Is the 18%-of-peak figure expected at these shapes, or is there a known config caveat (workspace buffer size, `VLLM_FLASHINFER_*`, autotune) we should check first?

### Repro sketch

```bash
vllm serve <Qwen3.8-27B-FP8> --tensor-parallel-size 2 --max-model-len 1000000 \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --block-size 16 --max-num-seqs 128 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.88 \
  --attention-backend FLASHINFER --speculative-config '{"num_speculative_tokens":2,...}' \
  --profiler-config '{"profiler":"torch","torch_profiler_dir":"/tmp/vprof","torch_profiler_with_stack":false}'
# warm a shared 124K prompt prefix, then run 10 concurrent /v1/chat/completions with max_tokens=3000
curl -X POST localhost:8001/start_profile   # ~42 s of steady decode
curl -X POST localhost:8001/stop_profile    # note: this RPC can time out while the dump succeeds
# parse rank*.pt.trace.json.gz, sum "dur" per kernel where "cat": "kernel"
```

Kernel timing closure: the six families above sum to 42.38 ms/step, matching an independent measurement of 41.8 ms/step from `generation_tokens_total` / `spec_decode_num_drafts_total`, so nothing material is missing from the accounting.

items.title: [Experimental] Packed-FP8 MSA sparse decode for MiniMax-M3 (SM100/SM103)
items.author: Analysis196884
items.body_excerpt:
## Tracking issue: experimental packed-FP8 MSA sparse decode

**Owner:** @Analysis196884

## Use case

MiniMax-M3 speculative decode serving (requested in #4567): per-token independent top-k sparse attention over a packed FP8 E4M3 paged KV cache `(num_pages, Hkv, 128, 256)`, consumed in place as strided K/V views, with BF16 Q and device scalar K/V scales. The path is the decode step after the existing MiniMax-M3 indexer produces `q2k_indices[Hkv, total_q, 16]`. Target hardware: SM100/SM103 (validated on B300/SM103). Benchmarks against the vLLM Triton baseline are in #5556.

## Reason for the experimental path

This is a new operation from a latest-model serving stack (admitted category: "new operations from the latest models"). The implementation is an adaptation layer over the existing TRT-LLM block-sparse decode kernel plus a small decode-metadata preparation kernel; the public contract (packed-cache view conventions, workspace requirements, trace surface) may still evolve with the serving integration, so it lands behind the experimental API `flashinfer.msa_ops.msa_packed_fp8_sparse_decode` with the implementation contained in `flashinfer/experimental/msa_fp8_decode/`.

## Scope

- Public API: `flashinfer.msa_ops.msa_packed_fp8_sparse_decode` (`@flashinfer_experimental_api`).
- Implementation: `flashinfer/experimental/msa_fp8_decode/` (backend + metadata-preparation kernel JIT).
- Tests: `tests/experimental/test_msa_packed_fp8_decode.py`; runnable usage example in `docs/api/sparse.rst` and `benchmarks/bench_minimax_m3_sparse_decode.py`.
- No AOT registration; not reachable from any `backend="auto"` dispatch.

## Graduation plan

Target: graduate (or revise) within four weeks of landing, i.e. by the first minor release after that window.

1. Collect serving-side integration feedback (vLLM MiniMax-M3) on the packed-cache contract and workspace ergonomics.
2. Complete SM100 runtime validation (only SM103 was validated at admission).
3. Add AOT registration and promote the trace templates to the graduation checklist requirements.
4. Graduate by removing the experimental marker, or fold the route into `msa_sparse_decode_attention` dispatch if maintainers prefer that shape.

## Removal conditions

Per the experimental policy: broken tests, loss of ownership, or lack of meaningful usage are sufficient for removal without stable deprecation guarantees.

items.title: Descriptor stores write past the tensor's inner extent, up to the next 16-byte boundary
items.author: alepot55
items.body_excerpt:
`tensor_descriptor.store` documents that values outside the tensor bounds are ignored, and the interpreter clips them per element, but on an H100 (`e08ec196b`) a store of a block that ends beyond the inner extent `N` also writes the elements from `N` up to the next 16-byte boundary of the row. With a column slice of a larger tensor as the destination, that is another tensor's data.

```python
@triton.jit
def copy(out_d, a_d, N, BLOCK_M: tl.constexpr, BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr):
    off_m = tl.program_id(0) * BLOCK_M
    for ni in range(0, tl.cdiv(N, BLOCK_N)):
        v = a_d.load([off_m, ni * BLOCK_N])
        out_d.store([off_m, ni * BLOCK_N], v)

out = torch.full((32, 512), 7, dtype=dtype, device="cuda")
out_d = TensorDescriptor.from_tensor(out[:, :N], [32, 128])
copy[(1,)](out_d, a_d, N, BLOCK_M=32, BLOCK_N=128)
```

Columns of `out[:, N:]` no longer equal to 7 afterwards (same with a `tl.make_tensor_descriptor` built in the kernel with `shape=[M, N], strides=[512, 1]`):

```
int8   N=466: 14 columns written (466..479)      N=464: none
int16  N=470:  2 columns written (470..471)
int32  N=466:  2 columns written (466..467)      N=468: none
```

So the store clips at 16-byte granularity of the global address, and only inner extents that are a multiple of 16 bytes behave as documented. `TensorDescriptor` checks the base and the strides for 16-byte alignment but not `shape[-1] * itemsize`. Is the intended contract that the inner extent must be 16-byte aligned too (in which case the descriptor could assert it and the interpreter should match the device), or is this a lowering issue? Found with a differential fuzzer of descriptor kernels against `TRITON_INTERPRET=1`, where it shows up in about half of the programs with a ragged inner dimension.

items.title: Should LMCacheMPConnector honor kv_transfer_config.kv_role — or is MP mode intentionally always-kv_both?
items.author: kezboard233
items.body_excerpt:
## Context

We run a production-shaped POC on 8×V100 (two vLLM TP4 instances of Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 sharing one LMCache MP server with a CPU L1 tier) and filed #5143 with a runtime-verified repro: an engine launched with `kv_role="kv_consumer"` still stores every request's KV into the shared L1 — a single 32K-token cold request produced `168 × "Stored 784"` lines (= full prefix × 4 TP ranks), and the only engine that received any request in that window was the `kv_consumer` one.

We later found #4665 (closed by its author without maintainer response) reporting the same mechanism from the CacheBlend angle: the single-process connector honors `kv_role` / `skip_save`, the MP connector honors neither. As of today's `dev`, `lmcache_mp_connector.py` still contains no occurrence of `kv_role` / `kv_consumer` / `kv_producer` / `force_skip_save`.

## The design question

Before we contribute a patch, we want to check intent: **is MP mode intentionally "every connected engine writes"?** Two readings:

1. **Contract gap** — vLLM makes `kv_role` mandatory, documents it as "Whether this vLLM instance produces, consumes KV cache, or both", and exposes `is_kv_producer` / `is_kv_consumer` for connectors to branch on; LMCache's own single-process adapter honors it (`force_skip_save` in `vllm_v1_adapter.py`). Under this reading we'd gladly contribute a small PR that skips store-metadata generation when `is_kv_consumer` (mirroring the single-process gate), so warm-then-read-only fleets and PD-style topologies become possible on the MP path.

2. **Intentional always-kv_both** — the MP tier is a shared scratch space where every connected engine contributes. Under this reading we'd instead ask for the intent to be documented, plus ideally a one-line warning at connector init when `kv_role != "kv_both"`, so users aren't misled (we only noticed via instrumented counter evidence ourselves).

Happy to do either — a steer from maintainers decides which.

(Impact context: no correctness issue — stored content is identical — but a consumer-role engine burns D2H bandwidth and shared-L1 capacity; a 32K prefix on our model is ≈8.6 GB across 4 ranks.)

items.title: [Bug] trtllm-bench hangs forever at shutdown when --iteration_log points into a directory that does not exist
items.author: nvegesna-netizen
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

If the parent directory of the path passed to `--iteration_log` does not exist, the
benchmark runs to completion and then hangs permanently instead of exiting.

The failure mode is costly and hard to diagnose:

- **It is deterministic.** Every run with such a path hangs.
- **It costs the whole run.** Generation finishes and the progress bar reaches 100%,
  but `stop()` never returns, so no report files are written and no statistics are
  printed. Everything the run computed is discarded.
- **It produces no diagnostic.** The last line logged is `Stopping LLM backend.`.
  The child process that failed does print a `FileNotFoundError` traceback, but it is
  unrelated in appearance to a hang and nothing in the parent reports the failure.
- **It is not interruptible.** `Ctrl-C` does not help; the process is blocked either
  inside a blocking `zmq_ctx_term()` call or on an `await` that can never resolve.
  `SIGKILL` is the only way out.

A single mistyped character in a path is enough to trigger it.

The hang is independent of model, dataset and parallelism, because it happens after
all generation has finished, when the iteration-logging plumbing is the only thing
still running.

Both the `throughput` and the `latency` subcommands are affected: both accept
`--iteration_log` and both drive `LlmManager`.

Verified on `main` at commit `3035d47286ef3e232b16430abf376600ef192517`; the line
numbers below refer to that commit.

## System Info

Not hardware-specific. The defect is in the `trtllm-bench` iteration-logging plumbing,
and it reproduces with no GPU and no TensorRT-LLM installation using the standalone
script under [Reproduction](#reproduction). The commit it was verified on is the one
above; the affected branches and release tags are listed in
[Versions affected](#versions-affected).

## Root cause

Three separate things have to be true, and all three currently are.

### 1. The writer process binds its socket before it opens the log file

`tensorrt_llm/bench/benchmark/utils/processes.py`, `IterationWriter.run` (lines
137-173):

```python
        try:
            # Create a ZeroMQ context and socket for inter-process communication
            logger.debug(f"Iteration logging: Binding to {address}...")
            context = Context(io_threads=1)
            socket = context.socket(PULL)
            socket.bind(address)                      # line 142

            # Open the log file for writing and start listening for messages
            logger.debug(
                f"Iteration logging: Listening for messages on {address}...")
            with open(log_path, "w") as f:            # line 147  <-- raises
```

`open(log_path, "w")` at line 147 raises `FileNotFoundError` when `log_path.parent`
does not exist. The only handler is `except KeyboardInterrupt` at line 158, so the
exception propagates, the `finally` at line 165 tears the socket down, and the child
exits with status 1. Nothing in the parent process ever inspects that exit code.

Note the asymmetry with `--report_json`, which is handled correctly:
`generate_json_report` in `tensorrt_llm/bench/benchmark/__init__.py` does
`report_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` at line 185. The
iteration-log path gets no equivalent treatment, so two adjacent reporting options
behave differently for the same user mistake.

The value also passes CLI validation silently. `--iteration_log` is declared in
`tensorrt_llm/bench/benchmark/throughput.py` at lines 281-290 as:

```python
@optgroup.option(
    "--iteration_log",
    type=click.Path(dir_okay=False,
                    writable=True,
                    readable=False,
                    path_type=Path,
                    resolve_path=True),
    required=False,
    help="Path where iteration logging is written to.",
)
```

Because `exists` defaults to `False`, `click.types.Path.convert` returns early from
its `except OSError` branch as soon as `os.stat` fails, so the `writable=True` check
is never reached for a path that does not yet exist. (Confirmed against click 8.3.1;
`requirements.txt` pins `click>=8.3.1,<8.4`.)

### 2. The producer cannot detect that the consumer is gone, and its teardown blocks

`tensorrt_llm/bench/benchmark/utils/asynchronous.py`, `LlmManager.iteration_worker`
(lines 320-366):

```python
            context = Context.instance(io_threads=1)       # line 327
            socket = context.socket(PUSH)                  # line 328
            socket.connect(iteration_addr)                 # line 329
            ...
            while not self._stop.is_set():
                async for stats in self.llm.get_stats_async(2):
                    await socket.send_json(stats)          # line 339
                await asyncio.sleep(0)
            ...
            async for stats in self.llm.get_stats_async(2):
                await socket.send_json(stats)              # line 348
        except asyncio.CancelledError:
            logger.debug("Iteration log worker cancelled.")
        except Exception as e:
            raise e
        finally:
            logger.debug("Iteration log worker sending None...")
            socket.send_json({"end": True})                # line 358
            if socket is not None:
                socket.close()                             # line 361
            if context is not None:
                context.term()                             # line 364
```

`socket.connect()` on an `ipc://` endpoint is asynchronous and does not fail when
nothing is listening, so the producer has no way to notice the dead consumer. libzmq
also creates the outbound pipe optimistically at connect time, which means the socket
is *not* in the mute state: sends keep succeeding into a queue that will never drain.

That yields two stalls, depending on how many iteration-stats messages the run
produces.

**Primary case (fewer than `ZMQ_SNDHWM` messages): the stall is in `context.term()`
at line 364.** Every send succeeds, the loop exits normally once `_stop` i

items.title: [Bug]: DisaggClusterManager drops remaining watch events when one event raises
items.author: DhineshPonnarasan
items.body_excerpt:
## System Info

```text
TensorRT-LLM commit: 67a0328029
GPU: NVIDIA Tesla T4, 16 GB VRAM
Compute Capability: 7.5 (SM75)
Driver: 580.178.04
CUDA: 13.0
Python: 3.12.10
OS: Linux (OpenHPC)
```

The reproduction itself is CPU-only and does not exercise CUDA, NIXL, UCX, or model execution.


## Information

* [ ] The official example scripts
* [x] My own modified scripts

## Tasks

* [ ] An officially supported task in the `examples` folder (such as GLUE/SQuAD, ...)
* [x] My own task or dataset

Testing the disaggregated-serving worker-event lifecycle.

## Reproduction

`DisaggClusterManager.worker_event_loop` can permanently drop later events from a watch-event batch when an earlier event raises.

The issue is reproducible on commit `67a0328029` using the real `worker_event_loop` and `WatchEventQueue.drain()` implementation.

Minimal event sequence:

1. Queue a `DELETE` event for an unknown worker (`ghost-worker`).
2. Queue a valid `SET` event for worker `w1` in the same batch.
3. Allow `worker_event_loop` to process the batch.

The resulting behavior is:

```text
drain() -> [DELETE ghost-worker, SET w1]
DELETE ghost-worker -> ValueError("Worker ghost-worker is unknown")
batch-level exception handler runs
SET w1 -> never processed
queue -> empty
```

A control case containing two valid `SET` events, `[SET w1, SET w2]`, processes both events normally.

## Expected behavior

Each event in a drained watch-event batch should be processed independently.

If one event is stale, invalid, duplicated, or otherwise raises an exception, the remaining events in the same batch should still be processed.

In particular, a failing `DELETE` for an unknown worker should not cause an unrelated subsequent `SET` event to be lost.

## Actual behavior

`WatchEventQueue.drain()` destructively removes all currently queued events.

`worker_event_loop` wraps the entire drained batch in a single `try/except`. When processing one event raises, the loop exits the batch immediately.

As a result, any later events that were already returned by `drain()` are silently discarded and are not retried.

In the reproduction:

```text
[DELETE ghost-worker, SET w1]
        |
        v
DELETE raises ValueError
        |
        v
SET w1 is skipped
        |
        v
queue is empty
        |
        v
w1 remains absent from the manager state
```

## Additional Notes

The relevant code paths are:

* `tensorrt_llm/serve/disagg_auto_scaling.py`

  * `worker_event_loop`
  * `_parse_worker_info`
  * `_get_workers_by_id`

* `tensorrt_llm/serve/cluster_storage.py`

  * `WatchEventQueue.drain`

`WatchEventQueue.drain()` is destructive, so events skipped after an exception cannot be recovered by the next polling iteration.

The current `worker_event_loop` has one exception handler around the entire drained batch. This differs from the `get_worker_events` path in the same component, which isolates failures per event.

The runtime reproduction was performed against commit `67a0328029` using the real implementation. The exercised repository files were verified to be byte-identical to the pinned commit.

The bug case:

```text
[DELETE unknown-worker, SET w1]
```

resulted in no `on_event` calls and an empty queue afterward.

The control case:

```text
[SET w1, SET w2]
```

processed both events successfully.

A likely fix is to isolate exception handling per event so that one failing event does not abort the remainder of the drained batch. Unknown-worker `DELETE` events may also need to be treated as an idempotent no-op.

I can contribute a CPU-only regression test and fix if useful.

## Before submitting a new issue...

* [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and checked the [[documentation](https://nvidia.github.io/TensorRT-LLM/)](https://nvidia.github.io/TensorRT-LLM/) and [[examples](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/tree/main/examples)](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/tree/main/examples) for answers to frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Bug]: trtllm-llmapi-launch: rank 0 never exits and follower ranks never stop when the engine dies with a wedged worker world
items.author: whiz-Tuhin
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info
- TensorRT-LLM 1.3.0rc25 (container build) and current main (83aed1a7): the relevant code is identical
- Multi-node launch with `srun --mpi=pmix ... trtllm-llmapi-launch <engine command>` (8 ranks, one engine process on rank 0)
- Cluster scheduler: Slurm with PMIx, `KillOnBadExit=1`.

### Who can help?
@NVIDIA/trt-llm-runtime-devs (owners of `tensorrt_llm/llmapi`)

### Information
- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Tasks
- [ ] An officially supported task in the `examples` folder (such as GLUE/SQuAD, ...)
- [x] My own task or dataset (give details below)

### Reproduction
Run the launcher under `srun --mpi=pmix -N1 -n4` with a fake engine on rank 0 that connects with
`RemoteMpiCommSessionClient`, submits a task in which even ranks raise and odd ranks block forever, and
then exits 1 (the same calls as `tests/unittest/llmapi/_run_mpi_comm_task.py`). Observed on a 4-rank
step, each case under a 75 s external timeout, with the released launcher (1.3.0rc25) and again with
the launcher script from main (83aed1a7) driving the same Python:
- task raises on every rank, engine exits 1: the launcher prints `Task exit code: 1`, the server logs
  `received shutdown signal`, then `MGMN leader node exit code: 0` and `Subshell exit code: 1`; the
  rank-0 task exits 1 and the step ends in 45 to 50 s. Handled today.
- task raises on ranks 0 and 2 and blocks forever on ranks 1 and 3, engine exits 1: the launcher
  prints `Task exit code: 1` and `MPI Comm server exit code: 0` and nothing more; no task exits; the
  step is still alive when the 75 s timeout kills it. Identical with both launcher versions. This is
  the shape seen in production, where the step lived for 37 minutes until the orchestrator's health
  timeout cancelled it.
- no task submitted (engine exits 3 without contacting the server), and a task that returns on every
  rank: both exit cleanly with the expected codes (3 and 0).
With the proposed fix applied (launcher and `mpi_session.py` from the PR branch mounted over the
released files, same job shape): the blocked-ranks case now logs `received shutdown signal while 4
worker future(s) are still running`, then after the 20 s grace used in the test
`RemoteMpiCommSessionServer: worker world did not shut down within 20.0s; calling MPI_Abort so no rank
outlives the leader`; all four tasks are killed by the abort and the step ends on its own after 63 s
with a non-zero exit. The other four cases are unchanged.

### Expected behavior
After the rank-0 task exits non-zero, the launcher should exit non-zero within a bounded time, and no
follower rank should outlive the leader: either the leader ends the communicator with `MPI_Abort`, or
the rank-0 task exits non-zero so `srun --kill-on-bad-exit=1` can end the step.

### actual behavior
The engine process started by `trtllm-llmapi-launch` on rank 0 failed during executor initialization
("Executor worker returned error", every rank logged "Failed to initialize executor") and exited 1.
The launcher printed `Rank0 Task exit code: 1` and, after the stop request,
`Rank0 MPI Comm server exit code: 0`. Then nothing: no `Rank0 MGMN leader node exit code`, no
`Rank0 Subshell exit code`, no `RankN MGMN worker node exit code`. The rank-0 launcher never exited,
the 7 follower launchers stayed in `MPICommExecutor`, and the srun step stayed alive with a dead engine
behind it for 37 minutes until the orchestrator's health timeout cancelled the step. The cluster has
`KillOnBadExit=1`, which did not help because no task ever exited.

### additional notes
Why, from the code:
- `trtllm-llmapi-launch` exits only after the foreground `python3 -m tensorrt_llm.llmapi.mgmn_leader_node`
  returns. The `--action stop` request is a single message on the ZeroMQ control socket; its exit code
  is 0 even if the server never reads it (`mgmn_leader_node.py:37-51`).
- `RemoteMpiCommSessionServer.serve()` reads the control socket only after every outstanding worker
  future has completed (`as_completed` loop), and once it has read the shutdown it still waits, through
  mpi4py, for every submitted task to return before the stop sentinel reaches the follower ranks
  (`MPICommExecutor.__exit__` -> `client_stop`). The sentinel is sent at interpreter exit, not in
  `serve()`. If any rank is wedged, none of this completes.
- `mgmn_worker_node.py` is `with MPICommExecutor(COMM_WORLD)`: the followers have no timeout and no
  exit path other than that sentinel, an `MPI_Abort`, or a signal from the scheduler.
- In this deployment mode the executor proxy's abort on init failure (`_fail_initialization` ->
  `shutdown_abort`) reaches a `RemoteMpiCommSessionClient`, whose `shutdown_abort` is a no-op, so no
  `MPI_Abort` is ever issued.

Proposed fix:
A PR follows: (1) `RemoteMpiCommSessionServer` polls the control socket while worker futures are
outstanding and runs shutdown as a bounded teardown that escalates to `MPI_Abort` after
`TLLM_MGMN_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_SECONDS` (default 60); (2) the launcher's rank-0 subshell waits at most
`TLLM_LLMAPI_LAUNCH_STOP_TIMEOUT` seconds (default 120) for the MPI Comm server to exit after the stop
request, then kills it so the launcher exits with the task's code.

items.title: [Bug] Mooncake master startup failure leaves a partially published address behind
items.author: adenzhou1350
items.body_excerpt:
### Problem

On current main `80f1809362f1a1e5d5eafc5ac0e744b98e13f271`, `_published_address` writes every address file before entering its `try/finally`. If publishing the second path fails, the master is stopped by `running_master`/`provision_pool`, but the first address remains and points at the stopped master. A failed `os.replace` also leaves the staging file behind.

### Reproduction

Use a persistent `run_dir` and set `address_file` (or `PoolSpec.master_address_file`) to an existing directory. The first `run_dir/master.addr` is published; replacing the second target raises `OSError`. After context entry fails, the launched master is stopped, but `run_dir/master.addr` and `<address_file>.partial` still exist. This uses actual filesystem operations, not a mocked `os.replace`.

The relevant paths are [publication](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/blob/80f1809362f1a1e5d5eafc5ac0e744b98e13f271/tensorrt_llm/_torch/pyexecutor/connectors/mooncake_store/master.py#L438-L463), [standalone master](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/blob/80f1809362f1a1e5d5eafc5ac0e744b98e13f271/tensorrt_llm/_torch/pyexecutor/connectors/mooncake_store/master.py#L491-L498), and [pool provisioning](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/blob/80f1809362f1a1e5d5eafc5ac0e744b98e13f271/tensorrt_llm/_torch/pyexecutor/connectors/mooncake_store/master.py#L537-L582).

### Proposed fix and checks

I prepared a [small fix with regression tests](https://github.com/adenzhou1350/TensorRT-LLM/commit/2e9863022): cover publication with `try/finally`, retract only successfully published paths, and clean the attempted staging file. The third regression ensures an unvisited path belonging to another master is preserved.

Windows and Linux CPU checks reproduce the three new failures on baseline; the patched master test file passes all 43 cases. These are **isolated leaf-module checks**: complete `config.py`/`master.py` and upstream tests are loaded, with package initializers bypassed and logging substituted; the suite's existing fake master process is used. This is not a claim that the full TensorRT-LLM package, Mooncake binary or GPU tests ran. Ruff lint/format and diff checks pass; the complete pre-commit hook suite was not run.

The same publication-before-finally structure is present in `_published_manifest` on #19171 at `997375ea351df93bf0b269fe8edf13871438bb89`; that renamed path was inspected statically, not executed. I can send the main-branch fix or help adapt it there, depending on the preferred review scope. Following CONTRIBUTING.md, I am requesting issue approval before opening a PR.

items.title: [Bug]: Nemotron dynamic-resolution tiler can return a zero-sized grid or divide by zero for panoramic images
items.author: adenzhou1350
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

Source: main at `f388b7c6a540364f356f200214497cdc34ce642e`.
CPU component reproduction with Python 3.12, PyTorch 2.11.0+cu130 and Pillow on Linux. CUDA was hidden and never initialized. No model weights, TensorRT native extensions or server were used.

### Information / Tasks

A small custom CPU reproduction of the unchanged dynamic-resolution preprocessing component. This is not a full-model reproduction.

### Reproduction

From a checkout at the commit above, this runs the complete unchanged tiler class and its two helpers, without importing unrelated model/native dependencies:

```python
import ast
import math
from dataclasses import dataclass
from pathlib import Path
from typing import List, Sequence, Tuple, Union

import torch
from PIL import Image

path = Path("tensorrt_llm/_torch/models/modeling_nemotron_h_multimodal.py")
names = {"_get_media_dimensions", "DynamicResolutionParams", "DynamicResolutionImageTiler"}
tree = ast.parse(path.read_bytes())
nodes = [n for n in tree.body if getattr(n, "name", None) in names]
assert {n.name for n in nodes} == names
ns = dict(globals())
exec(compile(ast.Module(body=nodes, type_ignores=[]), str(path), "exec"), ns)
tiler = ns["DynamicResolutionImageTiler"](
    max_model_len=4096, patch_size=16,
    min_num_patches=256, max_num_patches=4096,
    downsample_ratio=0.5,
    norm_mean=[0.5] * 3, norm_std=[0.5] * 3,
)
for size in [(256, 256), (768, 256), (65536, 16), (16, 65536)]:
    for tokens in [64, 256]:
        try:
            params = tiler.compute_params([Image.new("RGB", size)], tokens)
            print(size, tokens, params[0].patch_size, params[0].num_embeddings)
        except ZeroDivisionError as error:
            print(size, tokens, type(error).__name__, str(error))
assert not torch.cuda.is_initialized()
```

### Expected behavior

Either return a positive patch grid satisfying the pixel-shuffle/token-budget constraints, or reject an unsupported image shape with an explicit validation error. A positive-size image should not result in zero height/width or an unhandled arithmetic exception.

### Actual behavior

Both ordinary-image controls return positive grids. The panoramic cases return:

```text
(65536, 16) 64  (724, 0) 0
(65536, 16) 256 ZeroDivisionError division by zero
(16, 65536) 64  (0, 724) 0
(16, 65536) 256 ZeroDivisionError division by zero
```

### Additional notes

[`process_media`](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/blob/f388b7c6a540364f356f200214497cdc34ce642e/tensorrt_llm/_torch/models/modeling_nemotron_h_multimodal.py#L365-L403) floors the scaled patch dimensions before enforcing the minimum patch count. A dimension can become zero. Above the minimum budget, the upscaling division then divides by zero; at the minimum budget, that branch is skipped and zero survives the subsequent divisibility checks.

The normal input-processing path calls this tiler through `_process_images_dynamic` / `compute_params`, but I have not run a real model/server or established a quality-preserving fix. Is there an intended aspect-ratio limit, or should this path handle/validate collapsed patch dimensions? I can contribute a focused regression and fix once the intended behavior is confirmed.

- [x] Searched existing issues/PRs and checked the current implementation. The existing dynamic-resolution feature PRs do not appear to address this boundary.

items.title: How to make Tensor static and only call kernel by pointer?
items.author: peterbjorgensen
items.body_excerpt:
I am trying to turn Python cute dsl kernels into TensorRT QDP Plugins. It restricts the kind of parameters the PTX can have to (input_pointers..., scalar_arguments..., output_pointers...). I have it working for a simple "add_one_kernel" (see the program listing below if interested).

Instead of writing the kernel with pointer arguments, I would like to write it with some StaticTensorPointer class that automatically turns the layout etc. into compile-time variables and only the pointer ends up as a PTX parameter. I guess it's possible with a custom `DynamicExpression`, but I find the documentation a bit vague on this. Any ideas how to achieve this?

Another question: Is it possible to get the shared memory needed for a compiled kernel? I need it for the kernel launch parameters of the kernel in the plugin.

```
import tensorrt as trt
import numpy as np
from quack.cute_dsl_utils import torch2cute_dtype_map
import tensorrt.plugin as trtp
import torch
import torch_tensorrt
import cutlass.cute as cute

from quack.cute_dsl_utils import torch2cute_dtype_map

trt_logger = trt.Logger(trt.Logger.VERBOSE)

STATIC_SHAPE = (16, 16)
STATIC_STRIDE = (1, 16)

@cute.kernel
def add_one_kernel(x: cute.Pointer, y: cute.Pointer):
    STATIC_LAYOUT = cute.make_layout(shape=STATIC_SHAPE, stride=STATIC_STRIDE)
    tensor_x = cute.make_tensor(x, STATIC_LAYOUT)
    tensor_y = cute.make_tensor(y, STATIC_LAYOUT)
    tidx, _, _ = cute.arch.thread_idx()
    bidx, _, _ = cute.arch.block_idx()
    idx = bidx * cute.arch.block_dim()[0] + tidx
    if idx < cute.size(tensor_x):
        tensor_y[idx] = tensor_x[idx] + 1

@cute.jit
def apply_add_one_kernel(x: cute.Pointer, y: cute.Pointer):
    BLOCK_SIZE = 256
    num_blocks = (np.prod(STATIC_SHAPE).item() + BLOCK_SIZE - 1) // BLOCK_SIZE

    add_one_kernel(x, y).launch(
        grid = [num_blocks, 1, 1],
        block = [BLOCK_SIZE, 1, 1],
    )


@torch.library.custom_op("my::add_one", mutates_args=())  # type: ignore[misc]
def add_one(x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    assert x.is_cuda
    y = torch.empty_like(x)
    input_dtype = torch2cute_dtype_map[x.dtype]
    y_ptr = cute.runtime.make_ptr(input_dtype, y.data_ptr(), cute.AddressSpace.gmem, assumed_align=32)
    x_ptr = cute.runtime.make_ptr(input_dtype, x.data_ptr(), cute.AddressSpace.gmem, assumed_align=32)

    compiled = cute.compile(apply_add_one_kernel, x_ptr, y_ptr, options="--keep-ptx")
    compiled(x_ptr, y_ptr)

    return y


@torch.library.register_fake("my::add_one")
def _(X: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    return X

@trtp.register("my::add_one")
def add_plugin_desc(X: trtp.TensorDesc) -> tuple[trtp.TensorDesc]:
    # Output has the same shape and dtype as the input.
    return X.like()


@trtp.aot_impl("my::add_one")
def add_plugin_aot_impl(
    X: trtp.TensorDesc, outputs: tuple[trtp.TensorDesc], tactic: int
) -> tuple[
    str | bytes, str | bytes, trtp.KernelLaunchParams, trtp.SymExprs
]:
    # Choose the pointer type based on the input dtype.
    if X.dtype == trt.float32:
        x_dtype = torch2cute_dtype_map[torch.float32]
    elif X.dtype == trt.float16:
        x_dtype = torch2cute_dtype_map[torch.float16]
    elif X.dtype == trt.bfloat16:
        x_dtype = torch2cute_dtype_map[torch.bfloat16]
    else:
        raise ValueError("Unexpected dtype")
    input_dtype = x_dtype
    y_ptr = cute.runtime.make_ptr(input_dtype, 32, cute.AddressSpace.gmem, assumed_align=32)
    x_ptr = cute.runtime.make_ptr(input_dtype, 64, cute.AddressSpace.gmem, assumed_align=32)

    compiled_kernel = cute.compile(apply_add_one_kernel, x_ptr, y_ptr, options="--keep-ptx")


    # Build symbolic launch parameters.
    BLOCK_SIZE = 256
    num_blocks = (np.prod(STATIC_SHAPE).item() + BLOCK_SIZE - 1) // BLOCK_SIZE
    launch_params = trtp.KernelLaunchParams()
    launch_params.grid_x = num_blocks  # number of thread blocks
    launch_params.block_x = BLOCK_SIZE  # threads per block
    launch_params.shared_mem = 0  # bytes of shared mem (I have no idea how to get this)

    # ``extra_args`` are scalar arguments appended to the kernel's argument list at
    # launch. Here ``n_elements`` is passed as a 32-bit symbolic integer so TRT
    # evaluates it from the actual tensor size at runtime.
    extra_args = trtp.SymIntExprs(0)

    kernel_name_ptx = list(compiled_kernel.kernel_info.keys())[0]
    return (
        kernel_name_ptx,  # kernel function name in PTX
        compiled_kernel.artifacts.PTX,  # PTX source — embedded in TRT engine
        launch_params,
        extra_args,
    )


torch_tensorrt.dynamo.conversion.plugins.generate_plugin_converter(
    "my::add_one",
    supports_dynamic_shapes=False,
    requires_output_allocator=False,
    use_aot_if_available=True,
)


class MyModel(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()

    def forward(self, X: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        res = torch.ops.my.add_one.default(X)
        return res


if __name__ == "__main__":


    my_model = MyModel().to("cuda").eval()
    m = torch.full(STATIC_SHAPE, 2, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)

    assert my_model(m)[0][0] == 3.0
    assert my_model(m)[1][1] == 3.0

    with torch_tensorrt.logging.debug():
        trt_inputs = [m]
        model_trt = torch_tensorrt.compile(
            my_model,
            inputs=trt_inputs,
            min_block_size=1,
        )
        print("Model compiled successfully!")
        print("Running inference with compiled model...")
        with torch.no_grad():
            for i in range(10):
                res = model_trt(m)
                assert torch.allclose(res, my_model(m)), "Results do not match!"

        program = torch_tensorrt.dynamo.trace(
            my_model,
            arg_inputs=trt_inputs,
        )
        engine_bytes: bytes = torch_tensorrt.dynamo.convert_exported_program_to_seri

items.title: copy_if with a Copy_Atom dispatches on the src slice only and can store out of bounds when dst extents differ
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CuTe C++ - `include/cute/algorithm/copy.hpp`, the `copy_if` overloads

### Describe the bug

`copy_if(Copy_Atom<...>, pred, src, dst)` only static-asserts that src and dst have equal rank; it never compares extents. Per rest-slice it calls `Copy_Atom::call(pred_v, src_v, dst_v)`, and the atom's instruction dispatch tests the vector width against the **src** slice only (`copy_atom.hpp`, `is_constant<NumValSrc, size(src)>`). When dst has a smaller extent, one wide instruction is emitted into the smaller dst slice and stores out of bounds. There is no diagnostic of any kind before the corruption.

The sibling entry point `copy(src, dst)` handles the same mismatch safely: its vectorization machinery recomputes `max_common_vector`/alignment from both layouts and degrades to elementwise copies.

Minimal repro (host-only, ASan):

```cpp
#include <cute/tensor.hpp>
#include <cute/algorithm/copy.hpp>
#include <cstdio>
using namespace cute;

int main() {
  float sa[12], da[6];
  Tensor src = make_tensor(&sa[0], Shape<_4,_3>{});   // 12 elems
  Tensor dst = make_tensor(&da[0], Shape<_2,_3>{});   // 6 elems (typo)
  bool m[12]; for (int i=0;i<12;++i) m[i]=true;
  Tensor prd = make_tensor(&m[0], Shape<_4,_3>{});

  copy_if(Copy_Atom<UniversalCopy<uint128_t>, float>{}, prd, src, dst);
}
```

```
$ g++ -std=c++17 -g -fsanitize=address ... && ./a.out
==30==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: stack-buffer-overflow ...
WRITE of size 16 at 0x... thread T0
    #2 cute::copy_unpack<...> (include/cute/atom/copy_atom.hpp)
    #3 cute::Copy_Atom<...>::call(...)
    #4 cute::copy_if<...> (include/cute/algorithm/copy.hpp:69)
```

With plain `copy(src, dst)` on identical shapes the program runs ASan-clean and produces correct results, so the two entry points disagree on error behavior for the same misuse.

The generic elementwise `copy_if` at `copy.hpp:44-62` has a milder version of the same pattern: it bounds the loop by `size(dst)` and indexes `pred(i)`/`src(i)` without any cross-check.

### Expected behavior

Either a compile-time/static diagnostic when `size(src) != size(dst)` per rest-slice (mirroring what `copy()` effectively enforces), or dispatch keyed off both slices. Raw atom calls are normally fed by `TiledCopy` partitioning which guarantees matching widths, so this may be an accepted contract - but today the failure mode is silent memory corruption on a plausible typo, where the sibling API reports nothing yet also does the right thing.

### Environment details

- Current main, header-only, host-only repro (no GPU needed), g++ + AddressSanitizer
