items.title: [Feature]: CuTe DSL W4A8 MXFP4 SiTU MoE for Kimi K3
items.author: henrylhtsang
items.body_excerpt:
### Before submitting

- [x] I have searched existing issues and this request has not been filed yet.

### Problem

**tldr**:
* Request for a source visible cute dsl MXFP8×MXFP4 routed MoE backend
* Basically want to be able to inspect and hack around it
* Want feature parity to TensorRT-LLM Gen (e.g. routing and parallelism support, cuda graph)
* performance **doesn't** have to be as good as trtllm gen

## Motivation

We would like an open-source CuTe DSL alternative to the TensorRT-LLM Gen routed mixture-of-experts kernels exposed through FlashInfer. The main benefit is inspectability: we need to be able to read the kernel, profile it, diagnose scheduling or memory problems, make targeted fixes without treating a precompiled kernel as a black box, and hack around it.

The existing TensorRT-LLM Gen implementation should remain the reference for inputs, numerical behavior, and performance. The CuTe DSL implementation can be delivered incrementally rather than reproducing every TensorRT-LLM feature in one pull request.

FlashInfer already has CuTe DSL NVFP4 W4A4 and MXFP8-by-MXFP4 W4A8 MoE paths, but it doesn't have full feature parity. . This request is to make that implementation a practical TensorRT-LLM alternative. For our initial use case, it must support Kimi K3 with:

- NVIDIA B200/B300 as the primary target.
- Native MXFP4 E2M1 weights with UE8M0 group-32 scales.
- W4A8 execution: MXFP4 weights, FP8 E4M3 activations, and BF16 output.
- **SiTU activation. SiLU-and-multiply is not an acceptable substitute.**
- Optimized decode and prefill paths.
- Both 8-way expert parallelism and 8-way MoE tensor parallelism.
- CUDA Graph support without synchronization, allocation, or compilation in the execution path.

The reference entry point is:

```python
from flashinfer.fused_moe import trtllm_fp4_block_scale_routed_moe
```

## Shape and parallelism

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---:|
| Hidden size | 7168 |
| Expert intermediate size | 3072 |
| Routed experts | 896 |
| Experts selected per token | 16 |

Unsharded expert operations:

```text
GEMM1: [tokens_for_expert, 7168] x [7168, 6144]
GEMM2: [tokens_for_expert, 3072] x [3072, 7168]
```

`tokens_for_expert` is ragged and is often zero during decode.

Please support these two rank-local layouts:

| Mode | MoE TP | EP | Local experts | Per-rank intermediate size |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Expert parallel | 1 | 8 | 112 | 3072 |
| MoE tensor parallel | 8 | 1 | 896 | 384 |

Expert-parallel ranks receive global expert identifiers. Rank `r` owns experts `[r * 112, (r + 1) * 112)` and ignores non-local routes. Summing all eight rank-local outputs must reproduce the unsharded result.

MoE-tensor-parallel ranks receive the same inputs and routes, but each rank owns a `3072 / 8 = 384` intermediate-dimension weight shard. Each rank returns a partial `[T, 7168]` BF16 result suitable for a caller-managed all-reduce.

FlashInfer does not need to implement collective communication. Hybrid TP and EP layouts are not required initially.

## Required SiTU behavior

```text
gate_out = beta * tanh(gate / beta) * sigmoid(gate)
up_out   = linear_beta * tanh(up / linear_beta)  if linear_beta is present
           up                                      otherwise
output   = gate_out * up_out
```

Please add an explicit activation value such as `ActivationType.Situ`. `beta` and optional `linear_beta` must be runtime inputs, including per-expert values, rather than hidden compile-time constants.

## Kernel and API requirements

- Accept precomputed global top-k expert identifiers and router weights.
- Accept explicit global expert count, local expert count, and local expert offset.
- Select the parallel mode from explicit metadata, not tensor-shape inference.
- Consume packed MXFP4 weights without converting them to NVFP4.
- Allow a deterministic load-time shuffle without retaining duplicate full-size weights.
- Accept caller-owned output and workspace buffers and expose workspace size before execution.
- Keep workspace bounded for large prefills; fixed-size token slicing is acceptable.
- Run on the caller's CUDA stream without default-stream assumptions.
- Perform no host synchronization, device-to-host metadata reads, allocation, runtime compilation, or serving-time autotuning during execution.
- Capture and replay under CUDA Graphs for every integer token count from `T=1` through `T=16` in both parallel modes.
- Select decode and prefill variants internally using offline tuning data.
- Expose a capability query covering B300, MXFP4, SiTU, dimensions, top-k, parallelism, and CUDA Graph support.
- Fail clearly for unsupported configurations.

A finalized BF16 output is sufficient for the first pull request. A deferred form exposing rank-local GEMM2 rows, router weights, and the assignment-to-row mapping would be useful for fusing finalization with caller-owned collectives.

## Workloads

Decode:

```text
T = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16
```

Prefill:

```text
T = 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096
```

If practical, also test `T = 8192, 16384, 32768`.

Test balanced routing, many empty local experts, hot experts, and expert-parallel batches dominated by non-local routes. Report global and per-rank assignment histograms with performance results.


### Requested outcome

- Numerical comparison with TensorRT-LLM Gen at `T = 1, 16, 128, 512, 2048` using identical prepared weights, FP8 inputs, scales, routing, and SiTU parameters.
- Expert-parallel test: summing eight local expert ranges matches the unsharded reference.
- MoE-tensor-parallel test: summing eight intermediate-dimension shards matches the unsharded reference.
- CUDA Graph capture and repeated replay for every integer `T` from 1 through 16 in both modes.
- Correct execution under concurrent CUDA compute and memory-copy streams on B300, including repeated stress testing for intermittent stalls.
- Kernel and runner latency for each listed shape and mode, reported as a ratio to TensorRT-LLM Gen on the same B300.
- Documentatio

items.title: [RLlib] Potential infinite Env Runer sampling loop with non default algorithm parameters
items.author: corentinlger
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

Hi ! While investigating algo configs leading to silently discarded env runners results (https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/63302), I ran into a rare but weird case where RLlib training can hang forever without any error. It probably almost never happens, but it still seems a bit weird it's possible, so I'm still posting an issue in case it can help.

The issue: with a synchronous algo on the new API stack (e.g. PPO), if every `sample()` call takes longer than `sample_timeout_s`, each sampling round returns nothing. If `min_sample_timesteps_per_iteration > 0`, the iteration can never reach its minimum, so `train()` loops forever without crashing.

RLlib already warns while this happens and gives a useful advice to fix it, but can still keeps running the training indefinitely.

```
2026-10-01 12:54:33,281 WARNING rollout_ops.py:122 -- No samples returned from remote workers. If you have a slow environment or model, consider increasing the `sample_timeout_s` or decreasing the `rollout_fragment_length` in `AlgorithmConfig.env_runners().
2026-10-01 12:54:35,290 WARNING rollout_ops.py:122 -- No samples returned from remote workers. If you have a slow environment or model, consider increasing the `sample_timeout_s` or decreasing the `rollout_fragment_length` in `AlgorithmConfig.env_runners().
. . .
```

Do you think it would make sense to add a simple safeguard (e.g if no new samples are collected for N consecutive training steps, raise an error and crash the training) ? If so, I can open a quick PR for this (: (but idk if it's worth it as this bug is likely very rare)

### Versions / Dependencies

- Ray 2.58.0
- Python 3.11.13

### Reproduction script

```python
# Toy env whose episodes take ~10s (longer than sample_timeout_s)
class SlowEnv(gym.Env):
    def __init__(self, config=None):
        self.observation_space = spaces.Box(-1.0, 1.0, (2,), np.float32)
        self.action_space = spaces.Discrete(2)
        self._t = 0
        self.n_resets = 0

    def reset(self, *, seed=None, options=None):
        print(f"{self.n_resets = }")
        self.n_resets += 1
        super().reset(seed=seed)
        self._t = 0
        return self.observation_space.sample(), {}

    def step(self, action):
        time.sleep(0.2)          # 50 steps * 0.2s = ~10s per episode
        self._t += 1
        print(f"{self._t = }")
        done = self._t >= 50
        return self.observation_space.sample(), 0.0, done, False, {}

# algo config with low sample timeout + non null min_sample_timesteps_per_iteration
config = (
        PPOConfig()
        .environment(SlowEnv)
        .env_runners(
            num_env_runners=2,
            batch_mode="complete_episodes",
            sample_timeout_s=2.0,          # too low: episodes take ~10s
        )
        .reporting(min_sample_timesteps_per_iteration=100)  # the gate that causes the hang
    )

algo = config.build_algo()
result = algo.train()  # infinite env runner sampling loop
```

### Issue Severity

None

comments.author: lindicaphxag-tech
comments.body:
I put together a draft implementation in #66687 to explore the no-progress safeguard described here. It detects a successful training-step loop that repeatedly makes zero sampling progress while `min_sample_timesteps_per_iteration > 0` and `sample_timeout_s` is finite, and covers both the old counters path and the new lifetime-metrics path.

I have intentionally kept it draft because one design point deserves maintainer input: the current prototype uses `num_consecutive_env_runner_failures_tolerance` as the retry budget, which avoids a new config knob but couples EnvRunner failure tolerance to sampling-timeout/no-progress tolerance. If a separate internal/default budget or dedicated config is preferred, I can adjust before review.

Also happy to defer/close the draft if the original reporter would prefer to implement the fix.

items.title: [BUG] CuTeDSL >= 4.6 cannot compile NCCL GIN device ops — ptxas rejects the generated PTX (4.5.2 works)
items.author: kiwi3shark
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

Compiling any NCCL **GIN remote operation** (`Gin.put` / `Gin.signal` from
`nccl4py`'s `nccl.core.device.cute`) with `nvidia-cutlass-dsl >= 4.6` fails in
`ptxas`. The same kernels compile successfully with `nvidia-cutlass-dsl == 4.5.2`.

Two distinct `ptxas` errors appear, and **which one you get is selected by the
NCCL device-bitcode version**, while **whether it fails at all is selected by the
CuTeDSL version**:

| nvidia-cutlass-dsl | nccl4py | nvidia-nccl-cu12 | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4.5.2 | 0.3.1 | 2.30.7 | **compiles** |
| 4.5.2 | 0.3.1 | 2.31.2 | fails — `Parsing error near '.nvvm'` |
| 4.7.1 | 0.4.1 | 2.30.7 | fails — `Modifier '.volatile' cannot be applied to '.local' space` |
| 4.7.1 | 0.4.1 | 2.31.2 | fails — `Parsing error near '.nvvm'` |

`Gin.wait_counter` / `Gin.wait_signal` / `Gin.read_signal` / `Gin.read_counter`
(the local-poll operations, which do not issue a network operation) compile fine
in **every** combination above. Only the operations that post a remote action fail.

### Defect 1 — unlowered `llvm.nvvm.activemask` leaks into the PTX (NCCL 2.31.2 bitcode)

```
ptxas application ptx input, line 47; fatal : Parsing error near '.nvvm': syntax error
ptxas fatal   : Ptx assembly aborted due to errors
```

The generated PTX contains:

```ptx
.extern .func  (.param .b32 func_retval0) llvm.nvvm.activemask
()
;
```

The `llvm.nvvm.activemask` intrinsic is emitted as an external function
declaration rather than being lowered to `activemask.b32`, and `ptxas` rejects
it because `.` is not legal in a PTX identifier. It is the only leaked intrinsic
in the module (7 references).

This one reproduces on **4.5.2 as well as 4.7.1**, so it looks independent of
the DSL version. Note CuTeDSL's own `cutlass.cute.arch.activemask` is implemented
as inline PTX asm rather than via this intrinsic, so the intrinsic may simply
have no lowering path in the LLVM→NVVM import.

### Defect 2 — `.volatile` applied to `.local` space (NCCL 2.30.7 bitcode)

```
ptxas application ptx input, line 479; error : Modifier '.volatile' cannot be applied to '.local' space
ptxas application ptx input, line 481; error : Modifier '.volatile' cannot be applied to '.local' space
ptxas fatal   : Ptx assembly aborted due to errors
```

This is the interesting one: **the identical bitcode compiles cleanly under
4.5.2 and fails under 4.6.3 / 4.7.1 / 4.8.0.dev0**, which makes it look like a
CuTeDSL codegen regression introduced in 4.6.

### Not architecture specific

Reproduced with `CUTE_DSL_ARCH` set to `sm_90a`, `sm_100a` and `sm_120a` — same
failures. The measurements above were taken on a Blackwell sm_120 (cc 12.0) part,
CUDA driver 580.x.

### Not specific to the `_v2` entry points

`nccl4py` 0.4.1 calls `ncclGinPut_v2` / `ncclGinSignal_v2`, while 0.3.1 calls the
v1 `ncclGinPut`. Declaring the v1 symbols by hand with
`@cute.extern(name="ncclGinPut", source=BitCode(...))` and calling those instead
produces the **same** error for a given NCCL version, so the entry point makes no
difference.

### Reproducer

Single rank, any CUDA GPU; nothing is transferred, both failures are at compile
time.

```bash
pip install 'nvidia-nccl-cu12==2.31.2' 'nccl4py[cu12]==0.4.1' \
            'nvidia-cutlass-dsl==4.7.1' 'cuda-python==12.9.7'

python nvidia_issue_repro.py --case control   # Gin.wait_counter -> COMPILED_OK
python nvidia_issue_repro.py --case v2        # Gin.put / Gin.signal -> fails
python nvidia_issue_repro.py --case v1        # hand-declared v1 externs -> fails
```

Then swap `nvidia-nccl-cu12==2.30.7` to see defect 2 instead of defect 1, and
`nvidia-cutlass-dsl==4.5.2` + `nccl4py[cu12]==0.3.1` for the combination that
works. (0.3.1 and >= 4.6 cannot be mixed: 0.3.1 imports
`cutlass.base_dsl._mlir_helpers.op`, which 4.6.0 removed, and 0.4.1 requires
`~= 4.6`.)

The three cases must be run in **separate processes** — declaring the case `v1`
externs in the same module changes which error the stock path reports.

<details>
<summary>nvidia_issue_repro.py</summary>

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Minimal reproducer: CuTeDSL >= 4.6 cannot compile any NCCL GIN *remote*
operation, while local-poll operations compile fine.

Two independent defects, so the script runs ONE case per process -- declaring
the case B externs in the same module changes the failure reported for case A,
so they must not share a process:

    python nvidia_issue_repro.py --case control   # gin.wait_counter  -> OK
    python nvidia_issue_repro.py --case v2        # gin.put/signal    -> defect 1
    python nvidia_issue_repro.py --case v1        # v1 externs        -> defect 2

Dependencies are three public wheels, nothing else:

    pip install 'nvidia-nccl-cu12==2.30.7' 'nccl4py[cu12]==0.4.1' \
                'nvidia-cutlass-dsl==4.7.1' 'cuda-python==12.9.7'

A single rank on any CUDA GPU is enough; nothing is transferred, both failures
are at compile time.
"""
import argparse

import torch
import cutlass
import cutlass.cute as cute

import nccl.core as nccl
import nccl.core.device.cute as nccl_cute

items.title: Expert Parallelism (EP) roadmap for SM12x b12x MoE kernel (b12x_fused_moe / B12xMoEWrapper)
items.author: ItamarTerem
items.body_excerpt:
Hi flashinfer team,
We're deploying a large MoE model (384 experts, top_k=8) on 8x RTX PRO 6000 (SM120/Blackwell workstation) using the b12x_fused_moe CuteDSL kernel via TensorRT-LLM's pytorch backend, and have hit the Expert Parallelism restriction:

b12x_fused_moe does not yet support Expert Parallelism
(num_local_experts={X} != num_experts={Y}).
Use a different MoE backend for EP configurations.

This comes from the explicit guard in flashinfer/fused_moe/cute_dsl/b12x_moe.py (both in the free function b12x_fused_moe and in B12xMoEWrapper.__init__), confirmed in flashinfer version 0.6.12.
Context on why this matters for us specifically: without EP, every GPU must retain workspace/routing capacity sized for the full state_E (all 384 experts), even though tensor parallelism already shards each expert's weights across GPUs. This is a meaningful, measured memory cost — in our case, the dynamic workspace's packed_input buffer alone accounts for roughly 7–11GB/GPU across a 60-MoE-layer model, purely from having to size for the worst-case "all experts active" scenario rather than a num_experts/ep_size subset.

What we're asking:

1. Is EP support for the SM12x b12x kernel family (static/dynamic/micro backends) on the roadmap, even at a preliminary stage?
2. Is there a rough timeline or tracking issue we could follow?
3. Are there known architectural blockers specific to SM120 (vs. SM100/SM103, where other kernels like MegaMoE already support EP) that make this a harder problem here?

We also note that vLLM's FlashInferB12xExperts (_supports_parallel_config) explicitly declines to use this backend when EP is requested, for the same underlying reason — so this appears to be a shared, cross-framework limitation rather than something specific to our integration.
Happy to provide more detail on our exact shapes/config if useful. Thanks for your work on this — the b12x kernel has otherwise been the only correctness-verified MoE path we've found for SM120 (CUTLASS produces silently incorrect output on this architecture in our testing).

items.title: [dynamo] `IndexError` raised by a tensor op inside a compiled function skips the user's own `except IndexError` and escapes the compiled call (`RuntimeError` is routed to the handler since #184990; `fullgraph=True` does not complain)
items.author: cuiliaomei-beep
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

**Summary.** Inside a `torch.compile`d function, `try: x.sum(dim=5) except IndexError: <fallback>` runs the fallback in eager, while the compiled function raises `IndexError` out of the call and never executes the handler (torch 2.14.0 and nightly, `backend="eager"`, `fullgraph=True` or `False`); the same code with a `RuntimeError`-raising op (`x.view(5, 5)`) takes the handler. A user's defensive dimension / index fallback works in eager and silently disappears under compile, with no warning, so the program fails where it used to recover. Because `run_node` re-raises `IndexError` unchanged (the fix for #184340) before `get_fake_value` reaches the branch that turns fake-tensor `RuntimeError`s into observed exceptions, rather than routing every exception type to the user handler, every `IndexError` from dim / index validation (`x[i]`, `select`, `sum(dim)`, `softmax(dim)`, `transpose`, `squeeze`, `chunk`, `index_select`) bypasses `try/except` in compiled code.

```python
import torch

OPS = {
    "x[10]": lambda x: x[10],
    "x.select(0, 10)": lambda x: x.select(0, 10),
    "x.sum(dim=5)": lambda x: x.sum(dim=5),
    "x.softmax(dim=4)": lambda x: x.softmax(dim=4),
    "x.transpose(0, 5)": lambda x: x.transpose(0, 5),
    "x.view(5, 5)": lambda x: x.view(5, 5),  # RuntimeError: handled correctly
    "torch.cat([x, x.t()])": lambda x: torch.cat([x, x.t()]),  # RuntimeError: handled correctly
}


def guarded(x, op):
    try:
        return op(x)
    except (IndexError, RuntimeError) as e:
        return f"fallback after {type(e).__name__}"


x = torch.ones(3, 4)
for name, op in OPS.items():
    torch._dynamo.reset()
    eager = guarded(x, op)
    try:
        compiled = torch.compile(guarded, backend="eager", fullgraph=True)(x, op)
    except Exception as e:
        compiled = f"ESCAPED {type(e).__name__}: {e}"[:70]
    print(f"{name:22s} eager: {eager:28s} compiled: {compiled}")


# the usual defensive pattern, fullgraph=False: no fallback to eager either
def reduce_dim(x, dim):
    try:
        return x.sum(dim)
    except IndexError:
        return x.sum(-1)


torch._dynamo.reset()
print("eager   :", reduce_dim(x, 5).tolist())
try:
    print("compiled:", torch.compile(reduce_dim, backend="eager")(x, 5).tolist())
except IndexError as e:
    print("compiled: IndexError escaped:", str(e).splitlines()[0])
```

```
x[10]                  eager: fallback after IndexError    compiled: ESCAPED IndexError: index 10 is out of bounds for dimension 0 with siz
x.select(0, 10)        eager: fallback after IndexError    compiled: ESCAPED IndexError: select(): index 10 out of range for tensor of size
x.sum(dim=5)           eager: fallback after IndexError    compiled: ESCAPED IndexError: Dimension out of range (expected to be in range of
x.softmax(dim=4)       eager: fallback after IndexError    compiled: ESCAPED IndexError: Dimension out of range (expected to be in range of
x.transpose(0, 5)      eager: fallback after IndexError    compiled: ESCAPED IndexError: Dimension out of range (expected to be in range of
x.view(5, 5)           eager: fallback after RuntimeError  compiled: fallback after RuntimeError
torch.cat([x, x.t()])  eager: fallback after RuntimeError  compiled: fallback after RuntimeError
eager   : [4.0, 4.0, 4.0]
compiled: IndexError escaped: Dimension out of range (expected to be in range of [-2, 1], but got 5)
```

Nothing in the compiled path reports a problem: `fullgraph=True` compiles the function, there is no graph break, and the handler body is simply never reached. The caller-side `except IndexError` around the compiled call *does* work since #184340 / PR #184452 (the exception that escapes is a genuine `IndexError`), which is exactly why the in-function handler being skipped is easy to miss. A handler further out in the same compiled function (nested `try`, handler inside an `except` or `finally` block of another `try`) is skipped the same way; `NotImplementedError` from an op (`x.int() & 1.5`) also escapes; `TypeError`s become `Unsupported`.

**Root cause and possible fix.** `torch/_dynamo/utils.py`: `run_node` ends with

```python
except IndexError:
    # Re-raise IndexError from tensor dim validation (e.g. canonicalize_dim,
    # maybe_wrap_dim) so it reaches the user as IndexError, not RuntimeError.
    raise
except Exception as e:
    raise RuntimeError(make_error_message(e)) ...
```

so an `IndexError` from the fake kernel propagates as-is, while every other failure is wrapped into a `RuntimeError`. `get_fake_value` then handles `except RuntimeError as e:` and calls `raise_observed_exception(RuntimeError, tx, args=[msg])` (PR #184990), which jumps to a live user handler when there is one and otherwise surfaces a `FakeTensorObservedException`; that branch is what makes `except RuntimeError` inside compiled code work. The re-raised `IndexError` is not a `RuntimeError`, so it skips that branch entirely: it never becomes an observed exception, the handler is never jumped to, and the exception unwinds through Dynamo out of the compiled call. The fix is to route it the same way: catch `IndexError` (and `NotImplementedError`) in `get_fake_value` next to `RuntimeError` and call `raise_observed_exception(type(e), tx, args=[msg])` when a live user handler exists, keeping the current re-raise only for the no-handler case so the caller still sees an `IndexError`. A test that the whole `test_exceptions.py` family already has for `RuntimeError` (`try: op() except RuntimeError: fallback`) would catch this for the other exception types if parametrised over them.


### Error logs

`fullgraph=True` compiles without a graph break; the compiled call raises the exception the user's handler was written to catch, e.g.

```
IndexError: Dimension out of range (expected to be in range of [-2, 1], but got 5)
```

### Versions

```
PyTorch version: 2.14.0+cpu
OS: Microsoft Windows 11 Pro for Workstations (10.0.26200 64-bit)
Python version: 3.14.7 (64-bit runtime)
Is CUDA availabl

items.title: [DTensor] exponential_, log_normal_, geometric_ and multinomial give the same random values on every shard
items.author: oyiakoumis
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

When you call a random op on a sharded DTensor, each shard should get different random values. DTensor does this by sending random ops through its RNG tracker, which gives each shard its own part of the random stream.

Four ops are not sent through the tracker: `exponential_`, `log_normal_`, `geometric_` and `multinomial`. They run on each rank's local generator instead. Since every rank uses the same seed, **every shard gets the same values.** No error is raised.

Example: a `(8, 4)` tensor sharded by rows over 2 GPUs. After `dt.exponential_()`, rows 0-3 and rows 4-7 are identical.

**A second, narrower effect:** if the shards are uneven (for example 2 rows on one GPU and 1 row on the other) and large enough, each GPU's generator moves forward by a different amount. After that, a normal tracked op like dropout on a `Replicate` DTensor gives a different mask on each GPU, even though the tensor should be the same everywhere.

### Cause

DTensor decides whether an op is random by checking two hardcoded lists:

- `self._random_ops` in [`torch/distributed/tensor/_dispatch.py`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/a9ff16cf2fae5946d5fbe59864e1dd3b7c59e1f2/torch/distributed/tensor/_dispatch.py#L211-L226)
- `is_random_op()` in [`torch/csrc/autograd/python_variable.cpp`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/a9ff16cf2fae5946d5fbe59864e1dd3b7c59e1f2/torch/csrc/autograd/python_variable.cpp#L1337-L1371)

The four ops have sharding rules in [`_ops/_random_ops.py`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/a9ff16cf2fae5946d5fbe59864e1dd3b7c59e1f2/torch/distributed/tensor/_ops/_random_ops.py#L38-L55), but are missing from both lists.

**Tests didn't catch it**: [`test_init_ops`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/a9ff16cf2fae5946d5fbe59864e1dd3b7c59e1f2/test/distributed/tensor/test_random_ops.py#L73-L82) slices the other rank's shard using the full width instead of the shard width, so the shapes never match and `assertNotEqual` always passes. `test_multinomial_sharded` only checks shape and placement.

### Suggested fix

Add the four ops to both lists. `multinomial` may need a closer look: unlike the other three, it doesn't simply fill a tensor element by element, so it's worth confirming that each shard uses no more random numbers than the tracker reserves for it.

Repro (needs 2 CUDA GPUs; run with `torchrun --nproc-per-node 2 repro.py`):

```python
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
from torch.distributed.device_mesh import init_device_mesh
from torch.distributed.tensor import distribute_tensor, Replicate, Shard

dist.init_process_group("nccl")
rank = dist.get_rank()
torch.cuda.set_device(rank)
torch.manual_seed(0)
mesh = init_device_mesh("cuda", (2,))


def sharded(*shape):
    return distribute_tensor(torch.empty(*shape, device="cuda"), mesh, [Shard(0)])


# 1. Each rank holds one row; the two rows should differ
ops = {
    "uniform_ (control)": lambda t: t.uniform_(),
    "exponential_": lambda t: t.exponential_(),
    "log_normal_": lambda t: t.log_normal_(),
    "geometric_": lambda t: t.geometric_(0.5),
    "multinomial": lambda t: torch.multinomial(t.fill_(1 / 16), 16, replacement=True),
}
for name, op in ops.items():
    full = op(sharded(2, 16)).full_tensor()
    if rank == 0:
        print(f"{name:20s} rows equal: {torch.equal(full[0], full[1])}")

# 2. Uneven shards (2 rows vs 1 row), then dropout on a Replicate tensor;
#    the masks should be the same on both ranks
for name in ["uniform_ (control)", "exponential_"]:
    ops[name](sharded(3, 400_000))
    r = distribute_tensor(torch.ones(1000, device="cuda"), mesh, [Replicate()])
    mask = torch.nn.functional.dropout(r, 0.5).to_local()
    masks = [torch.empty_like(mask) for _ in range(2)]
    dist.all_gather(masks, mask)
    if rank == 0:
        print(f"{name:20s} then dropout, masks equal: {torch.equal(*masks)}")

dist.destroy_process_group()
```

Output (2x NVIDIA A10, torch 2.14.0+cu130):

```
uniform_ (control)   rows equal: False
exponential_         rows equal: True
log_normal_          rows equal: True
geometric_           rows equal: True
multinomial          rows equal: True
uniform_ (control)   then dropout, masks equal: True
exponential_         then dropout, masks equal: False
```

Expected: every `rows equal` line is `False`, and both `masks equal` lines are `True`. `uniform_` is already in the lists and shows the correct behavior.

I'd like to submit a fix, adding the four ops to both lists and fixing the test, if that sounds right to the maintainers.

### Versions

items.title: [Feature] Check free GPU memory before ModelClaim activation
items.author: jiangxiaobin96
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 Feature Description and Motivation

### Problem
Previously, ModelClaim ranked warm Pods using their observed free HBM but did not check whether a Pod had enough memory to start the requested model. A Pod with a cached artifact could be selected even when its free HBM was too low.
If the engine encountered GPU OOM while loading the model, `Activate` could already have returned after spawning the process. The model remained non-routable while the runtime retried it on the same Pod. After the restart budget was exhausted, the runtime and ModelClaim reported a terminal failure; placement did not automatically try another Pod.
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Controller selects a warm Pod"] --> B["Runtime Activate spawns the vLLM engine"]
    B --> C["Controller records Activating; route stays disabled"]
    C --> D["Engine loads model into GPU memory"]
    D --> E{"Enough GPU memory?"}
    E -- Yes --> F["Engine ready; ModelClaim becomes Active"]
    E -- No --> G["Engine exits; runtime cleans up and schedules restart"]
    G --> H{"Restart budget remaining?"}
    H -- Yes --> D
    H -- No --> I["Runtime reports failed"]
    I --> J["Controller marks ModelClaim Failed; route remains disabled"]
```

### Solution
Add optional spec.requiredHBMBytesPerGPU, expressed in bytes. When set, placement filters out Pods whose runtime snapshot has no GPU memory observation or whose available HBM is below the requested amount before applying artifact locality and load ranking. For multi-GPU placement, the existing snapshot summary uses the least free HBM across the required GPU group.
Claims that omit the field retain the previous placement behavior. If no Pod has confirmed sufficient capacity, the claim waits for a later reconciliation instead of calling Activate. The API schema, generated clients, tests, and ModelClaim documentation are updated.
This is a placement precheck, not a memory reservation. Concurrent activations and later KV usage can still change available HBM.

### Use Case

No response

### Proposed Solution

_No response_

### Area

Not sure

items.title: [Bug] KPA treats the per-pod mean as a total, so its replica count ignores the pod count
items.author: Zhuoxi2000
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

For `pod`, `resource` and `custom` metric sources, `collectFromPods` returns one value per pod. `MetricsClient.UpdateMetrics` (`pkg/controller/podautoscaler/metrics/client.go`) then records the **mean** of those values (`avg := sum / float64(len(metricValues))`) in both the stable and the panic window.

`KPAAlgorithm.computeTargetReplicas` (`pkg/controller/podautoscaler/algorithm/kpa.go`) turns that value into replicas with

```go
dspc = math.Ceil(observedStableValue / targetValue)
dppc = math.Ceil(observedPanicValue / targetValue)
```

This is Knative's formula, but in Knative the observed value is the **total** across ready pods. Here it is the per-pod mean, so KPA's answer does not depend on how many pods carry the load. APA uses the same mean and multiplies it by the current pod count (`ceil(currentPodCount * currentUsePerPod / expectedUse)`), so it gets this right.

Consequences:

- 4 pods, each at 90 against a target of 50 (80% over target), are scaled **down** to 2 (`ceil(90/50) = 2`, then limited by the max scale-down rate). APA gives 8 for the same input.
- The shipped `samples/autoscaling/kpa.yaml` (referenced from the metric-based autoscaling docs) uses `gpu_cache_usage_perc` with `targetValue: "0.5"` and `maxReplicas: 8`. A ratio metric averaged over pods is at most 1, so KPA can never recommend more than `ceil(1 / 0.5) = 2` replicas with it.

This looks like a regression from the metrics refactor. At v0.4.1, `metrics/client.go` recorded `sumMetricValue` (the sum over pods) in the window, and `scaler/kpa.go` used the same `ceil(observed / target)`, which was correct then. The current client records the mean. APA was adapted to it, KPA was not.

The KPA branch of the pending-replica guard (`computePendingAdjustedReplicas` in `autoscaler.go`, added in #2671) is inconsistent with itself as well. On scale-up it treats the value as a total (`ceil(adjusted / target)`). On scale-down it treats it as a per-pod mean (`MetricValue * readyReplicas`).

### Steps to Reproduce

Unit-level repro on `main`. Add this next to `TestComputeDesiredReplicasDoesNotHoldWhenNoReplicasPending` in `pkg/controller/podautoscaler/autoscaler_test.go`. It is the same input as that APA test, which expects 8:

```go
func TestComputeDesiredReplicasKPAScalesWithPodCount(t *testing.T) {
	pa := testPodAutoscaler(autoscalingv1alpha1.KPA)
	autoScaler := NewDefaultAutoScaler(&mockMetricFetcherFactory{
		mockMetricFetcher: mockMetricFetcher{metricsValue: 90},
	}, fake.NewClientBuilder().Build())
	scalingContext := testScalingContext(t, &pa)

	result, err := autoScaler.ComputeDesiredReplicas(context.TODO(), ReplicaComputeRequest{
		PodAutoscaler:   pa,
		ScalingContext:  scalingContext,
		CurrentReplicas: 4,
		ReplicaState:    ReplicaState{ReadyReplicas: 4},
		Pods: []corev1.Pod{
			{ObjectMeta: metav1.ObjectMeta{Name: "ready-1"}},
			{ObjectMeta: metav1.ObjectMeta{Name: "ready-2"}},
			{ObjectMeta: metav1.ObjectMeta{Name: "ready-3"}},
			{ObjectMeta: metav1.ObjectMeta{Name: "ready-4"}},
		},
		Timestamp: time.Now(),
	})
	require.NoError(t, err)
	assert.Equal(t, int32(8), result.DesiredReplicas)
}
```

```
$ go test ./pkg/controller/podautoscaler/ -run TestComputeDesiredReplicasKPAScalesWithPodCount -count=1
--- FAIL: TestComputeDesiredReplicasKPAScalesWithPodCount
    Error: Not equal:
           expected: 8
           actual  : 2
```

In a cluster: deploy `samples/autoscaling/kpa.yaml` and drive every pod to `gpu_cache_usage_perc` near 1.0. The PodAutoscaler never goes above 2 replicas.

### Expected behavior

When every pod is above the per-pod target, KPA should not scale down. For a per-pod metric it should size the workload from the total load, as Knative does: `desired = ceil(perPodMean * podCount / target)`. That is 8 for the input above, matching APA.

External and domain sources return a single value for the whole workload and should stay as they are. The existing `kpa external metric not adjusted` case, which expects 7, should keep passing.

### Environment

- AIBrix version: `main` (0779ef5), and every release since the layered autoscaler refactor (#1575)
- Deployment environment: unit test (Go 1.27, macOS). The code path is platform independent.
- LLM(s) being used: n/a

### Area

Orchestration (controllers, CRDs)

### Suggested fix

1. Pass the metric source type to the algorithm (a new `ScalingRequest.MetricSourceType` field).
2. In `KPAAlgorithm.computeTargetReplicas`, multiply the observed stable and panic values by the pod count for per-pod sources before dividing by the target. Keep the tolerance check on the per-pod value, so that pods within tolerance still hold the current count.
3. In `computePendingAdjustedReplicas`, use the APA formula (`ceil(currentReplicas * adjusted / target)`) for KPA as well, since both now treat the value as a per-pod mean.

I have this ready with tests and can open a PR.

Two points to confirm before the PR:

- This changes the expectations of the KPA cases in `TestComputeDesiredReplicasAdjustsKPAAPAConservativelyWhenReplicasPending` (#2671). Those inputs were written for total semantics: 250 per pod on 2 ready pods was meant as a scale-up and is now one by a much larger margin. I would change them to per-pod inputs that exercise the same guard paths. cc @googs1025
- Open PR #2804 describes the projected replicas as `ceil(value / targetValue)` for KPA, so it would need the same pod-count factor. cc @bolubo

---

The idea is to not compute FeedForward's on padded-out positions and skip attention computation for them as well

I guess the question also becomes of whether underlying flash attention implementation supports such jagged compact formats.

items.title: [Bug]: KVCacheManagerV2 + DSA: indexer (draft) cache pool is not part of admission; exhaustion under prefix-shared long-context load aborts the engine
items.author: PierreLeGuen
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- GPU: 8x NVIDIA H200 NVL (SM90; two 4-GPU NVLink islands, cross-island over PCIe/UPI), driver 595.71.05
- Host: Ubuntu 24.04.4, 2 TiB RAM, Xeon 6747P
- Container: `nvcr.io/nvidia/tensorrt-llm/release:1.3.0rc25` (CUDA 13.2, Python 3.12.3, torch 2.12.0a0+nv26.5, transformers 5.5.4)
- TensorRT-LLM: 1.3.0rc25 (tag `v1.3.0rc25`, 785c948); the code paths cited below were also checked on `main` @ a6616d6f (2026-09-03)
- Backend: PyTorch (`trtllm-serve --backend pytorch`)

### Who can help?

@yizhang-nv (KV cache manager V2 for DSA, #16060 / #18093)

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Tasks

- [ ] An officially supported task in the `examples` folder (such as GLUE/SQuAD, ...)
- [x] My own task or dataset (give details below)

### Reproduction

Model: GLM-5.3 (`GlmMoeDsaForCausalLM` -> DeepSeek-V3.2 path, DSA sparse attention), W4AFP8 checkpoint, `pp_size 2 --tp_size 4 --ep_size 4`, `speculative_config: {decoding_type: MTP, max_draft_len: 1}`, `kv_cache_config: {enable_block_reuse: true, free_gpu_memory_fraction: 0.8, dtype: auto}` (KV cache manager V2 auto-selected: `Resolved use_kv_cache_manager_v2='auto' to True for GlmMoeDsaForCausalLM`), `enable_chunked_prefill: true`, `max_num_tokens 8192`, `max_seq_len 262144`.

Traffic: replay of real agentic conversations at their original arrival pace, 16-32 requests in flight, prompt length p50 ~146k / p95 ~169k tokens, with long shared prefixes between turns of the same conversation (multi-turn tool use). Startup log:

```text
Splitting KV cache max_gpu_total_bytes: total=60.51 GiB, target=... (49968 bytes/token), draft=... (1284 bytes/token)
KVCacheV2Scheduler: tokens_per_block=64, max_num_tokens=8192, max_batch_size=64, draft_mgr=DSACacheManagerV2, ...
```

After ~180 requests (`max_batch_size 64`):

```text
[TRT-LLM] [E] [executor][RANK 0] submit request failed: Draft KV cache context resize failed for request 186: could not resize to 102991 tokens
  File ".../tensorrt_llm/_torch/pyexecutor/py_executor.py", line 2686, in _executor_loop_pp
    self.resource_manager.prepare_resources(scheduled_batch)
  File ".../tensorrt_llm/_torch/pyexecutor/kv_cache_manager_v2.py", line 2759, in _prepare_draft_resources
    raise RuntimeError(
RuntimeError: Draft KV cache context resize failed for request 186: could not resize to 102991 tokens
[TRT-LLM] [E] [_torch][RANK 3] HangDetector: propagating hard-kill to all ranks via MPI_Abort.
```

Same traffic with `max_batch_size 8`, after 26 requests:

```text
[TRT-LLM] [E] [_torch][RANK 0] Error in event loop: Failed to resume draft KV cache for request 78
RuntimeError: Failed to resume draft KV cache for request 78
[TRT-LLM] [E] [executor][RANK 0] Broadcasting event-loop error to 16 pending request(s): Failed to resume draft KV cache for request 78
```

Both go away with `kv_cache_config.enable_block_reuse: false` (which is what the GLM-5 deployment guide ships), at the cost of losing prefix caching entirely.

### Expected behavior

Admission accounts for the DSA indexer ("draft") cache so a context request is only scheduled when both pools can hold it, or the indexer mirror reuses blocks like the primary pool; and a failed resize/resume pauses or rejects the request instead of taking the engine down.

### actual behavior

The docstring of `_prepare_draft_resources` says "The main V2 scheduler only manages the primary KV cache manager", and the mirror calls `stop_committing()` (no block reuse). Both pools are sized to the same token count, but with block reuse the primary pool holds far fewer blocks than the sum of in-flight prompt lengths on prefix-shared traffic, so admission proceeds while the indexer pool is already full; the resize/resume failure is then fatal for the whole engine (HangDetector MPI_Abort). The HTTP frontend keeps running and answers `/health` with 503 while every request fails (#18663).

### additional notes

- #18093 (one-model draft KV reuse in cache manager V2) looks related because it coordinates target/draft reuse, but the pool that fills here is the DSA indexer K-cache mirror (`DSACacheManagerV2`, 1,284 B/token), not the speculative draft-model cache; please deduplicate if you consider it the same root cause.
- Reproducible without agentic traffic by sending many long prompts that share a long prefix (so block reuse keeps the primary pool small) at 16+ concurrency.
- Related but different: #15401 / #15462 concern windowed (SWA) pools; this model has no sliding window.
- Sibling reports from the same runs: #18661 (V2 `History length cannot exceed capacity` with reuse off), #18662 (MTP acceptance with V1), #18658 (indexer `wk` scale), #18659 (MIXED_PRECISION `kv_b_proj`).

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and checked the [documentation](https://nvidia.github.io/TensorRT-LLM/) and [examples](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/tree/main/examples) for answers to frequently asked questions.

items.title: cuTile MoE progress tracker
items.author: bkryu
items.body_excerpt:
Current issue tracks progress on the cuTile fused MoE implementation that started with #4646 

We expect cuTile can provide maintainability, as well as easy debugging and development experience for a "catch all" MoE implementation.

Here we track the MoE support across all target architectures, precision combinations, and activations through FlashInfer's unified MoE API.

The end goal is support for all SKUs, all relevant data types (including mixed weight/input precision) and activation parity with the CUTLASS and TRTLLM-gen fused MoE backends.

## PRs

PR #4646 provides:

- [x] BF16 on SM89, SM90, SM120, and SM121 with SwiGLU and ReLU²
- [x] NVFP4 W4A4 on SM120 and SM121 with SwiGLU and ReLU²
- [x] Unified MoE integration, autotuning, CUDA Graph support, tests, documentation, and benchmarks

PR #4888 adds support for all activations listed below

PR #5099 adds support for MXFP4 W4A4 and W4A16  (NVFP4, MXFP4).

PR #5332 adds support for per-tensor scaled FP8 and MXFP8 (W4A8, W8A8, W8A16)

## Target Architecture coverage

- [ ] SM80
- [ ] SM86
- [x] SM89
- [x] SM90
- [ ] SM100
- [ ] SM103
- [ ] SM107
- [ ] SM110
- [x] SM120
- [x] SM121

An architecture is complete when all hardware-applicable precision and activation combinations are tested. Hardware or cuTile-toolchain limitations should be recorded explicitly as N/A.

## Target Precision coverage

Support same-precision execution and higher-precision activations:

- [x] BF16 weights: W16A16
- [x] NVFP4 weights: 
  - [x] W4A4, NVFP4_NVFP4
  - [x] W4A16, NVFP4_BF16
- [x] MXFP4 weights: 
  - [x] W4A4,  MXFP4_MXFP4
  - [x] W4A8,  MXFP4_MXFP8
  - [x] W4A16 MXFP4_BF16
- [x] MXFP8 weights:
  - [x] W8A8 MXFP8_MXFP8
  - [x] W8A16 MXFP8_BF16
- [x] Per-tensor-scaled FP8 weights: W8A8, W8A16
  - [x] W8A8 FP8_FP8
  - [x] W8A16 FP8_BF16
- [ ] DeepSeek-style block-scaled FP8 weights: W8A8, W8A16

For W4A8, track each applicable activation scaling format—per-tensor FP8, block-scaled FP8, and MXFP8—separately. Every combination must define its packing, scale, accumulation, and output contracts.

## Target Activation coverage

- [x] SwiGLU, including parameterized/OAI semantics
- [x] SwiGLU-step
- [x] GeGLU
- [x] GeGLU-tanh
- [x] SiTU
- [x] ReLU²
- [x] GELU
- [x] ReLU
- [x] SiLU
- [x] Identity

## Expert parallelism

Expert parallelism is the final milestone, after single-rank coverage is stable.

- [ ] Local expert ranges and correct routing semantics
- [ ] Multi-GPU correctness and CUDA Graph support
- [ ] Representative EP performance characterization

items.title: [cake deslop] kimi_k3_tp12_tail: merge SM100/SM103 copies, drop identical k23 modules, runtime rank for one-shot K1
items.author: yzh119
items.body_excerpt:
The experimental Kimi-K3 TP12 fused tail (`flashinfer/experimental/kimi_k3_tp12_tail`, #5603/#5624/#5646/#5668) ships ~55K lines of Cake-generated code for 22 kernels per architecture.

**Findings**
- 20 of 22 sm_103a kernels differ from sm_100a only in the symbol and the shared-memory base line; 2 are identical; bindings differ only in symbol/namespace (26K redundant lines).
- `k23:n512:c*` and `k23:n640:c*` are byte-identical modules (column width only changes the host grid).
- `k1_oneshot_ess` is generated 12 times per architecture with the rank baked in, while every other kernel takes `rank` at runtime; the 12-way sum order is fixed, so a runtime rank preserves numerics.
- `k1_twoshot:grouped` and `k3_persist:grouped` serve exactly one token count (256).
- The GPU test needs 12 ranks on 3 NVL72 trays and never runs in CI; a unit test asserts generated arg-plan names.

**Proposed steps**
- [ ] One source per kernel compiled for SM100a and SM103a; one registry record per kernel.
- [ ] Remove the duplicate k23 width modules; key k23 by capacity.
- [ ] Shared binding header; remove unused helpers.
- [ ] Regenerate the one-shot ESS K1 with a runtime rank; expose poll schedule / bulk push / k23 capacity as template parameters.
- [ ] Add a single-GPU compile test for all registered modules.

Expected size: ~55K → ~22K (mechanical) → ~6K (regenerated).

items.title: [Performance]: sm89 ada blockwise FP8 GEMM copies block-scale factors to shared memory 4x/128x redundantly (stride-0 scale TV layouts)
items.author: jiazhihao
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

In the sm89 "ada blockwise" FP8 GEMM (`cpp/tensorrt_llm/kernels/cutlass_kernels/fp8_blockscale_gemm/ada_blockwise_gemm/`), the per-row A scale factors and the per-tile B scale factor are copied from global to shared memory redundantly: every one of the 4 warps issues the same `cp.async` for every SFA element, and all 128 threads issue the same `cp.async` for the single SFB element, once per k-tile and pipeline stage. The prologue `cute::clear` of those buffers is duplicated the same way. Restricting the clears and copies to one owning thread per element removes the duplicate shared-memory writes with no change in results.

**Where it comes from.** The gmem-to-smem thread-value layouts for the scale factors use stride 0 across warps (`sm89_utils.cuh`, lines 194-199 at `134fa245fe`):

```cpp
using GmemLayoutTVSFA = Layout<Shape<Shape<Int<ScaleMsPerTile>, Int<kThreadCount / ScaleMsPerTile>>, Shape<_1, _1>>,
    Stride<Stride<_1, _0>, Stride<_1, _1>>>;
using GmemLayoutTVSFB = Layout<Shape<Shape<_32, _4>, Shape<_1, _1>>, Stride<Stride<_0, _0>, Stride<_1, _1>>>;
```

With `ScaleMsPerTile = kTileM / ScaleGranularityM = 32` and `kThreadCount = 128`, thread `t` maps to SFA row `t % 32` and the warp mode contributes stride 0, so lanes with the same index in all four warps own the same element. For SFB both strides are 0, so all 128 threads own the one element. Every operation partitioned through these layouts is therefore executed by 4 (SFA) or 128 (SFB) threads writing identical bytes to the same shared address:

- `cute::clear(tAsSFA); cute::clear(tBsSFB);` in the prologue (`sm89_fp8_gemm_1d1d.cuh:265-266`)
- `cute::copy_if(g2s_copy_SFA, tApSFA, ...)` and `cute::copy(g2s_copy_SFB, ...)` in the prologue (`:283-286`) and in the mainloop for every k-tile (`:372-375`)

**Evidence from the compiled PTX** (traits `<float_e4m3_t, bfloat16_t, float, float, 3, 32, 128, 128>`, CUDA 13.2, `sm_100f`). The prologue clear compiles to

```
st.shared.b32  [%r13+61440], 0;   // smem_sfa stage 0
st.shared.b32  [%r13+61568], 0;   // stage 1
st.shared.b32  [%r13+61696], 0;   // stage 2
st.shared.v2.b32 [SharedStorageBase+61824], {0f00000000, 0f00000000};  // smem_sfb
st.shared.b32  [SharedStorageBase+61832], 0;
```

with `%r13 = SharedStorageBase + ((tid.x << 2) & 124)`, i.e. `smem_sfa + (tid.x % 32) * 4`, independent of the warp. Offset 61440 is `sizeof(smem_a) + sizeof(smem_b)` = 12288 + 49152. A static race checker over this PTX reports threads 0 and 32 as unordered writers of the same 4 bytes here; the writes are same-value and all consumers sit behind `cp_async_wait` + `__syncthreads` (`:336-337`, `:357-358`, `:407-408`), so this is not a correctness problem, only wasted shared-memory traffic and `cp.async` instructions.

**Cost per k-tile per CTA** (128 threads, 32x128x128 tile):

| Copy | Current | With one owner |
|---|---:|---:|
| SFA `cp.async` instructions | 128 | 32 |
| SFB `cp.async` instructions | 128 | 1 |
| Shared bytes written for scales | 1,024 | 132 |

That is 2 of the 12 `cp.async` instructions each thread issues per k-tile, and about 5% of the shared-memory write bytes next to the 20 KiB A/B tiles.

**Fix:** #19567 restricts the scale-factor clears and copies to one owning thread per element while keeping the stride-0 layouts; results are unchanged and the duplicate shared-memory writes disappear.

### Report of performance regression

_No response_

### Misc discussion on performance

The same stride-0 idiom appears in the smem-to-register scale layouts (`SmemLayoutTVSFA`/`SmemLayoutTVSFB`) but those are reads, so they are not affected.

### Your current environment (if you think it is necessary)

Not applicable: the analysis is on the compiled PTX (CUDA 13.2, `sm_100f`) at commit `ef567dd9b8919f6ee8b2da1f6f6d0c90206a78f8`; the code is unchanged on `main` at `134fa245fe`.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and checked the [documentation](https://nvidia.github.io/TensorRT-LLM/) and [examples](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/tree/main/examples) for answers to frequently asked questions.

  - TensorRT-LLM: v1.3.0rc9 line (source paths below verified against this line)
  - NCCL 2.30.4, PyTorch as shipped in the container
- OS: Ubuntu 24.04 (container)
- Orchestrator: MPI (`trtllm-llmapi-launch` → `mpirun`), i.e. the `MpiCommSession`/IPC-executor path (not Ray).

### Who can help?

Leaving blank for a core maintainer to route (executor / IPC / multi-node serving).

### The bug

On a **multi-node** `trtllm-serve` launched with the **MPI orchestrator** (ranks spanning two hosts),
startup **hangs at IPC-executor init**. Rank-0's orchestrator creates its ZMQ IPC queues bound to
**loopback** and advertises that `tcp://127.0.0.1:PORT` endpoint to all workers. The 8 worker ranks on
the *second* host try to connect to `127.0.0.1:PORT`, which resolves to *their own* loopback, never
reach rank-0, and exit — so `MpiSession`/IPC init blocks forever waiting for them to connect.

This is specifically an **IPC-executor** problem, not an MPI / NCCL / EFA problem: the `mpirun`
cross-node bootstrap is clean (all 16 ranks start; `orted` launches on the worker node over ssh), and
the hang is **before** NCCL init.

### The hang (reproduced, frozen 8+ minutes, GPUs idle)

`trtllm-serve` freezes right after these lines and never proceeds:

```
[TRT-LLM] [W] Orchestrator is creating IPC executor
rank 0 using MpiCommSession to bind to external MPI processes
[TRT-LLM] [I] Generating a new HMAC key for server proxy_request_queue
[TRT-LLM] [I] Generating a new HMAC key for server worker_init_status_queue
[TRT-LLM] [I] Generating a new HMAC key for server proxy_result_queue
```

Rank-0 waits for the 16 workers to connect to `worker_init_status_queue`; the 8 worker-node ranks
never connect (they start, fail to reach rank-0, exit → `orted` defunct), so init hangs.

### Root cause (source, v1.3.0rc line)

1. `tensorrt_llm/executor/ipc.py:58` — the queue bind address defaults to a hardcoded loopback:
   ```python
   self.address_endpoint = address[
       0] if address is not None else "tcp://127.0.0.1:*"
   ```
2. `tensorrt_llm/executor/proxy.py:494` — `worker_init_status_queue = IpcQueue(is_server=True,
   name="worker_init_status_queue")` is constructed with **no `address`**, so it uses that loopback
   default; `proxy.py:520` then advertises that `tcp://127.0.0.1:PORT` endpoint to the workers.
   Cross-host workers connecting to `127.0.0.1:PORT` hit their **own** loopback → fail.
3. **No routable-IP override exists.** A whole-tree grep of `tensorrt_llm/executor/` for
   `TLLM_*ADDR|*IP|*HOST`, `0.0.0.0`, `get_local_ip`, `use_hostname` finds nothing that sets the
   orchestrator IPC bind address. (`TLLM_SPAWN_PROXY_PROCESS_IPC_ADDR` is an `ipc://` unix socket for
   the RPC-proxy path — even more node-local — and `MASTER_ADDR` is for the Ray backend, not the MPI
   IPC executor.)

So on a single node everything binds and connects on loopback and works; the moment ranks span hosts,
the loopback-bound orchestrator queues are unreachable by the remote workers.

### Expected behavior

A multi-node MPI-orchestrated `trtllm-serve` should let the orchestrator IPC queues bind to a
**routable** address (or `0.0.0.0`) and advertise rank-0's **routable IP** (not `127.0.0.1`) to the
workers, so cross-host workers can connect and `/health` comes up.

### Reproduction

```bash
mpirun -np 16 -H <node0>:8,<node1>:8 \
  --mca plm_rsh_args "-p 2222 -o GSSAPIAuthentication=no" \
  -x TRTLLM_FORCE_COMM_METHOD=... \
  trtllm-llmapi-launch trtllm-serve <a-MoE-model> \
  --tp_size 16 --ep_size 16 --pp_size 1 ...
# hangs at "Orchestrator is creating IPC executor" (see log above); GPUs idle.
```
(`GSSAPIAuthentication=no` is only needed so ssh doesn't stall on GSSAPI KEX against a no-KDC node —
unrelated to the IPC bug.)

### A candidate direction — and why this is filed as an issue, not a "fix" PR

An env-overridable bind address gets *past* the freeze once, but is **not a reliable fix**, so I am
filing this as a defensive-note issue rather than presenting a patch as done:

```diff
--- a/tensorrt_llm/executor/ipc.py
+++ b/tensorrt_llm/executor/ipc.py
-        self.address_endpoint = address[
-            0] if address is not None else "tcp://127.0.0.1:*"
+        self.address_endpoint = address[
+            0] if address is not None else ("tcp://%s:*" % os.environ.get("TLLM_IPC_BIND_IP", "127.0.0.1"))
```
Run with `-x TLLM_IPC_BIND_IP=<rank-0 routable node IP>`.

**Caveat (measured):** with this change + `TLLM_IPC_BIND_IP=<node0 IP>`, **one** attempt advanced all
the way to `launch_server` (past the IPC freeze); a subsequent clean relaunch (stale procs + port
reaped) **re-hung at the same IPC freeze**. So a routable-IP bind is *necessary but not sufficient*.
Unconfirmed which of: (a) the env did not thread to rank-0 on the relaunch (env propagation), (b) a
second worker-connected queue still binds loopback, or (c) an ephemeral-port node↔node reachability
issue. A complete fix should (i) bind the orchestrator IPC to a routable/`0.0.0.0` address, (ii)
advertise the routable IP (not `0.0.0.0`/`127.0.0.1`) to workers, and (iii) ensure **every**
worker-connected queue (not just `worker_init_status_queue`) uses it — then prove a clean multi-host
`trtllm-serve` reaches `/health`.

### Proven workaround

Switching the orchestrator from MPI to **Ray** (`--orchestrator_type ray` / the Ray-backed launch
path, which uses `MASTER_ADDR` for a routable rendezvous) brings multi-node `trtllm-serve` up cleanly
on the same 2-node substrate. So the defect is specific to the **MPI IPC-executor** bind path, and
there is a working alternative

items.title: [Bug]: guided response_format is silently ignored without guided_decoding_backend
items.author: hhashmi4
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

TensorRT-LLM commit:
c76f4a856447820aa1f994b053da7580d69b657d

Container:
nvcr.io/nvidia/tensorrt-llm/release:1.3.0rc29.dev202609250232

Container environment:
- NVIDIA Release 26.08
- PyTorch 2.14.0a0+4fdf77b
- Python 3.12

Host:
- Linux x86_64
- Docker 29.1.3
- CPU-only host for the regression test

The container reports the same TRT_LLM_GIT_COMMIT as the source revision above.

### Who can help?

_No response_

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [ ] My own modified scripts

### Tasks

- [ ] An officially supported task in the `examples` folder (such as GLUE/SQuAD, ...)
- [ ] My own task or dataset (give details below)

### Reproduction

I ran into the remaining missing-backend case from NVIDIA/TensorRT#4855 and reproduced it against current TensorRT-LLM main:

`c76f4a856447820aa1f994b053da7580d69b657d`

I reduced the issue to the request-vs-engine validation path in `BaseLLM._check_arguments()`.

The regression test I used is:

```python
def test_check_arguments_rejects_guided_decoding_without_backend() -> None:
    llm = _TestLLM(guided_decoding_backend=None)
    sampling_params = SamplingParams(
        guided_decoding=GuidedDecodingParams(
            json={"type": "object"}
        )
    )

    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="guided_decoding_backend"):
        llm._check_arguments(
            prompt_len=1,
            sampling_params=sampling_params,
            is_gen_only=False,
        )
```

This test lives in:

`tests/unittest/llmapi/test_sampling_params.py`

Against unmodified current main, the regression test fails with:

`Failed: DID NOT RAISE <class 'ValueError'>`

The request contains an active guided-decoding constraint, but the missing backend is not rejected before execution.

I also traced the request path and confirmed that guided decoding is only installed when `guided_decoding_backend` is configured. Without a backend configured, the request can continue without the requested constraint being enforced.

I did not run full GPU inference locally because this host does not have an NVIDIA GPU. I ran the regression test inside NVIDIA's TensorRT-LLM release container built from the exact same source commit.

Container used:

`nvcr.io/nvidia/tensorrt-llm/release:1.3.0rc29.dev202609250232`

### Expected behavior

If a request includes an active guided-decoding constraint but the LLM/server was started without `guided_decoding_backend`, the request should be rejected before executor submission with a clear validation error.

Requests that do not use guided decoding should continue to work normally.

An empty/no-op `GuidedDecodingParams()` should also keep its current behavior and should not be rejected.

### actual behavior

The request is currently accepted even when `guided_decoding_backend=None`.

`BaseLLM._check_arguments()` does not reject the mismatch, so an active guided-decoding constraint can continue toward execution even though no guided decoder was configured.

On unmodified current main, the regression test fails with:

`Failed: DID NOT RAISE <class 'ValueError'>`

This means the structured-output request is not being rejected at the request-vs-engine validation boundary when the required backend capability is missing.

### additional notes

I tested a small fix locally in `BaseLLM._check_arguments()` that rejects an active guided-decoding request when no `guided_decoding_backend` is configured.

The check reuses the existing `SamplingParams._get_guided_decoding_params()` behavior instead of duplicating guide detection. That keeps the current behavior for:

- normal requests with no guided-decoding constraint
- empty/no-op `GuidedDecodingParams()`
- requests where a guided-decoding backend is configured

Validation on the patch:

- regression + control cases: 4 passed
- full `tests/unittest/llmapi/test_sampling_params.py`: 56 passed
- TensorRT-LLM pre-commit checks: passed

The separate OpenAI `json_schema` wrapper issue mentioned in NVIDIA/TensorRT#4855 is already fixed on current TensorRT-LLM main, so this issue is only about the missing-backend case.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and checked the [documentation](https://nvidia.github.io/TensorRT-LLM/) and [examples](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/tree/main/examples) for answers to frequently asked questions.

items.title: Matrix<R,C>::at() strides by row count: wrong values and out-of-bounds access for all non-square shapes (diagonal/hcat/vcat affected)
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

The value-semantics `Matrix<R, C>` specializations in include/cutlass/matrix.h implement `at(i, j)` with a **row-count** stride instead of a column-count stride:

```cpp
Element at(int i, int j) const {
    return data[i * kRows + j];   // should be i * kColumns
}
```

Every non-square specialization is affected (square ones coincide). Consequences for non-square shapes:

- wrong element returned/stored whenever row >= 1 and R != C;
- out-of-bounds reads **and writes** when R > C (e.g. `Matrix<float,4,1>::at(3,0)` touches `data[12]` of a 4-element array);
- GCC at -O2 even warns "iteration invokes undefined behavior" on loops over `at()` for 3x2/4x2/4x3.

Downstream members built on `at()` inherit the defect:

- `diagonal()` returns wrong values for every non-square shape and performs OOB accesses for R > C shapes (e.g. `Matrix<float,3,2>::diagonal()` writes 3 entries into its 2-element result while reading `data[8]` of 6); AddressSanitizer flags it: `heap-buffer-overflow READ ... Matrix<float,3,2>::diagonal() const matrix.h`.
- the element-wise forms of `hcat`/`vcat` read their operands through `at()`, so concatenations are wrong for any operand with more than one row and non-square shape. A full differential over all 15 shapes shows 28 hcat-lhs + 18 hcat-rhs + 19 vcat-lhs mismatches plus transpose round-trip failures (`t.transpose()` != original), all confined to non-square operands.

Everything else in the header (products, transpose storage maps, slice_/set_slice_, dot/sum/norm/trace, uniform constructors) sweeps clean against reference implementations; the defects are exactly the `at()`-derived paths. No in-tree caller exercises these members on non-square matrices today (`test/unit/core/matrix.cu` is 4x4 only), so this has stayed latent, but the class is public API.

### Suggested fix

Regenerate the specializations with `at()` striding by `kColumns`; make `diagonal()` emit `min(kRows, kColumns)` entries from `data[i * kColumns + i]` into a matching-size result; regenerate the element-wise `hcat`/`vcat` statics (or index operands directly). A unit test covering at/diagonal/hcat/vcat on non-square shapes would pin it.

items.title: [MPS] Out of memory error results in kernels not being executed
items.author: benkelaya
items.body_excerpt:
**What happens.** On MPS, take a bf16 tensor `(1, 128, H, W)`, permute it to `(1, H, W, 128)`, upcast it to float32, square it, and take the mean over the last dim. That is the variance step of an RMSNorm applied to an NCHW activation in channels-last order. Above 2**31 bytes of view, the result is all zeros, and nothing is raised. Below that size, it matches the CPU.

| view | bytes | max abs diff vs CPU | MPS result |
|---|---|---|---|
| (1, 2048, 2560, 128) | 1.342e9 | 4.9e-4 | correct |
| (1, 3072, 4096, 128) | 3.221e9 | 2580 | all zeros |

The same computation is correct on a tensor created contiguous at the large size. A bf16 reduction on the same view is also correct. We met it in a VAE decoder's final RMSNorm at a 3072 x 4096 output, where the image came out wrong, while running Sana 4K in [NeuroBrix](https://github.com/NeuroBrix/neurobrix), an open-source inference engine. Our workaround there, for anyone hitting the same wall: keep every op's output and float32 intermediates under a per-tensor byte ceiling declared for the MPS backend, and tile row-wise ops (norms, elementwise chains) over their non-reduced axes below it; the result is then exact.

**Reproducer** (torch 2.14.0, Apple M4 Pro 24 GB, macOS 27.0):

```python
import torch
torch.manual_seed(0)
H, W = 3072, 4096                      # 2048, 2560 is correct
xc = (torch.randn(1, 128, H, W) * 40).to(torch.bfloat16)
view_mps = xc.to("mps").permute(0, 2, 3, 1)
got = view_mps.to(torch.float32).pow(2).mean(-1, keepdim=True)[:, :64].cpu()
want = xc[:, :, :64].permute(0, 2, 3, 1).to(torch.float32).pow(2).mean(-1, keepdim=True)
print((got - want).abs().max().item(), bool((got == 0).all()))   # 2580.0 True
```

**Expected:** the CPU result, or an explicit error if the size is not supported.

**Where the zeros appear.** The cast alone is exact at the failing size. It keeps the permuted strides, `(1610612736, 4096, 1, 12582912)` for the float32 result, and matches the CPU to 0. The zeros appear in the float32 `pow(2).mean(-1)` that follows. Casting with `memory_format=torch.contiguous_format` before the reduction also returns zeros. A bf16 `pow(2).mean(-1)` on the same view matches the CPU to 0.0. The float32 chain on a bf16 tensor created in `(1, H, W, 128)` layout on the CPU and moved whole is correct, with a max difference of 4.9e-4. All checks compare the first 64 rows against the CPU at the failing size.

**Related, but not this case.** #197636 is the tiled `bmm` path past 2**32 output elements. #198471 is `nll_loss` past flat index 2**31. #154322 is a float16 to float32 cast returning zeros, whereas the cast here is correct. All sit under the large-tensor umbrella #149325 (`module: mps`, `module: 64-bit`). #198473 shows the same kind of silent result on 2.14.0 for `torch.arange`.

### Versions

```
PyTorch version: 2.14.0
OS: macOS 27.0 (arm64), build 26A428
CPU: Apple M4 Pro (24 GB unified memory)
```


cc @ezyang @gchanan @kadeng @msaroufim @malfet @kulinseth @DenisVieriu97 @jhavukainen @aditvenk @Isalia20

items.title: [Serve] [RFC] Computed Retry-After for backpressure rejections
items.author: vinay7373
items.body_excerpt:
## Motivation

PR #65193 added `BackpressureConfig`. Deployments can now reject backpressured requests with a 429 and a static `Retry-After` header. Each caller (proxy or `DeploymentHandle`) has its own request queue, and at the time of a backpressure rejection a static `Retry-After` value can be incorrect in both directions. If the queue is deep and the static value is too short, clients retry into another rejection, adding load exactly when the system is trying to shed it. If the queue drains fast and the value is too long, capacity sits idle while clients wait.

This proposal computes the `Retry-After` value from observed load. This makes the header a reliable estimate of when capacity will be available, instead of a number the operator guessed. This was the original shape of the production request behind #65193 and it fits the discussion there about making 429 the default at some point.

No OSS inference server does this today (TGI, Triton, NVIDIA Dynamo and TorchServe all reject without a retry hint). The closest prior art is cloud-side (Azure OpenAI's `retry-after-ms`, AWS's `x-amz-retry-after`) and per-client rate limiters, where the value can be exact because a rate window is a clock. Capacity recovery is not a clock, so here the value is an estimate at any layer.

## Goals

- An opt-in `BackpressureConfig` policy that computes `Retry-After` from load signals the rejecting component already has.
- Keep the rejection path as cheap as it is today. No RPCs, locks or extra work on reject-and-respond.
- Degrade gracefully: computed, else static, else no header. Never fail or delay a rejection.

## Non-goals

- Changing when requests are rejected. Admission control is a separate discussion.
- Guaranteeing admission at the suggested time. The header is a hint, not a reservation.
- Changing the default rejection status code. Tracked separately.
- Implementing any further policy, such as the cluster-informed one (see "Future policies").

## Proposed API

```python
from ray.serve.config import BackpressureConfig

@serve.deployment(
    max_queued_requests=64,
    backpressure_config=BackpressureConfig(
        status_code=429,
        retry_after_policy="queue_drain_rate",   # NEW: "static" (default) | "queue_drain_rate"
        retry_after_s=5,                         # static value; also the fallback for computed policies
    ),
)
```

`retry_after_policy` is a named policy instead of a bare `"auto"` so future strategies can be added without changing what existing configs mean.

## Proposed design

This design adds a new field to `BackpressureConfig` called `retry_after_policy`, and one new policy named `queue_drain_rate` that computes `Retry-After` from the rejecting component's observed queue depth and drain rate.

The overall mechanism has 3 basic aspects: (i) how to compute the `Retry-After` value (what the `queue_drain_rate` policy implements), (ii) where to compute it, and (iii) who stamps the header and emits it to the client.

These boil down to emission and estimation. Emission answers (iii) and is fixed: the rejecting component stamps the header. Estimation covers (i) and (ii): one shared implementation, invoked at the two places Serve rejects today, each feeding its own local signals.

### The `queue_drain_rate` policy (this proposal)

```
retry_after = ceil(observed_queue_depth / drain_rate)
```

- **The numerator is the depth observed at rejection.** It is at least `max_queued_requests`, since a rejection only fires once the queue has reached the cap, and occasionally a little above it: the router's check is not atomic, and replica-rejected requests re-enter the queue behind new arrivals. The raise site already holds this number (it is in the `BackPressureError` message today), so using the observed value costs nothing and is exact.
- **`drain_rate` is the live signal**: how fast the queue empties, updated at the end of every interval as `drain_rate = 0.3 * rate_over_last_interval + 0.7 * previous_drain_rate`. `rate_over_last_interval` is the fresh measurement: requests drained during the interval that just ended. `previous_drain_rate` is this same formula's output from the previous update, so it carries the whole history with older intervals fading out. The 70% weight on the trend keeps lumpy traffic from whipping the value around (completions land in bursts, so a single interval can read 0 or 3x the true rate), and the 30% on the fresh measurement keeps the estimate chasing real load changes within a few intervals. The split, the interval length and the warmup threshold are implementation constants with environment-variable overrides, like Serve's other internal tunables, not new `BackpressureConfig` fields. The update runs on a lightweight background timer in the component's existing metrics machinery (default 1s). An interval with zero completions counts as a real observation when work is in flight, since that is what slow drain looks like, but idle intervals (nothing running or queued) skip the update instead of decaying the rate. The rate counts as warm after a configurable minimum number of counted intervals; until then the fallback applies.
- **Two call sites, one implementation.** On the proxy path the router rejects; its drain rate is its own assignment throughput, from a monotonic counter added at the existing send event (the current per-replica counter is an in-flight gauge, so it can't provide a rate). The rate is fleet-blended: faster replicas take more assignments, so mixed hardware is priced in. On direct ingress the replica rejects; its drain rate is its own completion rate, and its queue is drained only by itself. Same formula, different local inputs, different values, each describing its own queue. A replica's value is a conservative upper bound, since a retry may be re-balanced to a replica that frees up sooner.
- **Clamp to [1, 60] seconds.** Common client SDKs ignore `Retry-After` above 60s.
- **Jitter (for example +/-20%) is applied in the shared heade

comments.author: suppagoddo
comments.body: @abrarsheikh - Sure, Will review

comments.author: johntaylor-cell
comments.body:
My main concern is how this RFC and direct-ingress work together.  Serve is moving toward direct-ingress with HAProxy as the default, and on that path the router is no longer the module that rejects the request.  HAProxy will sit between the client and Serve, and it already has retry-after functionality (as does Envoy).  Both implement it very differently from what the RFC proposes.  Their calculation is time-based so it is more exact than the proposed prediction.  It is also per-client, and HAProxy exposes queue-based metrics so the limit can fire only under real back pressure.  I suggest we provide a way to enable that functionality in HAProxy, which Serve already generates config for but does not use today.

If we also want retry-after on the router path (when direct-ingress is disabled), I would try to duplicate HAProxy's time-based functionality, rather than use a forecast. That is a larger change than this RFC scopes, since admission control is listed as a non-goal, but I think it is worth deciding explicitly rather than estimating.

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
Thanks for the review. Breaking it down into where we agree and where we don't.

**Where we agree:**

1. The RFC did not cover the direct-ingress path. That was a real gap and I updated the RFC. Short version: on direct ingress the same policy runs at the replica, using its own queue depth divided by an EWMA of its own completion rate. Same formula, one shared estimator implementation, two call sites. A replica's queue is drained only by itself, so that vantage is even simpler than the router's.

2. Per-client rate limiting at the HAProxy layer is valuable. It answers "this client exceeded its quota", and its Retry-After can be exact because a rate window is a clock. That is complementary to this RFC, which answers "the deployment is out of capacity, here is when to come back". I would support that as a separate proposal and am happy to file it.

**Where we don't agree, and why:**

1. "HAProxy will sit between the client and Serve" as the rejector. Not for backpressure today. On the direct-ingress path the replica rejects the request (see the "Request dropped due to backpressure" emission sites in [replica.py on the ray-2.58.0 tag](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/ray-2.58.0/python/ray/serve/_private/replica.py)). HAProxy passes the replica's response through, and its errorfiles only rewrite HAProxy-generated errors. #65193 shipped 429 + Retry-After on this path, tested with `RAY_SERVE_ENABLE_DIRECT_INGRESS=1`.

2. "Functionality Serve already generates config for but does not use". I checked `haproxy_templates.py`: no stick-tables, no track-sc, no deny rules, no Retry-After anywhere in the generated config. Enabling this would be new work, not switching on something dormant.

3. "Their calculation is time-based so it is more exact than the proposed prediction". I checked the [HAProxy docs](https://www.haproxy.com/documentation/haproxy-configuration-tutorials/security/traffic-policing/) on this. HAProxy's computed Retry-After is `http-after-response set-header Retry-After %[src,table_expire(...)]`: the time until the client's stick-table rate-limit record expires. That is per-client policing, and it is exact because a rate window is deterministic. For capacity overload (server maxconn queue full, `timeout queue` expiring) the docs show no Retry-After computation: that 503 ships without a hint. The queue timer measures elapsed wait, not time until capacity returns. When capacity frees depends on service completions and arrivals, and no layer can know that exactly, including HAProxy, which cannot see how long the inference ahead of a request will take. Any capacity Retry-After is an estimate at every layer. That is why the RFC ships an acceptance criterion and telemetry to measure the estimate, instead of claiming exactness.

Rate limiting and capacity backpressure are different problems. An exact time-based Retry-After exists for the first and cannot exist for the second. This RFC is scoped to the second, now explicitly works on both ingress paths, and leaves room for a HAProxy rate-limiting proposal alongside it.

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
@johntaylor-cell 

My thoughts on your a HA Proxy based admission control and what I see as limitations:

- As you mentioned the HAProxy queue resets on every reload and Serve reloads HAProxy on every replica-set change. So the primary queue evaporates exactly during autoscaling churn (your own finding).
- Composition traffic never passes HAProxy, so the Serve backstop must stay. That means 3 admission systems with 3 threshold vocabularies to keep coherent.
    - Users configuring three queueing layers instead of one: per-server `maxconn` plus timeout queue in HAProxy, `max_queued_requests` at handles, `max_ongoing_requests` at replicas. Three knobs at three levels in different units (connections vs requests, per instance vs per caller vs per replica) that all have to be sized against each other and re-sized as the cluster scales. Mis-size any pair and you get double queueing or shedding while replicas sit idle. That is more error prone, not simpler.
- The default proxy path gets nothing from it.
- Per-deployment BackpressureConfig granularity would have to be re-expressed in generated HAProxy config.
- Moving where queueing happens is an admission-control redesign, which this RFC explicitly scopes out as a non-goal.
- On jittered-static vs computed: 
    - jitter only spreads retries around a center, it cannot make the center reliable. With `retry_after_s` we already ship the option to set a fixed, guessed value at config time, so a jittered constant is not a new proposal, it is [#65193](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/65193) plus jitter. Drain rate moves 10-100x across load regimes, so the constant is wrong exactly when it matters. A 5s center against a 60s real drain means every jittered retry comes back early and gets refused again. Guessing that constant is the problem this RFC exists to remove. So a computed value using drain rate is more reliable. And @suppagoddo 's suggestion for A/B against a jittered-static baseline will show it under real workloads and make this measurable.
