@johntaylor-cell took your 6 and 7 into the RFC:

On 6: you are right that queue depth is the configured cap at rejection, and right about occupancy. I checked: `serve.llm` sets `DEFAULT_MAX_ONGOING_REQUESTS = int(1e9)` (python/ray/llm/_internal/serve/constants.py), so occupancy against configured capacity reads zero. The saturation factor is dropped entirely and the formula is now `ceil(max_queued_requests / drain_rate)`. 

One clarification on the drain rate, since implementability was questioned: the router already counts assignments per replica (num_requests_sent_to_replicas, router.py:152) and the rejection is raised from a method on the same `RouterMetricsManager` that owns those counters, so the EWMA is a derivation over state the raise site already holds, not new plumbing.

On 7: agreed and adopted. Jitter moves into the shared header helper, so the static retry_after_s path gets it too, which both fixes today's verbatim emission and keeps the A/B fair. Good catch, credited in the RFC.

Separately, your reload observation (HAProxy state wiped on replica-set changes when dynamic server updates would do) is a real standalone improvement to the HAProxy ingress, worth its own issue regardless of this RFC.

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
@suppagoddo thanks for your review, all of your points are in the updated RFC:

1. Renamed to queue_drain_rate, since the same policy runs at the router or the replica, whichever rejects.
2. On a local saturation factor for direct ingress: we ended up dropping the saturation factor everywhere instead. From @johntaylor-cell 's finding `serve.llm` defaults `max_ongoing_requests` to `1e9`, so occupancy measured against configured capacity reads zero for the main workload class, and the backoff term had no existing signal behind it. It isn't gone forever though: if the A/B data shows the simple formula consistently errs in a way a saturation signal would fix, that data is the justification to bring one back. Evidence first, term later.
3. EWMA warmup is configurable as an implementation constant with an environment-variable override, alongside the smoothing split and the interval length, same as Serve's other internal tunables. Deliberately not a new BackpressureConfig field, to keep the public API at two fields plus the policy name.
4. Adopted your measurement point: since retries can't be reliably correlated (new request IDs, different proxy, or no retry at all), the primary measure is suggested delay vs the locally observed queue drain time, with admitted-retry rate secondary where correlation does exist.
5. Your A/B against a jittered-static baseline is now the acceptance test itself.

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
@abrarsheikh to summarize the whole review thread and the current state of RFC:

Updated the RFC based on the review so far and it came out simpler. 
One policy, `queue_drain_rate` which computes `retry_after` on rejection using below formula:
```
retry_after = ceil(max_queued_requests / drain_rate)
```
Where:
- `max_queued_requests`: the numerator is the configured cap (depth at rejection is always the cap) and 
- `drain_rate` is a smoothed measure of how fast the rejecting component's queue empties which is assignment throughput at the router, completion rate at the replica. 

The value is clamped to [1, 60]s and jittered in the shared header helper so the static path gets jitter too, falls back to the static retry_after_s when the rate isn't warm, and the acceptance test is an A/B against a jittered-static baseline measured on suggested delay vs observed local drain time.

comments.author: suppagoddo
comments.body: @abrarsheikh @vinay7373 - Can I take this feature implementation?

comments.author: JerryChaox
comments.body:
hello guys, some information and test for this RFC.

I tested the proposal on Ray 2.58.0 and found two implementation details worth checking before coding it.

First, num_requests_sent_to_replicas is an in-flight gauge: it increments on send and decrements on completion. It cannot directly provide assignment throughput, so the router likely needs a monotonic counter at the accepted-assignment event.

Second, router queue depth is not always equal to max_queued_requests at rejection. Internal replica rejection can cause requests to re-enter after new requests occupy temporarily freed slots. With a cap of 8, 1,418 of 17,270 router rejection events had an observed depth of 9–11. I did not observe this on the direct-replica path.

I also compared the computed policy with a tuned jittered-static baseline over 90 held-out distributed runs. Conditional local-drain header MAE was 1.865s for the computed policy and 1.141s for static 2s. The computed policy generated fewer attempts, so this looks like a precision versus retry-cost tradeoff rather than a clear winner.

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
@JerryChaox Thanks for testing the approach and for those valuable findings. Here are my thoughts on each of them:

1. Agree (and my earlier comment was wrong on this) that `num_requests_sent_to_replicas` is an in-flight gauge, increments on send (`router.py:404`) and decrements on completion (`router.py:412`). I will fix this by adding a new monotonic assignment counter at the same send event. So the raise site and the counters live on the same object and the drain rate is still a derivation over local state.

2. This is a great find. Agreed. This finding makes the formula better: use the observed depth at rejection as the numerator instead of the configured cap. The raise site already holds that number, it is in the BackPressureError message today.

3. On your third observation, the A/B test: I see how a static value wins on a homogeneous workload, where a good constant like your 2s can be guessed or tuned in advance. But the whole purpose of this RFC is the case where the constant cannot be guessed in advance, because load regimes vary and move the drain rate. I'd like to know: a) Did drain time vary across your 90 runs? b) Was the 2s tuned per workload or once overall?

Your fewer attempts observation is the most interesting part. MAE weighs a 1s early and a 1s late suggestion equally, but the costs are not equal: early means a wasted attempt plus more load on a system that is already shedding, late means idle wait. So I think we should use a asymmetric or composite metric that penalizes wasted attempts (penalize early more than late).

comments.author: vinay7373
suppagoddo
comments.body: @vinay7373 - Sounds good, will start the implementation work!

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
Acceptance criteria spec:

1. Ground truth: Each rejection records the observed depth D and the drain counter value at that moment. Ground truth T is the wall time until the counter advances by D: assignments at the router, completions at the replica on direct ingress. This measures what the header claims, that the observed backlog clears. It does not measure whether a specific retry gets admitted, since that depends on other clients' arrivals. T stays measurable under continuous overload because the counter keeps advancing even when the queue never dips below the cap.
2. Metric: An asymmetric loss between the suggested delay `s` and `T`: `0.75 * max(T - s, 0) + 0.25 * max(s - T, 0)`. One second too early costs 3x one second too late, because an early retry wastes an attempt and adds load while the system is shedding and a late one only waits, bounded by the clamp. The minimizer of this loss is the 75th percentile of the drain time distribution, so the estimator gets a concrete target. MAE is reported as secondary for comparability. Scoring is offline over logged pairs, on the pre-jitter post-clamp value.
3. Baseline: The comparison arm is jittered static, with the constant tuned only on calibration runs disjoint from the evaluation set (rule: 75th percentile of calibration drain times, one global constant). A per-scenario tuned static is also reported. Runs are open loop (clients ignore the header) with autoscaling off and a pinned replica set.

@suppagoddo For me to run the above acceptance test I'll need one structured record per rejection with `policy id, fallback rung used, observed depth, drain rate estimate and warm flag, pre-jitter and post-jitter values, and the counter value at rejection`. Plus the counter itself readable by a test harness at sub-second granularity. Everything already exists at the raise site or in estimator state; the cost is one log line on a path that already logs a warning today. Please make sure this record emission is part of your implementation.

Pass bar (proposal): 
- Computed beats the static baseline on the primary loss by at least 20% in aggregate across the scenarios
- is never more than 10% worse in any single scenario
- the undershoot rate lands at 25 +/- 10 points
- and cold start falls back to the static value cleanly.

cc. @JerryChaox @abrarsheikh @johntaylor-cell

items.title: Illegal memory access in triton kernel and non-determinism codegen
items.author: xw285cornell
items.body_excerpt:
Hi team, we seem to identified an issue that triton is generating non-deterministic codegen results, and in certain cases (small chances) it seems to have illegal memory access due to out of bound access in shared memory. 
The triton code is fairly simple (shown below). We run the code many times (disabled pytorch's codegen cache) and it seems it produced different shared memory: 
Most of times: 
{"name": "triton__0d1d2d3d4", "shared": 2560, "num_warps": 4, "num_stages": 1}
Sometimes: 
{"name": "triton__0d1d2d3d4", "shared": 544, "num_warps": 4, "num_stages": 1}

So sometimes it only asks for 544 bytes for shared memory space which might lead to out of bound access to shared mem. We checked and ttir is the same across the two runs, but llir is different. Wondering if you can shed some lights on this (and whether the codegen is deterministic. Also this is still on llvm IR - not sure if it repros in MLIR. 

```
from torch._inductor.triton_ops.autotune import pointwise

@pointwise(
    size_hints=[262144, 64],
    tile_hint=TileHint.DEFAULT,
    filename="notebook",
    meta={
        "signature": {0: "*bf16", 1: "*fp32", 2: "*bf16", 3: "i32", 4: "i32"},
        "device": 0,
        "constants": {},
        "mutated_arg_names": [],
        "configs": [instance_descriptor(divisible_by_16=(0, 1, 2, 3), equal_to_1=())],
    },
)
@triton.jit
def triton_(
    in_ptr0,
    in_ptr1,
    out_ptr0,
    xnumel,
    ynumel,
    XBLOCK: tl.constexpr,
    YBLOCK: tl.constexpr,
):
    xnumel = 262144
    ynumel = 62
    xoffset = tl.program_id(0) * XBLOCK
    xindex = xoffset + tl.arange(0, XBLOCK)[:, None]
    xmask = xindex < xnumel
    yoffset = tl.program_id(1) * YBLOCK
    yindex = yoffset + tl.arange(0, YBLOCK)[None, :]
    ymask = yindex < ynumel
    x0 = xindex % 512
    x1 = xindex // 512
    y2 = yindex
    x3 = xindex
    tmp0 = tl.load(
        in_ptr0
        + (
            512
            + x0
            + (1536 * x1)
            + (786432 * y2)
            + (786432 * (((x0 + (512 * x1)) // 262144)))
        ),
        xmask & ymask,
    ).to(tl.float32)
    tmp1 = tl.load(in_ptr1 + (512 + x0), xmask)
    tmp2 = tmp1.to(tl.float32)
    tmp3 = tmp0 + tmp2
    tmp4 = 2.8284271247461903
    tmp5 = tmp3 / tmp4
    tl.store(
        out_ptr0 + (y2 + (62 * x3) + tl.zeros([XBLOCK, YBLOCK], tl.int32)),
        tmp5,
        xmask & ymask,
    )
```

items.title: Discussion: First-class image warmup workflow for AIBrix model workloads
items.author: googs1025
items.body_excerpt:
## Proposal

Add a first-class `ModelWarmup` workflow for AIBrix model workloads.

The initial scope is intentionally small: preload large inference/runtime images onto nodes before rollout or scale-out. This addresses cases where traffic arrives while a newly-created Pod is still waiting for the container runtime to pull and unpack images.

This issue is for design discussion. The API and controller behavior are not finalized.

## Business value

Image pulling is a major source of cold-start latency for model-serving workloads. It is especially visible during:

- autoscaler scale-out, when a new replica lands on a node without the required image cache;
- StormService or RoleSet rolling updates, when the new revision is not yet ready but traffic is already increasing;
- manual capacity preparation, where operators want to warm nodes before exposing them to serving traffic.

A first-class workflow should make image warmup observable through Kubernetes status and provide a verify-before-rollout/scale workflow.

## Proposed MVP

Introduce a standalone `ModelWarmup` CRD under `model.aibrix.ai/v1alpha1`.

```yaml
apiVersion: model.aibrix.ai/v1alpha1
kind: ModelWarmup
metadata:
  name: qwen-image-warmup
spec:
  targets:
  - nodes:
      names:
      - gpu-node-a
      - gpu-node-b
  - nodeSelector:
      matchLabels:
        resource-pool.aibrix.ai/name: latency-pool
  - workload:
      ref:
        apiVersion: orchestration.aibrix.ai/v1alpha1
        kind: StormService
        name: qwen
      subTarget:
        roleName: prefill

  imagePreload:
    images:
    - registry.example.com/vllm@sha256:...
    - registry.example.com/aibrix-runtime@sha256:...
    pullSecrets:
    - name: registry-secret

  policies:
    parallelism: 8
    globalTimeoutSeconds: 1800
    retryLimit: 2
    ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 3600
```

## Target selection

All of the following target sources should be supported:

1. **Explicit nodes**: a list of node names.
2. **Node labels, capabilities, or resource pools**: a Kubernetes `LabelSelector`, for example an AIBrix resource-pool label. This mode should discover matching nodes added later for autoscaler scale-out.
3. **AIBrix workloads**: resolve nodes from `StormService`, `RoleSet`, `Deployment`, `ModelClaim`, or `ModelAdapter` Pods, with role-level filtering such as `prefill` or `decode` where applicable.

Multiple target entries are allowed. The controller should take the union of all resolved targets and deduplicate by node name. This allows operators to combine a resource pool, a workload's current nodes, and explicitly reserved nodes.

A workload reference describes the current workload placement. It does not by itself guarantee coverage of future scale-out nodes; use a node selector/resource-pool target for that purpose.

## Execution model

The controller should:

1. Resolve all target sources.
2. Union and deduplicate target nodes.
3. Calculate a deterministic revision from the target and image configuration.
4. Create one node-pinned warmup Job per target node and revision.
5. Run one short-lived regular container per unique image so image pulls can proceed independently.
6. Update per-node and aggregate status from Job completion.
7. Reconcile newly matching nodes, failed Jobs, stale targets, retries, and TTL cleanup.

Warmup Jobs should use `nodeName` or required node affinity, support the target node's taints and architecture, use configured pull secrets, and avoid requesting GPU resources for image-only warmup. Image entrypoints should be overridden so an inference server does not start accidentally.

A Job is preferred over a bare Pod because it provides retry and completion semantics and can recreate a deleted warmup Pod.

## Suggested status

```yaml
status:
  phase: Pending|Running|Succeeded|Failed|Degraded
  observedRevision: ...
  desiredNodes: 2
  activeNodes: 1
  succeededNodes: 1
  failedNodes: 0
  startTime: ...
  completionTime: ...
  targets:
  - nodeName: gpu-node-a
    source: NodeSelector
    phase: Succeeded
    jobName: qwen-image-warmup-gpu-node-a
    reason: ImagePreloadSucceeded
    message: ...
  conditions: []
```

Image references should preferably be immutable digests, or the controller should record the resolved digest. A changed image list or target configuration must create a new revision and invalidate the previous result.

## MVP boundaries

The first implementation focuses on image preloading only. It should not yet include:

- model artifact/file download;
- engine startup or inference warmup;
- generic arbitrary commands or custom actions;
- automatic rollout blocking or autoscaler mutation;
- direct runtime sidecar RPC integration.

The status and API should remain extensible for later artifact, engine, and precheck stages. Existing StormService, RoleSet, ModelClaim, and PodAutoscaler behavior must remain unchanged unless warmup integration is explicitly enabled.

## Why keep warmup independent?

Warmup is useful before rollout, scale-out, and manual capacity preparation. A standalone resource provides reusable target selection, independent lifecycle and status, and a foundation for future integration with workload controllers without coupling the first implementation to a single workload type.

## Open questions

- Should the kind remain `ModelWarmup`, or should the image-only MVP use `ModelImageWarmup`?
- Should `StormService`, `RoleSet`, and `NodeSelector` be the initial supported target sources, with other workload kinds added later?
- Should failed Jobs be retained by default until TTL cleanup?
- Should the default failure behavior be fail-closed, degraded success, or require an explicit policy?

items.title: [Docs] Add Chinese localization and language switching for the documentation site
items.author: googs1025
items.body_excerpt:
## Feature Description and Motivation

 provide a Chinese version for the entire [AIBrix documentation site](https://aibrix.readthedocs.io/latest/)

A site-wide Chinese localization would make AIBrix more accessible to Chinese-speaking users and contributors, improve onboarding, and reduce the effort required to understand concepts, deployment guides, API references, and troubleshooting documentation.

## Use Case

Chinese-speaking users who are evaluating, deploying, or contributing to AIBrix currently need to translate the documentation page by page. A consistent official Chinese version would provide a more coherent reading experience across the whole documentation site.

## Proposed Solution

Consider adding Chinese localization for the documentation site with a visible language switcher, for example:

- Add a `中文` / `English` switcher in the documentation header or navigation.
- Use a stable localized URL structure such as `https://aibrix.readthedocs.io/zh-CN/latest/`.
- Translate the existing documentation progressively, starting with Getting Started, Installation, Architecture, and core user guides.
- Preserve matching navigation and page structure between English and Chinese where possible.
- Define a lightweight synchronization process so translated pages stay aligned with the English source, including a way to identify pages that need updates.
- Reuse any localization support already available in the current documentation toolchain.

items.title: [Testing] Triage of tests that never run: disabled specs and suites that no CI job compiles
items.author: bolubo
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

A read-only sweep of the tree at `4be9a600` (2026-09-27) looked for tests that cannot protect anything because they never execute. One family is disabled in place, some of it for two years. Another sits behind build tags that no test job passes, so its suites never run. A third family quietly skips itself on CI hosts.

This is a different axis from #2805, which tracks tests that are going red right now. A skipped test cannot go red, which is how these stayed invisible. One overlap (the console catalog skip, already named in #2805 A2) is listed in the appendix instead of repeated as an item.

The sweep grepped for skip markers across the Go and Python trees and cross-referenced every test file behind a build tag against every workflow under `.github/workflows`. Line numbers are against `4be9a600`.

If you want to take one, please comment on the item first so two people do not end up on the same thing, and link the PR here when it is up. Small focused PRs are the easiest to review.

## Items

- [ ] A1. The oldest in-place skip: the rayclusterfleet reconcile spec, skipped since 2024-09.
- [ ] A2. Roleset and StormService scaffold specs skip themselves in `BeforeEach` (2025-06).
- [ ] A3. ModelAdapter controller suite: all 18 specs parked behind `XDescribe` (2025-08).
- [ ] A4. OpenAI compatibility e2e: `TestCompletionStreaming` carries a bare fix-me TODO with no explanation (2025-10).
- [ ] A5. Two kvcache Python files skip at import time with no reason string (2025).
- [ ] A6. One storage factory test skips because a network probe is treated as flaky (2026-06).
- [ ] B1. `-tags zmq` test suites (9 files, 48 test functions) are run by no CI job (needs a wiring decision).
- [ ] B2. `-tags integration` tests under `pkg/controller` have no runner (needs a decision on where they belong).
- [ ] C1. Three rate limiter tests skip themselves in CI because no Redis is listening.

Grading:

- A: the skip is unconditional in the source; the fix is to re-enable and repair, or remove.
- B: no CI entry compiles the tag; the fix needs a wiring decision first.
- C: the test runs but skips itself under CI conditions; a green run hides it.

## A. Disabled in place

### A1. rayclusterfleet: the oldest skip

`pkg/controller/rayclusterfleet/rayclusterfleet_controller_test.go:112` is the only spec of its suite, and it skips under a deferral note that waits for the integration test to land:

> `Skip("Skipping this test for now")`

The skip dates to the initial controller PR `6828146f` (#194, 2024-09-20), so the spec has been skipped for two years. The integration work the note waits for now exists: `test/integration/controller/rayclusterfleet_test.go` runs in `make test-integration`.

- Acceptance: the spec runs in `make test` again, or it is deleted together with the TODO. If part of the reconcile is out of reach for the unit environment, say which part and where it is covered instead.
- Verify: `go test ./pkg/controller/rayclusterfleet/... -v` (the suite uses envtest, so run it via `make test` or with `KUBEBUILDER_ASSETS`).
- Size: S.

### A2. Roleset and StormService scaffold specs

`pkg/controller/roleset/roleset_controller_test.go:45` and `pkg/controller/stormservice/stormservice_controller_test.go:45` both skip inside `BeforeEach` with `Skip("skip this test and revisit once main logic is implemented")`. Both skips came in `8fd23efa` (#1226, 2025-06-25) and were never revisited. Each file has exactly one spec, so the skip takes the whole suite to zero.

- Acceptance: the specs pass against the current controllers, or the scaffold specs are deleted so the suites are empty on purpose.
- Verify: `go test ./pkg/controller/roleset/... ./pkg/controller/stormservice/... -v`.
- Size: S; both files share one origin, so one PR can carry both.

### A3. ModelAdapter: 18 specs behind XDescribe

`pkg/controller/modeladapter/modeladapter_controller_test.go:37` disables the whole suite with `var _ = XDescribe("ModelAdapter Controller", func() {`, under the comment "Disable Ginkgo tests that require Kubernetes environment". Every spec that needs a client builds it with `fake.NewClientBuilder()` (`:56`, `:196`, `:341`, `:396`), so the Kubernetes environment note may no longer apply. The package already has an envtest entry point: `suite_test.go:46` `TestControllers` with `testEnv *envtest.Environment` (`:44`). A separate integration suite lives at `test/integration/controller/modeladapter_test.go`.

- Acceptance: the specs run under the existing `TestControllers` entry (or against the fake client directly), or they are deleted with a note. The comment could be updated to match what the specs actually need.
- Verify: `go test ./pkg/controller/modeladapter/... -v` after switching `XDescribe` to `Describe`.
- Size: S.

### A4. OpenAI compatibility: one skipped streaming test

`test/e2e/gateway/api/openai_api_compatibility_test.go:29` holds 18 tests, and line 30 skips the first one with a bare fix-me TODO and no explanation. The file was added with that skip in `af635f2b` (#1678, 2025-10-18) and moved to the new layout in `fe7db93e` (#2676, 2026-09-07). The other 17 tests run in the Kind-based e2e suite (`./test/run-e2e-tests.sh`, `go test -p 1 ./test/e2e/gateway/...`).

- Acceptance: the test passes in the e2e pipeline, or the skip reason is replaced with what the test needs, and the test moves to a documented quarantine list.
- Verify: inside the e2e environment, `go test ./test/e2e/gateway/api/... -run TestCompletionStreaming -v`.
- Size: M (needs the e2e environment).

### A5. kvcache Python: two module level skips without a reason

`python/aibrix_kvcache/tests/test_group_aware_cache_manager.py:42` and `test_cache_ops.py:20` both call `pytest.skip(allow_module_level=True)` with no reason string, since `402c62c2` (#1064, 2025-05-07) and `a193a4c3` (#1247, 2025-07-05). items.title: [Bug] ModelRouter never recreates a missing HTTPRoute (deleted route, or model label added later)
items.author: btxu-db
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

ModelRouter only creates the HTTPRoute from a workload's Add event. There's no `UpdateFunc` and no periodic resync, so once the route is missing it stays missing until the controller restarts.

Two ways I ran into it:

- I deleted `deepseek-coder-7b-router` by hand. It never came back, and requests for the model kept failing with 503 while the pod was fine.
- I created a Deployment and added `model.aibrix.ai/name` with `kubectl label` afterwards. No route was created.

Without a routing strategy the gateway needs this route and returns 503 when it's missing. `config/default` doesn't set `ROUTING_ALGORITHM`, so plain OpenAI clients on a default install hit this.

#2831 fixed the delete-workload case from #2824. These two don't go through that path.

### Steps to Reproduce

kind (`hack/ci/kind-config.yaml`), AIBrix installed from `main` the way `test/run-e2e-tests.sh` does it, `aibrix/vllm-mock:nightly` from `development/app` as the engine.

**Deleting the route**

`deepseek-coder-7b` is served by the Deployment `deepseek-coder-7b-l20`, and requests return 200.

```bash
kubectl -n envoy-gateway-system port-forward svc/envoy-aibrix-system-aibrix-eg-903790dc 8888:80 &

req() {
  curl -s -o /tmp/resp.json -w '%{http_code}' localhost:8888/v1/chat/completions \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"model":"deepseek-coder-7b","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}],"max_tokens":8}'
}

kubectl -n aibrix-system delete httproute deepseek-coder-7b-router
start=$(date +%s)
for i in $(seq 1 30); do
  code=$(req)
  route=$(kubectl -n aibrix-system get httproute deepseek-coder-7b-router -o name 2>/dev/null || echo none)
  echo "t=$(( $(date +%s) - start ))s HTTP $code route=$route $(head -c 90 /tmp/resp.json)"
  sleep 3
done
```

Output (bodies truncated):

```
t=0s  HTTP 502 route=none upstream connect error or disconnect/reset before headers. reset reason: protocol error
t=3s  HTTP 502 route=none upstream connect error or disconnect/reset before headers. reset reason: protocol error
t=6s  HTTP 503 route=none {"error":{"type":"overloaded_error","code":"service_unavailable",...
...
t=89s HTTP 503 route=none {"error":{"code":"service_unavailable",...,"message":"httproutes.gateway.networki...
```

4 × 502 and 26 × 503 out of 30. The route never came back and the controller didn't log anything about it. The L20 pod stayed 1/1 Running.

**Adding the model label later**

A Deployment without `model.aibrix.ai/name`:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: late-label-2
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: late-label-2}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: {app: late-label-2}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: vllm-openai
        image: aibrix/vllm-mock:nightly
        command: ["python3", "app.py"]
        env:
        - {name: MODEL_NAME, value: late-model-2}
        ports: [{containerPort: 8000}]
```

```bash
kubectl apply -f late-label.yaml
kubectl rollout status deploy/late-label-2
kubectl label deploy late-label-2 model.aibrix.ai/name=late-model-2 model.aibrix.ai/port=8000
kubectl -n aibrix-system get httproute late-model-2-router
```

I checked for `late-model-2-router` every 10 seconds for 3 minutes. It wasn't there in any of the 18 checks, and the controller logged nothing about it.

**After restarting the controller**

```bash
kubectl -n aibrix-system rollout restart deploy/aibrix-controller-manager
```

After a restart, both routes come back right away. In the delete case, `deepseek-coder-7b-router` was back within about 8 seconds and requests returned 200 again. In the label case, `late-model-2-router` (backend `default/late-model-2:8000`) already existed when the rollout finished.


### Expected behavior

The route should exist whenever a workload serves the model, and come back on its own if it goes missing.

What I have in mind, keeping the current create-only behavior:

- An `UpdateFunc` that only reacts when the model labels or annotations change, and ignores objects that are being deleted.
- A ticker, like the periodic enqueue in ModelAdapter and PodAutoscaler, that lists workloads from the cache and creates any route that's missing. It checks the cache first, so nothing is written when all routes exist.

This doesn't try to update existing routes or handle the same model name in several namespaces. Happy to send a PR if this sounds OK.


### Environment

- AIBrix: tested on `main` @ `dcc8aa9a`. Latest `main` (`be4dcd30`, includes #2831) still only registers Add and Delete handlers in ModelRouter.
- Kubernetes: kind v1.30.0, 1 control-plane + 1 worker
- Envoy Gateway v1.2.8 from `config/dependency`
- Engine: `aibrix/vllm-mock:nightly` from `development/app`

### Area

Gateway

items.title: [Bug] KV event replay never applies the replayed batches
items.author: sohom-cs
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

`ZMQClient` asks the vLLM KV event publisher for a replay when it starts, from seq 0 ([zmq_client.go#L149](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/a26d827c0bbb0dd43079c7d7853a7bd32d89eb1e/pkg/cache/kvcache/zmq_client.go#L149)), and after every reconnect, from `lastSeq+1` ([#L251](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/a26d827c0bbb0dd43079c7d7853a7bd32d89eb1e/pkg/cache/kvcache/zmq_client.go#L251)). The replayed batches never reach the prefix index.

vLLM answers a replay request with one message per buffered batch and then an end marker with seq -1 ([`_service_replay`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/111f71a6dbf1fe517f6164e1059a2837bb0a8b4e/vllm/distributed/kv_events.py#L509-L527)). `requestReplay` reads a single frame ([#L394](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/a26d827c0bbb0dd43079c7d7853a7bd32d89eb1e/pkg/cache/kvcache/zmq_client.go#L394)), which is the empty delimiter of the first replayed message. It logs `Successfully requested replay from seq 0 for <pod> (response: 0 bytes)` and returns. The batches and the end marker stay unread in the DEALER socket.

What this breaks:

- A gateway that subscribes after the engine has cached blocks never indexes those blocks. Later `BlockStored` events whose parent is one of them are skipped as "unknown parent" ([sync_hash.go#L280-L287](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/a26d827c0bbb0dd43079c7d7853a7bd32d89eb1e/pkg/utils/syncprefixcacheindexer/sync_hash.go#L280-L287)), so prefixes that extend an earlier cached prefix are not indexed either.
- Events published while the client was disconnected are not recovered.
- The frames left in the socket are read by the next replay request as its response.

The unit tests did not catch it because the mock publisher answers a replay request with a single `"OK"` frame ([zmq_client_test.go#L635](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/a26d827c0bbb0dd43079c7d7853a7bd32d89eb1e/pkg/cache/kvcache/zmq_client_test.go#L635)).

A separate thing I noticed while reading this code, not part of this bug: the replay port is fixed at `DefaultRouterPort = 5558`, while `samples/semantic-router/models/qwen3-8b.yaml` publishes replay on 5559 and the vLLM P/D samples in `samples/disaggregation/vllm/` use 5558 for the NIXL side channel.

### Steps to Reproduce

A ROUTER that follows vLLM's replay protocol, plus the send and receive steps of `requestReplay` (pebbe/zmq4 v1.4.0, libzmq 4.3.5, Go 1.24):

```go
package main

import (
	"encoding/binary"
	"fmt"
	"time"

	zmq "github.com/pebbe/zmq4"
)

func seqBytes(s int64) []byte { b := make([]byte, 8); binary.BigEndian.PutUint64(b, uint64(s)); return b }

func main() {
	router, _ := zmq.NewSocket(zmq.ROUTER)
	router.Bind("tcp://127.0.0.1:15558")
	// vLLM side: replay buffer holds batches seq 7..9
	go func() {
		frame, _ := router.RecvMessageBytes(0) // [client_id, "", start_seq]
		client := frame[0]
		start := int64(binary.BigEndian.Uint64(frame[2]))
		for s := int64(7); s <= 9; s++ {
			if s >= start {
				router.SendMessage(client, []byte{}, []byte("kv-events"), seqBytes(s), []byte(fmt.Sprintf("payload-%d", s)))
			}
		}
		router.SendMessage(client, []byte{}, []byte{}, seqBytes(-1), []byte{}) // END_SEQ
	}()
	dealer, _ := zmq.NewSocket(zmq.DEALER)
	dealer.Connect("tcp://127.0.0.1:15558")
	time.Sleep(100 * time.Millisecond)
	// same send/receive steps as aibrix requestReplay
	dealer.SendMessage([]byte{}, seqBytes(0))
	dealer.SetRcvtimeo(5 * time.Second)
	resp, err := dealer.RecvBytes(0)
	fmt.Printf("requestReplay returns: err=%v, response %d bytes (logged as success)\n", err, len(resp))
	// what is left unread in the DEALER queue
	time.Sleep(200 * time.Millisecond)
	n := 0
	for {
		parts, err := dealer.RecvMessageBytes(zmq.DONTWAIT)
		if err != nil {
			break
		}
		n++
		fmt.Printf("  unread message %d: %d frames, seq frame=%v\n", n, len(parts), parts[len(parts)-2])
	}
	fmt.Printf("replayed batches never decoded/applied: %d messages left in socket\n", n)
}
```

Output:

```
requestReplay returns: err=<nil>, response 0 bytes (logged as success)
  unread message 1: 3 frames, seq frame=[0 0 0 0 0 0 0 7]
  unread message 2: 4 frames, seq frame=[0 0 0 0 0 0 0 8]
  unread message 3: 4 frames, seq frame=[0 0 0 0 0 0 0 9]
  unread message 4: 4 frames, seq frame=[255 255 255 255 255 255 255 255]
replayed batches never decoded/applied: 4 messages left in socket
```

This uses the framing of vLLM v0.26 and later, `[empty, topic, seq, payload]`. vLLM v0.25 and earlier send `[empty, seq, payload]` (the topic frame was added in vllm-project/vllm#45177). The first frame is the empty delimiter in both, so the result is the same.

### Expected behavior

`requestReplay` reads replies until the end marker, applies each replayed batch newer than `lastSeq` the same way as live batches, and bounds the whole replay by `ReplayTimeout`. A reply that times out is not read as the answer to the next request.

I'm opening a PR with a fix and tests.

### Environment

- AIBrix: main at a26d827
- vLLM: any version started with a `replay_endpoint` in `--kv-events-config`. I checked the replay code in `vllm/distributed/kv_events.py` for v0.11.0 through v0.30.0; only the topic frame changed.
- Found by reading the code and reproduced with the program above, not in a cluster.

### Area

Gateway

items.title: [Feature]: Add NVFP4 MegaMoE support on SM90
items.author: aleozlx
items.body_excerpt:
### Problem
The SM90 MegaMoE backends delivered in #4113 and #4069 cover FP8, while #3780 also requested NVFP4. Packed NVFP4 expert weights are not currently selectable as an SM90 MegaMoE backend through `MoEEpLayer`.

### Requested outcome
Support packed NVFP4 expert weights and scales on SM90 through the existing `MoEEpLayer` backend interface. The discussion in #3780 proposed keeping packed NVFP4 weights in HBM and unpacking inside the GEMM, initially with BF16 activations. The implementing team can confirm the precise kernel design.

### Acceptance criteria
- Multi-rank correctness against a reference for supported NVFP4 shapes and routing, including uneven or masked routing.
- Eager and CUDA Graph replay validation on SM90.
- Document supported formats, shapes, and fallback behavior; report representative latency against the current SM90 FP8 path.

### Related work
Follow-up to #3780 and the broader MegaMoE tracker #3692. Ownership and priority remain to be triaged.

items.title: [ModelClaim] Add operational metrics for pooled runtimes and policy actions
items.author: Jeffwan
items.body_excerpt:
### Feature Description and Motivation

ModelClaim exposes basic desired/ready/activation metrics and runtime KV/HBM gauges, but operators cannot currently tell whether an engine is repeatedly restarting, was re-adopted after an agent restart, exhausted its restart budget, or whether the pool KV policy applied or skipped a decision.

ModelClaim is still experimental, so this issue is limited to additive observability. 

### Use Case

When several model engines share one GPU, an operator needs to distinguish a healthy dense pool from a pool that is silently converging through engine restarts or repeatedly failing policy actions. The signals must support alerts and post-incident diagnosis without requiring runtime snapshot or controller log inspection.

### Proposed Solution

Add low-cardinality Prometheus metrics covering:

- engine restart attempts and restart-budget exhaustion;
- runtime agent re-adoption outcomes;
- engine state counts by phase (`active`, `sleeping`, `restarting`, `failed`);
- pool-policy evaluation and action outcomes (`applied`, `skipped`, `failed`) with a bounded reason label;
- requested and successfully applied KV limits per model;
- sleep and wake operation count and duration;
- duration for which a ModelClaim has no ready engine.

Keep labels bounded to namespace, model, pod/pool where necessary, action/result, and an enumerated reason. Do not expose free-form errors, operation IDs, PIDs, or claim UIDs as metric labels. Detailed errors should remain in logs and Kubernetes Events.

Add focused unit tests for registration, values, cleanup of deleted gauge series, and bounded label values. Document metric names and semantics alongside the ModelClaim runbook.

### Acceptance Criteria

- Metrics are exported from the existing controller-manager or runtime `/metrics` endpoints.
- A terminal engine failure, successful re-adoption, successful/failed KV update, and sleep/wake operation are observable without reading logs.
- Policy skip reasons are from a fixed enum and cannot introduce unbounded cardinality.
- Existing ModelClaim APIs and reconciliation behavior remain unchanged.

items.title: [Store] Does Mooncake store plan to support awareness of layers, chunk ordering, and TP?
items.author: Hadigan
items.body_excerpt:
It looks like the current Mooncake store does not have awareness of layer granularity, chunk order (earlier vs. later chunks), or TP ranks. This can cause problems during cache eviction:

1. The store might evict KVs for only some layers, forcing prefill to recompute all layer KVs for those tokens.
2. The store might evict the KVs corresponding to the earliest chunk(s) of a token sequence, forcing prefill to recompute KVs for all chunks/tokens.
3. The store might evict KVs produced by some TP ranks, forcing all TP ranks to recompute KVs.

I think the Mooncake store should be aware of layers, chunk ordering, and TP. On eviction, it should evict a token’s KV caches for all layers and for all TP ranks together (i.e., keep KV state complete per token). 
From the chunk-order perspective, eviction policies should prefer removing KVs for later chunks first rather than evicting early-chunk KVs that make prefill expensive.

items.title: gradcheck forward-mode AD fails for zero-element differentiable inputs (empty Jacobian max())
items.author: malfet
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.autograd.gradcheck(..., check_forward_ad=True)` in fast mode (the default) can crash when a **differentiable input has zero elements**:

```
RuntimeError: max(): Expected reduction dim to be specified for input.numel() == 0. Specify the reduction dim with the 'dim' argument.
```

This is a **gradcheck bug, not a device/kernel bug** (see "CUDA is not at fault" below). Observed intermittently on CUDA CI for `test_forward_mode_AD_nn_functional_linear_cross_entropy_cuda_float64` (the job showed `RERUN x2` then `FAILED`).

#### Reproducer

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
dtype = torch.float64
torch.manual_seed(0)

# zero-size in_features -> zero-element differentiable inputs
inp     = torch.randn(5, 0, device=device, dtype=dtype, requires_grad=True)
lin_w   = torch.randn(3, 4, 0, device=device, dtype=dtype, requires_grad=True)
target  = torch.randint(0, 3, (5, 4), device=device)
class_w = torch.rand(3, device=device, dtype=dtype) * 1.5 + 0.5

def fn(x, w):
    return F.linear_cross_entropy(x, w, target, weight=class_w, reduction="mean")

print(torch.autograd.gradcheck(
    fn, (inp, lin_w),
    check_forward_ad=True, check_backward_ad=False,
    check_undefined_grad=False, check_batched_grad=False,
))
```

CPU prints `True`. CUDA also usually prints `True` -- the failure is intermittent, which is itself the tell (see below).

#### Root cause (in `torch/autograd/gradcheck.py`)

1. `_adjusted_atol` scales `atol` by `sum(u)`, where `u` is the random direction vector for the input. For a zero-element input `u` is empty, so `sum(u) == 0` and the effective tolerance **collapses to exactly 0**.
2. The numerical reduced jvp is exactly `0` (there are no elements to perturb). With atol `0`, the fast-mode comparison in `_check_analytical_numerical_equal` requires the *analytical* jvp to be **bit-exactly 0**, leaving zero slack for even sub-epsilon differences.
3. When the comparison fails it calls `_run_slow_mode_and_get_error`, which does `(slow_numerical - slow_analytical).abs().max()` on an empty `(out_numel x 0)` Jacobian. `max()` with no `dim` raises on a 0-numel tensor. The comment right above it even states *"Assume jacobians are non-empty and have the same shape"* -- which is exactly the wrong assumption here.

So any op with a zero-element differentiable input is one sub-epsilon fluctuation away from turning a spurious "mismatch" into a hard crash instead of a readable error.

#### CUDA is not at fault

The earlier suspicion that CUDA left the zero-size-contraction (`in_features == 0`) matmul output uninitialized was **not confirmed**. Directly stressing it -- NaN-dirtying the caching allocator, then running `mm`/`einsum`/`bmm` with a zero-size K dimension thousands of times -- returns exact zeros every time on CUDA, matching CPU. **CUDA just works**: the primal and jvp for the empty case are computed correctly. The bug is entirely in gradcheck's handling of zero-element inputs.

#### Expected behavior / fix

`gradcheck` should handle zero-element differentiable inputs gracefully -- they carry no gradient to verify, so the comparison should be skipped (mirroring the existing `numel()` guards at `gradcheck.py:726` and `gradcheck.py:1016`), and `_run_slow_mode_and_get_error` must not assume non-empty Jacobians.

#### Workaround to revert once this is fixed

As a stopgap, the `in_features == 0` linear sample is excluded from `linear_cross_entropy`'s samples (it is kept for plain `linear`, whose forward-AD is fine). When this issue is fixed, remove the workaround so the empty sample flows back into `linear_cross_entropy`. In `torch/testing/_internal/common_methods_invocations.py` (added in https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/190051):

- `sample_inputs_linear(...)`: drop the `include_empty=True` parameter and the `if include_empty:` guard so the two `in_features == 0` samples are always yielded.
- `sample_inputs_linear_cross_entropy(...)`: drop `include_empty=False` from its internal `sample_inputs_linear(...)` call.

### Versions

main (2026-07)


cc @ezyang @albanD @gqchen @nikitaved @soulitzer @Varal7 @bobrenjc93 @ptrblck @msaroufim @eqy @tinglvv @nWEIdia

items.title: [Core][metrics] Duplicate metric headers being emitted
items.author: shayansadeghieh
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

**What happened**
When execing into a ray pod and running a curl against localhost:8080/metrics, I see duplicate headers for the same metric:
```
# HELP ray_component_cpu_percentage Total CPU usage of the components on a node.
# TYPE ray_component_cpu_percentage gauge
ray_component_cpu_percentage{Component="raylet",SessionName="session_2026-07-08_15-50-24_749109_290",Version="2.54.0",ip="10.72.69.156",pid="359"} 1.0
ray_component_cpu_percentage{Component="agent",SessionName="session_2026-07-08_15-50-24_749109_290",Version="2.54.0",ip="10.72.69.156",pid="412"} 1.2
# HELP ray_component_cpu_percentage Total CPU usage of the components on a node.
# TYPE ray_component_cpu_percentage gauge
ray_component_cpu_percentage{Component="ray::DashboardAgent",SessionName="session_2026-07-08_15-50-24_749109_290",Version="2.54.0",ip="10.72.69.156"} 1.2
```

This is not compliant with [prometheus spec](https://prometheus.io/docs/instrumenting/exposition_formats/#text-based-format:~:text=Only%20one%20HELP%20line%20may%20exist%20for%20any%20given%20metric%20name.) `Only one HELP line may exist for any given metric name`. As a result, anyone using the [official prometheus library](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/prometheus/common/expfmt) adhering to the spec will fail to export metrics. We end up losing a good amount of visibility on our jobs.

**What I'd expect to happen**
No duplicate headers. i.e. something like:

items.title: [Serve][Docs] In-place updates guide doesn't mention that code-update replica restarts are rolling
items.author: juanma9613
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

`doc/source/serve/advanced-guides/inplace-updates.md` is where you'd look to find out what a config change does to running replicas. It describes code updates as:

> "Changing the following values in a deployment's config will trigger redeployment and **restart all the deployment's replicas**."

> "Changing the following application-level config values is also considered a code update, and **all deployments in the application will be restarted**."

and contrasts them with lightweight updates, which:

> "modify running deployment replicas **without tearing them down and restarting them**, so there's less downtime as the deployments update"

Read together, that implies a code update restarts everything at once and incurs downtime. In fact the restart is a capped rolling update that preserves availability whenever `num_replicas > 1` — `DeploymentState._check_and_stop_outdated_version_replicas`:

```python
rollout_size = max(int(rolling_update_percentage * target_num_replicas), 1)
max_to_stop  = max(rollout_size - pending_replicas, 0)
```

Only `rollout_size` replicas stop per wave; the rest keep serving. Ray's own tests assert this: `test_rolling_update_percentage_configurable` checks that `num_replicas - expected_stopping` replicas stay `RUNNING` through a version change, and `test_redeploy_multiple_replicas` is documented as *"demonstrates zero downtime when redeploying a deployment with multiple replicas."*

The `max(..., 1)` floor is the surprising part: at `num_replicas: 1` it must stop the only replica. Measured on 2.57.0 over the HTTP proxy (open-loop 100 req/s, 4s replica startup, real code-version rollout): **n=1 → p99 4.9s with 42% of requests over 1s; n=2 → p99 3.3ms with none over 1s**, against a 2.4ms baseline. Zero errors in both — at n=1 it's a latency cliff rather than an outage, so it doesn't surface as 5xx.

We read this page, concluded a code update meant unavoidable downtime for our ingress deployment, and went some way into a redesign before finding the rolling behaviour in the source.

### Suggested addition

In the code-update section of `inplace-updates.md`: that replicas are replaced in waves of `max(int(rolling_update_percentage * num_replicas), 1)` rather than all at once, that `num_replicas > 1` therefore keeps serving through the rollout while `num_replicas: 1` does not, and a link to `rolling_update_percentage`.

Note that `rolling_update_percentage` appears nowhere under `doc/` — it only reaches the website via the autogenerated `DeploymentSchema` API reference, so there's no prose page a reader could find it from.

The behaviour is mentioned in passing on two other pages, both guides for unrelated opt-in features: `advanced-guides/gang-scheduling.md` ("### Rolling updates" — update waves, rollout size aligned to `gang_size`) and `advanced-guides/deployment-scoped-actors.md` ("## Understand rollout behavior" — *"old replicas keep talking to old actors while new replicas talk to new actors during the rollout window"*). Neither names the option or quantifies the wave size, and a reader not using gang scheduling or deployment-scoped actors wouldn't open either.

### Versions

Ray 2.57.0 (measurements); doc quotes and source from master @ e40b340eed.

items.title: [Core] Late RESOURCE_VIEW messages can reinsert dead nodes into the raylet resource map
items.author: hhhhjun
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

## Summary

A late RESOURCE_VIEW message can recreate a dead node's entry in the raylet's local resource map after its DEAD notification has already been processed.

In a long-running cluster with frequent worker churn, we observed approximately 1,079 live nodes in GCS but 223,654 entries in the head raylet's resource map.

## Sequence of events

1. Raylet R receives resource information for worker node N.
2. N dies, and R processes its DEAD notification through NodeManager::NodeRemoved().
3. NodeRemoved() records N in failed_nodes_cache_ and removes its resource entry through ClusterResourceManager::RemoveNode().
4. A delayed RESOURCE_VIEW message for N subsequently reaches NodeManager::ConsumeSyncMessage().
5. ConsumeSyncMessage() does not check failed_nodes_cache_ before updating labels and resources.
6. SetNodeLabels() inserts a new entry when N is missing, recreating the resource entry for a node already known to be dead.

The same issue can occur when DEAD arrives before the first resource message for N.

## Expected behavior

Once a raylet has observed DEAD for NodeID N, subsequent resource messages for N must not recreate its resource entry.

However, resource messages for an unknown/new NodeID should still be accepted before its ALIVE notification arrives. Rejecting every node that is not currently known alive would break this valid ordering.

## Impact

Obsolete entries can accumulate in the resource map under worker churn. SPREAD scheduling builds and sorts candidates from that map before filtering them, so an inflated map adds scheduling work.

During the captured incident, RequestWorkerLease handler statistics showed approximately 45 ms mean execution time and 1.4 s mean queueing time. These are production observations, not a controlled benchmark. We have not established that this issue caused every pending actor or insufficient-resource retry.

## Proposed fix

In NodeManager::ConsumeSyncMessage(), reject RESOURCE_VIEW messages for NodeIDs already in failed_nodes_cache_ before calling SetNodeLabels() or modifying resource state.

This is separate from the GCS dead-node metadata cache controlled by maximum_gcs_dead_node_cached_count.

We implemented this guard locally. Validation passed 36 NodeManager tests and isolated task, Dashboard, and Serve smoke tests. The full upstream suite has not been run.

## Relevant code

- src/ray/raylet/node_manager.cc
  - NodeManager::NodeRemoved()
  - NodeManager::ConsumeSyncMessage()
- src/ray/raylet/scheduling/cluster_resource_manager.cc
  - ClusterResourceManager::RemoveNode()
  - ClusterResourceManager::SetNodeLabels()
- src/ray/raylet/scheduling/policy/spread_scheduling_policy.cc

### Versions / Dependencies

- Ray: mainline (upstream master).
- Python: 3.12.
- OS: Linux.
- Deployment: Kubernetes, with a long-lived head and frequent worker replacement.
- Workload: Ray Serve GPU actors using SPREAD scheduling.

The affected code path was also inspected at upstream commit:
e430ec9ed0e1f9963d1a6b71ec1913eed0d98353

That commit pins the source inspection; it is not claimed to be the exact production build commit.

### Reproduction script

This is a C++ regression test, not a standalone Python script.

Add it to src/ray/raylet/tests/node_manager_test.cc alongside the existing NodeManagerTest tests, then build and run the NodeManager test target.

The test exercises the actual GCS node-liveness callback and ConsumeSyncMessage() handler. It covers both RESOURCE_VIEW-before-DEAD and DEAD-before-RESOURCE_VIEW ordering.

On the unguarded implementation, a late resource message recreates the dead node's resource entry, violating the assertions. With the known-dead guard, the entry remains absent, while a new NodeID is still accepted before ALIVE.

This test was validated locally; it has not been rerun against the exact upstream commit listed above.

[raylet-dead-node-reproduction.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32782810/raylet-dead-node-reproduction.txt)

### Issue Severity

High: It blocks me from completing my task.

items.title: SM120 (RTX PRO 6000) MoE backend gaps: MoeConfig.backend schema missing MegaMoE entries, and no EP-capable path for this hardware
items.author: ItamarTerem
items.body_excerpt:
Hi TensorRT-LLM team,
Deploying a large MoE model (Kimi-K2.7-Code-NVFP4, 384 experts) on 8x RTX PRO 6000 (SM120) via the pytorch backend, trtllm-serve, version 1.3.0rc20. Two related findings we wanted to raise:

1. MoeConfig.backend's pydantic Literal doesn't include MEGAMOE_CUTEDSL/MEGAMOE_DEEPGEMM, even though create_moe.py's dispatch logic already handles both as real branches. Setting moe_config.backend: MEGAMOE_CUTEDSL in extra_llm_api_options.yaml fails pydantic validation before create_moe.py is ever reached, even though the underlying backend selection logic supports it. This looks like the config schema hasn't caught up to the dispatch logic yet.
2. More fundamentally: none of the EP-capable MoE backends currently work on SM120 in this build.
 - MEGAMOE_CUTEDSL / MEGAMOE_DEEPGEMM: both explicitly require SM100/SM103 ("MegaMoECuteDsl requires SM100 family (SM100 or SM103); got SM120"), and fall back to CutlassFusedMoE.
 - WIDEEP: not SM-gated, but its GEMM compute still routes through the same CUTLASS kernel that produces silently incorrect output on SM120 in our testing, and additionally hit a binding mismatch in this build (run_moe() is missing value for argument '_37') before we could evaluate EP itself.
 - CUTEDSL (b12x): the only backend we've confirmed produces correct output on SM120, but has no EP support at the flashinfer level (num_local_experts != num_experts raises NotImplementedError in b12x_fused_moe).

Net result: there is currently no correct + EP-capable MoE path for SM120 in this stack, which limits per-GPU memory headroom for large-expert-count models on this hardware class.
Questions:

1. Is SM120 support planned for any of the MegaMoE/WideEP paths, or is SM100/SM103-first prioritization intentional for the near term?
2. Should we file the MoeConfig.backend schema gap as a separate, smaller issue, since that looks like a straightforward fix independent of the larger EP question?
3. Is there a recommended path for SM120 users running large MoE models today, or is CUTEDSL/no-EP the expected configuration for this hardware class in the current release?

Happy to share full repro steps/configs if helpful. Thanks for your work on this — appreciate the pointers.

items.title: [Data] read_iceberg migration to Datasource V2 (tracking issue)
items.author: AarryaSaraf
items.body_excerpt: ### Description `read_iceberg` is still on the V1 `Datasource` abstraction. We are porting it to Datasource V2 (`ListFiles` / `ReadFiles`), initially behind an opt-in flag. This issue tracks the work and collects design feedback before the flag flips. Three problems come out of the left column: 1. **The pushed-down filter never reaches planning.** Memoization happens at construction, before `.filter()` exists, and pushdown `copy.copy()`s the datasource, carrying the stale plan across. On a 3-file table where 2 match, `.filter(region == "US")` plans 3 files; the identical predicate as `read_iceberg(row_filter=...)` plans 2. Results stay correct, but the whole table is listed and planning is a single-node step that grows with table size. 2. **Sizing uses compressed bytes.** Measured expansion: 440x on one file, 1839x on another. A chunk nominally "128 MB" can be tens of GB decoded. 3. **Peak memory equals chunk size** — the chunk is materialized as one Arrow table before anything is yielded. On the right, `plan_files()` runs once inside the listing task with the filter already attached; its scan tasks become typed manifest columns rather than a driver-side object graph; bin packing counts estimated decoded bytes; and the reader yields one block per record batch. ### Status In progress. Stage 1 — the shared V2 seams Iceberg needs (schema without a file sample, an exact-metadata-count hook, a whole-file-indexer hook) — merged as #65908. Stage 2 is the Iceberg source itself: manifest codec, listing indexer, bin-packing partitioner, scanner, reader, and the flag and dispatch; it is built and green locally and lands as three PRs to stay reviewable. Stage 3 then makes `count()` metadata-only, answered from the manifest's per-file `record_count` wherever Iceberg's per-file residual is `AlwaysTrue` — so `WHERE partition_col = x` counts without reading data. Work planned after that is described in the draft PR linked below. All of it sits behind `DataContext.use_iceberg_datasource_v2` (default `False`, env `RAY_DATA_USE_ICEBERG_DATASOURCE_V2`), and the public `read_iceberg` signature does not change. One behaviour change for the release notes: `parallelism` / `override_num_blocks` become warning no-ops on this path, since task count now comes from bin packing. ### Use case Anyone reading a large Iceberg table with Ray Data: today a filtered read still lists and reads the whole table, and worker peak memory is sized from compressed bytes — a number that can be three orders of magnitude off. ### Related issues Related to #66147, #64464, #65581. Not a duplicate of any: no open issue or PR covers moving `read_iceberg` to Datasource V2 (#66133 / #66145 / #51951 are the write path). Feedback especially welcome on the opt-in-then-flip rollout and the `parallelism` no-op.

### This issue is to have a centralized place to list and track work on adding support to new ops for the MPS backend.

[**PyTorch MPS Ops Project**](https://github.com/users/kulinseth/projects/1/views/1) : Project to track all the ops for MPS backend. As Ops are requested we will add " *To Triage*" pool. If we have 3+ requests for an operation and given its complexity/need the operation will be moved "*To be implemented*" pool. If you want to work on adding support for such op, feel free to comment below to get assigned one. Please avoid pickup up an op that is already being worked on tracked in "*In progress*" pool. 

[Link to the wiki for details](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/wiki/MPS-Backend) on how to add these ops and example PRs.

[**MPS operators coverage matrix**](https://qqaatw.github.io/pytorch-mps-ops-coverage/) - The matrix covers most of the supported operators but is not exhaustive. **Please look at the `In vx.x.x` column, if the box is green, it means that the op implementation is included in the latest release; on the other hand, if the box is yellow, it means the op implementation is in the nightly and has not yet included in the latest release.** Before you comment below, please take a look at this matrix to make sure the operator you're requesting has not been implemented in nightly. items.title: Ray's site serves no /.well-known/security.txt (RFC 9116)
items.author: kobihikri
items.body_excerpt:
`https://docs.ray.io/.well-known/security.txt` returns 404 (and `ray.io` redirects without serving one). [RFC 9116](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116) defines `/.well-known/security.txt` as the standard, machine-discoverable place a security researcher (or automated tooling) looks first to find how to report an issue. Ray has a [SECURITY.md](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/master/SECURITY.md), but there's no security.txt advertising it at the well-known path.

A small security.txt (Contact → your reporting channel, a future `Expires` per §2.5.5, Policy → SECURITY.md) served from the site's static directory would resolve it. Happy to help however is easiest.

I used AI assistance to investigate and draft this; I reproduced the 404 myself.

shortlist.title: [good-first-issue] tests: make flaky vllm_bench throughput comparisons reproducible
shortlist.author: maobaolong
shortlist.body_excerpt:
Parent tracker: #5313 · Onboarding: #3372

## Confirmed flaky behavior

`k3-multiprocess-test / vllm / vllm_bench / zmq` changes its throughput verdict without a source update:

| Build #5340, September 29, 2026 (UTC) | Result |
| --- | --- |
| [Original job](https://buildkite.com/lmcache/k3-multiprocess-test/builds/5340#01a0eab1-a517-4a38-8163-b0ec7cfaff63) | LMCache throughput **7.34% slower** than baseline; fails the 5% limit |
| [Retry](https://buildkite.com/lmcache/k3-multiprocess-test/builds/5340#01a0eaba-4671-4f79-a910-4a02cfa0cadf) | LMCache throughput **0.62% faster** than baseline; passes |

Both are `dev` builds of **`9e8226dd49728769843bf6f586b00b33ab616125`**, with no PR-base merge, vLLM **`0.30.1rc1.dev244+g0da126676`**, and torch **`2.13.0+cu130`**. Both baseline and LMCache completed all 50 requests with 500400 input tokens. This is an intermittent benchmark verdict, not an installation failure.

The inputs are not reproducible across those attempts: the original uses seed `1790644335`, the retry `1790645482`. Each attempt uses the same seed for its own baseline/LMCache pair, but the default `RANDOM_SEED` comes from `date +%s`. The seed change is a confirmed confounder; it is **not proven to be the sole cause** of the throughput fluctuation.

## Bounded good-first task

Make this benchmark's inputs reproducible across retries, and make the comparison auditable. This is the first test-harness improvement for the confirmed flake, not a production performance optimization.

1. Replace the clock-derived default seed with a documented stable default; continue honoring an explicit `RANDOM_SEED` override.
2. Save a small comparison manifest next to `baseline.json` and `lmcache.json`: effective seed, model, request count and lengths, actual checkout SHA, installed vLLM/torch versions, and the two throughput values/verdict. Keep any new diagnostics local to this workload.
3. Preserve separate attempt results when used in CI. Follow the existing result-directory/cleanup conventions, and ensure the manifest is accessible in the job log or a public Buildkite artifact rather than merely naming a container-local file.
4. Add focused CPU-only regression coverage using stub benchmark commands: default seed is repeatable, both sides receive it, an override is honored, and success/failure summaries retain the actual numbers.

Keep the 5% throughput limit, request/token checks, and cache-retrieval validation. Do not add blanket retries, remove assertions, or present a fixed seed as proof of a resolved performance issue. #5227 already added retry mitigation; this task addresses reproducibility within the workload.

Starting points, checked at `42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052`:

- [Workload seed and result comparison](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052/.buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/scripts/workloads/vllm/vllm-bench.sh).
- [Result cleanup/copying](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052/.buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/scripts/cleanup.sh).
- [Buildkite step and existing retry policy](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052/.buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/pipeline.yml).

## Acceptance

- [ ] Default inputs are identical across attempts; explicit overrides still work.
- [ ] A reviewer can recover both results, the effective inputs, versions, and verdict from public job output/artifacts.
- [ ] Stubbed CPU coverage exercises default/override and passing/failing results.
- [ ] GPU validation reports first-attempt results with a fixed seed; remaining fluctuation is reported as unresolved rather than hidden.
- [ ] Existing behavioral assertions and thresholds remain effective.

## Reproduce the CI workload

The evidence below comes from CI; this issue does not claim a local GPU reproduction. Use a dedicated Linux x86_64 GPU test host with Docker and NVIDIA Container Toolkit, two available CUDA GPUs capable of running separate `Qwen/Qwen3-14B` servers, sufficient host RAM for the default 80 GiB LMCache buffer (plus the mock L2 storage for the L2 case), and disk/network access for the image, wheels, and model. CI uses CUDA 13.0, Python 3.12, and a 1 GiB `/dev/shm`. A maintainer can run the GPU validation for a contributor who only has a CPU machine.

These commands build the public CI image recipe, explicitly start Bash, and pin the historical LMCache and vLLM revisions. They are a reproduction recipe, not a fully locked copy of every historical dependency or GPU scheduling condition. Run from a fresh directory; make the actual PR against current `dev`.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache.git
cd LMCache
git checkout 9e8226dd49728769843bf6f586b00b33ab616125
docker build -t lmcache-flake-ci \
  -f .buildkite/k3_harness/ci-base.Dockerfile .
docker run --rm --gpus '"device=0,1"' --shm-size=1g \
  --entrypoint bash \
  -v "$PWD:/workspace/LMCache" -w /workspace/LMCache \
  -e MAX_JOBS=1 \
  -e INFERENCE_ENGINE=vllm \
  -e LMCACHE_REQUEST_TRANSPORT=zmq \
  -e LMCACHE_PR_BASE_MERGE=never \
  -e PINNED_VLLM_VERSION=0.30.1rc1.dev244+g0da126676 \
  -e PINNED_VLLM_ARCHIVE_INDEX_URL=https://wheels.vllm.ai/0da126676e38f5dc1b02b2c4f48dc85f90f5a79f/cu130 \
  lmcache-flake-ci -c '
    set -e
    source /opt/venv/bin/activate
    command -v git uv python3 nvcc gcc g++
    nvidia-smi
    git config --global --add safe.directory /workspace/LMCache
    .buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/run.sh vllm_bench
  '
```

Use the linked failed and passed jobs as the initial reproduction pair. For subsequent GPU runs, record the actual checkout SHA, installed package versions, GPU model, input settings, and first-attempt result. A green retry alone does not show that the underlying fluctuation was fixed.

shortlist.title: GGUF convert support for Vibevoice
shortlist.author: amin-jhn
shortlist.body_excerpt: Hey there! I am trying to convert my fine-tuned vibevoice into a gguf format for inference but cant find proper code or converter any where. The architecture is currently unsupported to any known converter like llama.cpp but I have already seen many variation of gguf-formated vibevoice. Can anyone help me with that?

comments.author: pwilkin
comments.body:
So the status currently is that there's no support for VibeVoice in llama.cpp (but llama.cpp *does* support TTS architectures, it's a question of somebody adding support for that specific model). 

What you have seen are probably repacks done by calcuis in his weirdly named "gguf-org project", but that project is not affiliated with ggml-org nor with llama.cpp in any way and from what I've analyzed the contents of those files, they are simply direct repacks of the original SafeTensors files, but with layers that are known to be quantizable by GGML converted to the respective quant format (with a side effect being that only a small percentage of the tensors that *should* be quantizable are really quantized, since the GGUF library does not know that for example `model.acoustic_tokenizer.decoder.stages.0.0.ffn.linear1.weight` should be a quantizable tensor). He then converts them back to F32 before running, so it's not a real GGML architecture, just a repack - not a very efficient one at that, since he unpacks all the quants to F32, so the memory usage will be the same as with the original model, just the quality will be lower (for example, the ComfyUI-GGUF solution, which supports GGUF quantization, does it by properly patching methods and dequantizing tensors on the fly as they're being used, so even though it does not utilize native quantized kernels for MAT_MUL like GGUF does, it actually allows to run those quants with a lower memory footprint).

TL;DR: You can try doing a repack in the same way, using `quantize` from the `gguf-py` library (a decent LLM coder will probably write that for you), but real VibeVoice support requires adding a proper MTMD model.

comments.author: amin-jhn
comments.body: Thank you so much for your detailed response!

comments.author: Ra5hidIslam
comments.body:
Hey @amin-jhn and @pwilkin,

Following up on pwilkin's suggestion, I went ahead and wrote a Python script using gguf-py that successfully repacks and quantizes the VibeVoice SafeTensors into a Q8_0 GGUF file.

While I know this doesn't close the issue (since it still needs the native C++ MTMD model support mapped out for llama.cpp), this script should fully solve the repackaging hurdle for anyone trying to run a compressed version through custom frontends like ComfyUI in the meantime.


```python

import argparse
import numpy as np
import torch
from safetensors.torch import load_file
import gguf
from gguf.quants import quantize
from gguf.constants import GGMLQuantizationType

def pad_tensor(tensor_np: np.ndarray, block_size: int = 32) -> np.ndarray:
    """Pads the last dimension of a 2D tensor to be a multiple of block_size."""
    rows, cols = tensor_np.shape
    if cols % block_size == 0:
        return tensor_np
    
    padding_needed = block_size - (cols % block_size)
    print(f"  --> Padding tensor: {cols} -> {cols + padding_needed} columns")
    return np.pad(tensor_np, ((0, 0), (0, padding_needed)), mode='constant', constant_values=0)

def vibevoice_repack_with_padding(path_input: str, path_output: str):
    print(f"Loading Safetensors from {path_input}...")
    try:
        tensors_loaded = load_file(path_input)
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Error loading file: {e}")
        return
        
    print("Initializing GGUF writer...")
    writer_gguf = gguf.GGUFWriter(path_output, arch="vibevoice")
    writer_gguf.add_string("general.name", "vibevoice")

    tensor_count = 0
    quantized_count = 0
    BLOCK_SIZE = 32 

    for tensor_name, tensor_data in tensors_loaded.items():
        tensor_np = tensor_data.cpu().float().numpy()
        
        is_2d_weight = len(tensor_np.shape) == 2 and "weight" in tensor_name
        
        if is_2d_weight:
            # 1. Pad to multiple of 32
            tensor_padded = pad_tensor(tensor_np, block_size=BLOCK_SIZE)
            
            # 2. Quantize into a structured array
            q_type = GGMLQuantizationType.Q8_0
            quantized_struct = quantize(tensor_padded, q_type)
            
            # 3. Cast the structured array to raw bytes
            quantized_bytes = quantized_struct.view(np.uint8)
            
            # 4. Add to GGUF using ONLY the raw bytes
            writer_gguf.add_tensor(
                name=tensor_name,
                tensor=quantized_bytes,
                raw_dtype=q_type,
            )
            quantized_count += 1
        else:
            # Standard F32 for 1D tensors
            writer_gguf.add_tensor(tensor_name, tensor_np)

        tensor_count += 1
        if tensor_count % 50 == 0:
            print(f"Processed {tensor_count} tensors...")

    print(f"Writing {tensor_count} tensors to disk...")
    writer_gguf.write_header_to_file()
    writer_gguf.write_kv_data_to_file()
    writer_gguf.write_tensors_to_file()
    writer_gguf.close()

    print(f"Successfully converted to GGUF at {path_output}.")
    print(f"Total: {tensor_count} | Quantized (Q8_0): {quantized_count}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Repack VibeVoice to GGUF with Q8_0 Fix.")
    parser.add_argument("--input", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--output", required=True)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    vibevoice_repack_with_padding(args.input, args.output)
```

Hope this helps anyone trying to get the file size down while we wait for native C++ support!

shortlist.title: Restart-proof KV cache for llama-server: 40K-token TTFT 155s to 6s after reboot
shortlist.author: qqkzlm
shortlist.body_excerpt:
Every restart wipes your prefill. Server crash, box reboot, model reload — a 40K-token agentic prompt pays the full ~155s prefill again before the first token.

I patched llama-server to persist KV-cache prefix checkpoints to disk and auto-restore the longest matching prefix on boot. Same prompt after a restart: **first token in ~6s instead of ~155s** (2.1s disk read once + decode). No client changes, no re-architecture — the server just remembers.

Measured on GTX 1080 8GB, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, `-c 92160`:

- Cold: 151s prefill → first token at ~155s
- Warm (post-restart): 2.1s disk read (first request only) → first token at ~6s
- Checkpoints keyed by model + ctx + KV quant (wrong config = ignored, never corrupted); disk-budget eviction included

Single-commit patch (86KB): https://github.com/qqkzlm/llama-cpp-prompt-disk-cache — `git am` onto the PrismML `prism` branch, four flags (`--slot-save-path`, `--checkpoint-min-step`, `--ctx-checkpoints`, `--prompt-cache-disk-budget`).

One MoE lesson from the same box: keep experts on GPU, let KV follow the layers — pushing 20 MoE layers to CPU collapsed prefill 265→30 tok/s, which no cache can fix.

Happy to upstream behind a flag if maintainers are interested.

comments.author: qqkzlm
comments.body:
Update to the README since this went up — three things worth calling out for anyone trying it:

**1. Prebuilt CUDA binaries exist for both platforms.** The `v0.2.3` release ships `llama-server-win-cuda-v0.2.3.zip` and `llama-server-linux-cuda-v0.2.3.tar.gz`. The Linux package is built for `sm_61`/Pascal, so it also runs on GTX 10-series. No build needed:

```bash
./llama-server -m model.gguf -c 32768 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \
  --slot-save-path /var/tmp/kvstore/model \
  --prompt-cache-disk-budget 20 --checkpoint-min-step 2048 --ctx-checkpoints 64
```

**2. Only one flag is actually required.** `--slot-save-path` is the only one you must pass — `--prompt-cache-disk-budget` and `--prompt-cache-disk-path` are silently ignored without it, and entries land in `<slot-save-path>/pdcache`. `--prompt-cache-disk` is **enabled by default**, so passing it is optional; use `--no-prompt-cache-disk` to turn the cache off.

**3. Cache hits require a byte-identical prompt prefix.** Only the common prefix from token 0 onward is reused. If you prepend a timestamp or a random ID, everything after it misses and the cache is effectively unused. Put stable content first (system prompt, tool definitions, long docs) and per-turn content last — opencode / Claude Code already do this, so it works out of the box.

The README now has a "when does the cache hit / when does it miss" section covering this, a flag-duty table, and a Chinese-first three-step guide (the repo README is now Chinese-primary). A Windows `start-llama-server.bat` is included in the zip if you want a prompt-driven launcher instead of a command line.

Still happy to upstream this behind a flag if maintainers are interested — the whole feature is one commit touching `tools/server/server-prompt-disk.cpp` (~900 lines) plus slot/task integration.
